archetype.name: Archetype
archetype.desc:
A recurring character type, situation or image that appears across many stories and traditions.

Jung used the term for inherited patterns in what he called the collective unconscious, surfacing in dreams, myth and religion; literary criticism, particularly Frye's, uses it more loosely for recurrent forms without committing to a psychological explanation. Vogler's screenwriting adaptation treats archetypes as functions a character performs for a scene rather than fixed identities, so that one figure may act as mentor in one encounter and as shapeshifter in the next.

The main objection to archetypal reading is that it can flatten what is specific to a culture into evidence for a universal.

hero.name: The Hero
hero.desc:
The figure whose choices drive a story and through whom an audience is invited to experience it.

The role has been defined very differently across traditions. Greek heroes are exceptional and often destroyed by that exception; folktale heroes are frequently the youngest, poorest or apparently stupidest of three; Campbell's hero is a psychological pattern more than a person. Frye's classification of fictional modes ranks the hero by their power relative to ordinary people and to their environment, from myth down to irony.

Protagonist, from the Greek for first contestant, is the more neutral term, since it carries no implication of virtue.

mentor.name: The Mentor
mentor.desc:
The figure who equips the hero with knowledge, training or a gift, and whose usefulness is usually limited by design.

The name comes from Mentor in the Odyssey, the old friend of Odysseus whose form Athena takes to advise Telemachus, so the archetype begins as a god in disguise. In folktale terms Propp classifies this role as the donor, defined by the test that precedes the gift, not by wisdom or age.

Mentors are frequently removed before the final ordeal, since a hero accompanied by a competent adviser cannot be forced into the decisive choice alone.

trickster.name: The Trickster
trickster.desc:
A figure who works by cunning, deception and boundary-crossing rather than strength, and who is as likely to create as to destroy.

Tricksters appear across many unrelated traditions, among them Anansi in Akan storytelling, coyote and hare figures in various Indigenous North American traditions, Loki in Norse myth, Hermes in Greek, and Sun Wukong in Chinese fiction. They are typically appetite-driven, frequently punished, and often responsible for some element of the world's order arriving by accident.

The cross-cultural comparison is useful but easily overdone: each of these figures belongs to a specific tradition with its own theology and social function.

shadow.name: The Shadow
shadow.desc:
In Jung's terms, the part of the psyche a person disowns, which is then met outside themselves; in narrative terms, an antagonist who embodies what the protagonist refuses to recognise in their own character.

The idea underlies the common construction in which hero and villain share an origin, a method or a desire, and differ only in a choice made at some earlier point. It also accounts for the persistent appeal of the double.

Vogler treats the shadow as a function, not a person, noting that it may be carried by an ally, an institution, or by the protagonist themselves.

threshold_guardian.name: Threshold Guardian
threshold_guardian.desc:
The figure or obstacle encountered at the boundary of the unfamiliar world, whose function is to test whether the hero is committed.

Campbell placed the crossing of the first threshold early in the journey and described the guardian who stands at it; Vogler adapted the role for screenwriting, observing that guardians are often not the main antagonist but subordinates, bureaucrats or personal doubts, and that they can be defeated, outwitted, befriended or absorbed.

Its practical use is structural. Placing a real cost at the boundary prevents the crossing from being a mere change of scene.

shapeshifter.name: The Shapeshifter
shapeshifter.desc:
A figure whose loyalty or identity will not stay fixed, generating doubt about whose side they are on.

In myth the shifting is literal, in the transformations of gods, in selkie and swan-maiden tales, and in werewolf legend; in modern narrative it is usually a matter of information, the ally who may be an informer or the lover whose account of themselves keeps changing.

Vogler adopted the term for screenwriting and argued that the role's function is to introduce instability and suspicion rather than to be resolved quickly, and that a single character may occupy it only temporarily.

herald.name: The Herald
herald.desc:
The figure or event that announces the need for change and sets the story moving.

In Campbell's account this is the call to adventure, and the herald may be a person, a letter, an accident or a piece of news; what matters is that it disturbs an equilibrium the protagonist would otherwise have maintained. Screenwriting vocabulary calls the same moment the inciting incident or catalyst.

The role is often filled by a character who then disappears, since the function is to deliver information with consequences, not to accompany the journey.

anti_hero.name: The Anti-Hero
anti_hero.desc:
A protagonist who lacks the conventional virtues of a hero, and whose interest for an audience lies elsewhere: in competence, candour, wit, or the reasons for their compromise.

The type has a long lineage, from the picaresque rogue and the Byronic outsider to noir detectives and the criminal protagonists of prestige television. Frye's ironic mode, in which the central figure is weaker or more constrained than the reader, describes much of the same territory.

The construction depends on a compensating hold on attention, since a story cannot proceed on a protagonist an audience neither admires nor finds interesting.

monster.name: The Monster
monster.desc:
The antagonist defined by its difference in kind: Grendel, the dragon, the Cyclops, Humbaba, the creature made in a laboratory.

Monsters mark the edge of the known and often carry what a culture finds intolerable. Criticism reads them as historically specific rather than universal. Booker made overcoming the monster one of his seven plots, and the confrontation is a standard stage in heroic narrative.

The sympathetic monster complicates the pattern: Shelley's creature and later horror fiction turn the encounter into a question about who is being excluded, and by whom.

the_double.name: The Double
the_double.desc:
The figure who resembles the protagonist closely enough to unsettle their sense of being a single person: the doppelganger, the twin, the mirror image, the reflection that moves independently.

The motif runs through nineteenth-century fiction in Hoffmann, Poe, Dostoevsky and Stevenson, and Freud discussed it in his essay on the uncanny as a mechanism by which something familiar becomes frightening.

It is closely related to the shadow as an archetype, and to the practical construction in which a story's antagonist is a version of the protagonist who chose differently.

anansi.name: Anansi
anansi.desc:
The spider trickster of Akan storytelling in what is now Ghana, and the figure after whom a whole genre of stories, anansesem, is named.

He wins by negotiation, flattery and misdirection rather than force, and one widely told story accounts for how the god's stories came to be his and thus came into the world. Traditions differ, and the tales exist in many versions, not a fixed canon.

Carried across the Atlantic through the transatlantic slave trade, Anansi survived in Caribbean and North American storytelling under names including Aunt Nancy, and remains a living presence in Jamaican folklore and children's literature.

plato.name: Plato
plato.desc:
Greek philosopher (c. 428-348 BCE) whose treatment of poetry precedes Aristotle's and opposes it. In the Republic he distinguishes between a poet speaking in his own voice and one speaking as his characters, which is the origin of the diegesis and mimesis pair, and treats the second as the more dangerous because the performer must become what he imitates.

His objection is educational and metaphysical at once: imitation is at a third remove from the truth, and dramatic poetry feeds the parts of the soul that reason should govern. The tenth book concludes by excluding most poetry from the ideal city while inviting a defence.

The Ion takes a different line, presenting poetic composition as divine possession, not as a skill its practitioner can explain, which is the position Aristotle's Poetics implicitly answers.

coleridge.name: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
coleridge.desc:
English poet and critic (1772-1834) whose Biographia Literaria of 1817 supplied the phrase that still describes an audience's contract with fiction, the willing suspension of disbelief for the moment.

The formulation arose from a specific working arrangement rather than from abstract theory. He described the division of labour on Lyrical Ballads, in which his own contributions would take supernatural subjects and aim to transfer enough human interest to them to secure that suspension, while Wordsworth took ordinary subjects and worked to make them strange.

His criticism also introduced the distinction between imagination and fancy, and his lectures on Shakespeare did much to establish the Romantic reading of character as the plays' governing interest.

abhinavagupta.name: Abhinavagupta
abhinavagupta.desc:
Kashmiri philosopher and aesthetician (c. 950-1016) whose commentaries are the decisive development of Indian literary theory after the Natyashastra. His Abhinavabharati is the most influential commentary on that treatise, and his Locana comments on Anandavardhana's work on suggestion.

His contribution to rasa theory is to explain how a spectator can take pleasure in emotions that would be painful in life. He argues that the response is generalised, detached from the individual's own circumstances and interests, so that what is experienced is grief itself, not a particular grief belonging to anyone.

That account moves rasa from a technical matter of performance to a theory of aesthetic experience with a philosophical basis.

scott_mccloud.name: Scott McCloud
scott_mccloud.desc:
American cartoonist and theorist whose Understanding Comics, published in 1993, made the case for comics as a medium with its own grammar and made it in comics form.

His central concept is closure: the reader supplies the movement, duration and causation that the gutter between panels leaves out, so the medium's basic operation happens in the audience rather than on the page. He classifies the transitions between panels by what the reader must do to bridge them, and argues that different comics traditions favour different types.

He builds on Will Eisner's term sequential art, and his account of the relationship between word and image has been taken up well beyond comics.

ovid.name: Ovid
ovid.desc:
Roman poet (43 BCE - 17 or 18 CE) whose Metamorphoses gathered the Greek and Roman transformation myths into a single continuous poem and became the principal channel through which classical mythology reached medieval and Renaissance Europe.

His manner is the opposite of Virgil's: witty, rapid, interested in desire and cruelty, and willing to treat the gods as capricious. The poem's transitions are deliberately ingenious, one story handing off to the next through a shared character, place or motif.

He was banished by Augustus to Tomis on the Black Sea in 8 CE for reasons he described only as a poem and a mistake, and he died there. The poem itself he claimed to have burned before exile, though copies survived.

virgil.name: Virgil
virgil.desc:
Roman poet (70-19 BCE) whose Aeneid deliberately answers Homer, taking the wanderings of the Odyssey for its first half and the warfare of the Iliad for its second, and attaching the result to the founding of Rome.

The poem is a literary epic rather than an oral one, composed in writing over eleven years with a consciousness of its models at every point. That makes it the model in turn for every subsequent epic that was written rather than sung.

He died with it unfinished and is reported to have asked that it be burned; Augustus overrode the instruction. Dante later made him the guide through hell and purgatory, which fixed his standing for medieval Europe.

dante.name: Dante Alighieri
dante.desc:
Florentine poet (c. 1265-1321) whose Commedia narrates a journey through hell, purgatory and paradise in the first person, with the poet himself as protagonist and a named, dated itinerary.

Writing it in Italian, not Latin was a decision with consequences well beyond the poem, and his defence of the vernacular as a literary language helped establish Tuscan as the basis of standard Italian.

He was exiled from Florence in 1302 in a political settlement and never returned, and the poem is populated with the people he knew, placed according to his judgement of them. That makes it a work of local score-settling as well as of cosmology.

dostoevsky.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
dostoevsky.desc:
Russian novelist (1821-1881) whose books stage arguments about God, freedom and guilt through characters who are permitted to make their cases at full strength.

His narration characteristically refuses to settle those arguments, which is the feature Bakhtin named polyphony: a plurality of consciousnesses that are never finalised by an authorial verdict, so that the most articulate case against belief in The Brothers Karamazov is put by a character the author opposed.

He was arrested in 1849 as part of a circle of intellectuals, subjected to a mock execution and sent to a Siberian prison camp for four years, an experience that runs through the later fiction.

aeschylus.name: Aeschylus
aeschylus.desc:
The earliest of the three Athenian tragedians whose work survives (c. 525-456 BCE). Ancient sources credit him with introducing the second actor, which made dramatic conflict between characters possible, where before it could only occur between a single figure and the chorus.

The Oresteia is the only complete tragic trilogy to survive from antiquity, and it uses that scale to carry an argument across three plays, moving from a cycle of blood vengeance to a court of law.

He fought at Marathon, and the epitaph attributed to him is said to have named the battle and to have passed over the plays. The story comes from later sources and is not documented.

aristophanes.name: Aristophanes
aristophanes.desc:
Athenian comic playwright (c. 446-386 BCE) and the only author of Old Comedy whose plays survive complete, eleven of them. The form he worked in was topical, obscene, fantastical and personally abusive, attacking living politicians, generals and intellectuals by name.

His plots proceed by taking an absurd premise entirely seriously: a private citizen makes his own peace treaty, the women of Greece withhold sex to stop a war, a poet is retrieved from the underworld to save the city.

He attacked Socrates in The Clouds and Euripides repeatedly, and Plato later has a character claim the play contributed to the case against Socrates.

menander.name: Menander
menander.desc:
Athenian playwright (c. 342-291 BCE) and the central figure of New Comedy, which replaced the political attack and fantasy of Aristophanes with domestic plots turning on mistaken identity, concealed parentage, thwarted lovers and reconciliation.

That machinery, transmitted through Plautus and Terence, is the direct ancestor of European comedy and of the romantic comedy plot still in use.

For most of recorded history he was known only through fragments and through the Roman adaptations. Papyrus discoveries in the twentieth century recovered one play, the Dyskolos, nearly complete, along with substantial portions of others.

plautus.name: Plautus
plautus.desc:
Roman comic playwright (c. 254-184 BCE) who adapted Greek New Comedy for a Roman audience, keeping the Greek settings and names while broadening the humour, expanding the musical passages and giving the scheming slave a far larger role.

Twenty of his plays survive, more than for any other ancient dramatist, and their stock figures and situations passed into Renaissance comedy directly, with Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors built from one of them.

The prologue to Amphitruo coins a Latin compound for a play in which gods and slaves share the stage, which is the earliest use of the idea later theorists developed as tragicomedy.

moliere.name: Molière
moliere.desc:
French playwright and actor (1622-1673) who combined the stock figures and physical routines of the Italian comedians with a satirical attention to particular social types: the hypocrite, the miser, the hypochondriac, the social climber, the misanthrope.

His company shared a Paris theatre with an Italian troupe, and the debt to their technique is visible in the timing and the business as much as in the characters.

Tartuffe was banned after its first performances following pressure from religious authorities and took five years to reach the public stage. He collapsed while performing in his own play about a hypochondriac and died the same night.

chretien_de_troyes.name: Chrétien de Troyes
chretien_de_troyes.desc:
French poet of the late twelfth century who did more than anyone to shape the Arthurian romance, writing in verse for the courts of Champagne and Flanders.

His surviving romances introduce Lancelot and the queen's love affair, establish the pattern of a knight who must repair a failure through a second sequence of adventures, and, in the unfinished Perceval, bring the grail into European literature for the first time.

He states in one prologue that the subject and treatment were supplied by his patron, which is a rare direct record of how such commissions worked. Almost nothing else about his life is known.

tolkien.name: J. R. R. Tolkien
tolkien.desc:
English philologist and novelist (1892-1973) who held chairs at Oxford in Anglo-Saxon and in English language and literature, and whose scholarly work on Beowulf reoriented its criticism toward the poem as a poem rather than as a historical document.

His fiction proceeded from invented languages, not toward them: the peoples and histories were developed to supply speakers for the languages he had been constructing since adolescence.

His lecture on fairy stories set out the argument that a writer performs an act of sub-creation, making a secondary world that commands belief from inside, and it remains the genre's most cited defence of itself.

laurence_sterne.name: Laurence Sterne
laurence_sterne.desc:
Anglo-Irish clergyman and novelist (1713-1768) whose Tristram Shandy appeared in nine volumes between 1759 and 1767 and dismantled the conventions of the novel almost as soon as they had formed.

The book is a first-person life story whose narrator cannot get himself born for several volumes, interrupted by digressions that are themselves interrupted, and printed with a black page, a marbled page, blank pages for the reader to fill and chapters that arrive out of order.

The Russian formalists later treated it as the clearest demonstration of their argument that plot is made by the deformation of story material.

metamorphoses.name: Metamorphoses
metamorphoses.desc:
Ovid's hexameter poem in fifteen books, completed around 8 CE, running from the creation of the world to the deification of Julius Caesar and gathering some two hundred and fifty transformation stories along the way.

Its organising principle is change of form, which allows almost any myth to be admitted, and its transitions between tales are deliberately ingenious, handing off through a shared character, a listener or a place.

It is the single most important source for classical mythology in later European art and literature, supplying subjects to Chaucer, Shakespeare, Titian and Bernini among a great many others, and it is the reason a large proportion of these myths survive at all.

aeneid.name: The Aeneid
aeneid.desc:
Virgil's epic in twelve books, left unfinished at his death in 19 BCE, following the Trojan Aeneas from the fall of his city to the war in Italy that precedes the founding of the Roman line.

Its structure answers Homer directly: wandering in the first six books, warfare in the second six. The sixth book takes the hero into the underworld to meet his father and see the unborn Romans, which is the most influential descent narrative in the Western tradition after the Odyssey.

The poem serves Augustan politics and undercuts them in the same breath, since its cost is counted throughout, and its final lines end on an act of rage, not on a settlement.

divine_comedy.name: The Divine Comedy
divine_comedy.desc:
Dante's poem in one hundred cantos, composed in Italian in an interlocking three-line rhyme he devised for it, and divided into hell, purgatory and paradise.

It is narrated in the first person by a protagonist who shares the author's name and history, guided first by Virgil and then by Beatrice, and it places real and recent people in each of its regions according to a scheme of judgement the poem sets out in detail.

The architecture is exact rather than atmospheric: every sin has its circle, every punishment matches its offence, and the reader is expected to follow the reasoning as well as the journey.

tristram_shandy.name: Tristram Shandy
tristram_shandy.desc:
Sterne's novel, published in nine volumes between 1759 and 1767, presents itself as the life and opinions of its narrator and spends most of its length failing to reach his birth.

Every attempt at narration is diverted by a digression, an anecdote about an uncle, a lengthy account of a nose, or a typographic intervention: a black page mourning a death, a marbled page, a blank page for the reader to draw on, dashes and asterisks standing in for what is not said.

Read in its own time as a comic performance, it was taken up two centuries later as the demonstration case for the argument that a novel's material and its arrangement are separable things.

lord_of_the_rings.name: The Lord of the Rings
lord_of_the_rings.desc:
Tolkien's novel, published in three volumes in 1954 and 1955, follows the destruction of a ring of power across an invented world supplied with its own languages, calendars, genealogies and several thousand years of prior history.

Much of that apparatus sits in appendices, not in the narrative, and the withholding is deliberate: the story is told as though the world existed before it and will continue after, and the reader is given the sense of depth without the exposition.

Its commercial success from the 1960s paperback editions onward created the modern fantasy market, and its conventions became the genre's defaults to an extent Tolkien would probably have regretted.

tragicomedy.name: Tragicomedy
tragicomedy.desc:
A mixed mode that refuses the settled ending of either of the forms it names, holding danger and absurdity in the same frame and resolving neither cleanly. The Latin compound behind the word appears first in the prologue to Plautus's Amphitruo, as a joke about a play in which gods and slaves share the stage.

Renaissance theorists took the joke up in earnest. Guarini's defence of his pastoral tragicomedy in the 1580s and 1590s argued at length that a play could take mortal risk seriously and still end without a death, a position strict neoclassicists regarded as a violation of decorum.

Shakespeare's late plays work the same ground, and modern drama pushed the mixture further, using comic structure to stage situations that admit no resolution at all.

jonathan_gottschall.name: Jonathan Gottschall
jonathan_gottschall.desc:
American literary scholar who applies evolutionary and empirical methods to literature, and whose The Storytelling Animal, published in 2012, asks the prior question most craft writing skips: why a species should spend so much of its attention on events that did not happen.

His answer is that fiction is useful rather than decorative, functioning as a low-cost simulation in which social and physical problems can be rehearsed without consequence, and he assembles evidence from children's pretend play, night dreams and the near-universal appetite for trouble in narrative.

His later work turns against the same subject, arguing that the persuasive power of story is a hazard as much as a resource.

storytelling_animal.name: The Storytelling Animal
storytelling_animal.desc:
Gottschall's 2012 book argues that human beings are shaped by fiction to a degree they do not notice, spending hours a day in imagined worlds through novels, film, daydream and sleep.

Its central proposal is that story functions as a flight simulator for social life, letting a person rehearse predicaments, betrayals and dilemmas at no cost, which would explain why narrative attention is drawn overwhelmingly to trouble.

The book is a synthesis and not an experimental report, and its evolutionary claims are argued from convergent evidence without being demonstrated, which is where its critics have concentrated.

peter_brooks.name: Peter Brooks
peter_brooks.desc:
American critic whose Reading for the Plot, published in 1984, reasserted plot as a serious object of study at a point when criticism had largely moved to language and structure.

His argument is that plot is a form of desire: a narrative sets an appetite going in the reader and the middle exists to delay its satisfaction, so the reading is driven by the anticipation of a retrospective understanding not yet available.

He takes the model from Freud's account of drives, treating the middle of a narrative as a deviance that postpones the ending, on the argument that the wrong end arrived at too quickly would not be an ending at all.

reading_for_the_plot.name: Reading for the Plot
reading_for_the_plot.desc:
Brooks's 1984 study treats plot not as the arrangement of events but as the force that carries a reader through them, and it is the fullest account available of why the middle of a narrative exists.

His proposal is that a story is driven by narrative desire, an appetite for the end that the text arouses and then refuses to satisfy directly, and that what a reader is doing throughout is anticipating the retrospective sense the ending will confer on everything preceding it.

The psychoanalytic apparatus dates the book, and the central observation has outlasted it: nothing in a plot means anything until it is read backwards from a conclusion the reader does not yet have.

janet_murray.name: Janet Murray
janet_murray.desc:
American academic working on digital media, whose Hamlet on the Holodeck, published in 1997, was among the first substantial attempts to ask what narrative becomes when the audience can act inside it.

She identifies three pleasures the medium can offer that print cannot combine: immersion in a world, agency within it, and transformation of the material or of the participant. She also distinguishes the computer's procedural nature as its defining property, which makes the author a designer of rules rather than a writer of sequences.

The book was written before the forms it anticipates existed, and its predictions have been argued with continuously since.

hamlet_on_the_holodeck.name: Hamlet on the Holodeck
hamlet_on_the_holodeck.desc:
Murray's 1997 book takes its title from a thought experiment about what a Shakespeare tragedy would be if an audience could walk into it and intervene, and uses the question to work out what a genuinely interactive narrative would require.

Its most used contribution is the separation of immersion, agency and transformation as distinct pleasures, and its insistence that agency means meaningful consequence, not the ability to press things.

It also framed the argument that followed, since a subsequent generation of games scholars defined their position partly against the assumption that a game is best understood as a story at all.

henry_jenkins.name: Henry Jenkins
henry_jenkins.desc:
American media scholar who has worked since the early 1990s on what audiences do with stories, inverting the usual question of what stories do to audiences.

His early work on fan communities treated rewriting, argument and unauthorised continuation as a legitimate mode of engagement, and his later Convergence Culture describes a media environment in which a single narrative is distributed across film, television, games, comics and print.

His term for that arrangement is transmedia storytelling, and his condition for it is strict: each platform should make a distinctive contribution rather than repeat the story in another format.

convergence_culture.name: Convergence Culture
convergence_culture.desc:
Jenkins's 2006 book describes the collision of old and new media as a cultural shift rather than a technological one, in which audiences move between platforms and expect to participate instead of receiving.

Its most cited chapter concerns transmedia storytelling, using the Matrix franchise as the case: a story deliberately distributed across a film trilogy, animated shorts, comics and a game, with material available in one place and nowhere else.

The book is optimistic about participation in a way later commentary has qualified, since the same architecture that invites audiences to contribute also captures what they contribute.

transmedia.name: Transmedia Storytelling
transmedia.desc:
A story distributed across several media so that each platform contributes material the others do not carry, and the whole exists only in the audience's assembly of the parts.

Jenkins's condition distinguishes it from adaptation and from merchandising: a novelisation retells the film and a transmedia component tells something the film does not, so a viewer who reads it knows more and a viewer who does not is still able to follow.

The arrangement is old in principle, since religious and mythological material has always circulated across sermon, image, drama and song, and new in being deliberately planned and commercially owned.

narrative_transportation.name: Narrative Transportation
narrative_transportation.desc:
The experience of being absorbed into a story to the point of losing track of the surrounding world, described in psychology as a convergent process of attention, imagery and feeling.

Green and Brock's work from 2000 made the state measurable and connected it to persuasion: readers who report high transportation show more story-consistent beliefs afterwards, and produce fewer counterarguments while reading, whether or not they are told the narrative is fictional.

The finding gives an empirical version of what suspension of disbelief describes impressionistically, and it also supplies the mechanism behind long-standing worries about what fiction does to the people who consume it.

kurt_vonnegut.name: Kurt Vonnegut
kurt_vonnegut.desc:
American novelist (1922-2007) whose fiction combines science-fictional premises, black comedy and a plain conversational voice, and whose experience as a prisoner of war during the firebombing of Dresden underlies Slaughterhouse-Five.

His contribution to the theory of narrative was made mostly outside his fiction, in a proposal that stories have simple shapes that can be drawn on a graph running from good fortune to ill over the length of the telling.

He submitted the idea as a master's thesis in anthropology at the University of Chicago and it was rejected. He gave the argument repeatedly as a lecture instead, drawing the curves on a blackboard.

emotional_arcs_study.name: The Emotional Arcs of Stories
emotional_arcs_study.desc:
A 2016 paper by Reagan, Mitchell, Kiley, Danforth and Dodds, published in EPJ Data Science, which tested Vonnegut's proposal computationally by measuring the emotional valence of successive passages across a filtered set of 1,327 works of fiction from Project Gutenberg.

Three separate methods converged on six recurring shapes: a rise, a fall, a fall then rise, a rise then fall, rise-fall-rise, and fall-rise-fall. The authors also compared the arcs against download counts and found some considerably more popular than others.

The corpus is English-language, out of copyright and filtered by popularity, which constrains what the finding can be taken to show.

carrier_bag_theory.name: The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction
carrier_bag_theory.desc:
Le Guin's essay of 1986 proposes that the first cultural device was not the weapon but the container, and that a literature organised around the hunt, the hero and the killing has mistaken a late and violent activity for the centre of human life.

She takes the premise from Elizabeth Fisher's carrier bag theory of evolution and applies it to narrative form, proposing the novel as a bag or medicine bundle: a container holding things in relation to one another, not an arrow driven at a target.

The essay is brief and has become one of the most cited pieces of writing about narrative form outside the academy.

yuval_noah_harari.name: Yuval Noah Harari
yuval_noah_harari.desc:
Israeli historian whose Sapiens argues that the decisive human capacity is the ability to believe in things that exist only because enough people agree they do.

Money, nations, laws, corporations, human rights and gods are on his account shared fictions, and their function is coordination: strangers who hold the same story about an imagined order can cooperate in numbers that kinship and personal acquaintance cannot support.

The argument places narrative at the centre of political and economic organisation rather than of art, and it has been criticised by historians for the breadth of its generalisations more than for the underlying claim.

nassim_taleb.name: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
nassim_taleb.desc:
Lebanese-American essayist and former options trader whose work concerns the limits of prediction and the mishandling of rare events.

His contribution to the subject of this graph is the narrative fallacy, set out in The Black Swan of 2007: the human compulsion to fit a story to a sequence of facts, which manufactures causation where there was only succession and makes a chaotic record feel explicable in retrospect.

He treats the tendency as a defect in reasoning, not a mode of understanding, which puts him in direct opposition to most of the positions represented here.

narrative_fallacy.name: The Narrative Fallacy
narrative_fallacy.desc:
The tendency to impose a story on a sequence of events, supplying causes, intentions and an arc that the events themselves did not contain.

Taleb named it in this form, and the underlying finding is well established in psychology: people remember, explain and predict better in narrative form than in statistical form, and are correspondingly confident about accounts that a record does not support. Success is explained by the qualities of the winner, and the failures who shared those qualities are not available to be counted.

It is the standing objection to every claim in this graph that storytelling is a mode of understanding rather than a distortion of one.

madame_bovary.name: Madame Bovary
madame_bovary.desc:
Flaubert's novel, serialised in 1856 and published as a book the following year, follows a provincial doctor's wife whose expectations have been formed by romantic novels and who ruins herself pursuing them.

Its technical importance rests on the narration. Free indirect style renders Emma's illusions in the vocabulary she would use while the surrounding prose declines to endorse them, so the reader occupies her position and can measure it at the same time.

The serial publication led to a prosecution for offences against public morals in 1857. Flaubert was acquitted, and the trial made the book notorious before it was famous.

emma_novel.name: Emma
emma_novel.desc:
Austen's novel of 1815 gives its heroine wealth, intelligence and social authority, and then builds the plot on her being wrong about almost everything she is most confident of.

The narration stays close to her judgement throughout without adopting it. That makes the book the standard demonstration of free indirect style used for sustained irony: the reader is given her reasoning and the means to see through it in the same sentences.

The book is a detective structure without a detective, in which the evidence for what is actually happening is available on a second reading and invisible on the first.

mrs_dalloway.name: Mrs Dalloway
mrs_dalloway.desc:
Woolf's novel of 1925 covers a single June day in London as a society hostess prepares for a party, moving between minds as characters pass one another in the street.

Its second strand follows a shell-shocked veteran the hostess never meets, and the two lives are connected only by the city, the hour and a death reported at the party. The chiming of a clock is used to pull the narration from one consciousness to another.

Woolf described her method as tunnelling behind characters to excavate a past that reaches the reader in fragments, not in flashback.

great_expectations.name: Great Expectations
great_expectations.desc:
Dickens's novel, serialised weekly in 1860 and 1861, is narrated in retrospect by a blacksmith's apprentice raised to gentility by an anonymous benefactor whose identity is not what he assumes.

The book inverts the usual shape of the novel of formation. What the protagonist acquires is shame, and what the plot delivers is the discovery that his rise was funded by the convict he helped as a child. That makes his education a stripping away rather than an accumulation.

Dickens wrote two endings, replacing a bleaker original after his friend Bulwer-Lytton advised against it, and both are printed in modern editions.

beloved.name: Beloved
beloved.desc:
Morrison's novel of 1987 concerns a woman who escaped slavery in Kentucky and the house she lives in afterwards, haunted by the daughter she killed rather than see returned to it.

The narrative refuses chronology, delivering the central act in fragments across the book as the characters become able to approach it, and it admits the ghost without explanation or scepticism, in the manner of the oral tradition the novel draws on.

It takes its starting point from the documented case of Margaret Garner, and it was awarded the Pulitzer Prize for fiction in 1988.

wizard_of_earthsea.name: A Wizard of Earthsea
wizard_of_earthsea.desc:
Le Guin's novel of 1968 is set in an archipelago where magic depends on knowing the true name of a thing, so power is a matter of exact knowledge and every use of it has a cost.

Its protagonist releases a shadow through pride while still a student, and the book's second half is the pursuit of it, ending when he names the thing with his own name and is made whole rather than victorious.

The protagonist and most of the archipelago's people are dark-skinned, a decision Le Guin made deliberately against the genre's defaults and one that cover artists spent decades ignoring.

if_on_a_winters_night.name: If on a Winter's Night a Traveller
if_on_a_winters_night.desc:
Calvino's novel of 1979 opens by addressing the reader in the second person, describing them buying and settling down with the book they are holding.

The reader-protagonist then begins ten novels in different styles, each broken off by a printing error, a mistranslation, a censor or a theft, and the search for the continuations becomes the plot that the interrupted openings never supply.

The construction is systematic, not whimsical, and it belongs to Calvino's association with the Oulipo group, whose interest was in the productive use of formal constraint.

ficciones.name: Ficciones
ficciones.desc:
Borges's collection, published in 1944 and gathering stories from the previous decade, contains most of the pieces his later reputation rests on.

Several take the form of a review or a scholarly note about a book that does not exist, on the stated grounds that composing vast volumes is laborious when one can pretend they are already written and supply a commentary. Others turn on infinite libraries, forking time, and a man who rewrites Don Quixote word for word and produces a different book.

The collection made the short story a vehicle for philosophical proposition and licensed later writers to abandon scene and character entirely.

cherry_orchard.name: The Cherry Orchard
cherry_orchard.desc:
Chekhov's last play, first performed in 1904, concerns an aristocratic family who cannot act to prevent the sale of the estate they have run out of money to keep.

Almost nothing is stated directly. Characters talk about the weather, a bookcase, a broken string heard somewhere off the property, while the auction proceeds elsewhere, and the significant material sits entirely under the dialogue.

Chekhov subtitled it a comedy and objected to Stanislavski's production for staging it as a tragedy. The disagreement has never been settled, and productions still choose a side.

andersens_tales.name: Andersen's Fairy Tales
andersens_tales.desc:
Andersen began publishing tales for children in 1835 and continued for nearly four decades, producing more than a hundred and fifty pieces that are largely original compositions rather than collected traditional material.

The voice is conversational and addressed to a child listener while the material frequently concerns adult disappointment, and several of the best-known tales end without consolation: the mermaid does not marry the prince, the little match girl does not survive the night.

His inventions include stories told from the position of an object or an animal, which gave the form a resource the traditional repertoire had barely used.

perraults_tales.name: Perrault's Tales
perraults_tales.desc:
Perrault's collection of 1697 gathers eight prose tales, among them Cinderella, Sleeping Beauty, Puss in Boots, Bluebeard and Little Red Riding Hood, each closed with a verse moral.

The versions here are the ones that entered European print and, through them, general circulation: the glass slipper, the fairy godmother and the pumpkin coach are Perrault's rather than the tradition's.

He was writing for an educated salon readership at the court of Louis XIV during a literary quarrel about ancient and modern authority, which makes the collection a sophisticated intervention, not an act of preservation.

psycho.name: Psycho
psycho.desc:
Hitchcock's film of 1960 spends its first act following a woman who has stolen money from her employer, and kills her roughly a third of the way through, transferring the audience's attention to the man who has to clean up afterwards.

The structural violence of that decision is the film's real innovation, since it removes the guarantee that the person being followed will survive to the end.

Hitchcock refused to admit latecomers to screenings, which was an unusual exhibition condition at the time, and is widely reported to have bought up copies of the source novel to protect the surprise. The second account is repeated everywhere and documented nowhere very firmly.

spirited_away.name: Spirited Away
spirited_away.desc:
Miyazaki's film of 2001 strands a sullen ten-year-old in a bathhouse for spirits after her parents are transformed, and requires her to work there under a name that is not her own in order to get them back.

The world is delivered without explanation: the bathhouse has an economy, a hierarchy and a plumbing problem, and the film assumes them and never introduces them. Its antagonist is not defeated but understood.

It won the Academy Award for animated feature in 2003 and was for some years the highest-grossing film in Japanese box-office history.

snow_white_1937.name: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
snow_white_1937.desc:
The Disney studio's first animated feature, released at the end of 1937, was widely expected in the industry to fail on the grounds that no audience would sit through a feature-length cartoon.

It did not, and the result established the economics and the house style of commercial animation: songs, animal companions, comic supporting characters, a softened source and a romantic resolution the Grimm text does not supply.

It also set the pattern by which the studio's versions of European tales became, for most of the world's audience, the definitive ones.

seven_samurai.name: Seven Samurai
seven_samurai.desc:
Kurosawa's film of 1954 has a village hire masterless samurai to defend it against bandits, and spends its first half on the recruitment, giving each man an introduction that establishes what he is for.

That assembly structure has been reproduced across genres so often that it now reads as a convention, not an invention, and the film was remade directly as a Western in 1960.

Its ending withholds the expected triumph: the surviving samurai observe that the victory belongs to the farmers rather than to them, and the film closes on the graves of the four who died.

macbeth.name: Macbeth
macbeth.desc:
Shakespeare's tragedy, written around 1606, has a soldier told by three witches that he will be king, and follows the murders required to make the prediction true and to keep it true afterwards.

The prophecies are the play's engine and its trap. Each is fulfilled in a sense other than the one he takes, and the security they seem to guarantee is what drives him to the actions that destroy him, so the prediction operates as a cause rather than a forecast.

It is the shortest of the tragedies and the most compressed, with almost no subplot and a protagonist who narrates his own deterioration.

biblical_narrative.name: Biblical Narrative
biblical_narrative.desc:
The narrative books of the Hebrew Bible, together with the gospels, constitute one of the most widely read bodies of story in the world and one of the most formally distinctive.

The prose is characteristically terse. Motive is rarely stated, physical description is minimal, and a great deal is left unexplained in a way that has invited commentary for two and a half thousand years. Auerbach contrasted this with Homer's fully externalised manner, arguing that the biblical style is fraught with background where the Greek leaves nothing unsaid.

The material has supplied European literature with the parable, the prophetic voice, the type and antitype, and a large proportion of its plots.

jataka_tales.name: Jataka Tales
jataka_tales.desc:
A body of several hundred stories concerning the previous lives of the Buddha, preserved most fully in the Pali canon and among the oldest surviving narrative collections in South Asia.

Most take the form of an animal fable with a moral, framed by an occasion on which the Buddha tells the story and closed by an identification of which character he had been. The frame turns a stock of popular tales into a single continuous biography across lifetimes.

Many of the stories circulate independently in other collections, and their relationship to the Panchatantra and to the Aesopic corpus has been debated since the nineteenth century without being settled.

erich_auerbach.name: Erich Auerbach
erich_auerbach.desc:
German philologist (1892-1957) whose Mimesis, written in Istanbul during the Second World War with almost no access to a research library, traces the representation of everyday reality across three thousand years of Western literature.

Each chapter begins from a single passage and reads outward from it. The first sets the scar of Odysseus against the binding of Isaac, arguing that Homer externalises everything into a continuous foreground while the biblical narrative leaves motive and background unspoken, and that the two styles impose entirely different demands on a reader.

His interest throughout is in when and how ordinary life becomes a fit subject for serious treatment.

wolfgang_iser.name: Wolfgang Iser
wolfgang_iser.desc:
German literary theorist (1926-2007) and a central figure in reception theory, which shifted attention from what a text contains to what a reader does with it.

His argument is that a text is full of gaps and indeterminacies which the reader necessarily fills, and that this filling is not an optional interpretive extra but the process by which the work comes into existence at all. The implied reader is his term for the position a text constructs for whoever reads it.

The approach is the complement to Booth's implied author, and the two together describe a transaction, not an object.

david_bordwell.name: David Bordwell
david_bordwell.desc:
American film scholar (1947-2024) whose work applied narrative theory to cinema with more rigour than the field had previously managed, and largely without the psychoanalytic apparatus that dominated film studies when he began.

He adapted the formalist separation of story material from its arrangement to film, treating narration as a process that cues and constrains the viewer's inferences, and he described the classical Hollywood style as a historically specific set of norms rather than as the natural way to make a film.

His later work on international variation argued against the assumption that those norms are universal.

hayden_white.name: Hayden White
hayden_white.desc:
American historian and theorist (1928-2018) whose Metahistory, published in 1973, argued that historical writing is shaped by the same narrative resources as fiction.

His claim is that a historian confronted with a record of events must emplot them, and that the choice of plot structure, romance, tragedy, comedy or satire, is a literary decision made before the argument begins and not derivable from the evidence.

The position was received as an attack on the discipline's claim to objectivity and remains contested. White consistently denied that it made history equivalent to fiction, arguing that the events are real and the shape imposed on them is not.

self_fulfilling_prophecy.name: Self-Fulfilling Prophecy
self_fulfilling_prophecy.desc:
A narrative pattern in which a prediction brings about the outcome it announces, because the attempt to avoid it or the confidence it produces supplies the necessary cause.

It is one of the oldest plot engines available: the king who exposes an infant to prevent a prophecy and thereby ensures the child is raised in ignorance of his parentage, the general who murders to secure a crown the prediction had already promised him. The structure converts fate from a background condition into a mechanism the plot can be built on.

The term itself is modern, coined by the sociologist Robert K. Merton in 1948 for the same process operating outside fiction, in bank runs and in expectations about people.

bluebeard_type.name: Bluebeard (ATU 312)
bluebeard_type.desc:
A tale type built on the forbidden chamber: a wife is given the keys to her husband's house, told that one room is closed to her, and finds in it the remains of the wives before her.

The structure makes the prohibition and the discovery a single event, since the test exists only to be failed and the husband's purpose in setting it is to have grounds for the killing. In Perrault's version she is saved at the last moment by her brothers; in related types collected across Europe the woman escapes by her own contrivance.

Its persistence in modern fiction and film owes to how directly it stages marriage as a matter of what a woman is permitted to know.

sleeping_beauty_type.name: Sleeping Beauty (ATU 410)
sleeping_beauty_type.desc:
A tale type in which a curse laid at a christening puts a princess and her household into a sleep of a hundred years, broken by the arrival of a prince.

The versions differ sharply in what happens on his arrival. Basile's Neapolitan telling of 1634 has the sleeping woman raped and giving birth without waking, with the story continuing for as long again afterwards; Perrault's of 1697 removes the assault but keeps a second half in which the prince's ogress mother tries to eat the children; the Grimms end at the waking.

The familiar version is therefore the last third of a much longer and much darker tale.

swan_maiden.name: The Swan Maiden
swan_maiden.desc:
A widely distributed pattern in which a man observes a woman who can take the form of a bird, seal or other creature, steals the skin or garment that allows the transformation, and marries her while it remains hidden.

The marriage lasts until she finds it, at which point she leaves, usually without hesitation and sometimes without her children. The tale is generally told from the man's point of view and reads very differently from hers.

Versions are recorded across Europe, Asia and the Pacific, including the Scottish selkie tales and the Japanese celestial maiden whose feather robe is taken while she bathes.

animal_bridegroom.name: The Animal Bridegroom
animal_bridegroom.desc:
A family of tale types in which a woman is married to a beast, a serpent, a bear or an invisible husband, and the marriage is redeemed instead of escaped.

The classical ancestor is the story of Cupid and Psyche, preserved in Apuleius in the second century, where the prohibition is against looking at the husband and the breach sends the wife on a sequence of impossible tasks to recover him.

Beauty and the Beast is the best-known modern descendant, written by Villeneuve in 1740 and abridged sixteen years later by Beaumont into the version that circulated. Its inversion of Bluebeard is exact: there the husband's secret destroys the wife, here her acceptance transforms him.

deal_with_the_devil.name: The Devil's Bargain
deal_with_the_devil.desc:
A pattern in which a person exchanges their soul, or something equivalent, for knowledge, power, wealth or skill, on terms that are honoured exactly and prove ruinous anyway.

The medieval legend of Theophilus supplies the Christian form, in which the bargain can still be revoked by intercession. Marlowe's Faustus removes that exit and ends in damnation; Goethe restores it two centuries later and lets his Faust be saved, which is the single largest divergence between the two great treatments.

The motif transferred readily to secular material, where the counterparty may be an institution, a patron or an industry rather than a devil.

changeling.name: The Changeling
changeling.desc:
A belief and narrative pattern in which a fairy or other being substitutes its own child for a human infant, leaving a substitute that fails to thrive, does not speak, or behaves in ways the family cannot account for.

The tales usually turn on detecting the substitution by trickery, commonly by doing something absurd in the creature's presence until it forgets itself and speaks.

Unlike most motifs this one had direct consequences. The belief was used to explain illness and disability in children and to justify cruelty toward them, and it persisted late enough to feature in documented cases, including the killing of Bridget Cleary in Ireland in 1895.

king_in_the_mountain.name: The Sleeping Hero
king_in_the_mountain.desc:
A legend pattern in which a king or hero is not dead but sleeping beneath a hill or in a cave with his companions, and will return at the hour of his people's greatest need.

The attached figures vary by region and include Arthur, Charlemagne, Frederick Barbarossa in the Kyffhauser, Holger the Dane, and Sebastian of Portugal, and the belief has repeatedly been put to political use by movements claiming the return is imminent or has arrived.

A common secondary motif has a shepherd or traveller stumble into the chamber, be questioned about whether the time has come, and be sent away.

riddle_contest.name: The Riddle Contest
riddle_contest.desc:
A pattern in which a question must be answered on pain of death, and the answer is available to the audience before it reaches the person required to give it.

It is one of the oldest narrative uses of withheld information, and it appears across unrelated traditions: the Sphinx before Thebes, Samson's riddle in Judges, the Anglo-Saxon riddles of the Exeter Book, the exchange of questions with a supernatural adversary in Norse material, and the princess whose suitors are executed for failing.

The contest also functions as a class device, since it is the one arena in which a poor or unarmed protagonist can defeat a powerful one legitimately.

magic_object.name: The Magic Object
magic_object.desc:
An item that confers a specific power on whoever holds it: a lamp, a ring, a cloak of invisibility, boots that cover leagues at a step, a purse that never empties.

In Propp's analysis the object arrives through a defined function, the donor who tests the hero and supplies a magical agent on the strength of the answer. That makes the acquisition a moral transaction, not a piece of luck.

Its modern descendant is a different device. Where the magic object does something the plot needs done, the MacGuffin need only be wanted, and its properties are deliberately left vague.

dragon_slayer.name: The Dragon Slayer (ATU 300)
dragon_slayer.desc:
A tale type in which a hero kills a monster that has been exacting tribute from a community, frequently rescuing a woman offered to it, and is then displaced by an impostor who claims the deed until proof identifies the true killer.

The token of proof is the type's distinctive element: the hero cuts out the tongues of the severed heads, and the impostor arrives with heads that are missing them.

The pattern underlies Perseus and Andromeda, the legend of Saint George, Sigurd and Fafnir, and countless collected variants, and it supplies the clearest folk instance of the plot Booker classified as overcoming the monster.

gothic_fiction.name: Gothic Fiction
gothic_fiction.desc:
A genre of dread, transgression and the returning past, conventionally dated from Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto in 1764, which was subtitled a Gothic story.

Its early machinery is architectural: ruined castles and abbeys, subterranean passages, locked chambers, hereditary curses and persecuted heirs. Ann Radcliffe developed a mode in which apparent supernatural events are eventually explained away, while Matthew Lewis's The Monk pursued open horror and violation, and the split between the two has persisted.

The form proved unusually hospitable to women writers and readers, and to anxieties about inheritance, confinement and sexual power that the realist novel handled less directly.

melodrama.name: Melodrama
melodrama.desc:
A mode of heightened emotional legibility in which moral positions are drawn clearly, feeling is externalised, and virtue is placed in visible distress.

The word combines music and drama, and the early nineteenth-century French stage form it names used orchestral accompaniment to underscore the action, a technique the cinema inherited wholesale. Its apparatus includes the innocent under threat, the unambiguous villain, the last-minute rescue and the recognition that restores a rightful identity.

Long treated as a debased opposite of tragedy, it was reassessed from the 1970s as the form a society without shared religious authority uses to make moral conflict visible.

thriller.name: Thriller
thriller.desc:
A genre organised around anticipated danger rather than around a completed crime, which is what separates it from detective fiction: the question is what will happen next, not what already happened.

Its characteristic protagonist is under-informed and out of position, an ordinary person caught in a conspiracy or a professional operating without support, and its plots run on pursuit, deadline and betrayal.

The espionage branch produced two opposed traditions, one treating the trade as adventure and the other, developed by Ambler, Greene and le Carre, treating it as bureaucratic, morally compromised and largely futile.

historical_fiction.name: Historical Fiction
historical_fiction.desc:
A genre in which invented characters act within a documented past, and in which the period is a set of conditions determining what is possible rather than a costume.

Walter Scott's Waverley of 1814 is the conventional starting point, and Lukacs argued that Scott's innovation was to present history as a process with winners and losers, not as a backdrop, using a middling protagonist caught between contending forces.

The genre's recurring difficulty is anachronism of mind: a character with modern moral reflexes reassures a modern reader and falsifies the period, while one with period reflexes may be unreadable as a protagonist.

dystopia.name: Dystopia
dystopia.desc:
A genre extrapolating a present tendency into a society organised around it, and following someone who begins to see the arrangement from outside.

It is the inverted twin of the utopia that Thomas More named in 1516, and the twentieth century produced its canonical examples in rapid succession: Zamyatin's We, written in 1920 and long suppressed in Russia, Huxley's Brave New World in 1932 and Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four in 1949, which between them established the two dominant models of control by pleasure and control by fear.

The form is argumentative by construction, which is also its standing weakness, since the protagonist frequently exists to be lectured.

western.name: Western
western.desc:
A genre set on the American frontier in the decades after the Civil War, organised around the arrival of law in a place that has been running without it.

Its standard figure is a man competent at violence who secures a community he cannot then belong to, which gives the form its recurring ending of a rider leaving a town he has made safe. Owen Wister's The Virginian in 1902 fixed the type in fiction and John Ford's films fixed it on screen.

From the 1960s the genre turned on itself, questioning the settlement it had celebrated and the treatment of the people already living on the land.

guslar.name: Guslar
guslar.desc:
A South Slavic epic singer who performs long narrative poems accompanied by the gusle, a single-stringed bowed instrument, sustaining a performance for hours and composing the verse as it is delivered instead of reciting a memorised text.

The tradition is the evidential basis of the oral-formulaic theory. Parry and Lord recorded singers in Yugoslavia in the 1930s specifically to test what could be inferred about Homer, and found performers producing thousands of lines from a stock of themes and formulas.

Among those recorded was Avdo Mededovic, whose performances ran to lengths comparable with the Homeric poems.

skald.name: Skald
skald.desc:
A Norse court poet, attached to a king or earl and paid to compose praise poetry recording his patron's campaigns and generosity.

Skaldic verse is metrically strict and syntactically dense, built on internal rhyme and stress patterns and on kennings, compressed metaphorical compounds that name a thing by circumlocution: the whale's road for the sea, the wound-sea for blood. The difficulty is deliberate and was a mark of the craft.

Because the form is so tightly constructed, verses attributed to named poets could be transmitted with unusual accuracy, and the sagas quote them as evidence for events they narrate.

naqqali.name: Naqqāli
naqqali.desc:
The Iranian tradition of dramatic storytelling, in which a solo performer narrates episodes from the Shahnameh and other epic material to an audience in a coffeehouse or public square, using voice, gesture and movement rather than staging.

A related practice performs the same repertoire in front of a large painted cloth, the performer moving along the scenes and drawing the audience's attention from panel to panel as the story advances.

The form declined with radio, television and the closure of the coffeehouses that supported it, and it was inscribed on UNESCO's list of intangible heritage in need of urgent safeguarding in 2011.

allegory.name: Allegory
allegory.desc:
A narrative in which the elements correspond systematically to a second scheme of meaning, so that characters, places and events stand for virtues, doctrines, institutions or historical actors and the correspondence holds across the whole work.

What distinguishes it from symbolism is completeness and intention: a symbol may resonate loosely, while an allegory can be decoded point by point, and medieval interpretation formalised this by reading scripture on several levels at once.

The mode's reputation has fallen and risen. Its critics object that a story whose meaning can be extracted has no reason to be a story, and its defenders point out that the extraction is rarely as clean as either party assumes.

soliloquy.name: Soliloquy
soliloquy.desc:
A speech delivered by a character alone on stage, or believing themselves alone, giving an audience direct access to a mind that the other characters cannot hear.

It is a convention, not a realistic depiction, and the Elizabethan theatre used it as the principal means of interiority available to a form with no narrator. Hamlet has seven, and they carry most of what the play is about.

Realist drama largely abandoned it as implausible, and the access it provided had to be recovered by other means: the confidant, the telephone call, the letter read aloud, and eventually the film voiceover.

greek_chorus.name: The Chorus
greek_chorus.desc:
A group of performers who sing, dance and comment on the action of a play without being able to alter it, standing between the events and the audience.

In Athenian tragedy the chorus supplies the community's perspective, asks the questions a spectator would ask, recalls the mythic background, and holds the moral position that the protagonists are violating. Its odes also divide the acts, which is where act structure originally comes from.

Drama shed it as individual character became the centre of interest, and its later revivals are usually deliberate archaism, used by writers who want the commentary and the distance it enforces.

mise_en_abyme.name: Mise en Abyme
mise_en_abyme.desc:
A work containing a smaller version of itself: a play within a play, a story whose characters read the story, a painting depicting the room it hangs in.

The term is borrowed from heraldry, where a shield may carry a small copy of itself at its centre, and was applied to literature by André Gide, who wanted a name for what he was attempting in his own fiction.

Its effect is to make the frame visible. The inner version invites comparison with the outer one, and the audience is put in the position of watching an audience. It is so often used at the moment a work wants to be understood as constructed.

exposition.name: Exposition
exposition.desc:
The delivery of information the audience needs and the characters already have: who these people are, what has happened before the story starts, and what the rules of the world permit.

It is the most consistently criticised part of the craft because the natural solutions are all detectable. Greek drama solved it with a prologue delivered straight to the audience; the well-made play used servants discussing their employers; the modern default is a newcomer who has to be told everything, which relocates the problem rather than removing it.

The alternative is to withhold, and let the audience assemble the situation from what the characters do not bother to explain.

verbal_irony.name: Verbal Irony
verbal_irony.desc:
A statement whose intended meaning differs from what it says, and which depends on the audience having enough context to register the gap.

It is distinct from the dramatic kind, which arises from what an audience knows rather than from what a speaker means, and from the situational kind, which requires no speaker at all. Sarcasm is a narrow and hostile subset, not a synonym.

In narrative it is a principal instrument of characterisation, since a character who speaks ironically is displaying a judgement they are declining to state, and a narrator who does so is inviting the reader into an alliance against someone.

leitmotif.name: Leitmotif
leitmotif.desc:
A short recurring element attached to a character, place or idea, returning in altered form as their situation changes.

The term comes from opera, where Wagner's practice of associating musical phrases with figures and objects was systematised and named by commentators rather than by him, and film scoring took the device over almost intact.

The literary equivalent is a repeated image, phrase or object whose meaning accumulates across a book. In both cases the effect depends on variation, not repetition, since a motif that returns unchanged reads as a label and one that returns transformed carries the history of everything between.

ellipsis.name: Ellipsis
ellipsis.desc:
The omission of a stretch of story time, so that a narrative jumps a night, a year or a generation without narrating it.

In Genette's analysis it is the limiting case of narrative speed, where a quantity of story is covered in no text at all, and it may be marked by a stated interval or left for the reader to detect. The corresponding film device is the cut between scenes, which audiences read so automatically that its conventionality is invisible.

What is skipped is rarely neutral. A narrative that omits the wedding and resumes ten years later has made an argument about which part mattered.

ballad.name: Ballad
ballad.desc:
A narrative song in stanzas, generally telling a single story of love, murder, supernatural encounter or crime, and transmitted orally in many variant versions.

The traditional ballad has a characteristic manner: it enters the story late, leaps between scenes without transition and lingers on the crucial exchange, delivers much of the action in dialogue, and repeats a phrase with one element changed at each occurrence.

Francis James Child's late nineteenth-century collection of English and Scottish ballads is the standard reference, and the broadside trade printed and sold new ballads on topical subjects alongside the older material.

musical_theatre.name: Musical Theatre
musical_theatre.desc:
A dramatic form in which song and dance carry part of the narrative instead of interrupting it, and in which characters sing at the point where speech will no longer do.

The integrated book musical, in which the numbers advance the plot and reveal character, is usually dated to Show Boat in 1927 and consolidated by Oklahoma! in 1943, replacing an earlier practice of hanging songs on a loose comic frame.

Its conventions are strong enough to be named by practitioners: the opening that establishes the world, the song in which a character states what they want, and the late reprise that shows what the wanting has cost.

documentary.name: Documentary
documentary.desc:
Film and television built from records of actual events and people, and shaped by the same selection, sequencing and emphasis that fiction uses.

John Grierson, who applied the word to film in the 1920s, described the form as the creative treatment of actuality, a phrase that concedes the tension at its centre. Flaherty's Nanook of the North, released in 1922, is a founding work and also a demonstration of the problem, since scenes were staged and arranged for the camera.

Later observational movements sought to remove the filmmaker's hand, and the ethical arguments about what a documentary owes its subjects have never settled.

sitcom.name: Situation Comedy
sitcom.desc:
A television form built on a fixed cast in a stable situation, in which each episode disturbs the arrangement and restores it by the end.

The reset is the form's defining constraint and its engine: characters cannot learn permanently. They can be funny indefinitely, and the comedy comes from watching the same people fail in the same ways against new material.

It developed out of radio serials, acquired the multi-camera studio format with a live audience, and later split, with single-camera production and season-long change eroding the reset that had defined it.

intertextuality.name: Intertextuality
intertextuality.desc:
The proposition that a text is not a self-contained object but a construction made from other texts, absorbing and transforming them whether or not the author intends it.

Julia Kristeva coined the term in the 1960s while introducing Bakhtin's work to a French readership, and it belongs to his account of language as always already used by someone else. Genette later built a detailed taxonomy of the relations involved: quotation, allusion, parody, pastiche, commentary and continuation.

The concept is broader than influence, which concerns what a writer read, and covers relations a reader constructs that no writer arranged.

narrative_closure.name: Closure
narrative_closure.desc:
The sense that a narrative has finished rather than merely stopped, produced by the resolution of the questions it raised and by formal signals that the reader recognises as an ending.

Frank Kermode argued that endings carry a weight out of proportion to their length because they retrospectively organise everything before them, and that human beings need fictions of ending in order to make sense of being in the middle of things.

What counts as closure varies by form and period. The nineteenth-century novel settled marriages and inheritances; the modern short story frequently ends where the meaning is still gathering, and treats a settled ending as a falsification.

character_arc.name: Character Arc
character_arc.desc:
The change a character undergoes across a narrative, usually described as a movement from one governing belief or need to another, tested by the events the plot supplies.

The term belongs to screenwriting instruction, not to older criticism, and it encodes an assumption that a protagonist ought to change, which a great deal of narrative does not share. Manuals accordingly supply a flat arc for the character who changes the world around them instead.

Episodic forms resist it by design: the picaro, the detective and the situation comedy cast all have to arrive at the next instalment unaltered.

equilibrium_model.name: Todorov's Equilibrium Model
equilibrium_model.desc:
A five-stage account of narrative in which a state of equilibrium is disrupted, the disruption is recognised, an attempt is made to repair it, and a new equilibrium is reached that is not identical to the first.

Its economy is the point. The scheme applies as readily to a folk tale, a news report or a sitcom episode as to a novel, and it identifies what must be true for a sequence of events to register as a story at all rather than prescribing where anything should fall.

The final stage carries the argument: the closing state resembles the opening one but has been altered by what happened, which is what distinguishes a narrative from a loop.

ring_composition.name: Ring Composition
ring_composition.desc:
An arrangement in which the elements of a narrative are placed symmetrically around a centre, so that the last answers the first, the second-last the second, and the turning point sits in the middle rather than at the end.

The pattern is common in oral and early written literature, including Homer, Herodotus and the Hebrew Bible, and it suits performance conditions in which an audience cannot turn back, since the echoes stand in for the rereading a page allows.

Recognising it changes where the emphasis falls, because the significant material sits at the centre of the structure, not at the climax a modern reader expects.

linda_seger.name: Linda Seger
linda_seger.desc:
American script consultant whose Making a Good Script Great, published in 1987, was among the first books to treat rewriting rather than writing as the subject.

Her approach works through diagnosis: identifying where a script's structure fails, where a character's motivation is unsupported, and what a scene is actually accomplishing, on the assumption that the reader is being paid to find the problem, not to admire the intention.

She also helped establish script consultancy as a profession distinct from development executive and teacher, which changed how screenplays are worked on in the industry.

john_truby.name: John Truby
john_truby.desc:
American screenwriting teacher whose The Anatomy of Story, published in 2007, argues against the three-act paradigm on the grounds that dividing a script into blocks says nothing about what has to happen inside them.

His alternative is a sequence of twenty-two steps running from a weakness and a need through desire, opponent, plan, battle and self-revelation, organised so that the antagonist attacks the protagonist's central weakness rather than merely obstructing the goal.

He treats theme as the organising principle, not an afterthought, which places him closer to Egri than to the structural manuals he criticises.

georg_lukacs.name: Georg Lukács
georg_lukacs.desc:
Hungarian critic and philosopher (1885-1971) whose early Theory of the Novel described the form as the epic of a world abandoned by meaning, in which a hero seeks a totality that is no longer available and the search rather than the finding constitutes the book.

His later Marxist criticism turned to realism, and The Historical Novel argues that Walter Scott's innovation was to present the past as a process of social conflict, not as a setting, using a middling protagonist caught between the contending forces so that both can be shown.

He defended nineteenth-century realism against modernism on the grounds that it could represent a society as a connected whole, a position that has been argued with ever since.

kenning.name: Kenning
kenning.desc:
A compressed metaphorical compound that names a thing by circumlocution: the whale's road for the sea, the battle-sweat for blood, the ring-giver for a king.

The device is central to Old Norse and Old English verse, where it supplies both ornament and metrical flexibility, since a poet needing a particular stress pattern can select among many available substitutes for the same noun. Skaldic practice nests them several deep, so that a kenning's determinant is itself a kenning and unpacking a stanza becomes a puzzle.

Snorri Sturluson catalogued the standard formations in the thirteenth century, partly because poets were already losing the mythological knowledge the older examples assume.

adaptation.name: Adaptation
adaptation.desc:
The transposition of a work into another medium, form or context, which is among the most common ways stories move and among the least respected.

Criticism long organised itself around fidelity, asking how far a film departs from its novel, a question that assumes the source is the standard and the adaptation an attempt at reproduction. Later work rejected the framing, treating adaptation as repetition with variation and noting that the practice is as old as narrative: Greek tragedy adapted epic, Shakespeare adapted chronicles and novellas, and the tale types have never existed in any other form.

What the medium can and cannot carry decides most of it, and the recurring difficulty is interiority.

frank_kermode.name: Frank Kermode
frank_kermode.desc:
English critic (1919-2010) whose The Sense of an Ending, published in 1967, asked why human beings need fictions of conclusion and what endings do to everything that precedes them.

His argument begins from the observation that we are always in the middle, without access to our own beginning or end, and that we borrow from narrative the shape that experience does not supply. He uses the ticking of a clock as the example: the sound is undifferentiated and we hear it as tick-tock, imposing a beginning and an end on an interval that has neither.

He also distinguished the apocalyptic expectation of an imminent end, which is repeatedly disconfirmed and repeatedly rescheduled, from the more supple fictions that literature offers instead.
