improvisation.name: Improvisation
improvisation.desc:
Composition in performance, in which the material is assembled in front of the audience from a stock of prepared elements rather than delivered from a fixed text.

It is never invention from nothing. The improvising performer works with routines, formulas, character types, scenarios and rules of exchange learned in advance, and the freedom lies in selection, ordering and response, not in origination. The same is true of the oral epic singer, the commedia troupe and the modern comedy stage.

Its characteristic constraint is that nothing can be revised, which rules out the effects that depend on a reader turning back and rewards those that depend on momentum.

rebirth.name: Rebirth
rebirth.desc:
The seventh of Booker's plots, in which a protagonist falls under a shadow, a spell, an obsession or a moral deadness, remains in it while it deepens, and is released near the end by an intervention usually involving love or grace.

It differs from the others in that the central figure is closer to the antagonist for most of the story, and the reader's sympathy has to be sustained through a long stretch in which the character is not admirable. The redemption cannot be earned by effort, which is what separates it from the quest, and it is generally supplied by someone else.

Booker's examples include Scrooge, the enchanted beast, the sleeping princess and Raskolnikov.

opera.name: Opera
opera.desc:
A dramatic form in which the text is sung throughout to an orchestral accompaniment, developed in Italy around 1600 by a circle attempting to reconstruct what they believed Greek tragedy had sounded like.

The reconstruction was mistaken and the result was new. Because music controls the pace absolutely, opera can hold a moment open for several minutes while a character examines a feeling, and can carry several characters' incompatible positions simultaneously in ways speech cannot.

Its narrative material has been drawn overwhelmingly from existing sources, myth, legend, plays and novels. That makes it one of the most consistently adaptive forms in the arts.

wilkie_collins.name: Wilkie Collins
wilkie_collins.desc:
English novelist (1824-1889), a friend and collaborator of Dickens, and the leading practitioner of the sensation novel of the 1860s.

His two major books are built on withheld information delivered through multiple first-person accounts, each narrator writing only what they witnessed, so the reader assembles a case from testimony as a jury would. He had trained in law and the arrangement is deliberate.

He wrote for weekly serialisation and engineered his instalment endings accordingly, and he is credited by later writers with establishing several of the devices the detective novel was built on.

the_moonstone.name: The Moonstone
the_moonstone.desc:
Collins's novel of 1868 concerns a diamond taken from an Indian shrine, given to a young woman on her birthday, and stolen from her room that night.

It assembles the case from a sequence of first-person narratives by household members, each writing to order and each limited to what they saw, which lets the author plant misdirection without any narrator lying. It contains a country-house theft, a bungling local constabulary, a celebrated detective from London, a reconstruction of the crime and a solution nobody suspects.

T. S. Eliot's description of it as the first and greatest of English detective novels is a judgement, not a fact, but the apparatus is unmistakably there.

agatha_christie.name: Agatha Christie
agatha_christie.desc:
English writer (1890-1976) and the dominant figure of the interwar detective novel, working the puzzle form harder than anyone before or since.

Her distinctive practice is to identify a place the reader assumes is safe and hide the culprit there: the narrator, the investigating officer, the victim, the child, everyone. Each book effectively tests one structural assumption of the genre and breaks it while observing the rule that the evidence must be shown.

She worked in a hospital dispensary during the First World War, which accounts for the unusual accuracy of the poisonings.

roger_ackroyd.name: The Murder of Roger Ackroyd
roger_ackroyd.desc:
Christie's novel of 1926 is narrated by a country doctor who assists the detective, records the investigation, and is revealed at the end to be the murderer.

The narration never states a falsehood. It omits, compresses and misdirects, with one paragraph in particular passing over a few minutes in language that is accurate and entirely misleading, so the reader convicts themselves of the assumption rather than being lied to.

It provoked an immediate argument about whether the device was permissible under the genre's fair-play conventions, an argument that has never fully closed and that Dorothy L. Sayers among others answered in its defence.

medea.name: Medea
medea.desc:
Euripides' tragedy of 431 BCE gives its protagonist a case, and then has her act on it in a way no case could justify: abandoned by Jason for a royal marriage and facing exile, she kills his bride, the bride's father and her own two children.

The play affords her the arguments, at length and in public, which is part of what made it uncomfortable to its first audience. It took third prize.

Its ending is the standard example of the god in the machine: Medea escapes above the stage in a chariot sent by her grandfather the sun, beyond any reach of justice, which is the resolution Aristotle objected to by name.

the_seagull.name: The Seagull
the_seagull.desc:
Chekhov's play of 1896 concerns a young writer, an established one, an actress mother and a girl who wants the stage, arranged so that everybody loves someone who is looking elsewhere.

The premiere failed badly enough that Chekhov left the theatre and swore off playwriting; the Moscow Art Theatre's production two years later succeeded, and the company took the bird as its emblem.

It is also the play most often cited for his principle about the gun: a firearm is present early, and the shot that matters is fired offstage in the final act and reported to the audience in a sentence.

oresteia.name: The Oresteia
oresteia.desc:
Aeschylus's trilogy of 458 BCE is the only complete tragic trilogy to survive from antiquity, following a killing through three plays: a king murdered by his wife on his return from Troy, the wife murdered by her son, and the son pursued by the Furies until a court is convened to try him.

Each play has a different chorus, and the sequence uses them to shift the point of view from the frightened elders of the city to the enslaved women of the household to the avenging powers themselves.

The resolution replaces the cycle of blood vengeance with a jury and a founding institution, which makes the trilogy an argument as well as a drama.

sergei_eisenstein.name: Sergei Eisenstein
sergei_eisenstein.desc:
Soviet director and theorist (1898-1948) whose films and writings established montage as the argument that cinema's meaning is produced between shots, not within them.

He held that two images in collision generate a concept neither contains, and classified the kinds of collision available: by rhythm, by graphic direction, by tone and by idea. The position was polemical against filmmakers who treated editing as a way of joining scenes.

His later career was constrained by the Soviet authorities, with projects abandoned, suppressed or completed under supervision, and his theoretical writing occupied much of the time this left him.

battleship_potemkin.name: Battleship Potemkin
battleship_potemkin.desc:
Eisenstein's film of 1925 dramatises a mutiny aboard a Russian warship in 1905 and the reprisals that followed, built entirely from editing rather than from star performance or plot.

Its most reproduced sequence, a massacre on a flight of steps in Odessa, has no historical original: the killings happened in the city but not there and not that way, and the scene was constructed for its effect. It has been quoted, parodied and taught continuously ever since.

The film is the standing demonstration of the claim that a shot means what the shot beside it makes it mean.

ernest_hemingway.name: Ernest Hemingway
ernest_hemingway.desc:
American novelist and short story writer (1899-1961) whose prose stripped the sentence back to declarative statement and concrete noun, and whose influence on twentieth-century writing in English is difficult to overstate and was frequently unfortunate for his imitators.

His stated principle was that a writer who knows what they are leaving out may omit it, and the omitted part will strengthen the story: the dignity of an iceberg lies in its being mostly submerged.

He worked as a reporter before and between the fiction, and the discipline of the news paragraph is visible in the method.

hills_like_white_elephants.name: Hills Like White Elephants
hills_like_white_elephants.desc:
Hemingway's story of 1927 consists almost entirely of a conversation between a man and a woman at a Spanish railway station while they wait for a train, about a procedure he wants her to have and she is not sure about.

The procedure is never named. Neither is the relationship, the history, or what either of them decides. The narration reports the drinks, the heat, the bead curtain and the hills across the valley, and does not enter either mind.

It is among the most taught demonstrations of the principle that a story's substance can sit entirely below the words on the page.

jonathan_swift.name: Jonathan Swift
jonathan_swift.desc:
Anglo-Irish satirist and clergyman (1667-1745), Dean of St Patrick's in Dublin, and among the most formidable ironists in English.

His method is to adopt a persona completely and reason from a monstrous premise with perfect composure, never breaking the mask and never signalling. The reader is left to supply the objection, which is the source of both the power and the recurring misreadings.

Gulliver's Travels operates the same way at book length, and its persistence as a children's story is one of literature's better jokes at its author's expense, since the final voyage is a sustained argument against the species.

a_modest_proposal.name: A Modest Proposal
a_modest_proposal.desc:
Swift's pamphlet of 1729, published anonymously, proposes that the children of the Irish poor be sold as food to wealthy landlords, and sets out the economic benefits in the calm register of contemporary improvement literature.

The persona is an earnest projector with figures, and the argument is conducted entirely in his voice: costings per child, seasonal availability, the effect on rents and on the number of papists. Nothing signals the joke.

The real target sits beneath the surface one, since the policies actually being pursued toward Ireland are what make the proposal's logic continuous with them, not a departure.

richard_wagner.name: Richard Wagner
richard_wagner.desc:
German composer and dramatist (1813-1883) who wrote his own librettos and argued for a total work of art in which music, text and staging would form a single dramatic instrument.

His practice of attaching short musical figures to characters, objects and ideas, and developing them as the drama develops, is the origin of the leitmotif as film scoring uses it, though the term was applied by commentators rather than by him.

His antisemitic writings are extensive, published under his own name, and inseparable from any account of him, and the argument about their relation to the music has continued since his lifetime.

ring_cycle.name: Der Ring des Nibelungen
ring_cycle.desc:
Wagner's cycle of four operas, written and composed over some twenty-six years and first performed complete at Bayreuth in 1876, follows a ring made from stolen gold that confers power on whoever renounces love to hold it.

The material is drawn from Norse and Germanic sources, the Eddas, the Volsunga saga and the Nibelungenlied, freely recombined, not adapted from any one of them.

Its musical fabric is built from short recurring figures attached to characters, objects and ideas, developed and combined so that the orchestra can contradict what a character on stage is saying.

john_bunyan.name: John Bunyan
john_bunyan.desc:
English preacher and writer (1628-1688), a tinker by trade and largely self-educated, imprisoned for twelve years for preaching without a licence.

He wrote for a readership that shared his religious framework and his plain speech, and the result was among the most widely read books in English for two centuries, second only to the Bible in many households.

His prose is concrete where his subject is abstract: the burden on the back, the slough, the hill, the river to be crossed at the end. The allegory has outlived the theology it was built to convey.

pilgrims_progress.name: The Pilgrim's Progress
pilgrims_progress.desc:
Bunyan's allegory of 1678 follows a man named Christian from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City, through the Slough of Despond, Vanity Fair, Doubting Castle and the river of death.

Every place and person is its meaning: Mr Worldly Wiseman, Giant Despair, Faithful, Hopeful. The correspondence is complete and declared. That makes it the reference case for allegory as a sustained method rather than an occasional figure.

It is framed as a dream, and Bunyan wrote a substantial part of it during imprisonment. Its influence on English prose reached readers who would have refused any other book of divinity.

bram_stoker.name: Bram Stoker
bram_stoker.desc:
Irish writer (1847-1912) who spent most of his working life as business manager to the actor Henry Irving at the Lyceum Theatre in London, and wrote fiction alongside it.

His notes for Dracula survive and show the book assembled over several years from folklore reading, travel writing and geography he had never visited, with the vampire's name and Transylvanian setting arrived at late in the process.

The novel's construction from documents suited a period fascinated by recording technology, and he put the newest of it into the book alongside the oldest superstition.

dracula.name: Dracula
dracula.desc:
Stoker's novel of 1897 is assembled entirely from documents: journals kept in shorthand, letters, telegrams, newspaper cuttings, a ship's log and recordings on phonograph cylinders, collected and typed up by one of the characters.

The method supplies the horror with corroboration, since each account is limited to one person's knowledge and the reader assembles the threat before any character does. It also dates the book precisely to a moment of new recording technology set against very old belief.

Its vampire has displaced every earlier one in the popular imagination, largely through adaptation, not through the novel itself.

to_the_lighthouse.name: To the Lighthouse
to_the_lighthouse.desc:
Woolf's novel of 1927 is built in three parts: a long afternoon and evening at a Hebridean holiday house, a short middle section covering the ten years that follow, and a return in which a postponed expedition is finally made.

The middle section is the book's most discussed passage. The house stands empty and decaying while the war happens elsewhere, and the deaths of three members of the family are reported inside square brackets, in single sentences, as interruptions to a description of weather and dust.

The effect is to make an ordinary domestic afternoon the substantial part of the book and a decade of catastrophe the parenthesis.

christmas_carol.name: A Christmas Carol
christmas_carol.desc:
Dickens's story of 1843 takes a miser through a single night in the company of three spirits who show him his past, the present he is refusing to see, and the death that is waiting, after which he wakes changed.

Its structure is unusually clean: the protagonist is shown rather than argued with, and the transformation is complete and permanent by morning. Dickens wrote it quickly, published it at his own expense, and it sold out within days.

It has done more than any other single work to fix the modern shape of the English Christmas, and the miser's name has become a common noun.

will_storr.name: Will Storr
will_storr.desc:
British journalist and author whose The Science of Storytelling, published in 2019, argues that the rules craft teaching arrived at by trial and error are describable in terms of how perception and personality actually work.

His starting position is that the brain does not receive the world but models it, and that a story succeeds by hijacking that process: attention is captured by unexpected change, and sustained by the question of who a person is that they would respond to change like that.

His other books work the same seam from outside fiction. Selfie examines how the modern idea of the self was assembled, and The Status Game argues that much human behaviour is organised around the pursuit of standing, which is also his account of what drives characters.

science_of_storytelling.name: The Science of Storytelling
science_of_storytelling.desc:
Storr's 2019 book applies research from psychology and neuroscience to the questions craft manuals usually answer from experience, and arrives at a scheme organised around character, not plot.

Its central proposition is the theory of control: everyone operates a model of how the world works, and a story begins when an unexpected change destabilises the protagonist's model and forces them to defend or revise it. The flaw at the centre of that model is what he calls sacred, because it is defended most fiercely where it is least examined.

The book closes with a practical appendix, the Sacred Flaw Approach, which works from a character's origin damage and ignition point outward to the plot that will test them.

mary_shelley.name: Mary Shelley
mary_shelley.desc:
English novelist (1797-1851), daughter of the philosopher William Godwin and the writer Mary Wollstonecraft, who died days after her birth.

She began Frankenstein at eighteen, during a wet summer at a villa on Lake Geneva where the party amused itself by attempting ghost stories. Her own account of the origin, written for the 1831 edition fifteen years later, describes a waking dream of a student kneeling beside the thing he had assembled.

She wrote six further novels, including an early work of apocalyptic fiction in which a plague destroys humanity, and edited her husband's poetry after his death.

horace_walpole.name: Horace Walpole
horace_walpole.desc:
English writer, politician and antiquarian (1717-1797), son of a prime minister, who built a small Gothic castle at Strawberry Hill and wrote the novel that named a genre.

He published The Castle of Otranto anonymously in 1764, presenting it as a translation of an Italian manuscript printed in 1529 and recently found in the library of a Catholic family in the north of England. The reception was warm; when he admitted authorship in the second edition, several reviewers turned on it.

He was also one of the great letter writers of the century, and the correspondence has outlasted the fiction as literature.

castle_of_otranto.name: The Castle of Otranto
castle_of_otranto.desc:
Walpole's short novel of 1764, subtitled a Gothic story in its second edition, opens with a giant helmet falling from the sky and crushing the heir to a usurped principality on his wedding day.

Everything the genre would run on for the next century is assembled here at speed: the castle with its subterranean passages, the tyrant pursuing a young woman through them, the prophecy, the portrait that steps out of its frame and the hereditary guilt working itself out on the innocent.

The first edition's claim to be a translated medieval manuscript is itself a Gothic device, and it established a habit of framing that the genre kept long after nobody believed it.

edgar_allan_poe.name: Edgar Allan Poe
edgar_allan_poe.desc:
American writer (1809-1849) who worked in poetry, criticism and the short story, and whose few tales of what he called ratiocination invented the detective story more or less complete.

His critical position matters as much as the fiction: he argued that a short work should be readable at one sitting and that every element of it must be subordinated to a single preconceived effect, which is the earliest clear statement of the short story as a designed form.

He also wrote foundational work in horror and in early science fiction, and died at forty in circumstances that have never been established.

murders_rue_morgue.name: The Murders in the Rue Morgue
murders_rue_morgue.desc:
Poe's tale of 1841 opens with an essay on analysis, introduces an eccentric and impoverished gentleman of great reasoning power, and then sets him to solve a double killing in a room locked from the inside.

In a few thousand words it establishes the amateur investigator who outthinks the police, the admiring companion who narrates, the locked room, the false arrest of an innocent man, the reconstruction from physical traces and the solution nobody has entertained.

Doyle acknowledged the debt directly, and every element listed above was still in use a century later.

walter_scott.name: Walter Scott
walter_scott.desc:
Scottish novelist, poet and antiquarian (1771-1832) who was among the most commercially successful writers in Europe in his lifetime and effectively created the historical novel as a form.

He published his fiction anonymously for years, and the books were known as the Waverley Novels after the first of them. His method was to set invented characters of middling rank inside documented events and to give the losing side of a conflict its case in its own voice.

He also collected border ballads, and the antiquarian and the novelist are the same person working on the same material by different means.

waverley.name: Waverley
waverley.desc:
Scott's first novel, published anonymously in 1814, follows a young English officer who travels north, is drawn into the Jacobite rising of 1745, and returns having seen a society destroyed.

Its protagonist is deliberately unremarkable, and the design is what Lukacs later identified as Scott's innovation: a figure of moderate convictions placed between two causes, so that both can be represented with sympathy and the reader is not told which to hold.

The subtitle sets the book sixty years before the present, which fixes the distance the historical novel works across and announces the period as a subject in itself.

giambattista_basile.name: Giambattista Basile
giambattista_basile.desc:
Neapolitan poet and courtier (c. 1566-1632) whose collection of tales, published after his death, is the earliest substantial literary treatment of the European fairy tale.

He wrote in Neapolitan rather than in Tuscan, in a dense, punning, extravagant style aimed at a courtly audience with an appetite for the grotesque, and the tales are considerably coarser and more violent than the versions that followed.

His collection was known to Perrault and to the Grimms, and it contains the earliest recorded forms of several stories now assumed to be much older in print than they are.

pentamerone.name: The Pentamerone
pentamerone.desc:
Basile's collection, published in Neapolitan in 1634 and 1636 after his death, holds fifty tales told over five days by ten women, inside a frame that is itself a fairy tale about a substituted bride.

It contains the earliest known literary versions of Cinderella, Sleeping Beauty, Rapunzel and Hansel and Gretel among others, and they are startling beside their descendants: the sleeping princess is raped in her sleep and bears twins before waking, and the cruelties are described with relish.

The Grimms called it the first national collection of tales, and its influence on both Perrault and their own work is documented.

alexander_afanasyev.name: Alexander Afanasyev
alexander_afanasyev.desc:
Russian folklorist (1826-1871) whose collection of Russian folk tales, issued in eight volumes between 1855 and 1863, is the largest and most important gathering of Slavic narrative material.

He worked largely from the archives of the Russian Geographical Society rather than in the field, and edited far more lightly than the Grimms, preserving dialect and inconsistency where they smoothed. That restraint is why the collection is usable as evidence.

A separate volume of bawdy tales could not be published in Russia in his lifetime and appeared abroad without his name on it.

afanasyev_tales.name: Russian Fairy Tales
afanasyev_tales.desc:
Afanasyev's collection of some six hundred Russian tales, published in eight volumes from 1855, is the corpus on which the formal analysis of the folk tale was built.

It is the source of the material most readers know as Russian: Baba Yaga in her hut on chicken legs, Koschei the Deathless who keeps his death in an egg, the firebird, the grey wolf and Vasilisa. The tales are given with their variants rather than merged into single authoritative versions.

Propp drew the hundred wonder tales of his Morphology directly from it, and the scope of his conclusions is the scope of this collection.

truman_capote.name: Truman Capote
truman_capote.desc:
American writer (1924-1984) who published fiction, reportage and a novella of considerable charm before spending six years on the book that defined the nonfiction novel and effectively ended his working life.

He travelled to Kansas in 1959 with Harper Lee to report a multiple murder, stayed through the investigation, the trial and the executions, and formed a close and much-discussed relationship with one of the condemned men.

He published little of substance afterwards, and an unfinished later project alienated the New York society that had been his subject and his circle.

george_lucas.name: George Lucas
george_lucas.desc:
American filmmaker whose 1977 space adventure altered the economics and the storytelling assumptions of commercial cinema more than any other single release.

He assembled it from serials, samurai films, Westerns, war pictures and comparative mythology, and has said that Campbell's account of the hero pattern helped him organise material he had already been drafting. The chronology of when the book entered the process is disputed by scholars working from the surviving scripts.

His retained merchandising and sequel rights, conceded by a studio that expected little, are the origin of the modern franchise.

wu_chengen.name: Wu Cheng'en
wu_chengen.desc:
Chinese writer of the Ming dynasty (c. 1500-1582), traditionally named as the author of Journey to the West.

The attribution is not secure. The novel was published anonymously in 1592, a decade after his death, and his name was attached to it by scholars in the twentieth century on the strength of a provincial gazetteer listing a work of that title among his writings. Some scholars accept it, others hold that the novel is a compilation with no single author.

What is not disputed is that the material had been developing in oral, dramatic and written form for four centuries before the novel fixed it.

ferdowsi.name: Ferdowsi
ferdowsi.desc:
Persian poet (c. 940-1020) who spent some thirty years composing the Shahnameh, an epic of the Persian kings from the creation of the world to the Arab conquest.

He wrote at a moment when Persian was reasserting itself as a literary language after two centuries of Arabic dominance, and he used a notably low proportion of Arabic vocabulary. Later tradition credits him with preserving the language, a claim he makes for himself in the poem.

The stories of his relationship with his patron, and of a promised payment that arrived too late, are legend rather than record.

shahnameh.name: The Shahnameh
shahnameh.desc:
Ferdowsi's epic, completed around 1010, runs to some fifty thousand couplets and narrates the Persian past in three movements: a mythical age, a heroic age dominated by the warrior Rostam, and a historical section ending with the fall of the Sasanians.

Its most famous episode has Rostam kill a young champion in single combat and discover afterwards that the man was his own son, which is among the oldest and most widely distributed of tragic patterns.

The poem remains a living performance repertoire, recited in coffeehouses and public squares, and is central to Persian cultural identity in a way few national epics match.

art_spiegelman.name: Art Spiegelman
art_spiegelman.desc:
American cartoonist and editor, born in 1948 to Polish Jewish parents who survived Auschwitz, whose work established that comics could carry material the form had never been asked to hold.

He serialised Maus over eleven years in Raw, the avant-garde comics magazine he edited with Francoise Mouly, and it received a Pulitzer special award in 1992, the first for a comic.

His subject throughout is the difficulty of the telling as much as the events told, and the books repeatedly show him failing to draw what he is drawing.

maus.name: Maus
maus.desc:
Spiegelman's account of his father's survival of the Holocaust, serialised from 1980 and completed in 1991, draws Jews as mice and Germans as cats.

The device is not a softening. The species are worn like masks, characters put them on and take them off, and the metaphor is repeatedly shown to fail under pressure, which is part of the argument. Interleaved with the wartime narrative is the present-day story of a difficult son interviewing a difficult father.

It is the work most often cited to establish that the medium can hold historical testimony, and it declines to be consoling about its own success at doing so.

the_wire.name: The Wire
the_wire.desc:
An American television series of sixty episodes broadcast between 2002 and 2008, created by a former police reporter, which gives each of its five seasons to a different institution in one city: the drug trade, the docks, city politics, the schools and the press.

Its method is to follow a process rather than a protagonist, so that characters recur across years without being the subject, and to withhold the resolutions the form conventionally supplies.

Its creator has described the institutions as functioning like the gods of Greek tragedy, indifferent forces that individuals cannot successfully oppose, which is his framing rather than a critical consensus.

nanook.name: Nanook of the North
nanook.desc:
Robert Flaherty's film of 1922 follows an Inuk hunter and his family through a year in the Canadian Arctic, and is conventionally treated as the first feature-length documentary.

It is also the form's founding problem. Scenes were staged and directed, hunting methods already abandoned were revived for the camera, an igloo was built open-sided so the interior could be lit, and the family group was assembled rather than found. The man credited as Nanook was named Allakariallak.

Flaherty's defence, that one sometimes has to distort a thing to catch its true spirit, is the argument every subsequent documentary has had to make or refuse.

war_of_the_worlds_broadcast.name: The War of the Worlds (radio)
war_of_the_worlds_broadcast.desc:
The Mercury Theatre's radio adaptation of the Wells novel, broadcast on the evening before Halloween in 1938, presented the invasion as a sequence of interrupted music programmes and live news bulletins from New Jersey.

The technique was the innovation: fiction wearing the exact format of reportage, complete with an on-scene reporter, an official statement and a silence where the transmission fails.

The mass panic it is said to have caused was overstated at the time by newspapers with an interest in discrediting radio as a news medium, and later research suggests the audience was small and the alarm limited.

aoi_no_ue.name: Aoi no Ue
aoi_no_ue.desc:
A noh play taking an episode from the Tale of Genji, in which the jealousy of an abandoned noblewoman leaves her body as a living spirit and attacks Genji's pregnant wife.

The staging is characteristic of the form's compression: the sick woman is represented by a folded robe laid on the stage floor and is never seen, and the entire drama is the spirit's appearance, her account of her humiliation, and her subduing by an exorcist.

It is among the most performed plays in the repertoire and among the clearest demonstrations of what noh does with a long prose source.

kanjincho.name: Kanjinchō
kanjincho.desc:
A kabuki play first staged in 1840, adapted from the noh play Ataka, in which a fugitive lord and his retainers attempt to pass a barrier disguised as travelling monks.

Its central scene has the retainer Benkei improvise a subscription list from a blank scroll under interrogation, and then beat his own disguised master to maintain the deception, an act the barrier keeper recognises for what it is and allows to pass.

It belongs to a category of kabuki pieces performed with a painted pine backdrop in imitation of the noh stage, and it is among the form's most celebrated vehicles for a leading actor.

chunhyangga.name: Chunhyangga
chunhyangga.desc:
The best known of the five surviving pansori works, telling of the daughter of a former courtesan who secretly marries the son of a magistrate, and is imprisoned and tortured by his successor for refusing him.

A full performance runs for several hours and is delivered by one singer with a single drummer, moving between sung passages, spoken narration and every character's voice.

The story circulates in Korea as prose fiction, film, television and stage as well as in performance, and its heroine functions as a national figure in a way that has been read politically since the colonial period.

robert_flaherty.name: Robert Flaherty
robert_flaherty.desc:
American filmmaker (1884-1951) who worked as a prospector and surveyor in the Canadian north before turning to film, and whose first feature is generally treated as the beginning of documentary.

His method was to live for long periods with the people he filmed, to show them the footage, and to restage what he judged characteristic of a way of life he believed was disappearing. That combination of long acquaintance and open direction is what makes his work both the form's founding achievement and its founding argument.

He worked the same way in Samoa and the Aran Islands, with the same objections following each time.

francis_james_child.name: Francis James Child
francis_james_child.desc:
American philologist (1825-1896), professor at Harvard, whose collection of English and Scottish popular ballads is the standard reference for the form.

He assembled it over decades from manuscripts, broadsides and earlier collections rather than from singers, printing every variant he could find under a numbered heading, so that a ballad appears as a family of versions with no authoritative text among them.

The numbering he devised is still how the ballads are identified, and singers who have never read him describe their repertoire by his numbers.

child_ballads.name: The Child Ballads
child_ballads.desc:
Child's collection, published in five volumes between 1882 and 1898, gathers three hundred and five traditional English and Scottish ballads together with every variant text he could locate.

The method is the achievement. Because the versions are printed side by side rather than merged, the collection shows a ballad as a process: the same murder, the same drowned sister, the same returning lover, told with different names, different regions and different endings.

It has functioned since as a working repertoire as much as a scholarly one, and the twentieth-century folk revival drew on it directly.

oscar_hammerstein.name: Oscar Hammerstein II
oscar_hammerstein.desc:
American librettist and lyricist (1895-1960) who did more than anyone to make the musical a dramatic form rather than a revue with a plot attached.

His 1927 collaboration on Show Boat took a serious subject and gave the songs narrative work to do, and his partnership with Richard Rodgers from 1943 established the pattern the form has followed since: numbers that advance the action, characters who sing because speech has run out, and a book strong enough to survive without the score.

He also took subjects the commercial theatre avoided, including racial prejudice, in shows that were nonetheless enormously popular.

oklahoma_musical.name: Oklahoma!
oklahoma_musical.desc:
The 1943 Rodgers and Hammerstein musical, adapted from a play about farmers and cowhands in the Oklahoma territory, is conventionally treated as the point at which the integrated book musical arrived.

It opens not with a chorus line but with a woman churning butter and a man singing offstage, and its numbers carry plot and character rather than interrupting for them. A long dream ballet stages the heroine's fear of the farmhand pursuing her, which is material the dialogue never states.

It ran for over two thousand performances and reset what a Broadway audience expected a musical to be.

community_series.name: Community
community_series.desc:
An American situation comedy created by Dan Harmon, broadcast from 2009, set among a study group at a failing community college.

Harmon wrote and taught his eight-step story circle during the show's production, and episodes are built on it, including the ones that abandon the format entirely for a western, a documentary parody or an animated episode. The structure is what allows the parodies to work as stories rather than as sketches.

Its characters also fail to develop in the way the form requires, and several episodes make that constraint their subject.

disco_elysium.name: Disco Elysium
disco_elysium.desc:
A 2019 video game in which a detective with no memory investigates a hanging in a strike-bound coastal city, and which contains no combat at all.

Its distinctive move is to turn the character sheet into a cast: two dozen skills speak to the protagonist as separate voices, arguing, lying and interrupting, so that a statistic in another game becomes a personality here. Failure is not a dead end, and a failed check frequently opens material a success would have closed.

It is among the strongest arguments that the medium's narrative resources are its own rather than borrowed from film.

george_orwell.name: George Orwell
george_orwell.desc:
English writer (1903-1950), born Eric Blair, who worked as a colonial policeman in Burma, fought in the Spanish Civil War and reported on poverty in Britain before the two late fictions that made his name a common adjective.

His essays argue for a prose stripped of received phrasing on political grounds, holding that stale language conceals bad thinking and makes atrocity easier to write about, a position his fiction acts on.

He wrote his last novel while seriously ill on Jura and died two years after finishing it.

nineteen_eighty_four.name: Nineteen Eighty-Four
nineteen_eighty_four.desc:
Orwell's novel of 1949 follows a minor functionary who edits the historical record for a state that has abolished the past, and who is broken for attempting a private life.

Its durable contribution is a vocabulary. Doublethink, thoughtcrime, unperson, memory hole and Newspeak have all entered general use, and the appendix on Newspeak argues that constraining a language constrains what can be thought in it.

Its ending refuses the consolation the form usually supplies: the protagonist is not martyred but converted, and the book closes with him loving the authority that destroyed him.

lazarillo.name: Lazarillo de Tormes
lazarillo.desc:
An anonymous Spanish novella published in 1554, narrated by a boy who serves a succession of masters, each of whom he describes with an eye trained by hunger.

The masters are the point: a blind beggar who teaches him cruelty, a priest who starves him, a squire with no money and impeccable manners who must be fed by his own servant. The book ends with Lazaro contentedly employed in an arrangement he takes care not to examine.

It established the picaresque and was placed on the Spanish Index in 1559, which is a reasonable indication of how its clergy were received.

george_eliot.name: George Eliot
george_eliot.desc:
English novelist (1819-1880), born Mary Ann Evans, who worked as an editor and translator of German biblical criticism before turning to fiction under a name adopted to keep her work from being read as a woman's.

Her subject is the moral consequence of ordinary choices in provincial communities, examined with an analytic seriousness the English novel had not previously brought to unremarkable people, and her narrators reason with the reader rather than merely reporting.

She lived for over twenty years with a man who could not obtain a divorce, at considerable social cost.

middlemarch.name: Middlemarch
middlemarch.desc:
Eliot's novel, published in eight parts across 1871 and 1872, follows several linked households in a Midlands town in the years before the first Reform Act.

Its method is to give every character the dignity of an interior case, including the ones the plot requires the reader to judge, and to trace how a marriage, a debt or a piece of local gossip alters a life without anyone deciding that it should.

Its closing sentences make the argument explicit, attributing the improvement of the world largely to people who lived faithfully and are now in unvisited tombs.

harriet_beecher_stowe.name: Harriet Beecher Stowe
harriet_beecher_stowe.desc:
American writer (1811-1896) from a prominent New England religious family, whose antislavery novel is generally described as the best-selling American book of its century after the Bible.

She wrote it in serial parts for an abolitionist paper, drawing on the accounts of formerly enslaved people and on the Fugitive Slave Act's requirement that northerners assist in returning them, and she published a documentary volume of sources afterwards in response to accusations of invention.

Her reputation has been argued over continuously since, with her sentimental method credited both with mobilising opinion and with fixing damaging types.

uncle_toms_cabin.name: Uncle Tom's Cabin
uncle_toms_cabin.desc:
Stowe's antislavery novel, serialised from 1851 and published as a book in 1852, sold in unprecedented numbers and was adapted for the stage in hundreds of unauthorised productions that reached audiences far larger than the book's.

Its machinery is melodramatic throughout: the innocent under threat, the pursuit across ice, the deathbed, the unambiguous villain, and a moral scheme in which suffering redeems.

The stage versions coarsened its figures into types that outlived the novel's arguments, and the title character's name became an insult. James Baldwin's 1949 essay attacking its sentimentality is the standard case against it.

thomas_malory.name: Thomas Malory
thomas_malory.desc:
English writer of the fifteenth century, most probably a Warwickshire knight imprisoned repeatedly on charges including robbery and assault, who compiled the Arthurian cycle in English while in custody.

He worked from the French prose romances and from English sources, translating, cutting and reordering rather than inventing, and produced a single continuous narrative out of material that had accumulated over three centuries in several languages.

He asks at the end of the book for prayers for his deliverance, which is the main evidence for the identification.

le_morte_darthur.name: Le Morte d'Arthur
le_morte_darthur.desc:
Malory's compilation, completed around 1470 and printed by Caxton in 1485, is the version through which Arthurian material reached the English-speaking world.

It runs from the begetting of Arthur to the collapse of the fellowship, and its second half is a study in how an order destroys itself: the grail quest that reveals most of the knights to be unworthy, the affair that cannot be ignored once it is spoken of, and the war that follows.

Its prose is spare and its dialogue abrupt, and almost every later English treatment of the legend works from it.

john_ford.name: John Ford
john_ford.desc:
American film director (1894-1973) whose work defined the Western for audiences worldwide and then spent decades interrogating it.

His compositions place small figures against enormous landscape, and his recurring subject is the community that a violent man secures and cannot join. He returned repeatedly to Monument Valley, which his films have made stand for the American frontier generally despite being a specific and unrepresentative place.

His late work reopens the settlement his earlier films celebrated, including its treatment of the people already living on the land.

the_searchers.name: The Searchers
the_searchers.desc:
Ford's film of 1956 follows a Confederate veteran across five years as he hunts for a niece taken by Comanche raiders, with the growing suspicion that he intends to kill her for having lived among them.

The film is built around a protagonist whose competence the story depends on and whose racial hatred it refuses to excuse, and it never resolves the tension between the two.

Its closing image, the man framed in a doorway as the family goes inside without him, is among the most quoted in cinema and states the genre's central problem without a line of dialogue.

the_winters_tale.name: The Winter's Tale
the_winters_tale.desc:
Shakespeare's late play, written around 1611, spends three acts on a king's sudden and unfounded jealousy, which kills his son, apparently kills his wife and results in his daughter being abandoned on a foreign shore.

The play then jumps sixteen years, changes country and register, and spends two acts in pastoral comedy before returning for a final scene in which a statue of the dead queen is revealed to be alive.

Nothing in either genre's rules accommodates the manoeuvre, and the play contains the most quoted stage direction in English, sending a character off pursued by a bear.

the_frogs.name: The Frogs
the_frogs.desc:
Aristophanes' comedy of 405 BCE sends Dionysus to the underworld to bring back a tragedian capable of saving Athens, which is losing a war it will lose within the year.

The second half is a formal contest between Aeschylus and Euripides, who weigh each other's prologues, quote each other's lyrics and finally put their verses on a literal balance. It is often described as the earliest surviving sustained work of literary criticism in any form, and it is conducted as a joke.

Aeschylus wins and is taken back to the living, which is a verdict on the drama and on the city at once.

egils_saga.name: Egil's Saga
egils_saga.desc:
An Icelandic saga of the thirteenth century, sometimes attributed to Snorri Sturluson, narrating the life of the poet and warrior Egill Skallagrimsson across the tenth.

Its subject is unusual for the form: a man who is monstrous, greedy and violent from childhood, and who is also the finest poet of his generation, with several of his compositions quoted in the prose as evidence.

The most affecting of them is a lament for a drowned son, which the saga presents as the thing that stopped him starving himself to death, so the poem is given a function within the narrative as well as a text.

wedding_of_meho.name: The Wedding of Smailagić Meho
wedding_of_meho.desc:
An oral epic performed by the Bosnian singer Avdo Mededovic and recorded by Milman Parry in 1935, running to some twelve thousand lines, a scale comparable with the Odyssey.

It was produced in performance over several days rather than recited from memory, and Parry also recorded Mededovic performing a song he had heard once, days earlier, from another singer, at several times its original length.

The recordings are the central evidence that a poem of Homeric dimensions can be composed without writing, and they are held with the rest of the Parry collection at Harvard.

julia_kristeva.name: Julia Kristeva
julia_kristeva.desc:
Bulgarian-French theorist and psychoanalyst, born in 1941, who arrived in Paris in the mid-1960s and introduced Bakhtin's work to a French readership that had not encountered it.

In doing so she coined intertextuality, describing a text as a mosaic of quotations built from the absorption and transformation of others, which detaches the idea from any question of what an author had read.

Her later work moved into psychoanalysis and into the study of abjection, and her account of the semiotic as a pre-linguistic register underlying symbolic language has been widely taken up in literary criticism.

stanislavski.name: Konstantin Stanislavski
stanislavski.desc:
Russian actor and director (1863-1938), co-founder of the Moscow Art Theatre, whose system for training performers is the basis of most naturalistic acting instruction since.

His method asks an actor to work from the character's objective in each unit of a scene, from the given circumstances surrounding it, and from what is meant rather than said, which makes it a practical technique for playing text that withholds its own subject.

His productions of Chekhov are what established those plays, and the collaboration between a dramatist writing under the surface and a company trained to play there is the clearest case of theory and practice arriving together.

ann_radcliffe.name: Ann Radcliffe
ann_radcliffe.desc:
English novelist (1764-1823) and among the most popular and best-paid novelists of the 1790s, whose Gothic romances established the mode's atmospheric method.

Her distinctive practice is the explained supernatural: apparitions, music from nowhere and figures behind curtains are supplied and then given natural causes, so the reader's fear is aroused and afterwards accounted for.

An essay published after her death distinguishes terror, which expands the soul by uncertainty and obscurity, from horror, which contracts it by making the object plain. The distinction still organises discussion of the genre.

david_simon.name: David Simon
david_simon.desc:
American writer and television producer, born in 1960, who spent thirteen years as a police reporter on the Baltimore Sun before taking a year's leave to sit with a homicide unit and write a book about it.

His method transferred directly to television: institutions observed at length from inside, procedure treated as inherently dramatic, and dialogue built from how people in a particular trade actually speak to each other.

He has been consistently hostile to the idea that his work offers solutions, describing it instead as an argument about what institutions do to the people inside them.

avdo_mededovic.name: Avdo Međedović
avdo_mededovic.desc:
Bosniak epic singer (c. 1875-1953) from Bijelo Polje in Montenegro, a farmer and butcher who could neither read nor write, and the most accomplished performer recorded in the Parry and Lord fieldwork.

His repertoire ran to dozens of songs and his performances to lengths no other singer approached. Asked to perform a song he had heard once, days earlier, from another singer, he produced a version several times longer than the original, elaborated rather than remembered.

He is the specific human evidence that a poem of Homeric scale can be composed without writing.

prodigal_son.name: The Prodigal Son
prodigal_son.desc:
A parable in the gospel of Luke in which a younger son takes his inheritance early, spends it, returns destitute intending to ask for work, and is met by a father who celebrates before he can finish his prepared speech.

The story does not end there. An elder son who stayed and worked refuses to come in, and the parable closes on the father outside with him, arguing, with nothing resolved.

No application is supplied and none of the figures is labelled, which is what makes it the form's clearest example: the listener has to decide which son they are.

storytelling.name: Storytelling
storytelling.desc:
The practice of relating events, real or invented, in a sequence that makes them mean something to a listener, reader or viewer.

It is older than writing and independent of any particular medium: the same story can be sung, spoken, printed, filmed or played. What travels between media is a structure of events, agents and consequences; what changes is who controls the pace, what can be shown and what must be inferred, and how much the audience can answer back.

Across cultures it has served to preserve knowledge, transmit law and belief, bind groups, teach children, entertain, and argue. Every element in this graph, from the smallest device to the largest tradition, is one answer to the question of how it is done.

plot.name: Plot
plot.desc:
The arrangement of events in a narrative, considered as a causal and emotional design, not as a simple list of what happened.

Aristotle called it mythos and ranked it first among the parts of tragedy, arguing that the incidents should follow by probability or necessity so that removing one would disturb the whole. Forster made the same distinction with his example of a king's death followed by a queen's: sequence alone gives a story, and the addition of cause gives a plot.

Competing traditions dispute its primacy. Character-centred teaching holds that plot should emerge from who the people are rather than being imposed upon them.

character.name: Character
character.desc:
The agents of a narrative, and by extension the methods by which an audience is given a sense of who they are.

Aristotle subordinated character to plot, holding that people are shown through what they choose to do. Later traditions reversed the emphasis: Egri began from character and derived plot from it, and the nineteenth-century novel developed elaborate means of interior access. Forster's distinction between flat characters, built from one idea, and round ones, capable of convincing surprise, remains the standard shorthand.

Structuralists went the other way again, treating characters as positions in a system, as in Propp's spheres of action and Greimas's actants.

setting.name: Setting
setting.desc:
The time and place in which a narrative occurs, together with the social and physical conditions that come with them.

Setting is rarely inert. It supplies the constraints that make action difficult, carries information about the people who live in it, and often determines what kind of story can be told at all, since the possibilities of a Heian court, a whaling ship and a colonised village differ in kind rather than degree.

Bakhtin's chronotope names the deeper version of this observation: that particular genres bind specific configurations of time and space, and that the road, the castle and the provincial town each generate their own sort of plot.

theme.name: Theme
theme.desc:
The idea or question a narrative pursues beneath its events, distinct from both its subject and its moral.

Theme is usually inferred, not stated, and is expressed through what the story chooses to test: which choices are given weight, which are punished, what the ending treats as a resolution. Craft teachers differ sharply on whether it should be settled before writing, as in Egri's premise, or discovered in revision.

A narrative can hold competing themes without resolving them, and readers may reasonably disagree about which the text supports; this indeterminacy is one of the things that distinguishes literature from argument.

conflict.name: Conflict
conflict.desc:
The opposition between what a character wants and what stands in the way, treated in most Western craft teaching as the engine of narrative.

The standard classroom taxonomy sets a protagonist against another person, against nature, against society, against fate or against themselves. Structural models generally assume it: the actantial model builds in an opponent, and the three-act shape depends on escalating obstruction.

Its universality has been questioned. Four-part structures such as kishotenketsu generate movement from juxtaposition, not opposition, and Le Guin's carrier bag essay argued that the identification of story with conflict is a cultural preference rather than a necessity.

fabula_syuzhet.name: Fabula and Syuzhet
fabula_syuzhet.desc:
The Russian Formalist distinction between the raw material of a story and the shaped form in which it is presented.

Fabula is the events in their chronological and causal order, reconstructed by the reader; syuzhet is the order and manner of their telling, including everything withheld, reordered, repeated or skipped. A detective novel makes the gap between them its whole method, since the fabula is complete before the syuzhet begins.

The pair reappears throughout narratology under other names: story and discourse in Chatman, histoire and recit in Genette, and, in a rougher form, Forster's contrast between story and plot.

mimesis.name: Mimesis
mimesis.desc:
Imitation or representation, the Greek term at the centre of ancient thinking about art.

Plato treated it with suspicion, arguing that art copies appearances and stands at a remove from truth; Aristotle took it as the natural human faculty from which poetry arises, and defined tragedy as the mimesis of an action. In later narratology the term is often paired with diegesis to distinguish scenic presentation, in which events seem to unfold before the audience, from summary narration.

Erich Auerbach's Mimesis, published in 1946, traced how European literature represented reality, from Homer and the Hebrew Bible to Woolf.

diegesis.name: Diegesis
diegesis.desc:
The narrated world of a story, and, in a related classical sense, the act of telling as opposed to showing.

Genette used the term to organise narrative levels: an extradiegetic narrator tells a story from outside it, an intradiegetic narrator is a character within that story who tells another, and events can be embedded several layers deep, as in One Thousand and One Nights. Film criticism uses the word for the boundary of the story world, distinguishing diegetic sound, which the characters can hear, from non-diegetic score and voice-over.

Crossing that boundary deliberately is called metalepsis, and produces the effects of metafiction.

narrator.name: Narrator
narrator.desc:
The agent that tells a narrative, distinct both from the author who wrote it and from any character it may also be.

Narrators differ in person, in how much they know, in how far they are involved in events, and in how much they intrude with commentary. Booth argued that even an apparently absent narrator makes constant rhetorical choices, and that behind every narrator the reader assembles an implied author, the version of the writer the text creates.

Where the narrator's account cannot be taken at face value, the reader must reconstruct events from it, which is the condition Booth named unreliable narration.

point_of_view.name: Point of View
point_of_view.desc:
The position from which a narrative is presented: first person, second, or third, and within third person the degree of access to characters' minds.

The choice governs what can be known and when, and therefore what suspense and irony are available. Henry James developed the practice of filtering a whole novel through one character's perception, which he called a centre of consciousness, and the technique became a standard of modern fiction.

Genette argued that the traditional term conflates two questions that should be separated, who speaks and who perceives, and proposed focalization for the second.

focalization.name: Focalization
focalization.desc:
Genette's term for the perspective through which narrative information is filtered, introduced to separate the question of who sees from the question of who speaks.

He distinguished zero focalization, where the narration is not restricted to any character's knowledge, internal focalization, where it is limited to what one character perceives and knows, and external focalization, where behaviour is reported without access to any interior.

The distinction resolves cases that point of view handles awkwardly, such as a first-person narrator recalling their younger self, where one person speaks and a different, earlier version of them sees.

catharsis.name: Catharsis
catharsis.desc:
The effect Aristotle attributed to tragedy: through pity and fear it accomplishes the catharsis of such emotions.

The sentence is brief, occurs once in the definition of tragedy, and is not explained further in the surviving text, which is why it has been argued over for centuries. Readings include purgation, a medical discharge of excess feeling; purification, a moral tempering; and clarification, an intellectual sorting of when pity and fear are properly felt.

The word carries all three senses in Greek. Any confident modern account of what Aristotle meant is an interpretation rather than a reading of the text.

hamartia.name: Hamartia
hamartia.desc:
The term in Aristotle's Poetics for the thing that brings the tragic protagonist to disaster, from a Greek verb meaning to miss the mark.

It is very often translated as tragic flaw, but many classicists argue that error or mistake is closer, and that Aristotle's point is precisely that the figure is neither wicked nor blameless: catastrophe follows from a misjudgement, not from vice, which is what makes pity and fear appropriate.

Oedipus, who acts on incomplete knowledge, is the case Aristotle returns to. Later criticism, particularly on Shakespeare, hardened the term into a defect of character.

peripeteia.name: Peripeteia
peripeteia.desc:
Reversal: in Aristotle's account, a change in which an action produces the opposite of what was intended.

He distinguishes it from a mere change of fortune. The messenger who comes to relieve Oedipus of his fear about his parentage is his example, since the reassurance is exactly what destroys the king. Aristotle held that the finest plots are complex, meaning that they turn on reversal and recognition, and that the two are strongest when they arrive together.

The idea survives in every modern discussion of the turn, the reversal or the plot point, though usually without the requirement of ironic self-defeat.

anagnorisis.name: Anagnorisis
anagnorisis.desc:
Recognition: the movement from ignorance to knowledge, in Aristotle's account, especially concerning identity and especially between people whose relationship determines the action.

He ranked the kinds, preferring recognition that arises from the events themselves over recognition produced by tokens, birthmarks or contrivance. Oedipus discovering what he has done is the paradigm, and Aristotle prized it because reversal and recognition coincide there.

The device is not confined to tragedy. Comedy and romance turn constantly on the revealed identity of a foundling or a disguised lover, and the detective story's closing explanation is a direct descendant.

suspension_of_disbelief.name: Suspension of Disbelief
suspension_of_disbelief.desc:
The audience's willingness to accept, for the duration of a work, premises they know to be untrue.

The phrase comes from Coleridge's Biographia Literaria of 1817, where he describes the aim of his contribution to Lyrical Ballads as procuring for supernatural subjects a willing suspension of disbelief for the moment, which he calls poetic faith.

Craft writing usually treats it as a contract with rules: an audience will grant a large initial improbability, a talking animal or a faster-than-light drive, but will not forgive a later inconsistency within it. Internal coherence, rather than realism, is what sustains it.

chronotope.name: Chronotope
chronotope.desc:
Bakhtin's term, borrowed from the language of physics and meaning time-space, for the way a genre binds temporal and spatial relationships into a single configuration.

His argument is that time and place are not separable settings but a joint structure that determines what kind of events and people a work can contain. The road produces chance meetings between strangers of any class; the ancient adventure novel unfolds in an empty time in which nobody ages; the idyll ties generations to one small patch of ground.

The concept has been widely applied outside literary study, in geography, anthropology and film analysis.

polyphony.name: Polyphony and Dialogism
polyphony.desc:
Bakhtin's account of the novel as a meeting of independent consciousnesses, not the expression of a single authorial view.

In his study of Dostoevsky he argued that those novels are polyphonic: the characters' ideas are given full argumentative force and are not overruled by the narrator, so the work stages a genuinely unresolved debate. Dialogism extends the claim to language itself, since every utterance answers previous utterances and anticipates a reply.

Heteroglossia names the social stratification of language a novel can hold, the professional, regional and generational idioms that the form is uniquely able to set against one another.

defamiliarization.name: Defamiliarization
defamiliarization.desc:
Shklovsky's principle, from the Russian ostranenie, that art exists to restore perception dulled by habit by presenting the familiar as if seen for the first time.

His examples include Tolstoy describing a flogging as a physical procedure without the word that normalises it, and a story narrated by a horse who does not understand property. The device lengthens and complicates perception, which for Shklovsky is the point: the difficulty is not an obstacle to the aesthetic effect but its substance.

Brecht's estrangement effect pursues a comparable disruption in the theatre, though with an explicitly political purpose.

rasa.name: Rasa
rasa.desc:
The central concept of Indian aesthetics, set out in the Natyashastra: the distilled emotional flavour that a performance produces in a prepared spectator.

Rasa is not the emotion of the character but its transformed aesthetic counterpart, arising when the underlying emotional state is combined with its causes, its physical expressions and its transitory accompaniments. The treatise enumerates eight, among them the erotic, comic, pathetic, furious, heroic and marvellous, and later commentators added a ninth, tranquillity.

The theory locates the work's completion in the audience's experience, which invites comparison with Aristotle on catharsis while resting on quite different premises.

subtext.name: Subtext
subtext.desc:
What a scene is about beneath what is said, carried by evasion, gesture, pauses and the choice of subject.

Dramatic writing since Chekhov and Ibsen has relied on the gap between the surface of conversation and the pressures underneath it, and the theatrical training traditions that followed built rehearsal methods around identifying what a character actually wants while saying something else.

It is a practical consequence of a broader principle: an audience that infers a meaning holds it more firmly than one that is told it. Explicit statement of what a scene has already shown is among the most common notes given on drafts.

world_building.name: World-Building
world_building.desc:
The construction of a coherent setting with its own geography, history, institutions, languages and rules, within which stories can be told.

Tolkien is the usual reference point for the practice in modern fiction, having built languages and mythologies long before the narratives that use them, and arguing in On Fairy-Stories that a secondary world commands belief through internal consistency rather than resemblance to this one.

The demands differ by medium. Games and shared universes need worlds that support many stories by many hands, which puts a premium on documented rules; a novel need only sustain the one story it tells.

georges_polti.name: Georges Polti
georges_polti.desc:
French writer whose Les Trente-six situations dramatiques, published in 1895, attempted to enumerate every dramatic situation available to a playwright.

Polti took the number from an assertion attributed to the eighteenth-century Venetian dramatist Carlo Gozzi, reported by Goethe and Schiller, that there are only thirty-six tragic situations. Polti set out to supply the list Gozzi never published, working through classical and modern drama and arriving at categories such as supplication, vengeance, rivalry of kin, and self-sacrifice for an ideal.

The book is best understood as a catalogue for invention, not a proof, and later plot taxonomies stand in the same tradition.

lajos_egri.name: Lajos Egri
lajos_egri.desc:
Hungarian-American writer and teacher (1888-1967) whose The Art of Dramatic Writing, published in 1946 as a revision of an earlier book, remains a standard text for dramatists.

Egri argued that a play begins with a premise, a short declarative proposition such as great love defies even death, which the action must then prove. From premise he derived character, insisting that figures be conceived in physiological, sociological and psychological dimensions, and that plot should grow out of what such people would do rather than being imposed on them.

His emphasis on character-driven causation runs counter to the Aristotelian priority of plot, and the disagreement is still live in writing instruction.

syd_field.name: Syd Field
syd_field.desc:
American screenwriter and teacher (1935-2013) whose Screenplay, published in 1979, gave Hollywood its most widely used working model of structure.

Field described the feature screenplay as a three-act paradigm with proportions attached: a setup, a longer confrontation, and a resolution, hinged by plot points at the ends of the first and second acts that turn the action in a new direction. He later added the midpoint and the pinches as further landmarks. Working from a standard of roughly one script page per screen minute, the model translates into page numbers a reader can check.

Critics argue it describes conventional commercial films instead of storytelling as such.

robert_mckee.name: Robert McKee
robert_mckee.desc:
American screenwriting lecturer, born in 1941, whose Story Seminar has been taught to very large numbers of writers since the 1980s and whose book Story appeared in 1997.

His account centres on the scene as the unit of construction, each turning on a value that shifts from positive to negative or back, and on the gap between what a character expects from an action and what the world actually returns, which forces the next choice. He distinguishes classical design from minimalist and anti-structural alternatives rather than treating the classical shape as the only option.

He was portrayed, with his permission, as a character in the 2002 film Adaptation.

christopher_vogler.name: Christopher Vogler
christopher_vogler.desc:
American story consultant, born in 1949, who translated Campbell's monomyth into a working tool for film development.

While reading scripts for Disney in the 1980s he circulated a short memo summarising The Hero with a Thousand Faces as a practical guide for screenwriters; it spread through the industry in photocopy before he expanded it into The Writer's Journey, published in 1992. His version reduces Campbell's many stages to twelve, and recasts Jungian archetypes as flexible functions a character can take up and put down, among them mentor, threshold guardian, herald, shapeshifter, shadow and trickster.

The book is a principal route by which Campbell reached commercial screenwriting.

blake_snyder.name: Blake Snyder
blake_snyder.desc:
American screenwriter (1957-2009) whose Save the Cat, published in 2005, set out a fifteen-beat sheet with page numbers attached, from opening image through catalyst, debate, break into two, midpoint, all is lost and dark night of the soul to the finale and closing image.

The title refers to his advice that a protagonist do something likeable early on so the audience will follow them. He also proposed that films fall into a small number of story categories, such as golden fleece, dude with a problem, and monster in the house, cutting across conventional genre labels.

The beat sheet's reach into film and publishing has drawn criticism for homogenising structure.

christopher_booker.name: Christopher Booker
christopher_booker.desc:
British journalist (1937-2019) whose The Seven Basic Plots, published in 2004, argued that stories across cultures resolve into seven shapes: overcoming the monster, rags to riches, the quest, voyage and return, comedy, tragedy and rebirth.

Booker said the book occupied him for more than three decades. Its second half turns from taxonomy to argument, contending that modern storytelling has lost its way by departing from these patterns, a normative claim reviewers treated far more sceptically than the taxonomy itself.

The scheme owes an acknowledged debt to Jungian psychology, and sits alongside earlier attempts by Polti and others to count the plots.

john_yorke.name: John Yorke
john_yorke.desc:
British television producer and executive, born in 1962, who has run drama for the BBC and Channel 4 and founded the BBC Writers Academy.

His book Into the Woods, published in 2013, surveys the competing structural models and argues that the familiar three-act shape is better understood as five acts, with the second act divided by a midpoint reversal into two movements. He grounds the argument in classical drama, in television practice where act breaks are dictated by transmission, and in an account of change as the thing all stories describe.

Writing from inside a commissioning organisation gives the book an unusual amount of practical detail about how episodes are actually built.

william_goldman.name: William Goldman
william_goldman.desc:
American novelist and screenwriter (1931-2018), the writer of Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid, All the President's Men and The Princess Bride, in both novel and screenplay form.

His memoir Adventures in the Screen Trade, published in 1983, is a candid account of how films are actually made, and supplied the industry's most repeated line, that nobody knows anything, meaning that no one can reliably predict what will succeed. He also argued that screenwriting is structure, and that a scene should be entered as late as possible and left as early as possible.

He was much used as a script doctor, often uncredited.

dan_harmon.name: Dan Harmon
dan_harmon.desc:
American television writer, born in 1973, the creator of Community and co-creator of Rick and Morty.

While running the short-film venue Channel 101 he set out a simplified version of Campbell's pattern as an eight-step circle: a character in a comfortable situation wants something, enters an unfamiliar world, adapts, gets what they wanted, pays a price, and returns changed. He published it on his own blog and in a series of articles, and it has since been widely adopted by television writers who found Campbell's stages too many and too mythological.

He has described it explicitly as a tool for generating and diagnosing episodes, not a theory of myth.

enheduanna.name: Enheduanna
enheduanna.desc:
Akkadian priestess of the twenty-third century BCE, daughter of Sargon of Akkad and high priestess of the moon god at Ur, and the earliest author anywhere whose name is attached to surviving work.

Her compositions are hymns rather than narratives, but one of them tells a story about its own making: a priestess driven from her temple in a rebellion, appealing to the goddess Inanna, and recovering her office through the power of the poem she is composing.

Some scholars question whether the attribution reflects authorship in the modern sense or a traditional ascription, and the texts survive in copies made centuries later.

exaltation_of_inanna.name: The Exaltation of Inanna
exaltation_of_inanna.desc:
A Sumerian hymn of some hundred and fifty lines attributed to Enheduanna, surviving in dozens of later scribal copies, in which the speaker praises the goddess Inanna and asks to be restored to the office she has lost.

Its unusual feature is self-reference. The poem names its author, describes her circumstances, and treats the act of composition as the instrument of her restoration, so a work of praise doubles as an account of its own occasion.

It is among the earliest surviving texts in which a first-person voice claims a specific identity rather than speaking for a community.

angela_carter.name: Angela Carter
angela_carter.desc:
English writer (1940-1992) whose fiction combined the fairy tale, the Gothic and the picaresque with a materialist analysis of what those forms carry.

She was explicit that she was not retelling tales but extracting what she called their latent content, and she objected to being described as gentling them. Her versions frequently give the woman the appetite, the agency or the transformation the source reserved for someone else.

She also translated Perrault, edited two collections of folk tales gathered from around the world, and wrote radio drama, journalism and a study of the Marquis de Sade.

the_bloody_chamber.name: The Bloody Chamber
the_bloody_chamber.desc:
Carter's collection of 1979 works ten tales out of familiar material, including three separate treatments of Beauty and the Beast and two of Little Red Riding Hood.

The title story is Bluebeard, narrated by the bride, and it replaces the rescuing brothers with the girl's mother arriving on horseback with a revolver. Elsewhere the beast is not transformed into a man and the girl becomes an animal instead, or the wolf is got into bed with rather than escaped.

Carter's stated intention was to open the tales up rather than to soften them, and the prose is deliberately ornate against a tradition of plainness.

marina_warner.name: Marina Warner
marina_warner.desc:
English historian and critic, born in 1946, whose work on fairy tale, myth and the figures cultures build out of women is the fullest account of the form's social history.

Her study of the fairy tale traces who actually told and wrote these stories, recovering the salon writers of seventeenth-century France, the nurses and servants who carried the oral material, and the persistent figure of the old woman as narrator that the printed collections both invoke and erase.

She also writes on the Arabian Nights, on scripture and on the visual iconography of allegorical figures.

zora_neale_hurston.name: Zora Neale Hurston
zora_neale_hurston.desc:
American writer and anthropologist (1891-1960) who trained under Franz Boas at Columbia and returned to the South to collect the folklore she had grown up inside.

Her position was unusual and productive: a fieldworker recording a tradition she belonged to, and a novelist whose fiction uses that material as narrative resource rather than as local colour. She wrote dialogue in the speech of her subjects at a time when contemporaries argued that doing so was a concession to caricature.

She died in poverty and was buried in an unmarked grave, and her work was recovered from near-oblivion in the 1970s.

mules_and_men.name: Mules and Men
mules_and_men.desc:
Hurston's collection of 1935 gathers African American folk tales recorded in Florida sawmill camps and in Louisiana, and presents them inside an account of the collecting.

The frame is the innovation. Rather than printing tales as specimens, she narrates the porch conversations, the competition between tellers, the interruptions and the reasons a story is produced at a particular moment, so the reader gets the performance situation as well as the text.

It is among the earliest substantial folklore collections made by someone gathering their own community's material.

octavia_butler.name: Octavia Butler
octavia_butler.desc:
American science fiction writer (1947-2006) whose work is preoccupied with power, hierarchy and the compromises available to people who have none.
