Her premises are unsentimental about their own implications: an unwilling time traveller who must keep a slaveholder alive to be born, a species that trades genetic material for survival on terms humans cannot refuse, a religion built from scratch by a teenager in a collapsing state.

She was the first science fiction writer awarded a MacArthur fellowship, and worked for years in menial jobs while writing before dawn.

kindred.name: Kindred
kindred.desc:
Butler's novel of 1979 pulls a Black woman from California in 1976 repeatedly back to a Maryland plantation in the early nineteenth century, where she must keep a white boy alive because he is her ancestor.

The device removes the distance that historical fiction usually supplies. The protagonist arrives with a modern person's reflexes and finds them useless, and the novel's subject is how quickly the accommodations required to survive begin to feel ordinary.

Butler described it as a grim fantasy rather than science fiction, on the grounds that it contains no science and offers no explanation for the mechanism.

hilary_mantel.name: Hilary Mantel
hilary_mantel.desc:
English novelist (1952-2022) whose trilogy about Thomas Cromwell reset expectations for what historical fiction could attempt.

Her method is a close third person in the present tense, so the reader occupies a man who does not know how his story ends, and the familiar events arrive as contingencies rather than as history. The prose withholds the retrospective knowledge every reader brings.

She wrote and lectured on the form directly, arguing that a novelist's obligation is to the shape of the evidence and that the gaps in the record are where fiction is permitted to work.

wolf_hall.name: Wolf Hall
wolf_hall.desc:
Mantel's novel of 2009 covers the years of Henry VIII's first divorce from inside the household and mind of Thomas Cromwell, a blacksmith's son who rose to run the country.

It reverses the received arrangement of the period, in which Cromwell is the calculating villain and Thomas More the man of conscience, without arguing the case directly: the reader is simply placed behind one pair of eyes and left there.

The present tense and the persistent unattributed pronoun are the technical means, and both were widely imitated afterwards.

maxine_hong_kingston.name: Maxine Hong Kingston
maxine_hong_kingston.desc:
American writer, born in 1940 to Chinese immigrant parents in California, whose first book made the boundary between memoir and myth a formal problem rather than a lapse.

She uses the word talk-story, from the Cantonese practice her mother worked in, for a mode in which family history, cautionary tale, legend and outright invention arrive in the same telling with no marker separating them.

Her books have been argued over on exactly that ground, with critics disputing whether her reworking of Chinese legendary material for an American readership is transmission or distortion.

the_woman_warrior.name: The Woman Warrior
the_woman_warrior.desc:
Kingston's book of 1976 is subtitled a memoir of a girlhood among ghosts and consists of five linked accounts, of which one is a first-person retelling of the legend of the woman who took her father's place in the army.

The reader is never told which material is remembered, which is inherited and which is invented, and the opening instruction not to repeat what follows is itself immediately disobeyed by the book containing it.

It is among the most taught works in American universities and among the most contested, on the question of what a writer owes a tradition they are working from.

mieke_bal.name: Mieke Bal
mieke_bal.desc:
Dutch theorist, born in 1946, whose introduction to narratology is among the most widely used textbooks the field has produced.

She separates narrative into three layers rather than two: the fabula of events, the story that arranges and focalises them, and the text in which a narrator presents that arrangement. The middle layer is her refinement, and it lets focalisation be analysed independently of who is speaking.

Her later work applies the same apparatus outside literature, to painting, sculpture, exhibitions and video, on the argument that narrative is not the property of any one medium.

liu_xie.name: Liu Xie
liu_xie.desc:
Chinese critic (c. 465-522) whose Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons is the earliest comprehensive work of literary theory in Chinese and among the most systematic produced anywhere before the modern period.

Its fifty chapters cover the origin of writing, the classification of genres, the construction of an argument, the use of ornament, the relationship between a writer's temperament and their style, and the training of a critic.

He worked as a Buddhist monastic librarian, and the treatise is organised with a bibliographer's thoroughness, moving from principles through genres to technique and finally to reception.

wenxin_diaolong.name: The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons
wenxin_diaolong.desc:
Liu Xie's treatise, completed around 501, is the fullest work of literary theory to survive from the pre-modern Chinese tradition, running to fifty chapters in parallel prose.

It takes the classics as the source of all later writing, classifies the genres descending from them, and then turns to technique: how a piece is planned, how thought becomes language, how ornament serves or obstructs, and why fashions in style change from one age to the next.

Its final chapters address the critic rather than the writer, arguing that most misjudgement comes from preferring the ancient or the contemporary as such.

jin_shengtan.name: Jin Shengtan
jin_shengtan.desc:
Chinese critic and editor (1608-1661) who did for vernacular fiction what no one had previously attempted, treating novels and plays as worthy of the close analysis reserved for the classics.

His editions carry running commentary in the margins and between chapters, examining how a scene is prepared, how a character is revealed by a gesture, how an author plants material to be used later, and how a reader is manipulated into an expectation.

He cut Water Margin to seventy chapters and rewrote its ending, and his version displaced the longer ones for two centuries. He was executed in 1661 after joining a protest against a local official.

water_margin.name: Water Margin
water_margin.desc:
A Chinese novel of the fourteenth century, assembled from earlier oral and dramatic material, in which a hundred and eight outlaws are driven one at a time out of ordinary life by corrupt officials and gather at a marsh stronghold.

Its structure is sequential rather than unified: each major figure receives an extended account of the injustice that made him an outlaw before the narrative moves to the next, so the book accumulates a society rather than following a plot.

It exists in versions of seventy, hundred and hundred-and-twenty chapters, which end very differently, and the choice between them is an interpretive decision.

cao_xueqin.name: Cao Xueqin
cao_xueqin.desc:
Chinese novelist (c. 1715-1763) born into a family that had served the Kangxi emperor and was ruined by imperial displeasure when he was a boy.

He spent his later years in poverty outside Beijing writing a novel about the decline of a great household, drawing on the world he had lost, and revised it repeatedly without finishing it. It circulated in manuscript among friends during his lifetime and was printed nearly thirty years after his death.

The surviving text's last forty chapters are generally attributed to a later editor working from his notes.

dream_of_red_chamber.name: Dream of the Red Chamber
dream_of_red_chamber.desc:
Cao Xueqin's novel, printed in 1791, follows the decline of an aristocratic family through the adolescence of a boy born with a jade in his mouth and his relationships with the girls and women of the household.

It holds several hundred characters, gives its women the intelligence and the interest, and works almost entirely through domestic detail: gardens, poetry contests, illnesses, the management of servants and the slow disappearance of money.

A mythological frame surrounds it, in which a stone left over from the repair of heaven asks to be sent into the world, so the whole is presented as a record of that stone's experience.

ibn_rushd.name: Ibn Rushd
ibn_rushd.desc:
Andalusian philosopher, jurist and physician (1126-1198), known in Latin Europe as Averroes, whose commentaries on Aristotle were the principal route by which that work reached medieval Christian thought.

His commentary on the Poetics is the most instructive failure in the history of criticism. Working in a culture with no theatrical tradition and from an Arabic translation of a Syriac version, he rendered tragedy as the poetry of praise and comedy as the poetry of blame, and produced a coherent account of an art he had no way to picture.

Borges wrote a story about the impasse.

ibn_al_muqaffa.name: Ibn al-Muqaffa'
ibn_al_muqaffa.desc:
Persian writer and administrator (c. 720-756) who converted from Zoroastrianism to Islam and became the principal shaper of Arabic literary prose.

His translations from Middle Persian carried a body of Indian and Iranian narrative and political material into Arabic, where it entered the wider Islamic and eventually the European tradition. He also wrote works of political counsel in his own name.

He was executed in his thirties on the order of a provincial governor, in circumstances that later accounts describe with considerable and probably embellished cruelty.

kalila_wa_dimna.name: Kalila wa-Dimna
kalila_wa_dimna.desc:
The Arabic version of the Panchatantra, made in the eighth century from a Middle Persian translation of a Sanskrit original, and the single most widely diffused book of narrative in the pre-modern world.

It keeps the nested animal fables and the frame of instruction for a ruler, and adds material of its own, including a preface about the difficulty of reading a book for anything but entertainment.

From Arabic it passed into Hebrew, Latin, Castilian, Persian and most European vernaculars, which is how the Indian material reached medieval Europe and, through it, the fable collections that followed.

somadeva.name: Somadeva
somadeva.desc:
Kashmiri poet of the eleventh century who compiled the Kathasaritsagara, reportedly for the diversion of a queen of the Kashmiri court during a period of political violence.

He worked from an earlier collection, the Brihatkatha, now lost, and his version is the fullest surviving descendant of it. He states that he has abridged rather than invented, and that his object was to preserve the substance while making the whole readable.

Almost nothing else about him is recorded, and the collection is dated from the reign named in its opening.

kathasaritsagara.name: The Kathāsaritsāgara
kathasaritsagara.desc:
Somadeva's eleventh-century Sanskrit collection, whose title means the ocean of the streams of story, holds several hundred tales inside a frame concerning a prince, his adventures and his acquisition of a kingdom.

The nesting is exceptionally deep. Characters inside tales tell tales whose characters tell further tales, and a reader can be five levels from the outermost narrative before returning through all of them in order.

It is among the largest such structures in world literature and a principal source for stories that turn up later in Persian, Arabic and European collections.

tale_of_heike.name: The Tale of the Heike
tale_of_heike.desc:
A Japanese account of the war between the Taira and Minamoto clans in the twelfth century, which reached its surviving form in the thirteenth and was performed rather than read.

Its opening lines state the theme directly, in the sound of temple bells and the colour of flowers, that the proud do not endure. The narrative then works that proposition through a specific dynastic collapse, with sympathy given to the losing side.

It supplies Japanese drama with much of its material, and noh in particular returns to its dead repeatedly as ghosts recounting the battles that killed them.

biwa_hoshi.name: Biwa Hōshi
biwa_hoshi.desc:
Itinerant Japanese performers, most of them blind and holding a nominal clerical status, who recited narrative to their own accompaniment on the biwa, a short-necked lute.

Their principal repertoire was the Tale of the Heike, delivered in instalments over many evenings in a chanted style that lay between song and speech, and they organised into a licensed guild that controlled training and the right to perform.

The tradition is the reason the text exists in the form it does: what survives is a performance repertoire written down, and its episodes are shaped for delivery in a single sitting.

coyote.name: Coyote
coyote.desc:
A trickster figure appearing across many Indigenous North American traditions, particularly in the Great Basin, the Plateau, California and the Southwest, in narratives that differ substantially between nations.

Where he appears he is generally both creator and fool: he brings fire, arranges the seasons or sets the pattern of death, and in the next story is defeated by his own greed or appetite in a manner that leaves him ridiculous.

The figure should not be treated as a single character across unrelated traditions, and many of these narratives are told under conditions of season and occasion that published collections ignore.

translation.name: Translation
translation.desc:
The carrying of a narrative into another language, which is how most stories reach most of their readers and which is generally treated as a transparent operation until it fails visibly.

It is not transparent. What survives a translation is the situation, the sequence and something of the tone; what is lost first is wordplay, metre, register and the associations a word carries in one language and not another. A translator's choices about how much to domesticate a text determine what a foreign tradition looks like to the readers who meet it that way.

Most of the transmission described in this graph happened through it, and most of the arguments about faithfulness in adaptation apply here with more force.

marie_de_france.name: Marie de France
marie_de_france.desc:
The earliest known French woman poet, writing in Anglo-Norman in the later twelfth century, probably in England and probably at or near a royal court.

Her twelve lais are short narrative poems drawn from Breton material, concerned with love that cuts across marriage, obligation and species, and told with a compression that leaves motive to be inferred. Her collection of fables is the earliest in French and among the largest medieval Aesopic collections.

She names herself in her prologues, which is why she is known at all, and states in one that she writes so that she will not be forgotten.

lais_of_marie.name: The Lais of Marie de France
lais_of_marie.desc:
Twelve short narrative poems of the later twelfth century, presented by their author as versions of Breton lays she has heard and set down so they will not be lost.

They are unusually direct about desire and unusually unsentimental about marriage: a wife imprisoned by a jealous husband, a knight who is a werewolf betrayed by his wife, lovers who die of the effort to be together. The supernatural is admitted without explanation and the endings are frequently unhappy.

They are contemporary with Chrétien's romances and much shorter, and they carry a great deal in a few hundred lines.

madame_daulnoy.name: Madame d'Aulnoy
madame_daulnoy.desc:
French writer (c. 1652-1705) at the centre of the salon culture in which the literary fairy tale was invented, and the person who named it.

Her collection of 1697 was titled tales of the fairies, and the phrase became the term for the genre in French and then, translated, in English. She published more tales than Perrault, at greater length and with more elaborate courtly machinery, and was the better known of the two in their own time.

Her life was irregular enough to be disputed, including an accusation against her husband that may have been fabricated and a long period abroad.

contes_des_fees.name: Les Contes des Fées
contes_des_fees.desc:
D'Aulnoy's collection of 1697, whose title supplied the name of the genre in French and, in translation, in English.

The tales are long, ornate and aimed at adults: courtly, ironic about the conventions they employ, and interested in the constraints on women who cannot choose their marriages. Her best-known pieces involve a princess transformed into a white cat and a prince turned into a blue bird by a rival's mother.

The salon writers she belonged to were mostly women, wrote a substantial share of the seventeenth-century French tales, and were largely written out of the genre's history by the collections that followed.

aphra_behn.name: Aphra Behn
aphra_behn.desc:
English writer (c. 1640-1689), a spy in the Netherlands for Charles II before turning to the theatre, and the first Englishwoman known to have earned her living by writing.

She wrote some nineteen plays, poetry and prose fiction, and was attacked in her lifetime for indecency on grounds her male contemporaries were not held to. Her reputation collapsed in the eighteenth century and was recovered in the twentieth.

Virginia Woolf's remark that women should let flowers fall on her grave, because she earned them the right to speak their minds, is the most quoted assessment of her.

oroonoko.name: Oroonoko
oroonoko.desc:
Behn's prose fiction of 1688 narrates the capture, enslavement and execution of an African prince in the English colony of Surinam, told by a woman who claims to have been present and to have known him.

The claim to eyewitness testimony is the book's central device and its central problem, since Behn's presence in Surinam is documented only by her own account. The narrator's position is compromised throughout: sympathetic, appalled and part of the colonial establishment.

It is one of the earliest English prose narratives of any length and among the earliest to take slavery as its subject.

emily_bronte.name: Emily Brontë
emily_bronte.desc:
English novelist and poet (1818-1848) who published one novel under a male pseudonym and died the year after it appeared, at thirty.

Her book was received as brutal and its authorship doubted, and her sister's preface to the posthumous edition apologises for it in terms that have shaped its reception since. Almost nothing of her working life is recorded and her letters do not survive.

Her poetry, written for a private imaginary world she and her siblings had maintained since childhood, was published only after her sister found it and, by her own account, was not forgiven for looking.

wuthering_heights.name: Wuthering Heights
wuthering_heights.desc:
Brontë's novel of 1847 covers two generations of mutual destruction between two Yorkshire households, and reaches the reader at two removes.

A visiting tenant records what a housekeeper tells him, and she was a participant with her own interests in how the story is understood, so every judgement in the book is somebody's. The narrative also runs backwards and forwards across forty years rather than proceeding in order.

Its refusal to supply a sympathetic centre was what appalled its first reviewers, and it is the reason the book survived the ones it appalled.

charlotte_bronte.name: Charlotte Brontë
charlotte_bronte.desc:
English novelist (1816-1855), the eldest surviving of the three sisters, who published under a male pseudonym and later acknowledged authorship after her sisters' deaths.

Her fiction takes plain, poor, unremarkable-looking women as its centres and gives them the first person, an argumentative intelligence and a claim to a full inner life, which was the aspect contemporaries found presumptuous.

She worked as a governess and a teacher, spent a formative period in Brussels, and outlived all five of her siblings before dying in the early months of a pregnancy.

jane_eyre.name: Jane Eyre
jane_eyre.desc:
Brontë's novel of 1847 follows an orphan through a charity school, a governess's post and a proposal she discovers to be bigamous, narrated in the first person by the woman it happened to.

Its innovation is the voice: a plain, poor, dependent woman who addresses the reader directly, argues with them, and asserts an equality her circumstances deny. The famous line reporting her marriage is spoken to the reader rather than about the event.

The first wife locked in the attic has generated a century of argument and at least one major novel written to answer it.

daphne_du_maurier.name: Daphne du Maurier
daphne_du_maurier.desc:
English novelist and short story writer (1907-1989) whose books were commercially enormous and critically dismissed as romance for most of her life, and have since been reread as studies of obsession and menace.

Her method is to take a Gothic situation and withhold the reassurance the mode usually supplies: houses that are not haunted but are not safe either, and narrators whose account of themselves does not survive scrutiny.

Hitchcock filmed three of her works, including a short story about birds that she set in Cornwall and he moved to California.

rebecca.name: Rebecca
rebecca.desc:
Du Maurier's novel of 1938 is narrated by a young woman who marries a widower, moves into his house and is steadily displaced by the presence of his first wife, who is dead.

The narrator is never named, which is the book's most discussed decision and the source of its atmosphere: she has no standing of her own in a house where everyone else does. The revelation about the first marriage reverses the reader's sympathies entirely and implicates them in what follows.

It reworks both Jane Eyre and Bluebeard, and Hitchcock filmed it two years after publication.

shirley_jackson.name: Shirley Jackson
shirley_jackson.desc:
American writer (1916-1965) who worked in horror and the uncanny while publishing domestic humour about her own household, and whose reputation has risen steadily since her death.

Her method is to leave the supernatural undecided. A house may be haunted or a woman may be disintegrating, and the narration is placed close enough to her that the reader has no way to check.

A story she published in 1948 about a village ritual produced more mail than the magazine had ever received for a piece of fiction, most of it hostile and much of it from readers asking where the ceremony took place.

the_lottery.name: The Lottery
the_lottery.desc:
Jackson's story of 1948 describes a summer morning in an unnamed American village where the residents gather for an annual draw, chatting about the weather and the farming while the boys collect stones.

The technique is flat reportage: the prose supplies no signal, no interior access and no comment, and the ordinariness holds until the final paragraphs.

The response was unprecedented for the magazine that printed it, running to hundreds of letters, and readers cancelled subscriptions or wrote to ask which town it was. It has been continuously taught and adapted since.

flannery_oconnor.name: Flannery O'Connor
flannery_oconnor.desc:
American writer (1925-1964) who produced two novels and thirty-odd stories before dying at thirty-nine of lupus, and whose essays and lectures on writing are among the most useful in English.

Her craft position is that fiction operates through the senses and the concrete, that a writer's business is with the specific rather than the abstract, and that a story cannot be reduced to its meaning without ceasing to be one.

Her fiction works through violence delivered to complacent people, which she defended as necessary on the grounds that a hostile audience must be shouted at.

margaret_atwood.name: Margaret Atwood
margaret_atwood.desc:
Canadian novelist, poet and critic, born in 1939, whose work ranges across historical fiction, speculative futures and the retelling of myth.

She applied a rule to her best-known novel: nothing would go into it that had not already been done somewhere, by some government, at some point. The result is a dystopia assembled from precedent rather than invention, and she has produced the source cuttings when asked.

She prefers speculative fiction to science fiction for her own work, a distinction she has argued about publicly with Ursula Le Guin.

handmaids_tale.name: The Handmaid's Tale
handmaids_tale.desc:
Atwood's novel of 1985 is narrated by a woman held as a reproductive servant in a theocratic state established on the territory of the United States.

Its closing section reframes everything preceding it: a transcript of an academic conference two centuries later, at which a male scholar discusses the narrative as a recovered document, jokes at its expense and declines to judge the regime that produced it.

The device turns the book from a warning into a question about who gets to interpret a survivor's account, and it is the element most adaptations have struggled with.

lady_gregory.name: Lady Gregory
lady_gregory.desc:
Irish folklorist, dramatist and theatre manager (1852-1932) who collected extensively from Irish speakers in the west of Ireland and co-founded the Abbey Theatre.

She worked by sitting with tellers in cottages and workhouses over many years, recording belief as well as narrative, and published the Ulster and Fenian cycles in a prose English shaped by Irish syntax that became a literary register in its own right.

Her collecting and her theatre are one project: the material she gathered supplied the national drama she was building a company to perform.

chimamanda_ngozi_adichie.name: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
chimamanda_ngozi_adichie.desc:
Nigerian novelist, born in 1977, whose fiction covers the Biafran war, migration and the politics of return, and whose short lecture on narrative has been watched tens of millions of times.

That lecture argues that the danger lies not in stories being untrue but in their being the only one available, and that a single story about a people, repeated, becomes the definitive one. She describes discovering as a child that books contained only white characters, and writing accordingly until she encountered African fiction.

Her position places power at the centre of the question of who tells what.

danger_single_story.name: The Danger of a Single Story
danger_single_story.desc:
Adichie's lecture of 2009, delivered in under twenty minutes and among the most watched talks ever recorded, sets out an argument about narrative and power.

A single story, she argues, is not false so much as incomplete, and its danger is monopoly: repeated often enough and from a position of power, one account of a people becomes the only one available, to outsiders and eventually to the people themselves. Her examples run in both directions, including her own assumptions about a poor family and about Mexico.

She connects the point to who holds the means of publication and distribution.

dorothy_l_sayers.name: Dorothy L. Sayers
dorothy_l_sayers.desc:
English writer (1893-1957) who wrote detective novels, defended the genre in criticism, and spent her later years on a verse translation of Dante she did not live to complete.

Her 1928 introduction to an anthology of detection is among the first substantial histories and theories of the form, tracing it from ancient tales of concealment to the contemporary puzzle and arguing about what fair play requires. She was a founder of the Detection Club and helped draft its oath.

She also argued that the form's constraints were its interest and that it would exhaust itself if it did not admit real characterisation.

jane_ellen_harrison.name: Jane Ellen Harrison
jane_ellen_harrison.desc:
English classicist (1850-1928), among the first women to make a career in the field, and the central figure of the group of Cambridge scholars who read Greek myth as an outgrowth of ritual.

Her argument is that the stories came after the ceremonies rather than explaining them: a rite performed for reasons long forgotten acquires a narrative to account for it, so myth is a secondary formation rather than a primitive science.

The ritual theory was overstated and has been substantially revised, and it shaped a generation of work on tragedy, comedy and the origins of drama.

mary_douglas.name: Mary Douglas
mary_douglas.desc:
British anthropologist (1921-2007) whose work on classification underlies a great deal of later thinking about monsters, taboo and disgust, generally without being cited.

Her central argument is that dirt is matter out of place: things are found polluting when they violate the categories a culture organises the world with, rather than because of any property they possess. Creatures that fit no class are treated as abominable for that reason alone.

Her late work on ring composition argues that a large body of ancient literature is arranged symmetrically around a centre, and that modern readers systematically miss it.

barbara_herrnstein_smith.name: Barbara Herrnstein Smith
barbara_herrnstein_smith.desc:
American theorist, born in 1932, whose study of how poems end is the closest thing the subject of closure has to a technical account.

Her argument is that a sense of conclusion is produced by identifiable formal means, including the resolution of a pattern the work has established, a shift in register at the close, and the exhaustion of a structural principle, and that a reader's sense of finality can therefore be explained rather than only reported.

Her later work on value argues that literary evaluation is contingent on the circumstances of readers rather than on properties of works.

laura_mulvey.name: Laura Mulvey
laura_mulvey.desc:
British film theorist and filmmaker, born in 1941, whose 1975 essay on visual pleasure is among the most cited pieces of writing about cinema.

Its argument is structural rather than about content: mainstream narrative film is organised so that the camera, the male protagonist and the audience share a position of looking, and women appear as the object of that look, which halts the narrative while it is being performed.

She has since revised the argument repeatedly, including on the question of what a female spectator does with a position built for someone else.

oral_storytelling.name: Oral Storytelling
oral_storytelling.desc:
Narrative composed and transmitted in performance rather than in writing, the oldest and most widespread form of the practice.

It has properties writing does not. The audience is present and shapes the telling; the text is remade at each performance; and memory does the storing where a page would, which favours formula, repetition, rhythm, concrete action and patterned structure. Parry and Lord showed with South Slavic singers that long narratives can be composed in performance from a learned system, never memorised whole, and Ong argued that these habits shape thought itself in cultures without writing.

It persists everywhere, in professional traditions and in ordinary conversation.

myth.name: Myth
myth.desc:
Traditional narrative concerning gods, origins and the order of the world, held within its own community as authoritative rather than as invention.

Folklorists conventionally separate myth from legend and folktale by the belief and setting a community assigns to it: myth is set in a primordial time and treated as sacred, legend in historical time and treated as having happened, and folktale as fiction. The boundaries are practical, not absolute and vary by tradition.

The modern colloquial use of myth to mean a false belief is a separate sense, and it obscures the fact that these narratives functioned as explanation, law and liturgy for the societies that told them.

legend.name: Legend
legend.desc:
Traditional narrative set in historical time and told as something that happened, however improbable its content.

Legends attach to named people, identifiable places and datable events, which distinguishes them from folktales set in an unspecified once upon a time. Saints' lives, the matter of Arthur, local accounts of buried treasure and haunted houses all belong here, as do the contemporary or urban legends studied by folklorists, which circulate as things that happened to a friend of a friend.

The category is defined by the claim to truth the telling makes, not by whether the events occurred.

folktale.name: Folktale
folktale.desc:
Traditional prose narrative circulating orally and told as fiction, without the sacred authority of myth or the historical claim of legend.

The category covers animal tales, jokes, tales of the stupid ogre, novellas and wonder tales, and its material is international: the same plots turn up across Europe, Asia and Africa in versions that cannot be ranked as more or less authentic. The Aarne-Thompson-Uther index exists to make that comparison possible.

Propp's structural analysis, Levi-Strauss's account of myth and the Finnish historic-geographic method all took folktale collections as their evidence, so much of narrative theory begins here.

fairy_tale.name: Fairy Tale
fairy_tale.desc:
The wonder tale: a short traditional narrative in which magic is unremarkable, set in an unlocated past, usually following an unpromising protagonist through tests to a transformed status.

The English name is a translation of the French conte de fees from the literary salons of the seventeenth century, and much of what is now read comes from written redactions, Perrault's of 1697, the Grimms' of 1812 onwards, and Andersen's original tales, not directly from oral tradition.

Jack Zipes and others have argued that each redaction carries the social lessons of its moment, so the tales are best read as historical documents rather than as timeless survivals.

fable.name: Fable
fable.desc:
A very short narrative, usually with animal characters standing for human types, ending in an explicit moral.

The form is extremely economical: a situation, a decision and its consequence, often in under a hundred words. That makes it a useful demonstration of the minimum a story needs. Its didactic purpose is stated rather than implied, which distinguishes it from most other narrative forms.

The Greek corpus attributed to Aesop and the Sanskrit Panchatantra developed independently but share plots, and the Panchatantra's route into Arabic, Latin and the European vernaculars is one of the best-documented cases of narrative travelling between cultures.

parable.name: Parable
parable.desc:
A brief realistic narrative told to convey a moral or spiritual point by analogy, with human characters and no supernatural machinery.

It differs from the fable in that its meaning is usually left to be drawn out, not appended, and that its events are ordinary: a farmer sowing, a son leaving home, a traveller helping a stranger. The parables of the Gospels are the best-known examples in the West, and comparable teaching stories appear in Buddhist, Jewish and Sufi traditions.

The form relies on the listener completing the analogy, which makes it a demonstration of how much interpretive work an audience will willingly do.

epic_poetry.name: Epic Poetry
epic_poetry.desc:
Long narrative verse on heroic or foundational subjects, in most traditions composed and performed orally before being written down.

The conventions recur widely: an invocation, an announced theme, catalogues, formulaic epithets, extended similes, journeys to the world of the dead, and a scale that binds a people's history to its gods. Metre and formula serve memory and performance as much as sound.

The form is not confined to Greece: the Mahabharata, the Ramayana, Gilgamesh, Beowulf, the Sundiata epic and many others are epics in this sense, and several are still performed today rather than only read.

drama.name: Drama
drama.desc:
Narrative enacted by performers before an audience, in which the story is carried by speech and action in present time rather than by a narrator.

The form imposes constraints that shape everything else: what cannot be shown must be reported, exposition must be motivated within conversation, and the audience's attention is held continuously, not at their own pace. Theatrical traditions have developed independently many times, in Greece, India, China, Japan and elsewhere, each with its own conventions of masking, chorus, music and stylisation.

Most early theory of storytelling, from Aristotle to Zeami to Freytag, is theory of drama.

novel.name: The Novel
novel.desc:
Extended prose fiction, read privately and at the reader's own pace, and the form in which interiority became the central subject of narrative.

Its European emergence is conventionally dated to Cervantes and the eighteenth century, though The Tale of Genji long predates that and prose fiction existed in antiquity. Print, literacy and a book trade made the form economically possible, and the nineteenth century added serialisation and a mass readership.

Bakhtin argued that its distinguishing feature is not length but the capacity to hold many social languages at once without subordinating them to a single authoritative voice.

short_story.name: Short Story
short_story.desc:
Prose fiction short enough to be read at a sitting, a condition Poe made central to his account of the form, arguing that unity of effect depends on uninterrupted reading.

The form as a commercial and literary category grew with nineteenth-century magazines, which supplied both a market and a length. Its economy pushes toward implication, a single situation, and endings that turn on recognition rather than resolution; Chekhov and Joyce developed the version that closes on a shift in understanding, not an event.

It sits close to the oral anecdote and the folktale, which are also built to be delivered whole.

film.name: Film
film.desc:
Narrative told through recorded moving images and sound, assembled by editing.

The form's specific resource is the cut: meaning arises from the relation between shots as much as from their content, a principle the Soviet montage theorists made explicit. Film controls duration absolutely, can move instantly through space and time, and can withhold or supply information through framing and sound in ways no other medium matches.

Its commercial structure has generated an unusually prescriptive craft literature, from Field's paradigm to Snyder's beat sheet, in part because scripts must be judged and financed before anything is shot.

television_serial.name: Television Serial
television_serial.desc:
Long-form narrative told in episodes, in which characters and situations continue across instalments instead of resetting.

The form's constraints are institutional: episode lengths, act breaks placed for advertising or scheduling, and seasons commissioned before their ending is known, which requires structures that can extend or contract. Writers' rooms make it a collaborative form in a way novels and films usually are not.

Streaming release altered the calculation again, removing the week between episodes that made the cliffhanger essential and encouraging serialisation so tight that individual episodes may no longer resolve anything.

comics.name: Comics
comics.desc:
Narrative told through images in deliberate sequence, usually with text, and read at a pace the reader controls.

Will Eisner's Comics and Sequential Art of 1985 and Scott McCloud's Understanding Comics of 1993 established the working vocabulary: the panel as a unit of time as well as space, the gutter between panels where the reader supplies the movement that is never drawn, and page layout as a means of controlling rhythm and revelation.

The form's economics have produced serialised universes maintained by many hands over decades, raising questions of continuity and authorship that other narrative media rarely face.

radio_drama.name: Radio Drama
radio_drama.desc:
Narrative performed for sound alone, using voice, music, effects and silence, with the listener supplying everything visual.

The absence of images is a resource rather than a limitation: scale costs nothing, and a scene can be relocated in a syllable. It also demands constant unobtrusive signalling of who is speaking and where they are.

The form's most repeated story concerns the 1938 Mercury Theatre broadcast of The War of the Worlds, presented as news bulletins. Later research has argued that the scale of the panic it supposedly caused was greatly exaggerated in contemporary newspaper coverage, making it a case study in how a story about a story survives.

video_game_narrative.name: Video Game Narrative
video_game_narrative.desc:
Storytelling in a medium where the audience acts, and where events must be produced by a system, not only recounted.

Designers distinguish the embedded narrative authored in advance from the emergent narrative produced by play, and lean heavily on environmental storytelling, where a space is arranged so that the player reconstructs what happened in it. Branching structures and player choice complicate authorship of the plot itself.

The term ludonarrative dissonance, coined by the designer Clint Hocking in 2007 in a critique of BioShock, names the mismatch that arises when what a game's story asserts is contradicted by what its mechanics reward.

narrative_journalism.name: Narrative Journalism
narrative_journalism.desc:
Reporting that uses the techniques of fiction, scene, dialogue, character and structure, while holding to a claim of factual accuracy.

The New Journalism of the 1960s made the approach visible, with Tom Wolfe as its noisiest advocate and Truman Capote's In Cold Blood as its most discussed case. The methods that make such work readable, compression, reconstructed scenes, access to what a subject was thinking, are also the points at which verification is hardest.

The form therefore carries a permanent tension: the narrative shape that gives events meaning is imposed by the writer, and events do not arrive with it attached.

memoir.name: Memoir and Autobiography
memoir.desc:
Narrative in which the author gives an account of their own life, or of a portion of it.

Augustine's Confessions established a durable pattern in the Western tradition, structuring a life as a movement toward conversion, and later secular versions retain the shape of a self explained by its turning points. The form's difficulty is that memory is reconstructive and that a life does not arrive divided into acts.

Bruner argued that this is not a defect peculiar to the genre but the ordinary condition of selfhood, since people continually compose and revise a narrative of who they are.

tragedy.name: Tragedy
tragedy.desc:
Drama, and later narrative generally, in which a serious action moves toward suffering and loss.

In Athens tragedies were performed in competition at festivals of Dionysus, drawn mostly from myth the audience already knew, so that interest lay in treatment rather than outcome. Aristotle described the effect as pity and fear resolved in catharsis, and preferred a protagonist neither wholly good nor wicked, brought down by hamartia.

Later traditions loosened the requirements. Renaissance and modern tragedy admitted mixed registers and, from the eighteenth century, protagonists of ordinary social standing, which Aristotle's account had not envisaged.

comedy.name: Comedy
comedy.desc:
Narrative that moves from disorder to a restored or improved social order, conventionally ending in reconciliation, marriage or feast.

Aristotle's treatment of comedy is lost, so its theory was rebuilt later. Northrop Frye described its typical movement as the young overcoming an obstructing older generation to form a new society, and traced the pattern from Greek and Roman New Comedy through Shakespeare.

The form's mechanisms, mistaken identity, disguise, the pairing off of couples and the exposure of pretension, are strikingly stable across two millennia, and much of the machinery of the Renaissance stage came directly from Plautus and Terence.

romance_medieval.name: Medieval Romance
romance_medieval.desc:
Narrative of chivalric adventure, developed in twelfth-century France and spreading across Europe, centred on knights, quests, marvels and love.

Chretien de Troyes gave the Arthurian material much of its literary form, and the matter of Britain, of France and of Rome supplied the standard subjects. Its structure is episodic, built from separable adventures strung along a journey, and it is the immediate ancestor of the quest as a narrative shape.

The genre's conventions had become sufficiently familiar by the sixteenth century to be parodied, most consequentially by Cervantes, whose parody produced the novel.

satire.name: Satire
satire.desc:
Narrative that attacks vice or folly by exposing it to ridicule, usually through exaggeration, inversion or false innocence.

Roman practice distinguished two temperaments, the genial mockery associated with Horace and the savage indignation associated with Juvenal, and the distinction is still used. Its characteristic technique is to adopt a position in order to destroy it, as in Swift's proposal that the Irish poor sell their children as food.

Because it depends on shared knowledge of what is being attacked, satire ages faster than most forms, and its irony is regularly mistaken for sincerity by readers outside its moment.

detective_fiction.name: Detective Fiction
detective_fiction.desc:
Fiction organised around the investigation of a crime, in which the reader is set a puzzle alongside the investigator.

It is the genre most explicitly built on the gap between story and telling: the events are complete before the narrative begins, and the plot consists of their reconstruction. That makes it a standing demonstration of the fabula and syuzhet distinction. Its devices, the red herring, the withheld clue, the closing explanation, follow from that structure.

Poe's The Murders in the Rue Morgue of 1841 is usually cited as the first modern example, and the interwar British and American schools formalised its rules of fair play.

science_fiction.name: Science Fiction
science_fiction.desc:
Fiction that extrapolates from science, technology or social change to construct a world differing from the present in specified ways.

Hugo Gernsback promoted the category in American magazines in the 1920s, coining scientifiction before settling on science fiction. Darko Suvin's influential definition described the genre through cognitive estrangement: a novum, some new element, that the reader is invited to reason about, not simply accept.

The form's strength is the thought experiment, using an invented world to isolate a variable in the actual one, as Le Guin does with gender in The Left Hand of Darkness.

fantasy.name: Fantasy
fantasy.desc:
Fiction set in a world where the impossible is real, and where that impossibility is part of the world's own rules, not a violation of them.

Tolkien's essay On Fairy-Stories, first given as a lecture in 1939, made the case for the form as sub-creation, arguing that a secondary world earns belief through internal consistency, and that recovery, escape and consolation are its proper effects rather than failings.

The genre draws its furniture from myth, folktale and medieval romance, and its modern commercial shape, the long quest across a mapped world, owes a great deal to The Lord of the Rings.

horror.name: Horror
horror.desc:
Fiction whose organising aim is to frighten or disturb, defined by intended effect rather than by subject or setting.

The Gothic novel, conventionally dated from Walpole's The Castle of Otranto in 1764, supplied the early machinery of ruins, tyrants and buried secrets. Freud's 1919 essay on the uncanny provided a durable account of why the familiar made slightly wrong disturbs more than the plainly alien.

The genre depends heavily on withheld information and on pacing, since a threat fully described is generally less frightening than one the audience is still assembling.

realism.name: Literary Realism
realism.desc:
The nineteenth-century project of representing ordinary contemporary life accurately, including the social and economic conditions that shape it.

Its practitioners extended narrative attention to subjects earlier hierarchies had excluded, and developed the techniques to do so: free indirect discourse, dense material detail, and plots driven by money, class and work. Flaubert, Eliot, Tolstoy and Balzac are standard reference points, and Auerbach's Mimesis traced the long approach to this way of writing.

Modernist writers reacted against its conventions, arguing that an inventory of surfaces missed the actual texture of consciousness instead of capturing it.

magical_realism.name: Magical Realism
magical_realism.desc:
Narrative in which marvellous events occur within an otherwise realistic world and are treated by the narration as unremarkable.

The term originates in art criticism, coined by the German critic Franz Roh in 1925 as Magischer Realismus for a style of post-expressionist painting, and was later taken up in Latin American criticism, where it attached to the fiction of the boom.

What distinguishes it from fantasy is the narrator's flat acceptance: no one in the story treats the marvellous as needing explanation. Garcia Marquez attributed the tone to the manner in which his grandmother told stories.

metafiction.name: Metafiction
metafiction.desc:
Fiction that draws attention to its own status as fiction, through self-reference, exposed devices, intrusive narrators or stories about their own composition.

The term was used by William H. Gass in 1970, but the practice is much older: Don Quixote, Tristram Shandy and the frame narratives of many traditions all display their machinery. Calvino's If on a winter's night a traveller makes the reader's attempt to read the book its plot.

The device is closely related to Shklovsky's laying bare of the device, and to Brecht's insistence that an audience be kept aware it is watching a construction.

bildungsroman.name: Bildungsroman
bildungsroman.desc:
The novel of formation, following a protagonist from youth to a settled relation with the adult world.

The term is generally credited to the German philologist Karl Morgenstern in the 1810s and was given wide currency by Wilhelm Dilthey later in the century; Goethe's Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship is the standard model. The pattern usually involves departure from home, a series of formative errors, disillusionment and some accommodation with society.

It has been adapted extensively, including by writers using it to describe formation under conditions of colonialism, migration or exclusion that the original model did not contemplate.

picaresque.name: Picaresque
picaresque.desc:
Episodic first-person narrative following a rogue of low birth through a series of masters and situations, satirising each in turn.

The Spanish Lazarillo de Tormes, published anonymously in 1554, established the pattern, and Guzman de Alfarache and later English and French imitations extended it. Its structure is additive, not causal: episodes can be reordered or removed, and the unity comes from the narrator rather than the plot.

The form provides the anti-hero to later fiction, and its episodic road structure survives in the picaresque strand of the novel from Fielding to the twentieth century.

creation_myth.name: Creation Myth
creation_myth.desc:
Narrative accounting for the origin of the world, of people, and of the order that governs them.

Recurring patterns include creation from a formless water or void, the separation of earth and sky, emergence from a world below, the dismemberment of a primordial being, and successive attempts at making humanity that fail before one succeeds. The Popol Vuh's sequence of failed creations is a well-documented instance of the last.

Such narratives are typically the most authoritative stories a tradition holds, tied to ritual and to the legitimacy of social arrangements. Comparison across traditions requires care.

flood_myth.name: Flood Narrative
flood_myth.desc:
The widely distributed story of a deluge that destroys humanity, survived by a few who are warned in advance and preserve life in a vessel.

The Mesopotamian version in the Epic of Gilgamesh, in which Utnapishtim recounts his survival, closely parallels the account in Genesis, including the release of birds to find land. The correspondence became public knowledge when George Smith identified the tablet passage in 1872, and it remains a central case in the comparative study of ancient Near Eastern narrative.

Flood stories occur in many other traditions as well, and explanations for the distribution, shared origin, independent invention, or common experience of flooding, are debated.

katabasis.name: Descent to the Underworld
katabasis.desc:
The journey of a living figure into the realm of the dead and back, a motif recurring across many unrelated traditions.

Odysseus consults the dead, Orpheus attempts to retrieve Eurydice, Inanna descends and is stripped at each gate, Izanagi follows his wife and breaks the prohibition on looking, and the Hero Twins of the Popol Vuh defeat the lords of Xibalba. The visit typically yields knowledge unavailable above ground, and imposes a condition that is often broken.

Campbell placed a version of the descent at the centre of his monomyth, and modern narrative retains it in figurative form as the protagonist's lowest point.

quest.name: The Quest
quest.desc:
A journey undertaken to obtain or reach something, structured by the obstacles encountered on the way.

As a narrative shape it is unusually accommodating: the object supplies motivation, the road supplies episodes, and companions can be added and removed at will. It dominates medieval romance, heroic fantasy and a great deal of game design. Booker lists it among his seven plots.

The object is frequently less important than the travelling, which is the observation behind the MacGuffin, and quest narratives commonly end by revealing that what was sought is not what was needed.

rags_to_riches.name: Rags to Riches
rags_to_riches.desc:
The pattern in which an overlooked or mistreated figure rises to wealth, recognition or marriage.

It is one of the most widely attested folktale shapes, appearing in Cinderella-type tales across Eurasia and beyond, and Booker includes it among his seven plots. The rise is typically not achieved by ambition but conferred once merit is recognised, often with supernatural help, which distinguishes the traditional pattern from the modern narrative of self-improvement.

Many versions attach a warning to the ascent, in the form of a deadline, a prohibition or a period of trial that must be survived first.

cinderella_type.name: Cinderella (ATU 510A)
cinderella_type.desc:
The persecuted heroine tale in which a girl mistreated at home is helped to attend a gathering, is recognised by a token, and marries.

Hundreds of versions have been recorded across Europe, Asia and North Africa. The Chinese Ye Xian, recorded in the ninth century, is among the earliest written; the Grimms' Aschenputtel supplies help from a tree at the mother's grave and has the stepsisters mutilate their feet; Perrault's version supplies the fairy godmother, the pumpkin and the glass slipper that most readers now assume to be original.

It is a standard demonstration of why folktales are catalogued by type rather than by any single text.

red_riding_hood_type.name: Little Red Riding Hood (ATU 333)
red_riding_hood_type.desc:
The tale of a girl sent through the woods who is deceived by a wolf at her grandmother's house.

Perrault's 1697 version ends with the wolf eating her and a verse moral about young women and smooth-tongued strangers; the Grimms added the huntsman who cuts her out alive, a rescue absent from Perrault. Oral versions collected in France, some recorded later, contain episodes found in neither, including a path of pins or needles and an escape achieved by the girl's own trick.

The variants make it a favoured case for arguments about what editors did to the tales they collected.

overcoming_the_monster.name: Overcoming the Monster
overcoming_the_monster.desc:
The pattern in which a community is threatened by a destructive being and a hero confronts and destroys it.

Gilgamesh and Enkidu against Humbaba, Beowulf against Grendel and later the dragon, Perseus against the sea monster, and Sundiata against Sumanguru all follow it, and Booker made it the first of his seven plots. The threat is typically established through its victims before the hero engages it, and the fight is often preceded by the acquisition of a specific weapon or knowledge.

The monster's meaning is rarely neutral, and criticism generally reads it in relation to what the telling culture excluded or feared.

voyage_and_return.name: Voyage and Return
voyage_and_return.desc:
The pattern in which a protagonist enters a strange world, is at first fascinated by it, comes under threat, escapes, and returns home altered by what they have seen.

Booker lists it among his seven plots, and it covers Alice's Wonderland, Gulliver's voyages, Odysseus among the Phaeacians and much science fiction of first contact. Its distinguishing feature is that the strange world is not conquered or fixed but left behind.

The return is where the pattern earns its meaning, since the point of comparison is the ordinary world seen again by someone who now has something to compare it with.

metamorphosis.name: Transformation
metamorphosis.desc:
The motif of a being changed into another form: human into animal, animal into human, person into tree, stone or star.

Ovid's Metamorphoses gathers a great many Greek and Roman instances into a single poem organised entirely around the device, and the motif is central to folktale, where enchantment and disenchantment structure whole tale types such as the animal bridegroom. In many traditions the transformation is a punishment, in others a rescue, and in others simply how the world's features came to exist.

Its persistence in modern fiction, from Kafka onward, generally turns the change into a condition to be lived with, not reversed.

three_act_structure.name: Three-Act Structure
three_act_structure.desc:
The dominant working model of dramatic construction in commercial film and television: a setup that establishes the situation and sets the story in motion, a long middle of escalating complication, and a resolution.

Its ancestry is often traced to Aristotle's remark that a whole has a beginning, a middle and an end, though Aristotle was describing completeness rather than proposing a template. The modern version with measurable proportions and turning points at the act breaks was codified for screenwriters by Syd Field in 1979.

Because act two is roughly twice the length of the others, practitioners subdivide it with a midpoint, which is what brings the model close to a five-part shape.

freytags_pyramid.name: Freytag's Pyramid
freytags_pyramid.desc:
The diagram derived from Gustav Freytag's 1863 analysis of drama, showing exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and catastrophe or resolution arranged as an ascent and descent around a central peak.

Freytag was describing five-act Greek and Shakespearean tragedy, in which a great deal happens after the turn. His falling action is as substantial as the rise. Applied to modern stories, where the climax usually sits near the end, the shape misleads: the descending side has almost nothing to hold.

It remains one of the most widely taught structural diagrams in schools, frequently without the context that produced it.

five_act_structure.name: Five-Act Structure
five_act_structure.desc:
The division of a play into five parts, recommended in Horace's Ars Poetica and standard in Renaissance and neoclassical European drama.

Shakespeare's plays are printed in five acts, but the divisions were largely imposed by editors and printers, not marked in performance at the Globe, where the action ran continuously. In the Roman and later theatre the act breaks corresponded to choral interludes or music.

Modern advocates, including John Yorke, argue that the familiar three acts are really five once act two is split at its midpoint, and that television, with its transmission breaks, works naturally in this shape.

monomyth.name: The Hero's Journey
monomyth.desc:
Campbell's name for the single pattern he claimed underlies heroic myth: the hero leaves the ordinary world, is tested in a region of supernatural wonder, wins a decisive victory, and returns with power to benefit others.

He called it the monomyth, taking the word from Joyce's Finnegans Wake, and elaborated it into stages including the call to adventure, the mentor, the threshold, the ordeal and the return.

Comparative folklorists object that the pattern is produced partly by selection, and that fitting a given tradition's stories to it requires ignoring what makes them distinct. Its practical afterlife in screenwriting, largely through Christopher Vogler, has been substantial regardless.

kishotenketsu.name: Kishotenketsu
kishotenketsu.desc:
A four-part narrative structure used in Chinese, Korean and Japanese composition, from the Chinese qi cheng zhuan he.

The parts are usually glossed as introduction, development, twist and conclusion. The third part is the distinctive one:, not a conflict escalating to a climax, it introduces something unexpected or apparently unrelated, and the fourth part reconciles it with what came before. Meaning arises from the juxtaposition rather than from opposition resolved.

It is often cited in discussions of story forms that do not depend on conflict, and can be seen in four-panel manga strips as well as in classical poetry and prose.

jo_ha_kyu.name: Jo-ha-kyu
jo_ha_kyu.desc:
A Japanese principle of pacing, meaning roughly beginning, break and rapid, describing a movement that starts slowly, gathers and elaborates, then finishes swiftly.

It originated in gagaku court music and was applied to noh by Zeami, who used it at every scale at once: within a single gesture, within a play, and across the order of plays in a full day's programme. The nesting is the point, since the same rhythm governs the smallest and largest units.

The concept has been extended by later writers to tea ceremony, martial arts and Japanese film editing.

proppian_functions.name: Propp's Thirty-One Functions
proppian_functions.desc:
The sequence of narrative functions Propp identified in Russian wonder tales: acts such as absentation, interdiction, violation, reconnaissance, trickery, villainy, departure, the donor's test, receipt of a magical agent, struggle, branding, victory, return, pursuit, unrecognised arrival, difficult task, recognition, exposure, transfiguration, punishment and wedding.

A function is defined by its consequence for the plot rather than by who performs it or how, so that a magical agent may be a horse, a ring or a piece of advice without changing the structure. No tale contains all thirty-one, but Propp argued that those present always appear in the same order.

The scheme underlies later formal models of story.

actantial_model.name: Actantial Model
actantial_model.desc:
Greimas's reduction of narrative roles to six actants in three pairs: subject and object, sender and receiver, helper and opponent.

An actant is a position in the structure rather than a person, so an abstraction can occupy one, a single character can hold several, and the object of desire may be a state of affairs, not a thing. The sender is whatever sets the subject in motion, the receiver whoever benefits.

The model generalises Propp's spheres of action beyond the folktale, and is used in analysing advertising, political discourse and organisational narratives as well as literature.

story_circle.name: Story Circle
story_circle.desc:
Dan Harmon's eight-step version of the heroic pattern, drawn as a circle divided into halves of order and chaos, and of the conscious and unconscious.

The steps run: a character is in a comfortable situation, needs something, enters an unfamiliar situation, adapts to it, gets what they wanted, pays a heavy price, returns to their familiar situation, and is changed. Because the circle closes, the final position invites comparison with the first.

Harmon published it while running the short-film venue Channel 101 and has described it as a practical tool for building and diagnosing television episodes, not a claim about myth.

seven_basic_plots.name: Seven Basic Plots
seven_basic_plots.desc:
Christopher Booker's taxonomy, published in 2004: overcoming the monster, rags to riches, the quest, voyage and return, comedy, tragedy and rebirth.

Each is described as having its own internal stages, and Booker argues they recur across cultures because they answer to shared psychological needs, an argument he grounds in Jung. The scheme belongs to a long line of attempts to count the plots, from Gozzi's reported thirty-six situations through Polti's list to more recent computational studies of emotional arcs in large text corpora.

Reviewers generally received the taxonomy more warmly than the accompanying claim that modern storytelling has gone astray.

save_the_cat_beat_sheet.name: Save the Cat Beat Sheet
save_the_cat_beat_sheet.desc:
Blake Snyder's fifteen-beat template for a feature screenplay, with target page numbers attached to each beat.

The beats run from the opening image and theme stated through the catalyst, debate, break into two, B story, fun and games, midpoint, bad guys close in, all is lost, dark night of the soul, break into three, finale and closing image. The specificity is the appeal and the objection: it is immediately usable, and its wide adoption has been blamed for a sameness of shape in studio films and commercial fiction.

Snyder also grouped films into story categories cutting across conventional genre labels.

frame_narrative.name: Frame Narrative
frame_narrative.desc:
A story that contains other stories, in which an outer situation supplies the occasion for the tales told inside it.

The device is very old and appears independently across traditions: the Panchatantra teaches princes through nested examples, One Thousand and One Nights makes the telling itself a matter of survival, the Decameron gathers its tellers away from plague, and the Canterbury Tales sets them competing on the road. Frankenstein uses it to bury its most sympathetic voice two layers deep.

The frame is rarely neutral. It establishes who is speaking to whom and why, and that context alters how the enclosed stories are read.

in_medias_res.name: In Medias Res
in_medias_res.desc:
Opening a narrative in the middle of the action, with the earlier events supplied later or left to be inferred.

The phrase comes from Horace's Ars Poetica, where he praises Homer for beginning the Trojan story at a late point rather than from the egg. The Iliad opens in the tenth year of the war, and the Odyssey places its famous adventures in a retrospective account given by Odysseus himself.

The technique buys immediate momentum at the cost of orientation, so it usually obliges a writer to smuggle exposition into scenes that are doing other work.

flashback.name: Flashback
flashback.desc:
A scene from earlier than the point the narrative has reached, inserted into the present line of the story.

Genette classed it as one of the two basic disturbances of narrative order, analepsis, with its forward-looking counterpart prolepsis. Its uses range from supplying withheld information at the moment it will do most damage to placing two times in a relation the reader must interpret.

Craft advice is generally suspicious of it early in a story, on the grounds that an audience will not care about a past it has no reason to be curious about yet. Many films withhold their flashbacks until a question has been planted.

foreshadowing.name: Foreshadowing
foreshadowing.desc:
The planting of a detail that gains its significance later, so that a subsequent development feels prepared.

It works on the reader's memory more than on their attention: the effect depends on the detail being noticed enough to be recalled and not enough to be solved. In Greek tragedy the audience often knows the outcome in advance, so the preparation operates as dread and never as puzzle.

The technique underlies the principle attributed to Chekhov about the gun on the wall, and its misuse is the source of the standard complaint that an ending was either predictable or came from nowhere.

unreliable_narrator.name: Unreliable Narrator
unreliable_narrator.desc:
A narrator whose account the reader has grounds to distrust, so that the story must be reconstructed against what is being said.

Wayne Booth introduced the term in The Rhetoric of Fiction in 1961, defining reliability by whether the narrator speaks in accordance with the norms of the implied author. Unreliability may come from self-interest, limited understanding, youth, madness or deliberate deception, and the reader detects it through inconsistencies and through the reactions of other characters.

The technique requires a second channel of information: if the text offers nothing but the narrator's word, there is nothing to correct it against.

stream_of_consciousness.name: Stream of Consciousness
stream_of_consciousness.desc:
The rendering of a character's thought as a continuous flow, including associations, fragments and shifts that ordinary reported thought would tidy away.

The phrase was used by the psychologist William James in his Principles of Psychology of 1890, and was applied to fiction by the novelist May Sinclair in 1918, writing about Dorothy Richardson's Pilgrimage. Joyce, Woolf and Faulkner developed it in different directions, from Molly Bloom's unpunctuated closing monologue to the compressed and disordered narration of Benjy in The Sound and the Fury.

Critics distinguish it from interior monologue, though the two terms are often used interchangeably.

free_indirect_discourse.name: Free Indirect Discourse
free_indirect_discourse.desc:
A method of reporting a character's thought or speech in the grammar of third-person narration but the idiom of the character, without quotation marks or a tag such as she thought.

The effect is a doubled voice: the narrator's and the character's occupy the same sentence, so irony and sympathy can be produced at once. Austen uses it to expose self-deception the character has not noticed, and Flaubert to quote a cliche while judging it.

The French term style indirect libre was given currency by the linguist Charles Bally in 1912, and the technique became a standard resource of the modern novel.

epistolary.name: Epistolary Narrative
epistolary.desc:
A story told through documents: letters, diaries, transcripts, newspaper cuttings, and in later versions emails, messages and recordings.

The form was central to the early European novel, in Richardson's Pamela and Clarissa and Laclos's Les Liaisons dangereuses, where the immediacy of writing to the moment gave psychological access before free indirect style existed to supply it. Dracula assembles its case from journals and telegrams.

It offers built-in multiplicity of viewpoint and a plausible reason for the reader to be reading, at the cost of continual invention of occasions on which the characters would plausibly write.

dramatic_irony.name: Dramatic Irony
dramatic_irony.desc:
The condition in which the audience knows something a character does not, so that ordinary speech acquires a second meaning.

Greek tragedy relies on it heavily, since the myths were known in advance: every vow Oedipus makes to find the murderer is heard by the audience as a sentence on himself. Hitchcock described the same asymmetry in cinematic terms, contrasting the few seconds of surprise from an unannounced explosion with the long tension available when the audience alone knows the bomb is under the table.

It reverses the usual economy of suspense: the interest lies not in what will happen but in when and how it will be understood.

chekhovs_gun.name: Chekhov's Gun
chekhovs_gun.desc:
The principle that everything given prominence in a narrative should be used, and that anything not to be used should be removed.

It reaches us from Chekhov's letters and from remarks reported by contemporaries, in several forms: that a rifle hanging on the wall in the first act must go off in a later one, and that a writer should not make promises they do not intend to keep. The exact wording varies with the source, so the principle is better attributed than quoted.

As stated it is a rule of economy, though in practice writers plant unused detail deliberately, which is how the red herring works.

macguffin.name: MacGuffin
macguffin.desc:
An object or goal that motivates the characters and matters little in itself: the papers, the formula, the briefcase whose contents are never shown.

Hitchcock popularised the term and, in his conversations with Truffaut and elsewhere, credited it to his colleague Angus MacPhail, illustrating it with a joke about a device for trapping lions in the Scottish Highlands where there are no lions. His point was that the audience's investment belongs to the characters' pursuit rather than to the thing pursued.

The device separates the mechanics of plot from its meaning, and is a useful test of whether a story's stakes are actually located in its people.

deus_ex_machina.name: Deus ex Machina
deus_ex_machina.desc:
A resolution brought about by an intervention from outside the established terms of the plot.

The phrase describes the literal machinery of the Greek theatre, a crane that lowered an actor playing a god into the scene, and Euripides used the device often enough for his name to be attached to it. Aristotle objected in the Poetics that a plot's unravelling should follow from the plot itself.

It is now almost always used as a criticism, though a story that has established divine intervention as part of its world is not doing the same thing as one that produces a rescue it never prepared.

cliffhanger.name: Cliffhanger
cliffhanger.desc:
An episode ending at a point of unresolved danger or revelation, designed to carry an audience across a gap in transmission.

It belongs to serial forms, and its history follows their economics: Victorian part-issue novels, magazine serials, cinema chapter-plays, radio and television, and now the streaming episode whose last thirty seconds are built to defeat the decision to stop watching.

The frame of One Thousand and One Nights makes the technique its subject, since Scheherazade survives only by leaving each night's tale unfinished. Popular etymologies tracing the word to a specific Victorian novel are commonly repeated but not securely established.

plot_twist.name: Plot Twist
plot_twist.desc:
A revelation that reorganises the audience's understanding of what they have already been shown.

A twist differs from a surprise in requiring retrospective coherence: the earlier material must support the new reading as well as the old. The strongest examples reward rewatching and the weakest collapse under it. The technique therefore depends on scrupulous fairness in what has been withheld, not concealed.

Its ancestor is Aristotle's peripeteia, though the modern twist is usually a change in the audience's knowledge rather than, as in his account, an action producing the opposite of its intended effect.

red_herring.name: Red Herring
red_herring.desc:
A detail planted to draw attention away from the real explanation, standard equipment in detective fiction and mystery plotting.

It works against the expectation set by Chekhov's principle of economy: the reader assumes that anything emphasised will matter, and the false lead exploits that assumption. Fair-play detective writing requires the misdirection to be honest, in that the true solution must remain visible to a sufficiently careful reader.

The usual origin story for the phrase comes from William Cobbett, who in 1807 described using a cured herring to divert hounds; his account may well be his own invention, and it is best attributed rather than asserted.

montage.name: Montage
montage.desc:
The construction of meaning in film through the joining of shots, not through what any single shot contains.

Soviet filmmakers of the 1920s made this the centre of their theory. The experiment attributed to Lev Kuleshov, in which the same neutral face cut against different images was read as expressing different emotions, is the standard demonstration, and Eisenstein argued for collision between shots as a means of producing an idea neither shot holds alone.

In ordinary usage the word now more often means a compressed sequence covering a long process quickly, which is a narrower and later sense.

show_dont_tell.name: Show, Don't Tell
show_dont_tell.desc:
The instruction to render experience in scene and detail instead of summarising or asserting it, so that the audience draws the conclusion themselves.

It is commonly attributed to Chekhov on the basis of a remark in his letters about describing the glint of light on broken glass rather than stating that the moon is shining; versions of the phrasing vary and it is safer attributed than quoted. As a rule of thumb it favours the concrete over the abstract.

Wayne Booth's The Rhetoric of Fiction was written substantially against the elevation of this advice into law, arguing that telling is a legitimate and often necessary technique.

fourth_wall.name: Fourth Wall
fourth_wall.desc:
The imaginary partition between a stage and its audience, through which spectators observe a world that behaves as though they were not there.

The conception is associated with Diderot's writings on theatre in the eighteenth century, and became a governing convention of naturalistic staging. Breaking it, by addressing the audience directly, is old in comedy and was used systematically by Brecht, who wanted spectators aware that they were watching a constructed argument rather than absorbed in an illusion.

In prose the equivalent is direct address to the reader, and in film and television the character who turns to the camera.

homer.name: Homer
homer.desc:
The name attached in antiquity to the Iliad and the Odyssey, and the figure around whom the oldest arguments about authorship in European literature revolve.

Ancient sources describe a blind poet from Ionia, but they disagree about his birthplace and date, and no reliable biographical evidence survives. From the eighteenth century onwards the Homeric Question asked whether the poems were the work of one poet, of many, or of a tradition, and the oral-formulaic research of Parry and Lord shifted the debate by showing how such poems can be composed in performance.

What is not in doubt is that the poems were shaped within an oral tradition before reaching written form.

valmiki.name: Valmiki
valmiki.desc:
The sage to whom the Sanskrit Ramayana is traditionally attributed, and who appears within the poem itself as a character, sheltering Sita and teaching the epic to her sons.

Tradition calls him the adi-kavi, the first poet, and tells that the shloka metre came to him in grief at seeing a hunter kill one of a pair of birds. Scholars treat the text as having grown over centuries, with a core often dated to the last centuries BCE and later books added, so that Valmiki names a tradition as much as an individual.

His version remains the reference point against which the many regional Ramayanas are read.

vyasa.name: Vyasa
vyasa.desc:
