The sage credited by tradition with composing the Mahabharata, and also with arranging the Vedas, which gives him the epithet Veda Vyasa, the arranger.

Like Valmiki he is a character in his own poem, the grandfather of its warring cousins, which places the narrator inside the events he narrates. The epic describes its own composition as dictation, with the god Ganesha writing while Vyasa recites.

Modern scholarship treats the text as a compilation that grew over several centuries into the vast work that survives, so Vyasa is best read as the name given to that accumulated tradition, not as a single historical author.

aesop.name: Aesop
aesop.desc:
The name attached to the Greek tradition of short animal fables ending in a moral. Ancient accounts describe him as an enslaved man of the sixth century BCE, ugly and sharp-witted, who won his freedom by cleverness and was later killed at Delphi, but these are legends of uncertain origin and his historical existence is not established.

The fables circulated orally long before they were collected; the earliest known written collection is attributed to Demetrius of Phalerum in the fourth century BCE and does not survive. Later Greek and Latin versions, notably by Babrius and Phaedrus, transmitted them onward.

Many tales in the corpus have parallels in Indian and Near Eastern collections.

scheherazade.name: Scheherazade
scheherazade.desc:
The frame narrator of One Thousand and One Nights, and fiction's most concentrated image of storytelling as survival.

In the frame, a king betrayed by his wife marries a new bride each night and has her killed at dawn. The vizier's daughter volunteers, and each night tells a story that is unfinished when morning comes, so that the king postpones the execution to hear the end. The device makes suspense a matter of life and death, and makes the cliffhanger a structural principle, not a trick.

She is a literary character rather than a historical figure, and her name appears in Persian and Arabic forms across the manuscript tradition.

sophocles.name: Sophocles
sophocles.desc:
Athenian tragedian (c. 497-406 BCE), one of the three whose work survives in quantity. Seven complete plays remain of a body of work ancient sources put at over a hundred.

He is credited with adding a third actor to tragedy, which allowed more complex confrontation on stage, and with increasing the size of the chorus. His Oedipus Rex became the model Aristotle returned to repeatedly in the Poetics for the handling of reversal and recognition.

His Theban plays, Oedipus Rex, Oedipus at Colonus and Antigone, were written decades apart for separate occasions and were not conceived or performed as a trilogy, despite being often published as one.

euripides.name: Euripides
euripides.desc:
Athenian tragedian (c. 480-406 BCE), the last of the three great fifth-century writers of tragedy, and the one whose plays survive in the largest number, in part because a volume of alphabetically ordered texts came down with the selection made for schools.

His drama gives unusual weight to women, enslaved people and outsiders, questions the justice of the gods, and often ends with a divinity appearing to settle matters from above, the device later named deus ex machina after the crane that lifted the actor into view. Aristotle criticised such endings for resolving a plot from outside it.

Aristophanes parodied him repeatedly, which is itself evidence of his prominence.

murasaki_shikibu.name: Murasaki Shikibu
murasaki_shikibu.desc:
Japanese noblewoman and lady-in-waiting at the Heian court who wrote The Tale of Genji in the early eleventh century. Murasaki Shikibu is a court sobriquet rather than a personal name, which has not survived.

Her diary records life at the empress's court and shows her reading Chinese, an accomplishment then thought unsuitable for women. The Tale of Genji follows the emotional life of a prince and, in its later chapters, of the generation after him, with an interior attention to feeling and social nuance that has led many readers to call it the first psychological novel.

It was written in Japanese at a time when prestige literature was written in Chinese.

geoffrey_chaucer.name: Geoffrey Chaucer
geoffrey_chaucer.desc:
English poet and civil servant (c. 1343-1400) who wrote The Canterbury Tales, an unfinished frame narrative in which pilgrims travelling to Canterbury tell stories in a competition.

He held posts as a customs controller and diplomat, and his travels in Italy exposed him to Boccaccio and Petrarch. Writing substantial literature in English, not French or Latin was a deliberate choice at a time when the language had little prestige.

The Tales are notable for matching story to teller: the fabliau given to the Miller, the courtly romance to the Knight, so that the tales characterise the pilgrims and the pilgrims comment on the tales.

giovanni_boccaccio.name: Giovanni Boccaccio
giovanni_boccaccio.desc:
Italian writer (1313-1375) whose Decameron collects a hundred tales inside a frame: ten young Florentines withdraw to a country villa to escape the plague of 1348 and pass ten days telling stories, ten each day on an announced theme.

The frame does real work. It sets an ordered, courteous storytelling ritual against a city described as collapsing, and it lets the collection range from bawdy trickery to tragedy without a single controlling voice.

Boccaccio wrote in Tuscan vernacular prose, and the book supplied plots to later writers across Europe, Chaucer and Shakespeare among them.

miguel_de_cervantes.name: Miguel de Cervantes
miguel_de_cervantes.desc:
Spanish writer (1547-1616) whose Don Quixote appeared in two parts, in 1605 and 1615. He had been a soldier, wounded at Lepanto, and spent five years captive in Algiers before returning to a precarious literary and administrative life.

Don Quixote begins as a parody of chivalric romance and becomes something larger: a book about what reading does to a reader, and about the distance between the world as narrated and the world as encountered. Part Two is startlingly self-aware, with characters who have read Part One, and with a response to an unauthorised sequel published under another name.

He also wrote the Novelas ejemplares and plays.

william_shakespeare.name: William Shakespeare
william_shakespeare.desc:
English playwright and poet (1564-1616), an actor and shareholder in the company that became the King's Men, writing for a commercial playhouse audience.

He worked almost entirely from existing material, chronicles, novellas, earlier plays and classical sources, and his originality lies in construction, character and language rather than invention of plot. The plays mix registers and classes freely, disregarding the neoclassical rules of decorum and unity that governed contemporary French drama.

About half the plays were printed in his lifetime in quarto; the collected volume of 1623, assembled after his death by colleagues, preserved eighteen that had not been published before. The five-act divisions now standard are largely editorial.

charles_perrault.name: Charles Perrault
charles_perrault.desc:
French writer and administrator (1628-1703) who published in 1697 a slim collection of prose tales, Histoires ou contes du temps passe, which fixed written versions of Sleeping Beauty, Little Red Riding Hood, Puss in Boots, Cinderella and Bluebeard.

He wrote for the literate salon culture of Louis XIV's court, not for children, adding verse morals that comment ironically on the stories, and his Little Red Riding Hood ends with the wolf's victory and no rescue. The title page named his son, and the authorship of the collection has been discussed on that basis ever since.

He was also a leading voice for the moderns in the literary quarrel of the period.

brothers_grimm.name: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm
brothers_grimm.desc:
German scholars, Jacob (1785-1863) and Wilhelm (1786-1859), whose Kinder- und Hausmarchen appeared in a first volume in 1812 and a second in 1815, and went through seven editions in their lifetimes, the last in 1857.

They were philologists pursuing a national literary inheritance, and also lexicographers who began the great German dictionary. Their informants were not, as the popular account has it, mostly peasants: many were educated middle-class acquaintances, among them Dorothea Viehmann and members of the Hassenpflug and Wild families, some of Huguenot descent, whose repertoire included French material.

Wilhelm rewrote the tales substantially across editions, smoothing the style and adjusting content for family reading.

hans_christian_andersen.name: Hans Christian Andersen
hans_christian_andersen.desc:
Danish writer (1805-1875) who, unlike Perrault and the Grimms, largely invented his tales rather than collecting them, beginning with a small booklet in 1835.

The Little Mermaid, The Ugly Duckling, The Emperor's New Clothes and The Little Match Girl are literary fairy tales with a distinctive tone: colloquial, ironic, addressed to a listener, and frequently unhappy in their endings. Objects and animals are given consciousness, and social humiliation is a recurring subject.

He also wrote novels, plays and travel books, and was ambitious for recognition in those forms, though it is the tales that carried his name into most of the world's languages.

jane_austen.name: Jane Austen
jane_austen.desc:
English novelist (1775-1817) whose six completed novels, published from 1811, were issued anonymously in her lifetime.

Her central technical contribution is a sustained use of free indirect style, in which a character's thoughts are rendered in the narrator's third person without quotation marks or attribution, so that judgement and self-deception can be presented at once and the reader is left to measure the gap. The irony of Emma depends on it entirely.

Her plots stay within a narrow social range of gentry courtship and inheritance, which she treated as a subject with real economic stakes, not as a backdrop.

charles_dickens.name: Charles Dickens
charles_dickens.desc:
English novelist (1812-1870) whose career began with The Pickwick Papers, issued in monthly parts from 1836, and who published most of his fiction serially thereafter.

Serialisation shaped the writing: each instalment needed its own shape and an ending that would bring readers back, which encouraged large casts, parallel plot lines and strong episodic hooks. Because he was publishing as he wrote, he could register public response mid-novel, and did.

He was also a formidable public performer, touring readings of his own work in Britain and America, and his editorial work on weekly magazines kept him close to a mass readership throughout his life.

gustave_flaubert.name: Gustave Flaubert
gustave_flaubert.desc:
French novelist (1821-1880) whose Madame Bovary, serialised in 1856 and published as a book in 1857 after its author was prosecuted and acquitted on charges of offending public morals, became a model of narrative impersonality.

Flaubert's use of free indirect discourse lets the prose slide into a character's idiom without announcing the shift, so that cliche can be quoted and judged in the same sentence. His letters describe an exacting search for the exact word and a wish to write a book about nothing, held together by style alone.

His practice was central to later arguments, including those of Henry James, about the novelist's disappearance from the novel.

anton_chekhov.name: Anton Chekhov
anton_chekhov.desc:
Russian short story writer and dramatist (1860-1904) who practised as a doctor for much of his life and treated fiction as a form of observation, not argument.

His stories decline the shaped climax, ending instead at a moment of altered understanding, and his plays, among them The Seagull, Uncle Vanya, Three Sisters and The Cherry Orchard, place the decisive events offstage while onstage life continues in fragments of talk.

He is also the source of two of the most repeated pieces of advice in craft teaching, on removing anything that will not be used and on rendering a scene rather than reporting it, both of which reach us through letters and reported remarks in varying forms.

henry_james.name: Henry James
henry_james.desc:
American-born novelist (1843-1916) who settled in England and wrote as much about the craft of fiction as any practitioner of his era.

His 1884 essay The Art of Fiction argued against prescriptive rules and for the novel as a serious form answerable only to its own execution. In the prefaces written for the collected New York Edition of his works he developed the idea of a centre of consciousness, a single reflecting character through whose perception a story is filtered, which shaped later thinking on point of view.

The Turn of the Screw is a much-analysed case of a narration whose reliability the text refuses to settle.

virginia_woolf.name: Virginia Woolf
virginia_woolf.desc:
English novelist and essayist (1882-1941), a central figure of literary modernism and a founder, with Leonard Woolf, of the Hogarth Press.

Mrs Dalloway, published in 1925, compresses its action into a single day in London while moving between minds and reaching back through memory, and To the Lighthouse divides its structure around a passage of elapsed time in which major events are reported in brackets. Her essays argued that the conventions of Edwardian realism, with their inventories of income and furniture, missed the texture of consciousness.

A Room of One's Own, published in 1929, set out the material conditions that had kept women from writing.

james_joyce.name: James Joyce
james_joyce.desc:
Irish writer (1882-1941) whose Ulysses, published in Paris in 1922, maps a single Dublin day onto the wanderings of the Odyssey, giving each episode its own style and technique.

He pushed interior monologue further than any predecessor, ending the novel with an unpunctuated stretch of a character's thought, and in Finnegans Wake dissolved English into a dense multilingual wordplay. It was in the Wake that Joseph Campbell found the word monomyth.

Dubliners, published in 1914, works by the opposite means: plain prose and small incidents that turn on a moment of sudden revelation, for which Joyce borrowed the religious term epiphany.

jorge_luis_borges.name: Jorge Luis Borges
jorge_luis_borges.desc:
Argentine writer (1899-1986) whose short fictions, collected in the 1940s in volumes including Ficciones, treat narrative itself as their subject.

He wrote reviews of imaginary books, stories built as labyrinths, libraries and forking paths, and fictions in which a text rewritten word for word acquires a different meaning. He worked almost entirely in the short form, arguing that it was absurd to write a long book when one could pretend it already existed and write a note on it.

He was a librarian for much of his life, and went blind in middle age, after which he composed by dictation and turned increasingly to verse.

italo_calvino.name: Italo Calvino
italo_calvino.desc:
Italian writer (1923-1985) who moved from neorealist fiction to formally inventive work, including Invisible Cities and If on a winter's night a traveller, a novel made of the opening chapters of ten different novels, addressed to a reader trying to finish one of them.

He also spent two years assembling Italian Folktales, published in 1956, selecting and translating from nineteenth-century regional collections into a single readable corpus, and writing an introduction on the nature of the tales. The work put him in the same relation to Italy as the Grimms to Germany, though from written archives rather than fieldwork.

His Six Memos for the Next Millennium were left unfinished at his death.

gabriel_garcia_marquez.name: Gabriel Garcia Marquez
gabriel_garcia_marquez.desc:
Colombian novelist and journalist (1927-2014) whose One Hundred Years of Solitude, published in 1967, follows several generations of one family in the invented town of Macondo.

He described the tone of the book as an attempt to write the way his grandmother told stories, relating extraordinary events with a completely straight face, and this deadpan treatment of the marvellous became the standard example of magical realism. His earlier career as a reporter is visible in the precision of the physical detail.

He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982, and remained a working journalist and a chronicler of Latin American political violence.

toni_morrison.name: Toni Morrison
toni_morrison.desc:
American novelist and editor (1931-2019) whose fiction draws on African American oral practice, communal narration, call and response, and a withheld secret circled by the community before it is told.

Beloved, published in 1987, takes as its starting point a historical case of an enslaved woman who killed her child rather than see her returned to slavery, and structures the telling around what cannot be said directly. Morrison worked for years as an editor at Random House, publishing Black writers whose work had little other route into print.

She received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1993, and her critical work examined how race operates in the American literary imagination.

chinua_achebe.name: Chinua Achebe
chinua_achebe.desc:
Nigerian novelist and critic (1930-2013) whose Things Fall Apart, published in 1958, narrates the arrival of British colonial administration and missionaries in an Igbo community from within that community's own understanding.

The novel folds proverbs, folktales and oral rhythms into English prose, and Achebe defended writing in English as a deliberate appropriation of the coloniser's language rather than a submission to it. His 1975 lecture on Heart of Darkness argued that Conrad's novel uses Africa as a backdrop against which European identity is tested, a reading that has framed debate about the book ever since.

He worked in radio broadcasting before turning to fiction and teaching.

ursula_k_le_guin.name: Ursula K. Le Guin
ursula_k_le_guin.desc:
American writer (1929-2018) of science fiction, fantasy, essays and poetry, the daughter of the anthropologist Alfred Kroeber and the writer Theodora Kroeber, and much concerned with how societies imagine alternatives to themselves.

The Left Hand of Darkness and The Dispossessed use invented worlds to examine gender and political economy, and the Earthsea books rework the shape of the heroic fantasy quest. Her 1986 essay The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction proposed that the earliest and most useful human technology was the container, not the weapon, and that stories built around gathering and holding are as fundamental as stories built around conflict and the hero.

She also translated the Tao Te Ching.

akira_kurosawa.name: Akira Kurosawa
akira_kurosawa.desc:
Japanese film director (1910-1998) whose work moved between adaptations of Japanese and Western sources and original screenplays, and who was a decisive influence on filmmakers outside Japan.

Rashomon, released in 1950, told one event through several irreconcilable accounts and won the Golden Lion at Venice in 1951, opening Japanese cinema to Western audiences. Seven Samurai established a structure of assembling a team for a defence that has been copied continually. He also adapted Shakespeare, transposing Macbeth to feudal Japan in Throne of Blood and King Lear in Ran.

His handling of weather, movement and screen geography is studied as closely as his narrative construction.

alfred_hitchcock.name: Alfred Hitchcock
alfred_hitchcock.desc:
British-American film director (1899-1980) whose name became attached to suspense as a technique with rules.

In his book-length conversation with Francois Truffaut he set out the distinction between surprise, where a bomb goes off without warning and the audience gets a few seconds of shock, and suspense, where the audience knows the bomb is there and the characters do not. That makes an ordinary conversation unbearable. He also popularised the term MacGuffin for the object everyone in a film is chasing and no one in the audience needs to care about, crediting the word to his colleague Angus MacPhail.

His working method depended on detailed pre-planning of shots.

orson_welles.name: Orson Welles
orson_welles.desc:
American director, actor and writer (1915-1985) who came to film from theatre and radio, where his Mercury Theatre company broadcast a 1938 adaptation of The War of the Worlds in the form of news bulletins.

Citizen Kane, released in 1941, assembles a life from the conflicting recollections of people who knew him, framed by a reporter's search for the meaning of a dying word. Welles shared the screenplay credit with Herman J. Mankiewicz, and the question of how the writing was divided between them has been argued over since Pauline Kael's 1971 essay, with substantial evidence advanced on both sides.

Much of his later work was made in fragments under difficult financing.

walt_disney.name: Walt Disney
walt_disney.desc:
American animation producer and studio founder (1901-1966) whose company turned European folktales into the versions most of the world now knows.

Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, released in 1937, was the first full-length cel-animated feature film, and was followed by adaptations of Perrault, the Grimms, Andersen and Collodi. The studio developed the storyboard as a planning tool, pinning drawings in sequence so that a film's shape could be assessed and revised before animation began, a practice that spread to live-action production.

Scholars of the fairy tale have examined how systematically the adaptations soften violence, add comic companions and resolve ambiguity.

hayao_miyazaki.name: Hayao Miyazaki
hayao_miyazaki.desc:
Japanese animator and director, born in 1941, a co-founder of Studio Ghibli whose films are built around flight, work, ecological damage and children moving through worlds that do not explain themselves.

Spirited Away, released in 2001, follows a girl into a bathhouse for spirits and won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature. His films frequently withhold a clear villain, allowing antagonists motives the story treats seriously, and include long passages of stillness that carry no plot function, a practice he has discussed as necessary breathing space.

He has worked primarily in hand-drawn animation and storyboards his films himself, often while production is under way.

bertolt_brecht.name: Bertolt Brecht
bertolt_brecht.desc:
German dramatist and director (1898-1956) who argued against theatre that absorbs its audience emotionally, and built a practice designed to keep spectators thinking.

His epic theatre uses placards, songs that interrupt the action, visible lighting rigs and narration of outcomes in advance, so that attention shifts from what will happen to why it happens and whether it had to. The German term Verfremdungseffekt, usually translated as alienation or estrangement effect, names the making-strange this is meant to produce, and is related to the Formalist idea of defamiliarization.

He worked in exile from 1933 and returned after the war to found the Berliner Ensemble in East Berlin.

aristotle.name: Aristotle
aristotle.desc:
Greek philosopher (384-322 BCE) whose Poetics is the earliest surviving systematic analysis of storytelling in the Western tradition. Written in the fourth century BCE and preserved as lecture notes, not a polished treatise, it treats tragedy as an imitation of an action, and ranks plot above character as the soul of the work.

His vocabulary still structures how stories are discussed: mythos (plot), mimesis (imitation), catharsis, hamartia, peripeteia and anagnorisis. He argued that a plot should have a beginning, middle and end, and that its parts should follow one another by probability or necessity rather than mere sequence.

A second book, thought to have covered comedy, does not survive.

horace.name: Horace
horace.desc:
Roman poet (65-8 BCE) whose verse letter known as the Ars Poetica became, alongside the Poetics, one of the two ancient texts that shaped European ideas of craft. It is advice rather than analysis: written as a letter to the Piso family, it argues for decorum, consistency of character, and revision.

Two of its phrases entered permanent circulation. In medias res describes the epic habit of opening in the middle of the action and filling in the past later, which Horace praised in Homer. Ut pictura poesis, as is painting so is poetry, was read for centuries as a licence to compare the two arts.

He also recommended that a play run to five acts, a suggestion later hardened by Renaissance critics into a rule.

bharata_muni.name: Bharata Muni
bharata_muni.desc:
The figure to whom the Natyashastra, the Sanskrit treatise on drama, dance and music, is traditionally attributed. Whether Bharata was a single author, a school, or a name attached to a compiled text is unresolved, and the treatise itself is usually dated somewhere between roughly 200 BCE and 200 CE.

The work sets out rasa theory: the idea that performance produces in the audience a distilled emotional flavour, drawn from underlying emotional states through gesture, speech, costume and situation. Eight rasas are enumerated in the text, with a ninth, shanta or tranquillity, added by later commentators.

It remains the foundational reference for classical Indian performance.

zeami.name: Zeami Motokiyo
zeami.desc:
Japanese actor, playwright and theorist (c. 1363-c. 1443) who, with his father Kan'ami, shaped noh into the form still performed today. He wrote many of the plays in the standing repertoire and a series of treatises, of which Fushikaden is the best known, intended for transmission within his own family, not publication.

His writing is concerned with how performance works on an audience over time: the pacing principle of jo-ha-kyu, the cultivation of hana or flower, the freshness that holds attention, and yugen, a subdued and suggestive beauty.

The treatises circulated privately for centuries and only became widely known to scholars in the twentieth century.

gustav_freytag.name: Gustav Freytag
gustav_freytag.desc:
German novelist and critic (1816-1895) whose Die Technik des Dramas, published in 1863, described the shape of five-act drama as a rising and falling movement around a central turning point.

He was analysing classical Greek and Shakespearean plays rather than issuing instructions, but the diagram drawn from his account, the pyramid of exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and catastrophe, was later detached from that context and taught as a template for stories in general. Modern writing courses often apply it to short stories and novels, which it was never built to describe.

His own reputation in Germany rested mainly on his novels and journalism.

vladimir_propp.name: Vladimir Propp
vladimir_propp.desc:
Russian folklorist (1895-1970) who took a corpus of Russian wonder tales, drawn from Afanasyev's collection, and asked not what they were about but what their characters did.

His answer, published in 1928 as Morphology of the Folktale, was that the tales are built from a limited set of narrative functions, acts defined by their consequence for the plot, which always occur in the same order even though no single tale uses them all. He identified thirty-one such functions and grouped the characters into seven spheres of action.

The book was little noticed outside the Soviet Union until an English translation appeared in 1958, after which it became a founding text of structuralist narrative analysis.

joseph_campbell.name: Joseph Campbell
joseph_campbell.desc:
American scholar of comparative mythology (1904-1987) whose The Hero with a Thousand Faces, published in 1949, argued that myths worldwide share a single underlying adventure of departure, initiation and return.

He took the word monomyth from Joyce's Finnegans Wake, and drew heavily on Jungian psychology, reading mythic figures as expressions of shared psychic patterns. Later he reached a very large audience through the 1988 television conversations with Bill Moyers.

Academic folklorists have criticised the approach for selecting and smoothing evidence to fit the pattern, and for flattening the specificity of the traditions it draws on. Its influence on popular screenwriting has nonetheless been enormous.

northrop_frye.name: Northrop Frye
northrop_frye.desc:
Canadian literary critic (1912-1991) who argued in Anatomy of Criticism, published in 1957, that literature is a single interconnected order that can be described systematically, not merely judged.

He mapped narrative onto the cycle of the seasons, associating comedy with spring, romance with summer, tragedy with autumn and irony or satire with winter, and classified fictional modes by the hero's power relative to ordinary people, running from myth down through romance, high and low mimetic, to irony.

His work drew on the Bible as a structuring source for Western literature, a theme he pursued further in The Great Code in 1982.

roland_barthes.name: Roland Barthes
roland_barthes.desc:
French critic and semiotician (1915-1980) who moved from structuralist analysis of narrative towards a looser and more playful reading of texts.

His 1966 introduction to the structural analysis of narrative proposed that stories, like sentences, could be described at distinct levels. In S/Z, published in 1970, he took a single Balzac novella apart into small units of reading and traced five codes running through it, among them the hermeneutic code of enigma and delay and the proairetic code of action.

His 1967 essay The Death of the Author argued that a text's meaning is made at the point of reading rather than fixed by its writer's intention, a claim still contested.

gerard_genette.name: Gerard Genette
gerard_genette.desc:
French literary theorist (1930-2018) who gave narratology much of its working vocabulary. Narrative Discourse, published in French in 1972 and in English in 1980, uses Proust as its main test case while building a general system.

He separated the events of a story from the way they are told, and analysed the telling under order, duration and frequency: whether events are related in sequence, how long the telling dwells on them, and how often a single event is narrated. He also distinguished who speaks from who sees, introducing focalization to replace the looser idea of point of view.

His later work on paratexts examined titles, prefaces and covers as part of how a text is read.

tzvetan_todorov.name: Tzvetan Todorov
tzvetan_todorov.desc:
Bulgarian-French critic (1939-2017) who introduced the term narratology in his 1969 study of the Decameron, and who did much to bring Russian Formalist work to French readers.

He described narrative as a movement between states of equilibrium: an initial balance is disturbed, the disturbance is recognised and acted upon, and a new balance is reached that is not identical to the first. His book on the fantastic defined that mode by hesitation, the reader and often the character unable to decide whether events are supernatural or explicable.

His later writing turned away from formal analysis towards history, ethics and questions of totalitarianism and cultural encounter.

claude_levi_strauss.name: Claude Levi-Strauss
claude_levi_strauss.desc:
French anthropologist (1908-2009) who applied structural linguistics to myth. His 1955 essay The Structural Study of Myth argued that a myth's meaning lies not in the order of its events but in the pattern of relations between its smallest units, which he called mythemes.

On this reading myths work through binary oppositions, raw and cooked, nature and culture, life and death, and function to mediate contradictions a society cannot otherwise resolve. He also held that a myth consists of all its versions, so that no telling is more authentic than another.

His four-volume Mythologiques traced transformations of myths across the Americas.

mikhail_bakhtin.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
mikhail_bakhtin.desc:
Russian literary thinker (1895-1975) whose work, much of it written in obscurity and internal exile, reached Western readers mainly from the 1960s onwards.

He treated the novel as fundamentally dialogic: a meeting of many voices and social languages, not the expression of a single authorial consciousness. His study of Dostoevsky argued that those novels are polyphonic, with characters whose viewpoints are not subordinated to the author's. Heteroglossia names the stratified variety of speech a novel can hold, and the carnivalesque names the temporary inversion of hierarchy he traced through Rabelais.

Chronotope, his term for the way a genre binds time and space together, remains widely used.

viktor_shklovsky.name: Viktor Shklovsky
viktor_shklovsky.desc:
Russian critic and novelist (1893-1984), a leading figure in the Formalist circles of the 1910s and 1920s. His essay of 1917, usually translated as Art as Technique or Art as Device, argued that habit makes perception automatic and that the purpose of art is to make the familiar strange again so that it is genuinely seen.

The Russian term ostranenie, rendered as defamiliarization or estrangement, comes from this essay. Shklovsky also drew the distinction, taken up throughout later narratology, between the raw chronological material of a story and the arranged form in which it is told.

His reading of Tristram Shandy treated its digressions as the novel laying its own devices bare.

wayne_booth.name: Wayne C. Booth
wayne_booth.desc:
American critic (1921-2005) whose The Rhetoric of Fiction, published in 1961, pushed back against the then fashionable rule that novelists should always show rather than tell.

He argued that every narrative choice is rhetorical, that authorial commentary is a legitimate technique and not a lapse, and that a reader always infers an implied author from the text, distinct from both the historical writer and the narrator. The book introduced the term unreliable narrator for a narrator whose account the reader has reason to correct.

His later work on the ethics of fiction asked what kind of company a book keeps with its reader.

seymour_chatman.name: Seymour Chatman
seymour_chatman.desc:
American film and literary theorist (1928-2015) whose Story and Discourse, published in 1978, set out a clear two-level model of narrative for English-speaking readers: story, the content of what happened, and discourse, the means by which it is conveyed.

He worked across media, arguing that narrative structure is not tied to language and that novels and films can be analysed with a shared vocabulary while differing in what each medium can do. He distinguished kernels, events the plot cannot lose without changing, from satellites, which can be removed without collapsing the sequence.

Coming to Terms, published in 1990, extended the argument to film narration.

carl_jung.name: Carl Jung
carl_jung.desc:
Swiss psychiatrist (1875-1961) whose ideas about the collective unconscious gave twentieth-century storytelling much of its archetypal vocabulary.

He proposed that beneath personal experience lies a shared inherited layer of the psyche, expressed in recurring figures and situations he called archetypes: the shadow, the anima and animus, the wise old man, the trickster, the great mother. Dreams, myths and religious imagery were for him different surfacings of the same material.

The clinical status of these claims is disputed within psychology, but their effect on how myth and narrative are read, particularly through Campbell and later screenwriting manuals, has been very large.

sigmund_freud.name: Sigmund Freud
sigmund_freud.desc:
Austrian neurologist and founder of psychoanalysis (1856-1939), who read stories as structured like dreams and dreams as structured like stories.

The Interpretation of Dreams described dream-work as condensation and displacement, disguising latent content as manifest content, a model later borrowed to analyse how narratives handle what they cannot say directly. He took the name of the Oedipus complex from Sophocles, and his 1919 essay on the uncanny examined the unease produced by the familiar made strange, a foundation for later criticism of horror.

His interpretations of specific literary works are widely contested, but his terms remain embedded in narrative criticism.

walter_ong.name: Walter J. Ong
walter_ong.desc:
American Jesuit priest and scholar (1912-2003) whose Orality and Literacy, published in 1982, synthesised research on what changes when a culture acquires writing.

He argued that thought in a primary oral culture, one with no experience of writing at all, must be shaped for recall: additive rather than subordinated, formulaic, redundant, close to the concrete situations of daily life, and organised around memorable human action, not abstraction. Writing, he held, restructures consciousness, and print and electronic media restructure it again.

His notion of secondary orality describes the speech-based culture of broadcast and recorded media, which depends on literacy to exist.

milman_parry.name: Milman Parry
milman_parry.desc:
American classicist (1902-1935) who transformed the study of Homer by treating the poems' repeated phrases as evidence of technique, not as decoration.

His analysis of formulaic epithets, the swift-footed Achilles and wine-dark sea of the Iliad and Odyssey, showed that they fit specific metrical positions with striking economy, implying a system built for composition in performance. To test the theory against living practice he recorded South Slavic singers in Yugoslavia in the 1930s with his assistant Albert Lord.

He died at thirty-three before publishing the full argument, which Lord carried to completion.

albert_lord.name: Albert Lord
albert_lord.desc:
American scholar of oral literature (1912-1991) who worked as Milman Parry's assistant on the South Slavic fieldwork and, after Parry's death, completed and extended the argument.

The Singer of Tales, published in 1960, described how a guslar learns not a fixed text but a system: a stock of formulas and typical scenes from which a song is remade at each performance. On this account there is no single original version of an oral epic, only performances, and the question of how a long poem could be memorised is the wrong question.

The book reframed debate about how the Homeric poems were composed, and shaped oral tradition studies well beyond Greek.

antti_aarne.name: Antti Aarne
antti_aarne.desc:
Finnish folklorist (1867-1925) who published in 1910 a classification of folktale types, giving recurring plots numbers so that versions collected in different countries could be compared as instances of the same tale.

He worked in the historic-geographic method associated with the Finnish school, which assembled all known variants of a tale in order to reconstruct its diffusion and, ideally, its original form. The index he produced was designed as a practical tool for archives rather than a theory of narrative.

It was later revised and expanded by Stith Thompson and again by Hans-Jorg Uther, and is now cited as the ATU index.

stith_thompson.name: Stith Thompson
stith_thompson.desc:
American folklorist (1885-1976) who translated and twice enlarged Aarne's tale-type index, in 1928 and again in 1961, extending its coverage well beyond its original European base.

His larger undertaking was the Motif-Index of Folk-Literature, a multi-volume catalogue of the smallest recurring elements of traditional narrative, magic objects, tests, ogres, tabus, indexed so that a scholar could trace a single element across unrelated tales. Where the type index organises whole plots, the motif index organises their parts.

The two indexes together underpin comparative folktale scholarship, and their limitations, particularly a European bias in categories, are much discussed.

algirdas_greimas.name: Algirdas Julien Greimas
algirdas_greimas.desc:
Lithuanian-French semiotician (1917-1992) who generalised Propp's findings into an abstract model of narrative roles.

His actantial model, set out in Semantique structurale in 1966, reduces the participants of any story to six actants arranged in three pairs: subject and object, sender and receiver, helper and opponent. An actant is a structural position rather than a character, so one figure can occupy several positions and one position can be filled by an idea or an institution, not a person.

He also developed the semiotic square, a diagram for mapping the oppositions and contradictions underlying a text's meaning.

kenneth_burke.name: Kenneth Burke
kenneth_burke.desc:
American critic and rhetorician (1897-1993) who treated language as symbolic action and human motives as best analysed in dramatic terms.

A Grammar of Motives, published in 1945, set out the dramatistic pentad: any account of what someone did can be examined through act, scene, agent, agency and purpose, and through the ratios between them, since an explanation that stresses scene implies a different view of responsibility than one stressing agent. He also described literature as equipment for living, offering strategies for recurring situations.

His account of form as the arousing and fulfilling of an audience's expectation remains widely quoted.

jack_zipes.name: Jack Zipes
jack_zipes.desc:
American scholar of fairy tales and translator, born in 1937, who has argued that fairy tales are historical documents, not timeless expressions of the human spirit.

His work traces how oral wonder tales were reshaped as they were written down for particular audiences, at court in seventeenth-century France, in the nineteenth-century German bourgeois household, and later in mass entertainment, and how each revision carried a lesson about behaviour, gender and class. Breaking the Magic Spell, published in 1979, set out the case.

He has also written extensively on the Grimms, on Andersen, and on the film adaptations that now supply most people's version of these stories.

jerome_bruner.name: Jerome Bruner
jerome_bruner.desc:
American psychologist (1915-2016) who argued that people think in two distinct modes, and that psychology had attended almost only to one of them.

The paradigmatic mode reasons by logic, category and proof; the narrative mode makes sense of experience by casting it as a story with agents, intentions and consequences, and is judged by lifelikeness rather than truth conditions. Actual Minds, Possible Worlds, published in 1986, developed the distinction.

He went on to argue that people construct their identity as an ongoing self-narrative, revised as circumstances change, an idea that has been influential in developmental and clinical psychology as well as in narrative studies.

e_m_forster.name: E. M. Forster
e_m_forster.desc:
English novelist (1879-1970) whose 1927 Cambridge lectures, published as Aspects of the Novel, are among the most quoted books of practical criticism in English.

He distinguished story from plot with an example that has been repeated ever since: a king dying and then a queen dying is a story, whereas a queen dying of grief at the king's death is a plot, because causation has been added. He also separated flat characters, built from a single idea and instantly recognisable, from round ones capable of surprising the reader convincingly.

His own novels, among them Howards End and A Passage to India, are studied alongside the criticism.

griot.name: Griot Tradition
griot.desc:
The West African tradition of hereditary specialists in speech, music and history, known in Mande languages as jeli and in French and English as griots.

A jeli's work is genealogical, historical and social as well as artistic: reciting lineages, praising and advising patrons, mediating disputes and holding a community's record. The role is generally inherited within particular families, and training is long, taking place within them.

The Sunjata epic is the best-known part of the repertoire, performed, not fixed in a text. Practices differ across the region, and the single word griot flattens a range of distinct roles and traditions.

seanchai.name: Seanchai
seanchai.desc:
The Irish tradition of the traditional storyteller and keeper of lore, whose repertoire could include local legend, genealogy, place-name explanation and long wonder tales.

Telling took place in the house-visiting gatherings that Irish calls airneal or ceili, in a domestic rather than a courtly setting, and the material was passed on by listening over years. Some tellers were recorded holding tales that ran for hours.

From the 1930s the Irish Folklore Commission collected extensively from tellers in Irish and English, producing one of the largest folklore archives in Europe and preserving repertoires at the point where the practice was in steep decline.

rakugo.name: Rakugo
rakugo.desc:
Japanese comic storytelling in which a single performer, kneeling on a cushion, plays every character in a story using only a fan and a hand towel as props.

The performer distinguishes speakers by turning the head and altering voice and posture, so the audience keeps track of a conversation held by one person. Stories end in a punchline, the ochi or sage, and the classical repertoire is shared, so listeners often know the ending and attend for the telling.

The tradition developed from the Edo period onward, is organised in master-apprentice lineages with ranked grades, and is still performed in dedicated yose theatres.

wayang_kulit.name: Wayang Kulit
wayang_kulit.desc:
Indonesian shadow puppet theatre, most fully developed in Java and Bali, in which flat perforated leather figures are manipulated against a lit screen.

A single puppeteer, the dalang, operates the figures, narrates, speaks all the parts and cues the gamelan orchestra through a performance that traditionally runs through the night. The repertoire draws heavily on Javanese versions of the Mahabharata and Ramayana, alongside local cycles, and includes clown-servant characters who comment on the action and on contemporary affairs.

UNESCO has recognised the tradition as intangible cultural heritage, and it continues both in ritual settings and as public performance.

noh.name: Noh Theatre
noh.desc:
Japanese masked theatre developed in the fourteenth century by Kan'ami and his son Zeami under shogunal patronage, and performed continuously since.

Its pace is extremely slow by the standards of most theatre, its movement codified, and its texts dense with poetic allusion. A common structure has a traveller meet a local figure who proves in the second part to be the ghost of someone bound to that place, so that the play becomes the telling and reliving of a past event.

Zeami's treatises on training, audience and the pacing principle of jo-ha-kyu were written for transmission within the family and are now central to Japanese aesthetics.

kabuki.name: Kabuki
kabuki.desc:
Japanese popular theatre known for stylised acting, elaborate costume and makeup, and stage machinery including the revolving stage and the hanamichi walkway through the audience.

It is generally traced to performances led by Izumo no Okuni in Kyoto in the early seventeenth century. Women were subsequently barred from the stage by the authorities, and male actors specialising in female roles, the onnagata, became a defining feature of the form.

Its repertoire includes history plays, domestic tragedies and dance pieces, and much of it is shared with the bunraku puppet theatre, for which several of its best-known plays were originally written.

commedia_dellarte.name: Commedia dell'arte
commedia_dellarte.desc:
Italian professional touring theatre from the sixteenth century onward, performed by companies working from a scenario, not a script.

Actors specialised for life in fixed masked types, among them Arlecchino, Pantalone, the Dottore and the Capitano, and improvised dialogue around an outline of entrances and plot beats, deploying rehearsed comic routines known as lazzi. Women performed professionally in these companies, which was unusual in Europe at the time.

The types and situations passed into scripted comedy through Moliere and others, and the practice remains a reference point for improvisation and physical comedy training.

norse_saga.name: Icelandic Saga
norse_saga.desc:
Prose narratives written in Iceland, mainly in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, recounting the feuds, settlements and lawsuits of families in the generations after the island's settlement.

Their manner is distinctive: laconic, externally focused, reporting speech and action without commentary and rarely entering a character's mind, so that motive must be inferred from behaviour. Genealogy and legal procedure are given close attention.

The relationship between written sagas and prior oral tradition has been debated for a century, between those who see them as transcribed tradition and those who emphasise the literary construction of the surviving texts.

troubadour.name: Troubadours
troubadour.desc:
Composer-poets of the courts of what is now southern France, writing in Occitan from the late eleventh century to the thirteenth.

Their songs elaborated the conventions of fin'amor, later called courtly love, in which a poet serves a lady of higher status through devotion, discretion and suffering. The related trobairitz were women poets working in the same tradition, and the trouveres of the north and Minnesanger of the German lands developed comparable practices.

The imagery and emotional grammar established there passed into the medieval romance and, through it, into a long line of European narrative about love.

pansori.name: Pansori
pansori.desc:
Korean musical storytelling in which a single singer performs a long narrative accompanied by one drummer, alternating sung passages with spoken narration and gesture.

A full performance of one of the surviving stories can last several hours, and the drummer punctuates it with calls of encouragement, as does the audience, so the telling is openly a shared event. Five narratives survive of a larger historical repertoire, among them the widely performed Chunhyangga.

The form developed from the seventeenth century onward, was carried by professional performers of low social status, and is listed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage.

hakawati.name: Hakawati
hakawati.desc:
The professional storyteller of Arab coffeehouses, particularly in Syria, Lebanon and Egypt, who performed long serialised narratives to a regular audience over many nights.

The repertoire included heroic cycles such as the romance of Antar and the epic of the Bani Hilal, as well as material overlapping with One Thousand and One Nights. Performances typically broke at a moment of suspense so that listeners would return the following evening, and audiences were vocal participants rather than silent.

The practice declined sharply with radio and television, though it has been revived in festival and theatrical settings.

songlines.name: Aboriginal Australian Songlines
songlines.desc:
In many Aboriginal Australian traditions, sung narrative sequences that follow the routes of ancestral beings across country, tying story, land, law, ceremony and navigation together.

Sections of a track are held by particular groups with responsibilities for them, and knowledge is often restricted according to age, gender and initiation, so it is neither public nor uniform. The English term songline was popularised by Bruce Chatwin's 1987 book and is regarded by many as an imprecise outsider's label for practices that differ greatly between peoples and languages.

They are living cultural property, not folklore of the past.

poetics.name: Poetics
poetics.desc:
Aristotle's short treatise on poetic composition, written in the fourth century BCE and surviving in a condensed form that reads like lecture notes.

It defines tragedy as the imitation of an action that is serious and complete, of a certain magnitude, and analyses it into six parts, of which plot is the most important and spectacle the least. It sets out the value of complex plots that turn on reversal and recognition together, prefers a unified action to a unified hero, and argues that the poet's task is to relate what could happen rather than what did.

The treatment of comedy that ancient sources describe as its second book has not survived.

epic_of_gilgamesh.name: Epic of Gilgamesh
epic_of_gilgamesh.desc:
Mesopotamian poem preserved on clay tablets in Akkadian, with earlier Sumerian poems about the same king behind it. The version usually read today, the Standard Babylonian text, is associated in ancient sources with the scribe Sin-leqi-unninni.

It follows the king of Uruk, his friendship with the wild man Enkidu, Enkidu's death, and Gilgamesh's failed search for immortality, ending with him back at the walls of his own city. A flood narrative told to him by a survivor closely parallels the account in Genesis.

The tablets were recovered from the library at Nineveh in the nineteenth century, and the flood passage was identified by George Smith in 1872.

iliad.name: The Iliad
iliad.desc:
Greek epic attributed to Homer, treating a few weeks in the tenth year of the siege of Troy, not the whole war.

Its announced subject is the anger of Achilles: his withdrawal from the fighting after a quarrel over honour, the death of Patroclus in his armour, his return and killing of Hector, and the night visit of Priam to beg for his son's body. Beginning in the middle of the war and ending before its conclusion, it is the standard illustration of an epic's selective focus.

The repeated epithets and typical scenes that Parry analysed run throughout, evidence of composition within an oral tradition.

odyssey.name: The Odyssey
odyssey.desc:
Greek epic attributed to Homer, following Odysseus's ten-year return from Troy and the situation at home, where his household is besieged by suitors.

Structurally it is far more elaborate than the Iliad. It begins with the son rather than the father, opens the main action years into the journey, and places the most famous adventures, the Cyclops, Circe, the underworld, the Sirens, in a long flashback narrated by Odysseus himself to his hosts, which makes the hero his own unreliable storyteller.

The pattern of departure, ordeal and disguised return has been treated by Campbell and others as a template for the heroic journey.

mahabharata.name: Mahabharata
mahabharata.desc:
Sanskrit epic traditionally attributed to Vyasa, telling of the dynastic war between the Pandava and Kaurava cousins, and one of the longest poems known.

It is built from nested frames: the story is recited to a king by a bard who heard it from another, and it absorbs vast quantities of genealogy, myth, and instruction on duty and statecraft, including the Bhagavad Gita, the dialogue between Arjuna and Krishna before the battle. The text itself claims that what is not in it is found nowhere.

It grew over centuries, and is a living source for theatre, film and television across South and Southeast Asia.

ramayana.name: Ramayana
ramayana.desc:
Sanskrit epic attributed to Valmiki, narrating Rama's exile, the abduction of his wife Sita by Ravana, the alliance with the monkey army, the war in Lanka and the return to Ayodhya.

It is a foundational religious and literary text and exists in many regional and linguistic versions, among them Tulsidas's Hindi Ramcharitmanas, the Tamil Kamba Ramayanam, and versions in Thailand, Indonesia, Cambodia and elsewhere, which differ substantially in emphasis and event.

The multiplicity is intrinsic, not incidental: the tradition has long accommodated many tellings, and the story is performed annually in the Ramlila theatre cycles of northern India.

natyashastra.name: Natyashastra
natyashastra.desc:
Sanskrit treatise on dramatic arts attributed to Bharata Muni, dated by scholars somewhere in the wide range between roughly 200 BCE and 200 CE.

It covers theatre building, gesture, movement, costume, music, plot types and the emotional effect of performance, and is the source of rasa theory, which describes how a performance transforms depicted emotional states into an aesthetic flavour experienced by the audience. Eight rasas appear in the text, including the erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the furious and the marvellous.

It remains a working reference for classical Indian dance and drama, and its account of audience response invites comparison with Aristotle on catharsis.

oedipus_rex.name: Oedipus Rex
oedipus_rex.desc:
Tragedy by Sophocles, first performed in Athens in the fifth century BCE, in which a king investigating a plague discovers that the murderer he is hunting is himself, and that the prophecy he fled has already been fulfilled.

The play is a detective story running backwards: nothing decisive happens on stage except the uncovering of what has already happened. Aristotle used it repeatedly in the Poetics as his example of reversal and recognition arriving in the same stroke.

Freud took its name for the complex he described, a use that says more about his theory than about Sophocles' play, in which Oedipus acts in ignorance throughout.

one_thousand_and_one_nights.name: One Thousand and One Nights
one_thousand_and_one_nights.desc:
A collection of stories in Arabic, assembled over centuries from Persian, Indian, Mesopotamian and Egyptian material, with no single authoritative text; the manuscripts differ widely in which tales they contain.

The frame of Scheherazade telling stories to defer her execution holds a body of tales that themselves contain further tales, several layers deep, making it among the most elaborate surviving examples of nested narration.

Antoine Galland's French translation, published from 1704, brought the collection to Europe and added stories not found in his Arabic manuscript, including Aladdin and Ali Baba, which he recorded from the Syrian storyteller Hanna Diyab.

panchatantra.name: Panchatantra
panchatantra.desc:
Sanskrit collection of animal fables in five books, traditionally attributed to Vishnu Sharma and conventionally dated to around the third century CE, though the material is older.

Its frame has a teacher undertaking to educate three unpromising princes in statecraft through stories, and tales are nested inside tales as characters illustrate arguments with further examples. The concerns are practical rather than pious: alliance, betrayal, the management of subordinates and the reading of intentions.

It travelled west through a Middle Persian version into Arabic as Kalila wa-Dimna and from there into Hebrew, Latin and the European vernaculars, making it one of the most widely translated secular books of the pre-modern world.

aesops_fables.name: Aesop's Fables
aesops_fables.desc:
A corpus of short Greek fables, mostly with animal characters and an appended moral, gathered under the name of Aesop, not written by a single hand.

The stories are extremely compressed: a situation, a choice, a consequence, often in a few dozen words. That makes them a useful demonstration of how little material a narrative needs. The fox and the grapes, the tortoise and the hare and the boy who cried wolf have entered ordinary speech as shorthand.

The collection grew by accretion over centuries, absorbing material from other traditions, and reached modern Europe largely through Latin verse versions and later through printed collections such as La Fontaine's.

beowulf.name: Beowulf
beowulf.desc:
Old English heroic poem of just over three thousand lines, surviving in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was damaged by fire in 1731.

The hero fights Grendel, then Grendel's mother, and returns fifty years later as an old king to face a dragon and die of the wound. The poem is set in Scandinavia, not England, and moves constantly between the main action and digressions into feuds and genealogies that its first audience evidently knew.

The date of composition is contested across a range of some three centuries. J. R. R. Tolkien's 1936 lecture argued that it should be read as a poem rather than mined as a historical document.

tale_of_genji.name: The Tale of Genji
tale_of_genji.desc:
Japanese prose narrative written by Murasaki Shikibu in the early eleventh century, following the life of an emperor's son and, in its final chapters, the generation that follows him.

It is frequently described as the world's first novel, a claim that depends on how the novel is defined, but its sustained interest in the inner life of many characters over decades is genuinely unusual for its date. Poems exchanged between characters carry much of the emotional weight, and social position governs everything.

It was written in Japanese by a woman of the court at a time when men wrote official prose in Chinese, and circulated in manuscript among court readers.

journey_to_the_west.name: Journey to the West
journey_to_the_west.desc:
Chinese novel published in the sixteenth century, conventionally attributed to Wu Cheng'en though the attribution is not certain, based on the historical pilgrimage of the monk Xuanzang to India for Buddhist scriptures.

The historical journey is transformed into a comic and fantastical quest in which the monk is escorted by the Monkey King Sun Wukong, the pig Zhu Bajie and the monk Sha Wujing through a long series of encounters with demons. Sun Wukong's rebellion against heaven occupies the opening chapters and made him one of the most adapted characters in East Asian culture.

It is counted among the four great classical Chinese novels.

the_decameron.name: The Decameron
the_decameron.desc:
Boccaccio's collection of a hundred novellas, written in the years around 1350, set within a frame in which ten young people leave plague-stricken Florence for the countryside and tell stories over ten days.

Each day has an appointed theme and a ruler who sets it, and the tellers comment on each other's tales, so the frame is a functioning society, not a mere container. The stories range from farce and sexual trickery to accounts of generosity and grief.

The book supplied plots to later European writers, including Chaucer and Shakespeare, and Todorov used it as the subject of the 1969 study in which he introduced the term narratology.

canterbury_tales.name: The Canterbury Tales
canterbury_tales.desc:
Chaucer's unfinished collection, written in Middle English mostly in verse, in which pilgrims travelling from Southwark to Canterbury tell stories in a competition proposed by their host.

The plan announced in the General Prologue, four tales from each pilgrim, was never completed; what survives is a set of fragments whose order varies between manuscripts. The interest lies in the friction between tellers: tales are told in reply, in mockery, or in drunken interruption, so that the frame keeps commenting on its own contents.

The range of registers, from the Knight's romance to the Miller's fabliau, is unusually wide for a single work of its period.

don_quixote.name: Don Quixote
don_quixote.desc:
Cervantes's novel, published in two parts in 1605 and 1615, about a gentleman who reads so many chivalric romances that he sets out to live one.

The comedy comes from the collision between his narration of events and everyone else's, and the book layers this further by presenting itself as a translation of an Arabic manuscript by a historian whose reliability the narrator questions. In Part Two the characters have read Part One and treat the knight accordingly, and the text takes public notice of a spurious sequel published under another writer's name.

It is routinely cited as the point at which the European novel begins.

hamlet.name: Hamlet
hamlet.desc:
Shakespeare's tragedy, written around 1600, in which a prince is charged by his father's ghost to avenge a murder and delays.

The play draws on a Scandinavian legend recorded by Saxo Grammaticus and transmitted through Belleforest, and probably on a lost earlier English play. It puts a play within itself, staged to catch the conscience of the king, and gives its protagonist soliloquies that turn the revenge plot into an interrogation of action and knowledge.

Three substantially different early texts survive, the 1603 and 1604 quartos and the 1623 folio, and every modern edition is an editorial decision about how to combine them.

grimms_fairy_tales.name: Grimms' Fairy Tales
grimms_fairy_tales.desc:
Kinder- und Hausmarchen, the Grimms' collection of German tales, published in two volumes in 1812 and 1815 and revised through seven editions to 1857.

The first edition was an annotated scholarly work; later editions were reshaped for household reading, with Wilhelm expanding dialogue, adding Christian colouring and removing sexual material, while violence against wrongdoers was often intensified rather than softened. Comparison of editions is a standard exercise in fairy tale scholarship.

The brothers presented the tales as an inheritance of the German folk, though several came to them through French-descended informants and some derive from printed sources.

frankenstein.name: Frankenstein
frankenstein.desc:
Mary Shelley's novel, published anonymously in 1818 and revised in 1831, in which a student animates a body and abandons what he has made.

It is built as a set of nested narrations: letters from an Arctic explorer enclose Victor Frankenstein's account, which encloses the creature's own first-person narrative at the centre, so the reader reaches the most sympathetic voice only through two hostile intermediaries.

By Shelley's own account in the 1831 introduction, the story began with a waking dream during a ghost-story competition among the party at Lake Geneva in 1816; this is her retrospective telling, and its details have been much discussed.

morphology_of_the_folktale.name: Morphology of the Folktale
morphology_of_the_folktale.desc:
Propp's study, published in Russian in 1928 and translated into English in 1958, analysing a corpus of Russian wonder tales taken from Afanasyev's collection.

Its method is to set aside subject matter and describe each tale as a sequence of functions, acts defined by their significance for the course of the action, such as the interdiction, the violation, the departure, the donor's test, the struggle, the return and the recognition. Propp lists thirty-one, argues their order is fixed even where many are absent, and assigns the characters to seven spheres of action.

Levi-Strauss's critical review and Propp's reply became a set text in structuralist debate.

hero_with_a_thousand_faces.name: The Hero with a Thousand Faces
hero_with_a_thousand_faces.desc:
Campbell's comparative study, published in 1949, which assembles myths from many cultures to argue that they share one adventure, described in three broad movements of separation, initiation and return, elaborated into a longer series of stages.

The stages include the call to adventure, refusal of the call, supernatural aid, crossing the threshold, the belly of the whale, the road of trials, atonement with the father, apotheosis and the return with the boon. Campbell reads these psychologically, following Jung.

Folklorists have criticised the selection of evidence and the flattening of cultural difference; the book's influence on twentieth-century screen storytelling has been all the same very large.

atu_index.name: Aarne-Thompson-Uther Index
atu_index.desc:
The standard catalogue of international folktale types, begun by Antti Aarne in 1910, translated and twice enlarged by Stith Thompson in 1928 and 1961, and revised by Hans-Jorg Uther in 2004.

Each recurring plot receives a number, so that versions collected in different times and places can be identified as the same tale: ATU 510A is Cinderella, ATU 333 is Little Red Riding Hood, ATU 425 covers the search for the lost husband. The numbers make comparative work possible without privileging any one version as the original.

Its European origins and categories have been criticised as a poor fit for some other traditions.

popol_vuh.name: Popol Vuh
popol_vuh.desc:
The narrative of the K'iche' Maya of highland Guatemala, covering the creation of the world, the failed attempts to make human beings, the adventures of the Hero Twins in the underworld of Xibalba, and the origins of the K'iche' lineages.

The surviving text descends from an alphabetic manuscript in K'iche' made in the sixteenth century, copied and translated into Spanish in the early eighteenth century by the Dominican friar Francisco Ximenez, whose copy is the earliest known.

Episodes in it correspond to imagery on Maya ceramics of far earlier date, which indicates the material long predates the colonial-era manuscript.

epic_of_sundiata.name: Epic of Sundiata
epic_of_sundiata.desc:
Mande epic of West Africa, telling of Sundiata Keita, the thirteenth-century founder of the Mali Empire: his birth to a hunchbacked mother, his inability to walk as a child, his exile, and his return to defeat the sorcerer-king Sumanguru.

It is transmitted by jeliw, the hereditary bards often called griots in French and English, and exists in performance, not in a single fixed text; published versions are transcriptions of particular performances by named singers, such as the widely read one recorded from Mamadou Kouyate.

It is a working example of a long narrative sustained by oral tradition into the present day.

one_hundred_years_of_solitude.name: One Hundred Years of Solitude
one_hundred_years_of_solitude.desc:
Garcia Marquez's novel, published in 1967, following seven generations of the Buendia family in the town of Macondo from its founding to its disappearance.

Repeating names and repeating events give the chronicle a circular shape, and marvellous occurrences, a rain of yellow flowers, a woman ascending into the sky, are reported in the same flat register as the weather. A massacre of banana plantation workers, based on a historical episode in Colombia, is remembered by one survivor and denied by everyone else.

It became the most widely read work of the Latin American boom and the standard reference point for magical realism.

things_fall_apart.name: Things Fall Apart
things_fall_apart.desc:
Achebe's first novel, published in 1958, centred on Okonkwo, a wrestler and titled man of an Igbo village, and on the arrival of missionaries and colonial administration.

The first part establishes the community's law, festivals, kinship obligations and disagreements in their own terms before any European appears, so that what follows is a disruption of a functioning order rather than an encounter with a blank. The prose is dense with proverbs, which Achebe's narrator describes as the oil with which words are eaten.

The closing paragraph shifts to the District Commissioner's planned book, reducing the whole novel to a paragraph in his study of pacification.

ulysses.name: Ulysses
ulysses.desc:
Joyce's novel, published in Paris in 1922, covering a single day in Dublin, 16 June 1904, and mapping its episodes onto the Odyssey.

Each chapter takes a different technique: newspaper headlines, a catechism of questions and answers, a parody sequence tracing the history of English prose, and a closing monologue of unpunctuated thought. The correspondence with Homer is structural, not plot-level, and Joyce supplied schemas to friends that assign each episode an organ, art, colour and symbol.

Its serialisation in the United States was halted by an obscenity prosecution, and the book was not legally published there until 1934.

rashomon_film.name: Rashomon
rashomon_film.desc:
Kurosawa's film of 1950, which recounts an assault and a death in a forest through the irreconcilable testimonies of a bandit, a woman, the dead man speaking through a medium, and a woodcutter.

It adapts two stories by Ryunosuke Akutagawa, taking its setting and title from Rashomon and its structure from In a Grove. No account is confirmed, and the film declines to supply the true version.

Its success at Venice in 1951 brought Japanese cinema to wide Western attention, and its name has passed into general use for situations in which participants give incompatible accounts of the same event.

citizen_kane.name: Citizen Kane
citizen_kane.desc:
Film released in 1941, directed by Orson Welles, in which a reporter investigating a newspaper magnate's dying word interviews people who knew him, and the life is assembled from their partial and conflicting recollections.

The structure withholds chronology and gives the answer to the audience alone in the final shot, without telling anyone in the film. Its deep-focus photography by Gregg Toland and its overlapping sound design were widely imitated.

Welles and Herman J. Mankiewicz share the screenplay credit, and the division of the writing between them has been disputed since Pauline Kael's 1971 essay, with detailed cases made on both sides.

star_wars.name: Star Wars
star_wars.desc:
Film released in 1977, written and directed by George Lucas, in which a farm boy leaves a desert planet with an old mentor, rescues a princess and destroys a battle station.

It is the most cited modern example of the heroic pattern that Campbell described, and Lucas has spoken publicly about Campbell's importance to him; the two later appeared in conversation, and Lucas has said the work helped him give shape to his drafts. Accounts differ on how early in the writing that influence took hold.

Its commercial success reshaped studio economics around sequels, merchandising and effects-driven event films.

in_cold_blood.name: In Cold Blood
in_cold_blood.desc:
Truman Capote's account of the 1959 murder of a Kansas farming family and the trial and execution of the two men convicted of it, serialised in 1965 and published as a book in 1966.

Capote described it as a nonfiction novel, applying scene construction, dialogue and shifting viewpoint to reported material, and the book became a founding text for literary journalism. He worked on it for years with Harper Lee, who conducted much of the early interviewing.

Journalists and scholars have since documented invented and altered details, including the closing scene. That makes it a standing test case for the limits of narrative in reporting.

links.details:
The Poetics survives in a compressed form that reads like notes for lectures rather than a finished treatise, which accounts for its abruptness and for the amount of argument its key terms have generated.

What it does contain is the earliest systematic account of how narrative works in the Western tradition: the definition of tragedy, the ranking of its six parts, and the analysis of plot into simple and complex kinds.

The attribution is traditional. Ancient sources assign both epics to a single poet, but the formulaic technique that Parry identified in them implies composition within an oral tradition, so authorship in the modern sense may not be the right question.

The Iliad's selection of a few weeks from a ten-year war shows an organising intelligence at work on inherited material, whoever exercised it.

Antiquity assigned the Odyssey to the same poet as the Iliad, and ancient scholars already disputed it. Differences in vocabulary, outlook and structure have kept the question open.

The Odyssey's handling of narrative is markedly more complex: it begins late, withholds its hero for four books, and gives its most famous episodes to the hero himself to narrate.

Tradition names Valmiki as the poem's author and also places him inside it, sheltering Sita and teaching the epic to her sons, so that the poem contains the scene of its own transmission.

Scholars treat the surviving text as the growth of centuries around an earlier core. That makes the attribution a statement about a tradition, not a claim about one writer.

Vyasa is credited with composing the epic and appears within it as an ancestor of both warring families, so the traditional author is also a participant in the events.

The poem describes its own making as dictation to Ganesha, and frames the whole as a recitation to a king by a bard who heard it from another, layering the transmission into the text itself.

The treatise is attributed to Bharata, but whether that names an individual, a lineage of teachers or an editorial tradition is unresolved, and the text shows signs of compilation.

Its scope goes far beyond playwriting to cover theatre construction, gesture, music, costume and the emotional effect of performance, which is what makes it a source for rasa theory.

The attribution is conventional, not documented. The fables circulated orally and were collected under Aesop's name long after the period to which the ancient legends assign him, and the corpus continued to absorb new material for centuries.

What the name marks is a manner, extreme brevity with an appended moral, rather than the output of a known writer.

Sophocles wrote the play for the Athenian dramatic festivals, working with a myth his audience already knew, so that the interest lay wholly in the handling.

His solution was to make the entire action an investigation: everything decisive has already occurred, and the play stages only its discovery. Aristotle repeatedly used it as his example of the finest kind of plot construction.

Murasaki wrote it in Japanese as a lady-in-waiting at the Heian court, in a period when men wrote prestige prose in Chinese, and it circulated in manuscript among court readers.

Her diary of court life survives alongside it, which is unusual for a writer of that date and supplies some context for the world the tale describes.

Chaucer left the collection unfinished, well short of the scheme announced in the General Prologue, and the surviving manuscripts disagree about the order of the fragments.

His distinctive move was to make the tellers matter as much as the tales, so that a story is understood partly as a bid in an argument among the pilgrims.

Boccaccio wrote in Tuscan vernacular prose in the years after the plague of 1348, which he describes in the introduction and uses as the reason his ten storytellers withdraw to the countryside.

Setting an orderly ritual of storytelling against a city in collapse gives the collection its frame and much of its point.

Cervantes published the two parts a decade apart, in 1605 and 1615, and the interval became part of the book: in Part Two his characters have read Part One and are known by it.

He also used Part Two to answer a spurious continuation issued under another name, absorbing the rival book into his own fiction.

Shakespeare worked from existing material, a Scandinavian legend transmitted through Belleforest and probably a lost earlier English play, and the originality lies in what he did with the revenge structure rather than in the story.

Three substantially different early texts survive, so every modern edition of the play is an editorial construction from them.

The brothers gathered and edited, not invented, but the editing was extensive: Wilhelm reworked the tales across seven editions, expanding dialogue, adjusting content for family reading and shaping a consistent style.

Comparing the 1812 first edition with the 1857 last is a standard exercise, because it shows how much of what readers take to be traditional is editorial.

Propp published the study in 1928 in Leningrad, working on a corpus of Russian wonder tales drawn from Afanasyev's collection.

It attracted little attention outside the Soviet Union until an English translation appeared in 1958, after which it became a founding document of structuralist narrative analysis three decades after it was written.
