Campbell assembled myths from many traditions to argue for a single underlying adventure, reading the pattern psychologically after Jung.

The book was published in 1949 and reached a far larger audience decades later, partly through its adoption by filmmakers and partly through his 1988 television conversations with Bill Moyers.

Aarne published the original tale-type index in 1910 as a working tool for archives, giving recurring plots numbers so that versions collected in different countries could be filed and compared.

His categories reflected the Northern European material he knew best, a bias later revisions have been criticised for carrying forward.

Thompson translated Aarne's index and enlarged it twice, in 1928 and 1961, extending its coverage well beyond its original European base and giving the catalogue the form in which most scholars used it for half a century.

His separate Motif-Index catalogued the smaller recurring elements from which tales are built, so the two indexes work at different scales.

Garcia Marquez has described looking for years for the tone that would let him write the book, and finding it in the manner of his grandmother's telling, in which extraordinary things were reported without any change of expression.

His earlier work as a reporter shows in the precision of physical detail that anchors the marvellous events.

Achebe wrote his first novel in English while working in Nigerian broadcasting, and structured it so that the Igbo community is established in its own terms before any European appears.

The prose carries proverbs and oral rhythms into the English sentence, a deliberate appropriation of the coloniser's language that he defended in his essays.

Joyce worked on the novel for seven years and published it in Paris in 1922 after its American serialisation was stopped by an obscenity prosecution.

He gave each episode its own technique and supplied friends with schemas assigning organs, arts and colours to them, which has shaped how the book is read ever since.

Kurosawa combined two stories by Ryunosuke Akutagawa, taking the setting and title from one and the structure of conflicting testimony from the other.

The film's success at Venice in 1951 opened Japanese cinema to Western audiences, and its title has since become shorthand for irreconcilable accounts of a single event.

Welles directed, starred in and shares the screenplay credit with Herman J. Mankiewicz. How the writing was divided has been disputed since Pauline Kael's 1971 essay, with detailed cases advanced on both sides, and the question is not settled.

What is not disputed is the film's assembly of a life from partial recollections, a structure Welles had already explored in radio.

Aristotle opens the Poetics by grouping epic, tragedy, comedy and dithyramb together as kinds of imitation, differing only in medium, object and manner. Imitation is treated as natural to human beings and as the source of the pleasure audiences take in representations of things they would find painful to witness directly.

The move matters because it makes storytelling a craft with describable rules, not a form of inspiration or possession, which is roughly the position Plato had taken.

The definition of tragedy in the sixth chapter of the Poetics ends by saying that the imitation of a serious action accomplishes, through pity and fear, the catharsis of such emotions. The sentence is a single clause and Aristotle never returns to explain it.

Everything since has been interpretation: a purging of excess feeling, a clarification or tempering of it, or a structural resolution belonging to the plot, not to the audience. The ambiguity has kept the term productive rather than settled.

Aristotle argues that the best tragic plot involves a person neither outstandingly virtuous nor wicked, whose change of fortune comes about through hamartia rather than through vice. The reasoning is functional: a wholly good figure destroyed produces revulsion, a wicked one destroyed produces satisfaction, and neither yields pity and fear.

Later criticism narrowed the term into the moralised idea of a tragic flaw, a reading the Greek does not require, since it covers error and misjudgement as readily as defect of character.

Peripeteia is named in the Poetics as one of the two devices that distinguish a complex plot from a simple one: a reversal in which an action produces the opposite of its intended effect. Aristotle's requirement is that it follow by probability or necessity from what has gone before, not that it merely surprise.

His example is the messenger who comes to relieve Oedipus of his fear about his parentage and, by telling him what he knows, destroys him.

The second mark of a complex plot is anagnorisis, a change from ignorance to knowledge, which Aristotle rates most highly when it coincides with the reversal and arises from the structure of the events themselves.

He ranks the available kinds, placing recognition through tokens and birthmarks lowest and recognition that follows from the action highest. The hierarchy is an early statement of a durable craft principle: the revelation should be earned by the plot, not delivered by a device.

The phrase comes from the Ars Poetica, where Horace praises the poet who plunges the audience into the middle of things instead of beginning at the egg from which Helen was hatched. He offers Homer as the model, since the Odyssey opens with its hero already stranded in the tenth year of his return.

The advice was formulated for epic and inherited by the novel and by film, where it is now standard rather than daring.

The Natyashastra sets out rasa as the flavour or aesthetic essence that a performance produces in a prepared spectator, generated from the combination of determinants, consequents and transitory states that the treatise catalogues in detail.

Its enumeration of the principal rasas, together with the corresponding durable emotions, gave Indian dramaturgy a systematic account of audience response centuries before European criticism attempted one. Later commentators, notably Abhinavagupta, developed the theory considerably beyond the text.

Jo-ha-kyu was not the invention of Zeami, the fourteenth-century actor and playwright who shaped noh: the three-part movement from slow introduction through development to rapid conclusion was already established in court gagaku music. What Zeami did in his treatises was generalise it into a governing principle of noh.

He applies it at every scale at once, to a whole day's programme of plays, to a single play, to a scene, and to an individual gesture, so that the pattern nests inside itself. It remains one of the clearest formulations of pacing as a structural rather than decorative concern.

Freytag's 1863 study of dramatic technique diagrammed the five-act play as a rising and falling movement through introduction, rise, climax, return and catastrophe. He drew his examples from Greek tragedy and Shakespeare, and intended the shape as a description of a specific historical practice.

In later use the diagram detached itself from its evidence and became a general template applied to novels, short stories and screenplays, usually flattened into a single peak with a long tail.

Working from a corpus of Russian wonder tales, Propp argued that the characters and their attributes vary endlessly while their actions do not. He reduced the tales to thirty-one functions, defined as acts significant for the course of the action, which always occur in the same order even though no single tale contains all of them.

The method was deliberately morphological, not historical or psychological: he was describing the grammar of a tale type, not its meaning or origin.

The Lithuanian-French semiotician Algirdas Greimas generalised Propp's findings into six actants arranged in three pairs: subject and object, sender and receiver, helper and opponent. An actant is a structural position, not a person, so one character may occupy several and one position may be filled by an abstraction, an institution or an absent ideal.

The abstraction is the point. It let the analysis extend beyond folk tales to any narrative, and to texts in which the antagonist is a condition rather than a villain.

Campbell drew the word monomyth from Finnegans Wake and used it for the single pattern he claimed underlies hero narratives across cultures: separation from the ordinary world, initiation through trials, and return with something of value.

His synthesis was comparative and psychological, leaning on Jung, and it has been criticised by folklorists for selecting evidence to fit the template and for flattening the specificity of the traditions it draws on. Its influence on twentieth-century popular storytelling is nonetheless difficult to overstate.

Jung used archetype for the inherited, universal forms he held to structure the collective unconscious, distinguishing the archetype itself, which he considered unrepresentable, from the images through which it appears in dreams, myths and art.

The concept passed into literary and popular use largely stripped of that distinction, becoming a vocabulary of recurring character types. Whatever its standing as psychology, it supplied criticism and screenwriting with a durable set of terms.

The shadow in Jung's scheme is the part of the personality that the conscious self refuses to recognise as its own, and which is therefore encountered outside, projected onto other people or figures.

Translated into narrative terms, this makes the antagonist a function of the protagonist rather than an independent obstacle, and it explains the recurring structure in which defeating the enemy requires acknowledging a likeness to it. Story manuals adopted the term wholesale.

Freud's 1919 essay on the uncanny takes up Otto Rank's study of the double, arguing that the figure begins as an insurance against extinction and becomes, once that stage of thought is passed, a harbinger of death.

He reads the uncanny generally as the return of something long familiar that has been repressed, which accounts for the particular discomfort of encountering a duplicate of oneself. The essay remains the standard reference point for critical work on doubles, mirrors and automata.

In his 1917 essay on art as device, Shklovsky argued that habit devours objects, and that the purpose of art is to restore the sensation of things by making the familiar strange and by deliberately prolonging the process of perception.

His examples include Tolstoy's technique of describing a practice without naming it, so that it must be seen, not recognised. The idea gave formalism its most portable concept and fed directly into Brecht's theatre.

The formalist separation of fabula from syuzhet distinguishes the events in their chronological and causal order from the arrangement in which the work presents them. Shklovsky used the distinction to argue that plot is made precisely by the deformation of the story material.

Every later narratological pair of terms for the same split, including story and discourse, descends from this one. It is the analytic move that makes flashback, withheld information and unreliable narration describable rather than merely noticeable.

Bakhtin's chronotope names the intrinsic connectedness of time and space in a narrative, treating the two as a single fused category that defines a genre. The road, the threshold, the provincial town and the castle each carry their own temporality and their own possibilities for encounter.

His essay traces the chronotopes of the Greek romance, the adventure novel and the chivalric romance, arguing that changing the chronotope changes what kinds of event can occur at all.

In his study of Dostoevsky, Bakhtin argued that the novels are polyphonic: they contain a plurality of independent consciousnesses that are not subordinated to a single authorial viewpoint, and whose voices are never finalised by the narrator.

He contrasted this with the monologic novel, where every voice is ultimately placed by the author. The concept underwrites his broader account of the novel as the genre in which competing social languages meet without being resolved.

Genette introduced focalization to separate two questions that point of view had confused: who speaks and who sees. A narrator may report events from outside while restricting the reader's knowledge to what a particular character perceives.

He distinguished zero focalization, where the narration exceeds any character's knowledge, internal focalization, tied to one or more characters, and external focalization, which reports behaviour without access to thought. The scheme remains the standard analytic vocabulary.

Booth coined the term in The Rhetoric of Fiction in 1961, defining a narrator as reliable when speaking or acting in accordance with the norms of the work, and unreliable when not. The formulation depends on his related idea of the implied author, the version of the writer the text itself constructs.

By locating the unreliability in a gap between narrator and work, not in mere dishonesty, he made it possible to analyse narrators who are sincere and still wrong.

In Aspects of the Novel, Forster separated story from plot with an example that has outlasted the book: a sequence of events reported in order is a story, and the same events joined by causation are a plot. The reader of the first asks what happened next, the reader of the second asks why.

His distinction is looser than the formalists' but reached a far wider audience, and it survives in every workshop that asks whether a scene is connected to the one before it by therefore or merely by and then.

Forster's division of characters into flat and round is the other term from Aspects of the Novel in general circulation. A flat character is constructed around a single idea or quality and can be summarised in a sentence; a round one is capable of surprising the reader convincingly.

He was careful not to treat flatness as failure, noting that flat characters are easily recognised, easily remembered, and indispensable to comic and satirical writing.

Field's Screenplay in 1979 codified the paradigm that dominated American screenwriting instruction for the next generation: three acts of roughly a quarter, a half and a quarter, joined by two plot points that turn the action in a new direction, with page numbers attached.

The three-act division was old; the innovation was the timing. By specifying where the turns should fall in a standard hundred-and-twenty-page script, Field turned a descriptive scheme into a template that could be checked.

Snyder's 2005 manual reduced the screenplay to fifteen named beats with page numbers, from the opening image through the catalyst, the midpoint and the dark night of the soul to the final image. The title comes from his advice that the hero do something likeable early on.

The sheet is the most prescriptive of the popular structures and the most criticised for it, with detractors arguing that its adoption has made studio films interchangeable in shape.

Booker's book, published in 2004 after decades of work, argues that all storytelling reduces to seven plots: overcoming the monster, rags to riches, the quest, voyage and return, comedy, tragedy and rebirth. He grounds the scheme in Jungian psychology and treats deviation from it as a symptom of cultural decline.

The classification is widely used as a rough taxonomy and widely rejected as an argument, particularly for the evaluative second half of the book.

Harmon adapted Campbell's monomyth into an eight-step circle for television writing: a character in a comfortable situation wants something, enters an unfamiliar situation, adapts to it, gets what they wanted, pays a price for it, and returns changed.

The compression is deliberate. Reduced to eight beats on a wheel, the pattern can be applied to a twenty-two-minute episode, to a subplot, or to a season arc, which is what made it usable in a writers' room rather than a lecture hall.

Egri's The Art of Dramatic Writing, which reached its familiar form in the 1940s, insists that every play must begin from a premise stated as a proposition, such as great love defies even death, and that everything in the work exists to prove it.

The demand is stricter than most later manuals make it, and it puts theme at the head of the process rather than treating it as something that emerges. Egri also argued, against the received hierarchy, that character generates plot, not the reverse.

The French writer Georges Polti, in his Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations of 1895, catalogues every dramatic conflict he took to be possible, from supplication and deliverance through revolt, rivalry and fatal imprudence, each with a required set of roles and a list of examples drawn from world drama.

The project descends from an earlier claim by the Italian playwright Carlo Gozzi, repeated by Goethe, that thirty-six such situations exist. Its value now is less as theory than as a provocation: a finite list of the ways interests can be set against one another.

Bruner argued that human beings organise experience through two irreducible modes of thought, the logico-scientific and the narrative, and that the second is not a lesser form of the first. Narrative deals in intention, particularity and the breach of the expected, and it is how people construct both a version of reality and a version of themselves.

The position moved storytelling out of aesthetics and into psychology, and it underlies much later work on narrative identity, testimony and clinical practice.

The principle survives in several formulations from Chekhov's letters and reported conversation rather than in a single published statement: a rifle hanging on the wall in the first act must be fired by the last, and anything that will not be used should not be there.

The advice is about economy, not about guns. It assumes an audience that reads every introduced element as a promise, and it is quoted as often in the negative, to explain why a detail planted and abandoned registers as a fault.

Hitchcock did not invent the term, and credited it to the screenwriter Angus MacPhail, but he defined and popularised it, most fully in his conversations with Truffaut. The MacGuffin is the thing the characters pursue and the audience does not need to care about: the plans, the formula, the uranium in the wine bottle.

His point was that its content is arbitrary and its function is not. It exists to set the pursuit in motion, and the more the film explains it, the less well it works.

In the prefaces written for the New York Edition of his novels, James worked out the idea of the central consciousness or reflector: a character through whose perception the material is filtered, chosen for being intelligent enough to register what happens and limited enough not to see everything.

The prefaces treat this as a technical problem with technical solutions, and they are the point at which point of view becomes a craft question in English, not an incidental feature of narration.

Freytag's analysis of dramatic technique proceeds from the Poetics and from the Greek and Shakespearean drama Aristotle's categories were used to describe. The unity of action, the ranking of plot, and the requirement that events follow by necessity are all inherited, not argued for.

What Freytag adds is the diagram. Aristotle describes a plot as having a beginning, a middle and an end; Freytag draws the middle as a rise to a peak and a fall away from it, and the picture proved more portable than the argument.

The three-act model is routinely traced back to the Poetics, and the lineage is real but loose: Aristotle says a whole has a beginning, a middle and an end, and defines each functionally rather than by proportion.

He does not divide a play into three acts, and Greek tragedy was not built that way. The act divisions of the European stage come from Roman practice and Renaissance codification, and the specific proportions of the modern paradigm come from twentieth-century screenwriting instruction.

Greimas took the Morphology as his point of departure and generalised it, arguing that Propp's seven spheres of action could be reduced to six actantial positions arranged in three pairs.

Greimas was drawing on Etienne Souriau's work on dramatic situations as well, and the resulting model was designed to escape the limitation Propp had accepted, that his findings applied to a particular corpus of Russian wonder tales, not to narrative in general.

Campbell's comparative method is organised around Jungian assumptions: that the recurrence of figures and sequences across unrelated traditions indicates something common in the psyche rather than diffusion or coincidence, and that myth performs psychological work for the individual as well as the group.

The debt is explicit throughout The Hero with a Thousand Faces, and it is also where the book takes most of its criticism, since the framework guarantees in advance the kind of unity it sets out to find.

Jung worked closely with Freud from 1907 and was for several years treated as his successor in the psychoanalytic movement, before the association broke down and ended in 1913.

The split was substantive as well as personal: Jung rejected the primacy Freud gave to sexuality, and developed the collective unconscious and the archetypes as inherited structures, not as material repressed within an individual life. Both accounts went on to shape literary criticism, in different directions.

Vogler encountered The Hero with a Thousand Faces as a story analyst and wrote a short memo applying it to screenplays, which circulated widely in the studios before becoming The Writer's Journey.

Vogler reduced Campbell's stages to twelve and turned the archetypes into assignable functions. The result was a working template rather than a comparative thesis, and it is the form in which Campbell's ideas reached most working screenwriters.

Lucas has said that he had drafted Star Wars before reading Campbell and that the book helped him organise material he was already assembling from serials, samurai films and mythology.

The two later appeared together in a widely broadcast series of conversations, which cemented the association in public accounts. The chronology of exactly when the book entered the drafting process has been disputed by scholars working from the surviving script material.

Brecht's Verfremdungseffekt and Shklovsky's ostranenie describe the same operation, making the familiar strange so that it must be perceived, not recognised, and the resemblance has been noticed since both terms entered circulation.

Whether Brecht took the idea from the formalists is not settled. The usual route proposed is Sergei Tretyakov, who knew both traditions and whom Brecht met in the early 1930s, and Brecht himself credited his encounter with Chinese acting for the formulation he published.

Chaucer knew Boccaccio's work and drew directly on the Teseida and the Filostrato for individual poems. Whether he knew the Decameron itself is a long-running scholarly dispute.

The two collections share a frame of tellers taking turns and several tale analogues, but the analogues also circulated independently, and Chaucer never names Boccaccio. What is not in doubt is that the Italian collection is the earlier and the more rigorously structured of the two.

The Italian companies toured widely from the sixteenth century and left their stock figures and routines embedded in European comic practice: the miserly old man, the pedant, the boastful soldier, the clever servant who drives the plot.

Moliere worked alongside an Italian troupe in Paris and took a great deal from them, and the lazzi, the rehearsed physical set pieces, passed through pantomime into silent film comedy with their timing largely intact.

Several tales in the Grimms' collection reached them through informants of Huguenot descent, notably the Hassenpflug family, whose repertoire derived from Perrault's printed French versions.

The Grimms presented their collection as German popular tradition, and the presence of French literary material inside it complicates that framing. Their own later editions moved some texts further from the Perrault versions as the difficulty became apparent.

Disney's first feature, released in 1937, was drawn from the Grimms' Snow White, and the studio returned to the collection repeatedly afterwards.

The adaptations altered the tales substantially, softening the punishments, supplying romantic resolutions and giving the heroines songs and animal companions. For most audiences since, the Disney versions have displaced both the Grimm texts and the oral variants they were edited from.

Andersen's tales, unlike the Grimms', are literary inventions by a named author, and the studio has drawn on them across its history, most consequentially with The Little Mermaid in 1989 and later with a very loose treatment of The Snow Queen.

The adaptations characteristically reverse his endings. Andersen's mermaid does not marry the prince, and the sustained melancholy of his originals is the element the films most consistently remove.

Lucas has repeatedly credited The Hidden Fortress, and the debt is visible in the decision to tell the opening from the point of view of two bickering low-status characters, not from the hero's, as well as in wipe transitions and elements of the swordplay.

Kurosawa's own films drew heavily on Western sources in turn, including Shakespeare and the American Western. That makes the exchange a circuit rather than a line.

Don Quixote is treated as the point at which prose fiction turns on its own conventions, setting a character formed by reading against a world that has not read the same books.

Its second part, published ten years after the first, goes further by populating the story with people who have read part one and with a response to a spurious continuation published by someone else. The devices modern novelists use to acknowledge their own artifice are largely already there.

James knew Flaubert in Paris in the 1870s, attended his gatherings and wrote about him at length, treating him as the novelist of the sentence and the most serious available example of the craft taken as a vocation.

James's admiration was not uncritical, and he thought Flaubert's subjects too narrow for the technique lavished on them. But the doctrine of the impersonal author, worked out in James's own prefaces, is unimaginable without him.

Borges wrote reviews of books that do not exist, summaries in place of the novels they summarise, and stories built on invented encyclopaedias, apocryphal authors and infinite libraries.

The strategy was partly temperamental and partly practical, since he claimed it was a laborious madness to compose vast books when one could pretend they already existed and offer a note upon them. The stories became a founding reference point for later self-conscious fiction.

Calvino built books out of combinatorial schemes: cities described to an emperor, a novel made entirely of interrupted first chapters, narratives generated by a spread of tarot cards.

His association with the Oulipo group placed the interest in constraint on a formal footing, and his lectures on the qualities he hoped literature would carry into the next millennium remain a standard defence of writing that shows its own machinery.

The second part of Don Quixote is the earliest thoroughly self-referential novel in the European tradition. Its characters have read the first part, discuss its errors, and meet readers who recognise them.

Cervantes also frames the whole as a translation of an Arabic manuscript by a historian whose reliability the narrator questions, so the authority of the text is undermined from within before the parody of chivalric romance begins.

A Wizard of Earthsea, published in 1968, offered a fantasy built on restraint rather than on scale: a small archipelago, magic that costs something and depends on knowing true names, and a young protagonist whose antagonist turns out to be an aspect of himself.

Her essays were equally influential, particularly the attack on the assumption that fantasy must be written in a mock-antique register, which she argued signals nothing but the writer's tin ear.

Le Guin treated the genre as a thought experiment conducted in narrative form, most directly in The Left Hand of Darkness, whose inhabitants have no fixed sex, and in The Dispossessed, which sets an anarchist society against a propertied one without exempting either from criticism.

She worked in an anthropological register, not a technological one, and her insistence that the genre could carry serious social and ethical argument shaped its reception well beyond its own readership.

The romances of chivalry are the material Cervantes works on. His protagonist has read them into madness, and the novel repeatedly measures their conventions against an unimpressed world.

The treatment is affectionate as well as destructive: the priest's inspection of the library spares several titles, and the parody depends on the reader knowing the form well enough to recognise what is being twisted. The genre's decline after Don Quixote is often attributed to the book, though its popularity was already falling.

Modern fantasy takes most of its furniture from medieval romance rather than from myth or folk tale: the quest undertaken by choice, the enchanted forest, the sword with a name, the code of conduct that binds the hero more tightly than law does.

The route runs through the nineteenth-century medievalism of William Morris and the Pre-Raphaelites, and then through writers with professional philological knowledge of the originals. The genre's default setting is a version of the European Middle Ages.

The Occitan lyric poets developed the conventions of fin'amor, the service of an unattainable lady expressed as feudal obligation, and those conventions became the emotional grammar of the romance when the material moved into narrative in northern France.

The transmission is traceable through patronage as well as poetics, with Eleanor of Aquitaine's court and that of her daughter Marie de Champagne connecting the troubadour lyric to Chretien de Troyes.

Morrison drew on African American oral tradition as narrative material, not as local colour, most visibly in Song of Solomon, which is built on the tale of enslaved Africans who flew home.

She described wanting the novels to work the way that material works, with a community's voice audible in the telling and the supernatural admitted without explanation, and she was explicit that the tradition supplied a set of formal resources and not subject matter.

David Copperfield and Great Expectations gave the English novel of formation its most widely read models, both narrated in retrospect by the grown protagonist and both organised around the discovery that the account of his own rise he has been given is false.

Dickens differs from the German model in refusing a settled accommodation with society as the endpoint. Great Expectations in particular treats the education as a stripping away of expectation rather than an acquisition of place.

The studio's animated features have become, for most audiences worldwide, the default versions of the tales they adapt, to the point where the printed and oral variants read as departures from them.

The influence runs both ways in commercial terms, since the tales' status as common property made them available without cost, and the resulting films are protected. Critics including Jack Zipes have argued that this amounts to the enclosure of a shared tradition.

Joyce read Homer first in Charles Lamb's Adventures of Ulysses as a schoolboy and named Odysseus as the most complete character in literature, on the grounds that he is son, father, husband, lover, soldier and king in turn.

Ulysses uses the Odyssey as a structural scaffold rather than a source of plot, assigning each of its episodes a Homeric correspondence. The relation is comic and deflationary throughout, which requires the reader to hold both texts at once.

Italian companies were performing in England and across Europe during Shakespeare's working life, and his comedies use the stock configuration of clever servants, obstructive elders, boastful soldiers and twinned lovers that the form had standardised.

Direct influence is inferred, not documented, since no record places him at a performance, and much of the same material reached him through Roman comedy independently. The resemblance is clearest in the early plays.

Shakespeare's tragedies broke with the neoclassical rules the continental theorists were codifying at the same moment, mixing comic material into tragic action, ranging freely across time and place, and giving the protagonist an interior life extensive enough to compete with the plot.

The effect on the genre was decisive in English and, once translated, on German and Romantic criticism, which used him as the standing argument that the classical unities were a convention rather than a law.

The plays are printed in five acts and are among the most cited examples of the structure, though the divisions in the early quartos are inconsistent and much of the act marking in modern texts was supplied by later editors working from the Folio and from neoclassical expectation.

Freytag built his account of dramatic construction largely on Shakespeare and Greek tragedy, so the five-act model as it was taught in the nineteenth century is substantially a description of these plays.

The Tale of Genji sustains psychological consistency across a very large cast and several generations without supernatural machinery driving the plot, which is why it is regularly advanced as the earliest work answering to the description of a novel.

The claim depends on the definition adopted, and the work had no direct influence on the European novel, which developed independently. Its influence within Japanese literature was immediate and continuous, and it became the standard against which later prose was measured.

One Hundred Years of Solitude made the mode internationally legible and supplied the surface most imitators copied: an unhurried chronicle voice, generations of repeated names, and marvels reported without emphasis.

Garcia Marquez attributed the register to his grandmother, who he said told the most outrageous things with a completely unruffled expression, and the anecdote is his own account, not an independent record. He was consistently sceptical of the label itself.

Achebe built Igbo speech practice into the texture of his English, using proverbs as a working element of dialogue and negotiation, not as decoration, and the novel itself pauses to say how central they are to the way people speak.

The method was part of an argument about the language question: rather than abandoning English, he set out to make it carry the weight of another way of speaking, a position African writers have debated with him ever since.

The Grimms' collection established the study of folk narrative as a scholarly field as well as supplying its most famous corpus, and their annotations and comparative notes did as much for the discipline as the tales did for readers.

Their method also set a bad precedent that took a century to correct: they edited heavily while presenting the results as transcription, and the assumption that a printed tale is a record of an oral one has misled collectors and readers ever since.

Aarne's original index was compiled from the Finnish and Danish collections and the Grimms', which means the Grimm corpus is built into the classification scheme at its foundation rather than merely catalogued by it.

The consequence is a documented bias in the system toward European wonder tales, which Thompson's expansions and Uther's 2004 revision worked to reduce without being able to remove entirely.

Frye's archetypal criticism takes from Jung the assumption that recurring images and figures across unrelated literatures point to something structural rather than to borrowing, though Frye located the structure in literature itself, not in an inherited psyche.

Frye was explicit about wanting criticism to become a systematic body of knowledge, and the archetype gave him units to build the system out of.

Frye's Anatomy of Criticism did more than any other work to establish the archetype as a working critical term in English departments, treating recurring images and narrative shapes as the elements of an ordered literary universe.

His version is deliberately less psychological than Jung's: the archetype is a convention of literature that a reader has learned to recognise, not an inherited contents of the mind. His scheme survives disagreement with the psychology it borrowed from.

Lord was Parry's student and assistant on the fieldwork in Yugoslavia in the 1930s, and after Parry's early death he completed the project and published its findings.

The division of labour was this: the hypothesis about formulaic composition and the fieldwork design were Parry's, while the full comparative demonstration and the account of how a singer learns and composes are Lord's, in The Singer of Tales.

Ong's account of orality rests on the Parry-Lord findings and generalises them from epic composition to habits of thought and expression across cultures without writing.

The extension is where the argument becomes contested, since a description of how a singer composes is evidence about performance, not about cognition, and critics have objected that Ong's contrast between oral and literate mentality is drawn too sharply.

Todorov's 1965 anthology of Russian formalist writing in French translation is the main channel by which the movement reached Western European criticism, and the structuralist narratology of the following decade proceeds from it.

Todorov's own work applies the formalist separation of story from discourse systematically, and the term narratology comes out of this line of enquiry rather than from the Russians themselves.

The Ars Poetica shares enough vocabulary and doctrine with the Poetics that the two were treated as a single inherited authority throughout the Renaissance, and the rules of neoclassical drama were assembled from both together.

Whether Horace read Aristotle directly is doubted. The usual account traces his immediate source to the Hellenistic critic Neoptolemus of Parium, which would make the relation an inheritance through the tradition, not a reading.

Zeami and his father Kan'ami shaped noh into the form that survives, and Zeami's treatises, written for transmission within his own family and unknown outside it until the twentieth century, set out its aesthetics, training and dramaturgy.

He wrote most of the plays that remain central to the repertoire, developed the doctrine of yugen, and formulated the principle that the flower of a performance lies in what is withheld from the audience.

Woolf's essays argued that the novel had been captured by the wrong conventions, cataloguing houses, incomes and clothing while missing what she called an ordinary mind on an ordinary day.

Her own books acted on the argument, dissolving plot into consciousness and distributing narration across several minds within a continuous passage. The criticism and the fiction were a single project, and both were widely imitated.

Austen narrowed the novel's subject to a few families in a country village and demonstrated that the restriction cost nothing, since the questions of money, marriage, standing and self-knowledge were all available inside it.

Her technical contribution was free indirect style used systematically for irony, which gave the English novel a way to report a character's judgement and undercut it in the same sentence, and which Flaubert, Eliot and James all developed further.

Perrault's 1697 collection gave several of the best-known tales the form in which they entered European print, including the glass slipper, the fairy godmother and the wolf in the grandmother's bed.

He was writing for a literate salon audience rather than transcribing peasant tradition, and the verse morals he appended are addressed to that readership. The Grimms' informants later returned some of this material to Germany as oral tradition.

Andersen's tales are largely original compositions, not collected material, and they changed what the form could contain: an unhappy ending offered without consolation, a sustained melancholy, and objects and animals given interior lives.

His narrating voice speaks directly to a child listener while the material frequently addresses adult disappointment, and that double address became one of the form's standard resources.

Euripides pushed tragedy toward psychological extremity and social argument, giving major roles to women, slaves and foreigners and treating the gods as arbitrary rather than just.

He won fewer festival prizes than Aeschylus or Sophocles and was mocked by Aristophanes for lowering the form, but more of his plays survive than either of theirs, and his influence on later Greek and Roman drama and on the modern reception of tragedy has been correspondingly large.

Sophocles is credited in ancient sources with adding a third actor and with abandoning the connected trilogy in favour of self-contained plays, both changes that increased what a single tragedy could hold.

His surviving work supplied Aristotle with most of his examples, and Oedipus Rex in particular became the model against which the genre was defined, which has given his practice a normative status the other tragedians never acquired.

Hitchcock worked out a grammar for controlling an audience's attention and anxiety through editing, camera placement and the distribution of information, and he explained it at length in his conversations with Truffaut, which turned a body of practice into a teachable method.

His reappraisal by the Cahiers du cinema critics as an artist, not an entertainer was also a founding case for the argument that a director can be the author of a studio film.

Before Citizen Kane, Welles built a reputation in radio with the Mercury Theatre, whose 1938 War of the Worlds broadcast presented an invasion through simulated news bulletins.

The scale of the panic it is said to have caused was overstated at the time by newspapers with an interest in discrediting radio, and later research has argued the audience was far smaller than the legend requires. The technique itself, fiction wearing the format of reportage, was genuinely new.

Kurosawa's international success from 1951 opened Western distribution to Japanese cinema and made him the most widely imitated director of his generation, with several films remade as Westerns.

His own sources ran in the other direction, taking from Shakespeare, Dostoevsky, Simenon and John Ford, which makes the exchange circular rather than one-way. His compositional practice and use of weather and movement have been absorbed into mainstream action filmmaking.

The studio's 1937 Snow White established that animation could sustain a feature-length narrative for a general audience, at a scale of investment that was widely expected to fail.

What followed was an industrial system, with story departments, multiplane cameras and a division of labour, that set the template for commercial animation worldwide and shaped the economics of family entertainment for the rest of the century.

Miyazaki's features demonstrated that hand-drawn animation could carry ambiguous antagonists, unhurried passages with no plot function, and protagonists who are frequently young girls with practical problems, not destinies.

His international standing, confirmed by the reception of Spirited Away, changed the assumptions Western distributors held about what animation was for and who its audience was.

Dickens established the mass-market novel as a serial commodity and demonstrated the audience that existed for it, publishing in parts, reading his work aloud on tour, and writing to a schedule that shows in the books.

His technical inheritance is mixed and identifiable: caricature that carries social argument, plots built on concealed connection and inheritance, and part-endings engineered to compel a return, all of which passed into subsequent popular fiction and into serial drama.

Flaubert supplied realism with its most influential discipline: an impersonal narration that reports without endorsing, sentences worked over until the rhythm satisfied him, and a refusal to supply the reader with a position of comfort.

He disliked the label. What later novelists took from him was the technique rather than a programme, and his practice of free indirect style is the single most consequential inheritance the movement passed on.

James turned the novel's technique into an explicit subject through the prefaces he wrote for the New York Edition of his works, which set out the problems of centre of consciousness, dramatic presentation and the management of point of view as craft questions with solutions.

Those prefaces, more than the novels, are the origin of the Anglo-American tradition of teaching fiction as a set of techniques, not as a body of works.

The picaresque was the dominant new prose form in Spain when Cervantes was writing, with Lazarillo de Tormes long in circulation and Guzman de Alfarache a recent bestseller, and its episodic road structure and social panorama are visible throughout Don Quixote.

What Cervantes does not take is its central premise. His protagonist is not a survivor working the social ladder from below but a gentleman with an idea, which changes the meaning of every episode on the road.

Modern fantasy draws on Norse and Icelandic material for a great deal of its furniture, and the route is largely academic: the writers who established the genre's conventions in the twentieth century included professional philologists who read the sagas and the Eddas in the original.

What came across is not only names and creatures but a tone, in which doom is known in advance and fought anyway, which sits oddly alongside the genre's other inheritance from chivalric romance.

Horace's two books of Satires established the conversational, self-implicating manner that later criticism named after him: an urbane speaker who laughs at folly, includes himself among the fools, and aims to correct rather than to wound.

The contrast with the indignation of Juvenal became the standard way of describing the mode's two registers, and English satirists from the Renaissance onward positioned themselves explicitly on one side of it or the other.

Chekhov detached the short story from the anecdote and the twist, ending pieces on an unresolved gesture, not a revelation, and refusing to state the judgement the material invites.

His stated aim was to describe a situation truthfully enough that the reader would reach a verdict unassisted, and the practice of ending where the meaning is still gathering has shaped the literary short story in most languages since.

Borges worked almost entirely at short length and made the constraint an argument, treating the story as a form capable of holding an idea that a novel would only dilute.

His pieces frequently take the shape of a review, a note or an encyclopaedia entry rather than a narrative, which expanded what could count as a story and gave later writers a licence to abandon scene and character altogether.

Plot is the arrangement of events, and in the Western critical tradition it has usually been treated as the component everything else rests on. Aristotle ranked it first of the six parts of tragedy and called it the soul of the work, on the grounds that a story is an imitation of an action rather than of a person.

The priority has been contested ever since, most persistently by writers who hold that character generates event, not the reverse, but no account of storytelling manages without some version of the term.

Character supplies the agents whose wants and limits make events legible as a story, not a sequence. Aristotle placed it second to plot and defined it in terms of choice, since it is revealed by what a person decides in circumstances where the decision is not obvious.

The modern novel largely reversed the ranking, treating interiority as the primary material and plot as what happens to be necessary to expose it. Both positions still circulate, often within the same workshop.

Setting supplies the where and when, and with them the constraints that make particular actions possible, difficult or unthinkable. It ranges from a specified street to an invented cosmology, and it can be inert background or an active force.

Bakhtin's chronotope argues for the stronger position, treating time and space as fused into a single category that determines what kind of story can be told at all. A road, a threshold and a provincial town each carry their own rate of change and their own sorts of encounter.

Theme is what a story is about beneath the level of its events, and it is the component practitioners argue about most, since it can be treated as a starting proposition to be demonstrated or as something that emerges from the work and should never be stated.

The risk at one extreme is illustration, where characters exist to carry an argument; at the other, incoherence. Most craft teaching splits the difference by insisting that theme be legible in the pattern of choices rather than in dialogue.

Conflict is the mechanism by which plot advances: an intention meets resistance, the resistance forces a larger action, and the sequence acquires causal necessity instead of mere succession.

The familiar classroom taxonomy of person against person, self, society and nature is a rough sorting, not a theory, and craft writers generally prefer to locate the conflict inside a scene, asking what is at stake and how the balance has shifted by the end of it. Narratives without visible conflict tend to substitute another engine, such as pattern or accumulating dread.

Hamartia belongs to Aristotle's account of the best tragic plot: the change of fortune should come about not through vice but through an error made by a person of substantially decent character. The device is what allows an audience to feel pity, which requires undeserved suffering, alongside fear, which requires resemblance.

Whether the error is intellectual or moral has been argued for centuries, and the English rendering as tragic flaw commits the term to one side of that argument.

Catharsis appears in the Poetics as the effect proper to tragedy, the clause that completes Aristotle's definition of the form. Whatever it means precisely, it identifies tragedy as a genre defined by what it does to an audience rather than by its subject matter or its ending.

That has made it the natural target for anyone rejecting the form's politics: Brecht's objection to catharsis is an objection to a theatre that discharges feeling instead of leaving it unresolved and available for use.

Peripeteia is one of the two components that distinguish what Aristotle called a complex plot from a simple one, the other being recognition. It is a reversal in which the action produces the contrary of what was intended, and Aristotle insists it must follow from what precedes by probability or necessity.

The requirement is a structural constraint, not a stylistic preference: a reversal that does not arise from the established situation is a coincidence, and coincidence weakens the causal chain that makes the sequence a plot at all.

Recognition is the movement from ignorance to knowledge, and Aristotle rates it highest when it falls together with the reversal and arises from the events themselves rather than from tokens, scars or announcements.

In practice it is the component that most often determines where a plot can end, since the story usually cannot continue once the withheld knowledge has arrived. It also links directly to dramatic irony, which is the state of an audience waiting for a recognition it has already made.

Focalization is Genette's attempt to rescue the useful part of point of view by isolating one question from the several the older term confused. Point of view had been asked to cover voice, position, knowledge and sympathy at once; focalization covers only the restriction of information to a particular perceiving consciousness.

The separation makes describable a common arrangement that the older vocabulary could not name: a narrator who speaks from outside and above the story while seeing only what one character can see.

The thirty-one functions are the substance of Propp's book, not a scheme he published separately. The Morphology derives them from a hundred wonder tales, defines each by the act's significance for the course of the action, and demonstrates that they occur in a stable order.

The book also supplies the seven spheres of action, or roles, into which the tales' characters fall. Function and role together are what allow the same underlying tale to be told with entirely different casts and settings.

The monomyth is the pattern Campbell's 1949 book sets out to demonstrate, organised into departure, initiation and return, with named stages inside each. The book supplies the comparative evidence, drawn from myth, scripture and folk tale across many cultures.

The pattern has since travelled independently of the volume, usually in the condensed twelve-stage form that Vogler prepared for screenwriters, which is how most people who use the term encounter it.

Zeami made jo-ha-kyu the organising principle of noh at every scale, from the sequence of five plays that made up a full day's programme to the internal shape of a single dance and the delivery of a line.

Because the pattern nests, a performer working inside the slow opening section is still expected to observe the same three-part movement within it. Pace becomes structural in this dramaturgy rather than a matter of local emphasis, and in which the accelerating close is prepared from the first moment.

Overcoming the monster is the first of Booker's seven plots, covering narratives in which a community is threatened by a hostile power and a protagonist confronts it, from Beowulf and Perseus through dragon-slaying tales to the modern thriller.

Booker treats the monster as a psychological, not a zoological category, which is what allows him to place a criminal conspiracy and a sea serpent in the same class. It is also the point where critics object that the abstraction has been set high enough to guarantee the fit.

Rags to riches is Booker's second plot, in which an overlooked or mistreated figure rises to a station that reveals a worth already present. Cinderella is the type case, and the pattern extends to Aladdin, David Copperfield and a great deal of popular fiction.

Booker distinguishes the complete form, in which the rise is earned through loss and return, from the truncated version in which fortune simply improves, and treats the second as the weaker shape.

Voyage and return covers narratives in which a protagonist falls out of the ordinary world into one governed by unfamiliar rules, survives it, and comes home altered by the passage. Booker's examples include Alice in Wonderland, Gulliver's Travels and Robinson Crusoe.

The pattern differs from the quest in that the destination is not chosen and the object is escape rather than acquisition, and it overlaps with the mythic descent, which supplies its oldest instances.

Cinderella occupies its own position in the international type index, and the entry is the standard demonstration of what such an index is for. Versions have been recorded across Europe, the Middle East and Asia, including a ninth-century Chinese telling that long predates the familiar European ones.

Without a shared number, a folklorist reading a collection in another language would have no way to establish that these are one tale, not a resemblance, and the comparative study of its variants would be impossible.

The tale of the girl and the wolf carries its own type number, and its documented history shows how much editing separates an oral tale from its printed form. Versions collected from oral tradition include episodes absent from the familiar text and often end without a rescue.

Perrault's 1697 version closes with the girl devoured and a verse moral attached; the Grimms supplied the huntsman. The type entry is what makes those differences visible as variants of one tale rather than separate stories.

Shahrazad is not one of the collection's tales but the device that holds them: the vizier's daughter who marries a king in the habit of executing his wives after a single night, and survives by breaking off each story at daybreak.

Because the contents of the Nights varied enormously between manuscripts and recensions, the frame is the most stable thing in the work. It is also its argument, since the tales are told to postpone an execution and eventually to change the mind of the man ordering it.

The Iliad is among the earliest surviving works of European literature and the model against which the epic was subsequently defined: a long narrative poem in a fixed metre, treating heroic action of consequence to a whole people, opening with an invocation and beginning in the middle of a longer war.

Its formulaic language and repeated type-scenes, once read as signs of an unpolished text, are now understood as the technique of oral composition in performance.

The Odyssey shares the Iliad's metre, diction and scale but establishes a second and equally durable epic pattern: the return home, structured as a series of episodic tests and organised around delayed recognition rather than around a battle.

Its opening in the tenth year of Odysseus' wandering supplied Horace with his example of beginning in the middle of things, and its embedded first-person narration of earlier adventures is one of the oldest surviving frame structures.

The Gilgamesh poems are the oldest substantial narrative literature known, preserved on cuneiform tablets in Sumerian and later Akkadian and recovered only in the nineteenth century from the library at Nineveh.

The standard version supplies the epic's core elements well before the Greek examples: a hero of superhuman rank, a companion whose death forces the confrontation with mortality, a journey to the edge of the world, and an account of a great flood told to the hero by its survivor.

The Mahabharata runs to several times the combined length of the Iliad and Odyssey and is among the longest poems ever composed, though the Tibetan and Mongolian Gesar cycle is longer still, and it accumulated over centuries, not being composed at one moment.

It contains not only the dynastic war that forms its spine but a vast body of embedded story, genealogy, law and philosophy, including the Bhagavad Gita. Its own frame presents it as recited at a snake sacrifice, a telling within a telling within a telling.

The Ramayana is the more tightly plotted of the two Sanskrit epics, following a single arc of exile, abduction, search, war and return. Its form is verse in shloka metre, and the tradition attributes both the poem and the metre to Valmiki.

It has circulated for two millennia across South and Southeast Asia in versions that differ substantially in language, emphasis and outcome, and it remains a living performance repertoire for shadow puppetry, dance drama and television alike.

Beowulf is the major surviving Old English heroic poem, composed in alliterative verse organised around a caesura and dense with compound kennings. It survives in a single manuscript that was damaged by fire in 1731.

Its three monster fights, separated by decades and framed by digressions into feud and dynastic history, give it a structure quite unlike the classical epics, and the poem is one of the standard test cases for arguments about oral composition in a written tradition.

The Sundiata epic recounts the founding of the Mali empire in the thirteenth century, and it survives as a performed repertoire maintained by griots rather than as a fixed text. The written versions in circulation are transcriptions of particular performances by named singers.

It is the standard example of a living oral epic: no version is authoritative, the performer adapts to occasion and audience, and the genealogical material carries real social weight outside the performance.

The Popol Vuh is the principal surviving account of K'iche' Maya cosmology, covering the creation of the world, the repeated failed attempts to make human beings, and the exploits of the Hero Twins in the underworld.

It reaches us through a mid-sixteenth-century alphabetic transcription in K'iche' and a later Spanish translation, which places it among the small number of pre-Columbian narrative traditions to survive the conquest in substantial written form.

Hamlet takes the machinery of the Elizabethan revenge tragedy, a ghost with a grievance, a delayed retribution, a play within the play and a stage littered at the close, and slows it down around a protagonist who examines the obligation instead of discharging it.

The delay is the innovation. It converts a plot of action into one of consciousness, and it produced the longest role in the canon and the most heavily interpreted character in English drama.

Oedipus Rex is the tragedy most often used to define the genre, largely because Aristotle used it that way. Its plot is a single investigation that turns out to be an investigation of the investigator, so that the reversal and the recognition arrive in the same moment.

Everything an audience needs is delivered within a day's action, and the catastrophe follows from the protagonist's determination to know, not from any external agency.

Don Quixote is conventionally treated as the first modern novel, and the claim rests on what it does with other books rather than on its length or realism. Its protagonist has read the romances of chivalry into madness, and the narrative measures his inherited literary expectations against an unimpressed world.

The second part compounds the device by having characters who have read the first part, which makes the book an early and unusually thorough exercise in fiction commenting on its own circulation.

Written at the Heian court in the early eleventh century, the Tale of Genji follows several generations through a closed aristocratic world, sustaining psychological consistency across an enormous span and a large cast.

Its claim to be the first novel rests on that sustained interiority and on the absence of any supernatural machinery driving the plot; what drives it instead is temperament, rank, obligation and the passage of time.

The sixteenth-century Chinese novel builds a vast comic and allegorical structure around the historical pilgrimage of the monk Xuanzang, giving him a monkey with supernatural powers, a pig and a river spirit as companions and eighty-one ordeals to survive.

It draws on centuries of oral and dramatic treatments of the same material, and its episodic architecture, in which each trial is a self-contained tale within a governing arc, has made it endlessly adaptable to serial media.

Ulysses maps a single Dublin day onto the structure of the Odyssey, assigning each episode a Homeric correspondence along with an organ, an art and a dominant technique. The parallel is a scaffold, not a retelling, and much of its comedy comes from the mismatch of scale.

Its real innovation is technical: sustained interior monologue, a different prose style for each episode, and a final chapter of unpunctuated thought that has become the standard reference for stream of consciousness.

The novel narrates seven generations of the Buendia family and the town of Macondo, reporting ascensions, plagues of insomnia and a four-year rain in exactly the same register as births, wars and business dealings.

That equanimity of tone is what makes it the defining case of the mode: nothing in the narration marks the marvellous as marvellous, and the reader is given no vantage point from which to separate the two orders of event.

Frankenstein carries the Gothic apparatus of transgression, isolation and pursuit, and locates the source of dread in a scientific act rather than a supernatural one, which is why it is also claimed as an origin point for science fiction.

Its horror is structural as much as visual: the nested first-person narratives, with the creature's account held inside Victor's and both inside Walton's letters, force the reader to hear the case from the thing that should only be feared.

Achebe's novel narrates the disintegration of an Igbo community under missionary and colonial pressure from inside it, giving the pre-colonial society its own texture, proverbs, humour and internal disputes instead of presenting it as a state of nature.

The closing paragraph shifts to the district commissioner contemplating the paragraph he might spare for the story just told, which is the book's compressed argument about who has been permitted to narrate Africa.

Capote's account of the 1959 murders of a Kansas farming family and the pursuit and execution of the two men convicted of them was published as a nonfiction novel, using scene construction, interior perspective and withheld information drawn from fiction.

It became the model for the form and also its standing controversy, since subsequent scrutiny has raised questions about invented and reconstructed material, including the book's final scene.

Citizen Kane assembles a life from the conflicting accounts of people who knew the man, structured as a reporter's failed search for the meaning of a single word. No narrator is authoritative and the film declines to resolve them.

Its reputation rests as much on technique as on structure: deep focus that keeps foreground and background simultaneously legible, ceilinged sets, extreme low angles, and overlapping sound montages that compress years into seconds.

Kurosawa's film presents four irreconcilable accounts of the same encounter in a wood, given by participants and a witness, with no version confirmed and one delivered through a medium by the dead man.

The design gave its name to the situation in which an event is knowable only through incompatible testimony. Its international success in 1951 also opened Japanese cinema to Western audiences and to festival distribution.

The Aesopic corpus is the reference collection for the form: short prose or verse narratives with animal actors, a single reversal, and an explicit moral, many of them older than the sixth-century BCE figure to whom they are attributed.

The collection accreted over centuries and passed through Greek, Latin, medieval and vernacular recensions, gaining and losing tales at every stage. That makes it a body of tradition rather than a book by an author.

The Panchatantra is a Sanskrit collection of animal fables framed as instruction for princes in the conduct of affairs, organised into five books each governed by a theme such as the loss of friends or the gaining of allies.

Its tales are nested several layers deep, with characters telling stories that contain further stories, and it travelled west through Persian and Arabic versions into medieval Europe, making it one of the most widely diffused narrative collections in existence.

The Grimms' collection is the corpus most people mean by the fairy tale, and its influence has been strong enough to standardise which versions of these stories count as the real ones.

It is nonetheless a heavily edited text, not a transcript. Across seven editions the prose was smoothed and lengthened, moral framing was added, and the informants included literate middle-class women and a family of Huguenot descent, whose repertoire brought French literary tales back into German circulation.

The Nights is a composite collection assembled over centuries from Arabic, Persian and Indian material, with no fixed contents; several of the best-known tales in Europe entered the corpus through Antoine Galland's early eighteenth-century French version rather than from any Arabic manuscript.

What holds it together is the frame, in which Shahrazad tells stories through the night and breaks off at dawn, making narrative itself the instrument of survival.

The hero is the archetype defined by function, not by virtue: the figure who leaves the known world, undergoes the ordeal and returns carrying something the community needed.

Campbell's comparative treatment placed founders, prophets and legendary kings in the same category on those grounds, and screenwriting manuals inherited the role as a slot to be filled. The abstraction is what gives the term its reach and also what critics object to.

The mentor is the figure who equips the protagonist for a crossing and characteristically cannot accompany them through it. The role so often ends in departure or death at the threshold of the final ordeal.

The name comes from the Odyssey, where Athena takes the form of Odysseus' old friend Mentor to advise Telemachus, so the archetype's label carries its own origin story in it.

The trickster is the boundary-crossing figure who wins by deception, appetite and improvisation rather than by strength, and who is as likely to be humiliated as to triumph.

Unlike most archetypes the trickster is morally unstable by definition, functioning at once as a culture hero who brings fire, language or story to humanity and as a disruptive force who breaks the order he helps establish. Anansi, Coyote, Hermes, Loki and Br'er Rabbit occupy the same position across unrelated traditions.

The shadow names the antagonist as a projection of what the protagonist will not acknowledge. The strongest versions resemble the hero, not merely opposing them.

In narrative terms it accounts for a recurring structure: the confrontation resolves only when the likeness is admitted, and defeating the figure outright without that recognition tends to feel unfinished. The term reaches storytelling through Jung by way of the popular manuals.

The threshold guardian blocks the passage from the familiar world into the unfamiliar one, and the role is defined by position, not by malice: the figure may be a gatekeeper, a rival, a sceptic or a bureaucratic obstacle.

Its function is to test whether the protagonist is committed enough to proceed. The guardian is often bypassed, recruited or absorbed rather than destroyed.

The shapeshifter is the figure whose loyalty or nature cannot be fixed, and whose function is to keep the protagonist and the audience uncertain about where they stand.

The literal versions in folklore, selkies, swan maidens, werewolves and gods in borrowed bodies, and the figurative versions in modern fiction, the ally who may be an informant, do the same structural work: they make trust a variable rather than a given.

The herald delivers the news that unsettles the existing situation and sets the story in motion, and the role can be filled by a person, a letter, a summons, a symptom or an arrival.

It is the archetype most obviously reducible to a plot function. Screenwriting manuals treat it as interchangeable with the inciting incident. In older narrative the herald frequently carries supernatural authority, which removes the option of refusing.

The anti-hero occupies the protagonist's position without the qualities the position conventionally implies, lacking courage, moral standing or competence while still commanding the audience's attention and often its sympathy.

The figure is not a modern invention, since the picaresque rogue and the trickster both predate the term, but it became central to twentieth-century fiction and later to serialised television, where sustained running time makes prolonged moral discomfort commercially viable.

The monster is the figure that violates a category, being neither properly animal nor human, neither living nor dead, and the horror it produces has been argued to come from that classificatory failure rather than from danger alone.

Narratively it externalises what a culture will not accommodate, which is why the same creature can be read as a threat to a community or as its casualty, and why the sympathetic monster is a recurring correction, not a modern novelty.

The double is the figure who duplicates the protagonist and thereby threatens the assumption that a self is singular and continuous. It appears as a twin, a portrait, a mirror image, a shadow, an automaton or an identical stranger.

Freud, following Rank, read it as an idea that begins as a defence against death and becomes an omen of it once that stage of thinking is abandoned, which accounts for the particular unease the figure produces even in comic treatments.

Anansi is the spider trickster of Akan tradition, and in the best-known tale cycle he acquires all the world's stories from the sky god by capturing creatures the god believed uncatchable, which is why stories are called spider stories.

Carried across the Atlantic through the slave trade, he persisted in Caribbean and North American traditions, where a figure who survives by wit against overwhelming power had an obvious application.

The griot is a hereditary specialist in West African societies whose repertoire covers genealogy, history, praise and epic, and whose function includes advising, mediating and holding a lineage's record.

The role is professional and inherited, not casual, and the performance is typically accompanied on the kora, ngoni or balafon. The Sundiata epic survives as a griot repertoire. It exists in many authoritative performances and no authoritative text.

The seanchai was the Irish keeper of lore and tradition, carrying genealogy, local history, legend and tale, and performing in domestic settings rather than in courts.

The repertoire and the setting made the role vulnerable to social change, and much of what survives was recorded in the twentieth century by collectors working for the Irish Folklore Commission, so the tradition is now known largely through an archive of late performances.

The hakawati performed serialised story cycles in the coffeehouses of the Arab world, working through long romances over many nights and breaking at a point calculated to bring the audience back.

The practice supplies a direct working model for the frame narrative of the Nights, in which continuation is contingent on the listener's appetite, and it declined sharply with radio and television, though it has been revived as a heritage performance.

Pansori is a Korean form in which a single singer, accompanied by one barrel drummer, performs an entire narrative lasting several hours, alternating sung passages with spoken narration and using a fan and gestures as the only staging.

Five of the traditional repertoire survive in performance. The form demands an extraordinarily developed rough vocal technique, and the drummer's calls of encouragement are part of the performance, not audience noise.

Rakugo is a Japanese comic storytelling form in which a seated performer plays every character in a long tale using only voice, posture and two props, a folding fan and a hand towel, which stand in for whatever the story requires.

The stories are a fixed repertoire passed from master to apprentice, and the form takes its name from the punchline that ends each one. Its constraints are severe by design: no set, no costume change, no leaving the cushion.

In Javanese and Balinese shadow puppetry a single dalang manipulates the entire cast of perforated leather figures against a lit screen, voices every character, narrates, and cues the gamelan, in performances that traditionally run all night.

The repertoire draws mainly on the Mahabharata and Ramayana, adapted with local characters and comic servants who comment on contemporary affairs, so the ancient material carries current commentary inside it.

Songlines are Aboriginal Australian tracks across country in which narrative, song, ceremony, law and geography are held together, so that the sequence of a song corresponds to the sequence of places along a route.

The form makes storytelling inseparable from land and from custodial responsibility: particular songs belong to particular groups and are performed under particular conditions, and treating them as a body of tales detachable from country misrepresents what they are.

The troubadours composed and performed lyric poetry in Occitan in the courts of southern France between the eleventh and thirteenth centuries, developing the conventions of courtly love that shaped European romance for centuries afterwards.

Unlike most oral traditions their work was written down in songbooks compiled after the fact, so a substantial body of attributed texts survives alongside a much smaller number of melodies.

The Icelandic sagas narrate feuds, settlements and lawsuits among named families in a plain declarative prose that reports actions and speech and almost never enters a character's mind.

They were written in the thirteenth century about events of the ninth to eleventh, drawing on oral tradition, and their status as history is contested. The restraint of the narration is their most distinctive feature: motive must be inferred from conduct, which produces an effect modern readers often describe as cinematic.

Noh is a Japanese form dating from the fourteenth century in which masked performers, a chorus and a small ensemble present highly compressed plays, many of them structured around an encounter with a ghost who returns to recount an attachment that has prevented release.

Movement is extremely slow and codified, the texts are dense with poetic allusion, and the dramaturgy assumes an audience that knows the source material, so the interest lies in treatment rather than in outcome.

Kabuki developed in the seventeenth century as a popular counterweight to the aristocratic noh, with spectacular staging, revolving stages and trapdoors, elaborate makeup, and a repertoire drawn from history, domestic scandal and puppet theatre.

All roles have been played by men since women were barred from the stage in the 1620s, and the onnagata specialism that resulted developed its own transmitted technique. The audience relationship is direct and vocal in a way noh does not permit.

Commedia dell'arte was a professional improvised theatre that spread from sixteenth-century Italy across Europe, built on masked stock characters with fixed traits, a stock of rehearsed comic routines, and a scenario posted backstage, not a script.

Its figures, the miserly Pantalone, the pedantic Dottore, the boastful Capitano and the servant Arlecchino, passed into Moliere, into pantomime and Punch and Judy, and into the physical vocabulary of silent film comedy.

Tragedy took shape as a theatrical genre before it became a general narrative mode, and its formal features, the chorus, the messenger speech, the unity of a single day's action, are inseparable from the conditions of the Athenian festival stage.

When the term was later applied to novels and films it kept the shape while losing the apparatus. Arguments about whether a modern work is truly a tragedy usually turn out to be arguments about what survives the transfer.

Comedy likewise begins as a competitive theatrical genre at the Athenian festivals, with a chorus, direct address to the audience and topical political attack, before narrowing to the domestic plots of New Comedy that Rome inherited and Europe adopted.
