The stage machinery of mistaken identity, disguise, obstructive fathers and a closing marriage passed from Menander through Plautus and Terence into Shakespeare and Moliere, and from there into the structure of romantic comedy on film.

Creation myths account for the origin of the cosmos, the world or humanity, and comparative study groups them into recurring patterns: emergence from a primordial sea, the dismemberment of a giant body, separation of sky from earth, world parents forced apart, and creation by word or by craft.

They typically also establish an order, explaining why the social and natural arrangements a community lives under are the ones that hold. They are so often recited in ritual rather than told casually.

Flood narratives are among the most widely distributed of all mythic patterns, appearing in Mesopotamian, Hebrew, Greek and South Asian traditions among many others, generally with a warned survivor, a vessel, a remnant of living creatures and a covenant or renewal afterwards.

The Mesopotamian versions are the earliest recorded, and the close correspondence between the Gilgamesh account and the biblical one was recognised immediately when the tablets were deciphered in the 1870s.

Transformation is one of the most persistent motifs in narrative: people become animals, plants, stars or stone, and creatures take human form. In myth it commonly serves as punishment, escape or aetiology, explaining why a bird calls as it does or a river runs where it does.

Ovid's Metamorphoses gathered the Greek and Roman instances into a single continuous poem and became the channel through which most of them reached European art and literature.

Joyce mapped a single day in Dublin in June 1904 onto the structure of the Odyssey, assigning each episode a Homeric correspondence, and circulated schemas listing them to friends and early critics.

The relation is structural and ironic rather than narrative: the Cyclops becomes a belligerent nationalist in a pub, the descent to the dead becomes a funeral, and the returning husband walks home to a wife who has not been waiting. The parallel supplies the architecture and most of the comedy.

The story reached Shakespeare from Scandinavian legend, recorded by Saxo Grammaticus in the twelfth century as the tale of Amleth and retold in French by Francois de Belleforest.

A lost play on the same subject, generally called the Ur-Hamlet, was on the London stage some years before Shakespeare's version. In the legendary material the feigned madness is a straightforward tactic and the revenge is carried out; the delay and the interiority are the additions.

Several plays in the noh repertoire take their material from the Tale of Genji, the best known being Aoi no Ue, which dramatises an episode in which a jealous rival appears as a living spirit at the sickbed of Genji's wife.

The adaptation is characteristic of the form: a long prose narrative is reduced to a single charged encounter, usually with the returning spirit as the central figure, on the assumption that the audience already knows the story around it.

Kabuki drew on the older form both for individual plays and for a whole category of pieces staged with a painted pine backdrop in imitation of the noh stage.

The best-known instance, Kanjincho, is a kabuki treatment of the noh play Ataka, taking the confrontation at the barrier where a retainer must beat his own disguised master to maintain the deception. The transfer characteristically loosens the compression and adds spectacle.

Parry's fieldwork and philology transformed the Homeric question by shifting it from authorship to method. He showed that the fixed epithets and repeated phrases in the Iliad and Odyssey form an economical system, with a formula available for each metrical position and almost no wasteful duplication, which is not how a lettered poet composes.

The conclusion was that the poems are the product of oral composition in performance, worked out over generations of singers. Parry tested it against living epic singers in Yugoslavia, not by argument alone.

Lord completed the research programme Parry began and set out its results in The Singer of Tales in 1960. From recordings of South Slavic guslari he described how a singer learns a stock of themes and formulas and composes a fresh version at every performance, so that no two tellings are identical and none is a memorised text.

The finding replaced the assumption that oral tradition preserves a fixed original with a model in which the tradition is the compositional technique itself.

Ong's Orality and Literacy synthesised the Parry-Lord findings into a broader account of how thought and expression differ in cultures without writing. He described oral discourse as additive rather than subordinative, aggregative, redundant, agonistic and situational, since nothing can be looked up and everything must be held in memory.

He also coined secondary orality for the electronically mediated speech of radio and television, which is oral in form but produced by a literate culture and dependent on writing.

Levi-Strauss argued that a myth should be analysed not as a story but as a structure of relations, broken into constituent units and read across its versions rather than along any single telling. No variant is the authentic one; the myth is the sum of them.

He held that myths work by mediating contradictions a society cannot resolve in practice, arranging them into pairs of oppositions that are progressively softened. The method treats narrative as a form of thought, not as entertainment or belief.

Propp's corpus was the Russian wonder tale, and his conclusions are explicitly limited to it: he claimed a common structure for the tales in Afanasyev's collection, not for narrative in general.

The restriction is routinely ignored by later users, who apply the thirty-one functions to films and novels. What the analysis does establish for the fairy tale is that its characters are defined by what they do rather than who they are. The same tale can be told with wildly different casts.

Aarne's 1910 index gave folklorists a shared numbering for recurring tale types, built from the Finnish, Danish and Grimm collections available to him and organised into animal tales, ordinary folk tales and jokes.

The point was practical, not theoretical. Without a common index, a scholar in one country could not tell whether a story collected in another was the same tale, and comparison across languages was guesswork. The system made the historic-geographic method possible.

Thompson translated and twice enlarged Aarne's index, extending its coverage well beyond northern Europe, and separately compiled the Motif-Index of Folk-Literature, which catalogues the smaller recurring elements out of which tales are built.

The two indexes work at different scales: the type index identifies a whole plot, the motif index a component such as a magic object, a prohibition or a transformation. Together they remain the basic reference apparatus of comparative folk narrative study.

Zipes reads fairy tales as social documents rather than timeless wisdom, tracing how the oral tales were selected, rewritten and published for particular audiences, and how the editing carried the values of the editors.

His work follows the process by which peasant tales became bourgeois children's literature, with the sexual content removed, the violence sometimes retained and the moral instruction added. He also argues for the tales' subversive potential. The same corpus has been repeatedly rewritten.

Zipes has translated the Grimms' collection and written extensively on its formation, including the first edition of 1812 and 1815 and the substantial revisions made across the seven editions that followed.

His account documents how Wilhelm Grimm progressively smoothed the prose, sharpened the moral framing and altered the sources' social specifics, and how the brothers' informants included educated women and a Huguenot family, not the anonymous peasantry the collection's framing implies.

Frye's Anatomy of Criticism arranges literature into four narrative categories he called mythoi, corresponding to the seasons: comedy to spring, romance to summer, tragedy to autumn and irony or satire to winter. The scheme treats genres as displacements of a common mythic material.

His claim is that literature as a whole forms an ordered system, and that criticism can describe it structurally instead of judging works one at a time. The archetypal method he built on it dominated Anglophone criticism for a generation.

Bakhtin treated the novel not as one genre among others but as the form that resists the closure of genre, absorbing other kinds of writing and staging the collision of the many social languages that make up a culture.

He called this heteroglossia, and argued that the epic, by contrast, addresses an absolute past that cannot be argued with. The novel is where a language can be quoted, parodied and answered back to. He considered it the only genre still in the process of becoming.

Forster's Aspects of the Novel, delivered as lectures in 1927, refuses chronology and takes the novel apart by component instead: story, people, plot, fantasy, prophecy, pattern and rhythm.

The informality is deliberate and has kept the book in print, but the analytic distinctions it introduced, particularly between story and plot and between flat and round characters, entered general critical usage and have proved more durable than the more systematic schemes of the same decade.

Booth's Rhetoric of Fiction attacked the prevailing doctrine that authors should show rather than tell and should vanish from their own books. He argued that authorial presence is unavoidable, that every choice of what to narrate is rhetorical, and that the real question is not whether the author intervenes but how well.

To describe the presence without confusing it with the living writer, he introduced the implied author, the sensibility a reader reconstructs from the text and measures its narrators against.

The American narratologist Seymour Chatman argued that point of view had become an unusable term because it collapses several distinct things: the physical position from which events are perceived, the interests they are reported in, and the mind whose knowledge limits them.

He proposed replacing it with a pair of terms, slant for the narrator's attitude and filter for the character consciousness through which the material passes. The distinction runs parallel to Genette's focalization and is aimed at the same confusion.

Barthes opened his introduction to the structural analysis of narratives by observing that narrative is present in every age, place and society, carried by speech, image, gesture and their mixtures, and that it begins with the history of humanity itself.

The essay then proposes a linguistic model for describing it, dividing narrative into levels of function, action and narration. It is the manifesto of the structuralist project on narrative, and later Barthes himself moved beyond it.

In his essay on the reality effect, Barthes examined details in realist fiction that serve no function in the plot or characterisation, such as a barometer on a piano, and argued that their apparent uselessness is the point: they signify nothing except that this is the real.

In S/Z he distinguished the readerly text, which positions the reader as a consumer of a settled meaning, from the writerly text that requires the reader to produce it. Classic realism is his exemplar of the first.

Burke's dramatism treats language and thought as modes of action, not of knowledge, and analyses any account of motive using five terms: act, scene, agent, agency and purpose.

The method's leverage comes from the ratios between them, since an explanation that emphasises scene over agent produces a different account of responsibility than one that reverses the pair. Devised for rhetoric and philosophy, the pentad is regularly borrowed by critics as a tool for analysing dramatic structure.

Freud used Sophocles' play in The Interpretation of Dreams as evidence that the desires it dramatises are universal, arguing that its continuing power over audiences could not be explained by the fate of one legendary king or by the idea of destiny alone.

The reading gave the complex its name and made the play the most heavily interpreted text in the psychoanalytic canon. Critics have objected that Freud reads the myth and not the tragedy, and that Sophocles' Oedipus acts in ignorance throughout.

Oedipus Rex is the Poetics' standing example of a well-constructed plot. Aristotle uses it for the complex plot in which reversal and recognition coincide, for the tragic error committed in ignorance, and for the principle that the events should be such that a reader who only hears them recounted will shudder.

He also praises its economy: everything the audience needs is delivered within the action, and the discovery emerges from the investigation rather than from an outside revelation.

Campbell's hero is a functional role rather than a character type, defined by a journey out of the known world and back, not by virtue, strength or rank. The figure who returns carries a boon that the community could not have obtained without the crossing.

His comparative method sets Buddha, Moses, Odysseus and Christ side by side as instances of one pattern, which is the source of both the book's reach and the objection that the resemblances are produced by the level of abstraction.

Vogler condensed The Hero with a Thousand Faces into a seven-page memo for Disney story development in the mid-1980s, later expanded into The Writer's Journey. He reduced Campbell's stages to twelve and recast the archetypes as functions a screenwriter can assign.

The adaptation, not the original, is how Campbell reached the film industry. It is also where the monomyth acquired its prescriptive character, since Campbell described a pattern he claimed to find and Vogler supplied a sequence to follow.

Into the Woods, by the British television producer John Yorke, argues that the three-act model taught in screenwriting manuals conceals a five-act shape underneath, and that the midpoint that three-act teaching treats as a marker is in fact the centre of a symmetrical structure.

His account grounds the claim in the practice of British television drama as well as in classical dramaturgy, and treats structure as a consequence of how audiences process change, not as an arbitrary convention.

McKee's Story places conflict at the centre of its system, arguing that a story advances when the gap opens between what a character expects an action to achieve and what the world actually returns, forcing a larger action.

He organises conflict on three levels, inner, personal and extra-personal, and treats a scene as working only when a value at stake has changed by the end of it. The seminar the book comes from has been running since the 1980s and its vocabulary is widespread in the industry.

Todorov's Grammaire du Decameron applied a linguistic model directly to Boccaccio's hundred tales, treating characters as nouns, their attributes as adjectives and their actions as verbs, and deriving the tales' plots from a small set of transformations.

The study is one of the clearest demonstrations of what structural narratology claimed to be able to do, and Todorov coined the term narratologie in the course of this line of work.

Austen's narration slips into a character's idiom without quotation marks or attribution, so that a sentence carries the character's judgement while retaining the narrator's grammar. The technique is what allows Emma's self-satisfaction to be reported and mocked in the same clause.

Critics generally treat her as the first English novelist to use it systematically for irony, not occasionally, and it is the main reason her narrators can be devastating without ever stating a verdict.

Flaubert used free indirect style to render Emma Bovary's romantic expectations in the vocabulary she would have used, while the surrounding prose declines to endorse them. The reader is placed inside a set of illusions and given the means to measure them at the same time.

His practice, together with his stated aim of an impersonal author present everywhere and visible nowhere, made the technique central to the realist novel and to the criticism that followed it.

Joyce pushed interior monologue further than his predecessors, cutting the connective tissue that would explain a thought and letting associations run without signposting. Molly Bloom's closing chapter dispenses with punctuation altogether.

He credited the French novelist Edouard Dujardin with the precedent. What is his own is the range: the technique is applied to several different minds in Ulysses, each with its own vocabulary and rhythm, so the method registers as characterisation rather than as effect.

Woolf's version of the technique moves between consciousnesses within a single continuous passage, so that a thought begun in one character's mind is completed in another's while the external scene proceeds uninterrupted.

Her essay on modern fiction argued for the change on representational grounds: life is not a series of symmetrically arranged events but a luminous halo, and a novel built on plot and furniture misses what it is trying to record.

The Canterbury Tales sets its stories inside a pilgrimage, with a host proposing a competition and the tellers drawn from across the social range, from knight to miller to pardoner.

The frame does more than contain the tales: the tellers quarrel, interrupt and answer each other's stories, so that a tale is coloured by who tells it and why. The scheme was never completed, and the surviving fragments leave the order of the tales unsettled.

The Decameron's frame has ten young Florentines withdraw to the countryside to escape the plague of 1348, telling ten tales a day for ten days under a rotating monarch who sets each day's theme.

The structure is unusually rigorous, and the plague is not a pretext: the description of the city's collapse at the opening establishes the stakes of the storytelling that follows, which is organised, decorous and life-affirming precisely against that background.

The Nights gives the frame more to do than any comparable collection. Shahrazad's survival depends on suspending each story at a point that obliges the king to postpone her execution, so the mechanism of the frame is also the mechanism of suspense.

Stories are nested several levels deep, with characters inside a tale telling tales of their own to buy time in the same way, which reproduces the frame's logic inside itself.

The Mahabharata is enclosed in several layers of telling: the poem is recited to an audience at a sacrifice by a bard who heard it from another, who in turn had it from Vyasa, and further narrations sit inside the main action.

The layering is not decorative. It allows the epic to absorb didactic, legal and philosophical material as things somebody tells somebody else, which is one reason the work could keep growing over centuries without breaking.

The Panchatantra is built entirely of nested telling: a teacher undertakes to instruct three princes, and instructs them by means of stories in which animals themselves tell stories to make a point, sometimes three or four levels down.

The nesting is functional, not ornamental, since each embedded tale is offered as an argument in a dispute inside the tale containing it, and the reader is invited to weigh it as such.

Euripides is the playwright most associated with resolving a plot by lowering a god onto the stage by crane, and Aristotle named his Medea when objecting to the practice.

Modern criticism is less certain that the objection lands. Several of the interventions are read as deliberately unsatisfying, arriving to impose an order the preceding action has shown to be arbitrary, so the machinery may be deliberate.

Oedipus Rex is the standing example of the device because the audience arrives already knowing the answer to the question the protagonist spends the play investigating. Every line he speaks about finding and punishing the killer is heard twice over.

Sophocles compounds it deliberately: Oedipus curses the murderer, promises to fight for the dead king as for his own father, and mocks the blind seer for his darkness, each time supplying the audience with a meaning he cannot hear.

Hitchcock's account of suspense to Truffaut turns on withholding nothing from the audience: two men talk at a table and a bomb goes off, giving fifteen seconds of surprise, or the audience is shown the bomb and the clock first, and the same conversation becomes unbearable.

The formulation makes suspense a matter of information distribution rather than of shock, and it is the clearest practical statement of why dramatic irony is a tool and not an effect.

Chekhov's plays place the significant material below the spoken line: characters discuss the weather, work, a sold estate or a departing train while the thing at issue goes unnamed, and the audience assembles it from evasions and non-sequiturs.

The method requires an acting technique to match, and its adoption by Stanislavski and the Moscow Art Theatre is inseparable from the plays' eventual success, after early productions that had treated the texts as conventional drama failed.

Brecht's theatre breaks the imaginary wall as a matter of policy, not as a joke: actors address the audience directly, songs interrupt the action to comment on it, and placards announce what is about to happen so that no one watches to find out.

Removing the outcome as a source of interest is deliberate. The attention it frees is meant to go to how the situation came about and whether it had to.

Dickens published almost all his novels in monthly or weekly parts, which made the end of an instalment a commercial instrument as well as a structural one: the reader had to be brought back in a month's time.

The practice shaped the books themselves, producing the recurring pattern of a revelation or a threat placed at a part-ending, and it left a structural inheritance that serial television took up directly.

The film establishes the ending in its first minutes and then assembles the life backwards through five accounts given to a reporter, each covering a period the previous witness could not see and none of them disinterested.

The flashbacks are attributed rather than neutral, which is the design: the same man is a different figure in his guardian's memoir, his colleague's recollection and his second wife's account, and the film never adjudicates between them.

Each of the film's four accounts is internally coherent and flattering to its teller, and no external evidence is offered to settle them. One is delivered by the dead man through a medium, which removes even death as a guarantee of candour.

The woodcutter's final version is not privileged either, since he has already admitted to concealing what he saw. The film's structure makes unreliability a condition of the testimony, not a trick played on the viewer.

The poem opens in the tenth year of Odysseus' attempt to get home, with the hero held on Calypso's island and his household under siege, and only later supplies the intervening adventures through his own narration at the Phaeacian court.

Horace used exactly this arrangement as his example when advising poets to plunge into the middle of things, and the Odyssey is therefore both the earliest surviving instance in the European tradition and the source of the precept.

The novel is presented as a sequence of letters from the explorer Walton to his sister, inside which Victor's narration sits, and inside that the creature's own account.

The epistolary framing supplies a plausible reason for the story to exist as a document and puts a fourth party between the reader and the events. It also means the creature's case reaches us at three removes, filtered by two men with reasons to present it as they do.

Miyazaki's films are built outward from place, and the settings carry information the dialogue never states: how a bathhouse is staffed, what a flying machine is made of, which parts of a landscape have been abandoned and why.

He has described working from images and drawing the world before knowing the story, and several of his features went into production without a completed script, which is possible only because the setting is doing so much of the narrative work.

Le Guin's invented societies are constructed as anthropological propositions rather than as backdrops: a world without fixed gender, a moon colonised by anarchists, an archipelago whose magic depends on knowing true names.

The plots then function as tests of the premise. She was explicit that the method came from her upbringing among anthropologists, and equally explicit that a thought experiment is not a prediction.

Games distribute a large share of their narrative into the environment itself, through documents, audio logs, architecture, wreckage and the arrangement of a space, on the assumption that a player who explores will assemble the account.

The approach suits a medium in which the audience controls pace and route and cannot be relied on to encounter anything in order, and it produces stories that are found, not delivered.

The false lead is structural in detective fiction rather than incidental: the puzzle requires that the correct inference be available to the reader and yet not made, which means competing explanations must be supplied and made attractive.

Golden Age practice formalised the ethics of this, since a clue planted to mislead is fair while a fact withheld is not, and the codes of fair play drawn up in the 1920s are largely about where that line falls.

The genre is built on a terminal reversal: the solution must overturn the arrangement of suspicion the story has established, or the reading has been pointless.

The constraint is severe, because the twist must also be retrospectively inevitable, assembled from material already shown. Christie's most discussed novels are the ones that push hardest on where the culprit may be hidden, including inside the narration itself.

Serial television inherited the instalment ending from serialised fiction and radio, and made it a scheduling instrument: the episode ending secures next week, the season ending secures renewal and a year of speculation.

Streaming release has weakened the first function while leaving the second intact, and the resulting shift in how episodes end is one of the clearer structural effects of a distribution change on narrative form.

The coffeehouse storyteller worked long romances over many nights and stopped at a point calculated to bring the audience back the following evening, since the return of the audience was the livelihood.

It is the same mechanism the Nights dramatises in its frame, where a story broken off at dawn buys another day, and it demonstrates that the device belongs to oral performance economics long before it belonged to print or broadcast.

Saga prose reports what people did and said and declines to report what they felt. A character's state is conveyed by a delayed reply, a change of colour, or an understated remark before an act of violence.

The restraint is a convention of the form, not a limitation of its writers, and it produces an effect modern readers describe as cinematic, since motive must be inferred from conduct exactly as it is on screen.

Montage names both the general assembly of shots and the specific compressive sequence in which a stretch of time is conveyed by a chain of fragments.

Soviet filmmakers of the 1920s made the stronger claim, that meaning is produced by the collision between shots, not by their content, and their experiments established editing as the medium's distinctive narrative resource rather than a way of joining scenes.

If on a Winter's Night a Traveller opens by addressing the reader in the second person, describing them settling down to read the book they are holding, and then repeatedly interrupts the novels it begins.

The device is sustained, not gestural: the reader is a character, the interruptions are the plot, and the ten opening chapters that go nowhere are the substance of the book rather than a frame around it.

The poem is the founding instance of the pattern: a protagonist thrown out of the known world into one governed by other rules, surviving encounters with monsters, enchantresses and the dead, and returning to a home that has changed in his absence.

The return is not a restoration. Odysseus arrives disguised, has to establish his identity against claimants, and the reckoning that follows occupies a substantial part of the poem, so the passage back is as demanding as the passage out.

The eleventh book takes Odysseus to the edge of the world to consult the dead, where he speaks with the prophet Tiresias, his mother, and the shades of his former comrades from Troy.

Strictly the episode is a nekyia, a summoning of the dead by ritual, rather than a full descent into the underworld, and ancient and modern readers have argued about which it is. Either way it established the pattern of a hero who acquires necessary knowledge only by going to the place of the dead.

The poem is organised around three fights against creatures that a community cannot handle: Grendel, his mother, and fifty years later the dragon roused by a stolen cup.

The structure sets the pattern against a hero's whole life instead of repeating it for effect. The final victory kills him, and the poem closes with the survivors expecting the feuds his death has left them exposed to, which qualifies the triumph the pattern would normally deliver.

The expedition against Humbaba, the guardian of the cedar forest, follows the pattern closely: a monstrous power, a journey to reach it, and a killing that establishes the heroes' reputation.

The epic then withdraws the reward. The killing is one of the offences for which the gods require a death, Enkidu dies for it, and Gilgamesh's grief drives the rest of the poem, so the victory is presented as the cause of the loss rather than as a resolution.

The opening books describe a world made by successive attempts, with beings formed from mud and then from wood found inadequate and destroyed, before humanity is finally made from maize.

The sequence gives the account its distinctive shape: creation as a process of trial and failure by gods who deliberate and revise, and human beings as the version that could finally speak and give thanks, which is what the earlier attempts could not do.

The Hero Twins descend to Xibalba, the underworld, to face its lords in a series of contests and deadly houses, having been summoned as their father and uncle were before them and killed there.

They succeed by trickery and by allowing themselves to be killed and returning, and the episode ends with the defeat of the underworld lords, not with a bargain. It is one of the fullest surviving descent narratives from the Americas.

The 1977 film follows the pattern closely enough to serve as its standard teaching example: a call refused, a mentor who supplies a weapon and dies at a threshold, a descent into the belly of a larger vessel, a trial and a return.

How much of that was designed and how much was arrived at through the serials and samurai films Lucas was drawing on is disputed, but the fit is close, and the film's success is the main reason the monomyth became a working template in the industry.

The Grimms' Aschenputtel differs from the version most readers know: there is no fairy godmother, the help comes from a hazel tree on the mother's grave and the birds that live in it, and the stepsisters cut off a heel and a toe to force the shoe before the birds expose them.

Setting it beside Perrault's earlier French version and the many other recorded variants is the standard demonstration of how much a tale type varies while remaining recognisably one tale.

The Grimms supply the huntsman who cuts the wolf open and the grandmother who emerges alive, an ending absent from Perrault's version of a century earlier, which stops with the girl devoured and appends a verse warning to young women.

Oral variants recorded later contain episodes found in neither, and several end with the girl escaping by her own wit. The type entry is what allows the three to be read as one tale with different politics rather than as separate stories.

The novel's spine is an object-and-journey structure of the plainest kind: a monk must travel from China to India and bring back Buddhist scriptures, and the road supplies eighty-one ordeals along the way.

What complicates it is that the pilgrim is the least capable member of the party and the ordeals are largely survived by his unruly companions, so the quest doubles as the disciplining of the monkey who accompanies him.

The central movement of the epic is a search: Sita is carried off to Lanka, and Rama's recovery of her organises the alliance with the monkey forces, the crossing of the sea and the war that follows.

The recovery does not settle the poem. The later material, in which Sita's time in captivity is held against her and she undergoes ordeal and eventual exile, is the part most argued over, and several regional versions handle it very differently.

Cinderella is the reference case for the pattern, and it shows what distinguishes the full form from mere improvement of fortune: the heroine's worth is established before her circumstances change, and the recognition at the end confirms something already true rather than conferring it.

The ordeal in the ashes is therefore structural, not decorative, since a rise without a prior fall would leave nothing for the ending to reveal.

The flood account in the eleventh tablet is the earliest surviving extended version, told to Gilgamesh by its survivor, and it contains the elements the later Near Eastern accounts share: the warning, the vessel, the animals, the birds released to test for land and the offering afterwards.

When George Smith deciphered and presented the tablet in 1872, the correspondence with the biblical narrative was immediately recognised as the most consequential result of Mesopotamian archaeology to that date.

The surviving early epics carry the marks of oral composition in performance: fixed epithets economically distributed across metrical positions, repeated type-scenes for arming, feasting and burial, and a diction that operates as a working system and never as a personal style.

Parry and Lord established that these are the technique of composition rather than the residue of a lost original, which places the written epics at the end of a long performance tradition and not at the start of literature.

Athenian tragedy drew most of its subject matter from the same body of heroic legend the epics treated, and worked on the assumption that the audience already knew the outcomes. So much of its effect depends on irony, not on suspense.

An ancient anecdote has Aeschylus describe his plays as slices from Homer's great banquet. The remark is reported rather than documented, but the relation it describes is visible throughout the surviving repertoire.

Early cinema took its performers, its stories and initially its camera position from the theatre, filming scenes as if from a good seat in the stalls.

What separated the two was editing. Once a scene could be assembled from shots taken at different distances and times, film acquired a narrative grammar the stage does not possess, and the theatrical inheritance became one resource among others rather than the medium's basic method.

Film inherited from the novel the expectation of a sustained story with interiority and social breadth, and from the first drew a substantial share of its material directly from novels.

The transfer is lossy in a specific way: the novel's most distinctive resource, direct access to a mind through language, has no exact cinematic equivalent, and voiceover, point-of-view shots and performance are the partial substitutes that adaptation debates have circled ever since.

Broadcast radio established the practices television took over: the fixed weekly slot, the continuing cast, the sponsor, the episode ending built to secure the next appointment, and the daytime serial that ran for years.

Many early television programmes were direct transfers, with the same titles, writers and performers moving across. What television added was the picture, which removed the medium's most demanding constraint and, with it, much of radio's reliance on sound to carry place.

Freytag's 1863 diagram is the nineteenth-century ancestor of twentieth-century structural teaching, and the two are frequently confused. His model has five parts and describes the classical and Shakespearean five-act play he was analysing.

The three-act paradigm that replaced it in screenwriting instruction is a different scheme with a different purpose: not a description of an existing repertoire, but a set of proportions and page numbers offered to writers as a target.

Five acts was the prescriptive norm for serious European drama from Horace onwards, taken up by Renaissance theorists and standard in Elizabethan and neoclassical practice, though the act divisions in Shakespeare's texts were largely imposed by later editors.

The reduction to three came with changed staging and intervals in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and was then formalised for screenwriting. Some critics, John Yorke among them, argue that the five-act shape persists underneath the three-act description.

Snyder's beat sheet is built on the three-act paradigm and specifies it further, replacing two turning points with fifteen named beats and giving each a page number.

The difference is one of degree that becomes one of kind: a description flexible enough to fit most films becomes a template a script can be checked against, and it is checked against it. The sheet is credited with a measurable effect on the shape of studio releases.

Harmon's circle is a deliberate compression of Campbell, reduced to eight steps and drawn as a wheel so that the return is the same point as the departure.

The purpose of the reduction is production. A pattern with seventeen stages cannot be applied to a twenty-two-minute episode, a subplot and a season arc simultaneously; one with eight can. The circle spread through television writing, not through criticism.

Greimas's six actants are a direct generalisation of Propp's seven spheres of action, reorganised into three oppositional pairs and stripped of any dependence on a particular corpus.

The move trades descriptive precision for range. Propp's functions describe Russian wonder tales in detail and nothing else with authority; the actantial model applies to any narrative and tells you correspondingly less about any particular one.

The Sundiata material is held and performed by griot lineages, and the printed versions in circulation are transcriptions of particular performances by named singers rather than editions of a text.

The custodianship is hereditary and carries obligations, since the epic contains genealogy that has standing outside the performance. The most widely translated version derives from a performance by Mamadou Kouyate, recorded and prepared for publication by Djibril Tamsir Niane in 1960.

The coffeehouse storytellers of the Arab world performed long romances and story cycles over successive nights, including material belonging to the Nights, working from memory and from prompt books, not from a fixed text.

That practice is the working reality the collection's frame dramatises, in which a story broken off before its end obliges the audience to return. The tradition declined sharply with broadcasting, and survives now mainly as revived heritage performance.

The Irish seanchai carried a repertoire of local legend, wonder tale, genealogy and lore, performed in domestic settings and passed on by hearing rather than by reading.

Most of what survives was recorded in the twentieth century by collectors working for the Irish Folklore Commission, whose questionnaires and field recordings preserved a large body of material at the point when the social conditions that sustained the telling were disappearing.

The five surviving pansori works derive from popular narrative material rather than from literary composition, among them the tale of Chunhyang, the faithful woman who resists a magistrate, and that of Simcheong, the daughter who sells herself to restore her father's sight.

The same stories circulated as prose fiction and as folk tale, and the pansori performance is one branch of that transmission, not the origin of the plots.

The Javanese and Balinese shadow theatres take most of their repertoire from the Mahabharata, performed all night by a single dalang who voices every character and cues the gamelan.

The material is thoroughly localised, not translated: episodes unknown in the Sanskrit epic have been added, the Pandawa brothers are accompanied by indigenous clown-servants who comment on current affairs, and the genealogies have been extended to connect the epic families to Javanese dynasties.

The Ramayana supplies the second of the two great cycles in the shadow puppet repertoire, with Rama's exile, the abduction of Sita and the war in Lanka distributed across many separate night-long performances.

As with the Mahabharata material, the local versions differ substantially from the Sanskrit poem in emphasis and in cast, and the performances carry ritual as well as entertainment functions, being commissioned for weddings, harvests and other occasions.

The pair descends from Plato's distinction between a poet who speaks in his own voice and one who speaks as his characters, and it underlies every later version of showing against telling.

Genette pointed out that the opposition is not symmetrical in prose. Narrative can only ever tell, since it is made of language throughout, and what looks like pure showing is a rhetorical effect produced by the amount of detail and the absence of overt commentary, not a different mode of existence.

The two genres were formally paired from the outset, competing at the same Athenian festivals under separate rules, and criticism has treated them as a matched set ever since.

The conventional account contrasts an individual destroyed with a community restored, a fall in rank with a rise, and death with marriage. The contrast is durable but leaky: the same plot material can be resolved either way, and tragicomedy exists because writers kept declining to choose.

The four-part scheme inherited from Chinese poetics moves from introduction to development to a turn and then to a reconciliation, and the turn is the point of interest: something unexpected is introduced that recasts what has come before.

What it does not require is conflict. Where Western structural teaching treats opposition as the engine of narrative, this pattern can produce a complete and satisfying story without any antagonist at all. It is regularly cited as evidence that the conflict model is a convention rather than a law.

The two modes share a narrative surface and differ in what that surface is permitted to contain. Both report events in a level register with attention to social and material detail; one restricts itself to the verifiable and the other does not.

The magical variety depends on the realist one for its effect, since the marvellous only registers as unremarkable if the prose around it is behaving exactly as realist prose behaves. Remove the realism and what remains is fantasy.

Oral narrative is composed in performance for a present audience, varies with occasion, and is shaped by what a listener can follow and a performer can hold; the novel is composed in solitude, fixed in print, and read privately at whatever pace the reader chooses.

The consequences are formal. Repetition, formula and episodic structure are strengths in performance and faults on the page, while sustained interiority and long-range structure are available to print and difficult in the hall.

Noh is aristocratic in origin, extremely slow, masked, spare in staging and dense with poetic allusion; kabuki is a popular form with elaborate makeup, revolving stages, trapdoors, spectacular reveals and a vocal audience.

The contrast is one of register, not of nationality or period, and the two traditions have never been sealed off from each other: kabuki borrowed plays and staging conventions from noh, and both have been maintained continuously alongside one another.

The two occupy the same structural position and differ in what they supply once they are in it. The hero's qualities justify the audience's attention; the anti-hero's do not, and the interest has to come from somewhere else, usually from candour, competence or the pleasure of watching someone refuse a role.

The pairing is old rather than modern, since the picaresque rogue and the trickster both predate the term, but sustained serial narrative has made the second position far more commercially viable than it once was.

Both claim to have found a repeating pattern beneath many stories, and they arrive by opposite routes. Propp worked from a defined corpus of a hundred wonder tales and derived his functions inductively, restricting his conclusions to that material.

Campbell drew comparatively from myth, scripture and folk tale across the world and grounded the result in depth psychology. The first is testable and narrow; the second is expansive and, its critics argue, unfalsifiable by construction.

The two name opposite intentions toward an audience. Catharsis describes an emotional involvement carried to a point of discharge, leaving the spectator settled; defamiliarization describes an interruption of habitual perception, leaving them unsettled and attentive.

Brecht made the opposition explicit in his attack on what he called Aristotelian theatre, arguing that a spectator whose feelings have been resolved has been given an experience instead of a question.

The two principles govern the same relationship between preparation and payoff from opposite ends. The gun on the wall requires that anything introduced be used; the god in the machine is the fault of using something never introduced.

Both rest on the assumption that an audience reads a narrative as a system of promises, and both are stated as prohibitions, not as techniques, which is unusual among craft rules and suggests how reliably readers notice the breach.

The conventional distinction is that science fiction proposes a change consistent with, or extrapolated from, the known world, while fantasy proposes one that is not, and asks only for internal consistency in return.

The boundary does not hold well under pressure, since faster-than-light travel is no more available than magic, and both genres were shelved together for most of their commercial history. Many writers, Le Guin among them, treated the division as a marketing convenience rather than a formal one.

Both follow a young protagonist of low or uncertain standing through a series of social settings, and they draw opposite conclusions from the journey. The picaro survives, learns tactics and does not change; the protagonist of a novel of formation is altered by what happens and arrives somewhere.

The difference shows in the shape as well as the ending: an episodic chain that could be extended indefinitely against a structure that has to close once the formation is complete.

The two work the same material from different sides. Foreshadowing plants an element so that a later development feels prepared; Chekhov's principle says that anything planted must be used, or the preparation registers as a broken promise.

One describes what a writer should do to make an outcome land, the other what a writer must not do once something has been introduced, and together they account for most of the craft advice given about setup and payoff.

Dramatic irony is the state of an audience that knows what a character does not; recognition is the moment the character catches up. One is a condition sustained across a stretch of narrative, the other an event that ends it.

Oedipus Rex is the standard demonstration of the pair working together, since the entire play is an extended irony resolved in a single recognition that arrives simultaneously with the reversal.

The flashback is the most familiar instance of the gap the formalists named: the events in their own order against the order in which the work delivers them.

Stating the distinction is what turns the device from a convention into an object of analysis, since it allows a critic to ask what is gained by withholding an event from its chronological place, and to describe narratives in which the order of telling carries most of the meaning.

Unreliability is a possibility opened up by the decision to narrate from a position inside the story. A narrator with an interest in the account, limited access to the facts or a reason to misrepresent them can only exist once narration is attached to a person.

Booth's formulation makes the dependence explicit, since a narrator is unreliable relative to the norms of the work as a whole, which means the reader must be able to triangulate a second position from the same text.

Both are devices whose content matters less than their function, and they are frequently confused. The MacGuffin motivates the characters and can be anything at all; the red herring misdirects the audience and must be plausible enough to be believed for a while.

One is aimed at the people inside the story and the other at the people watching it. A MacGuffin can be left unexplained without cost and a red herring cannot be left unresolved.

The pattern and the role define each other in Campbell's account: the hero is whoever undertakes the journey, and the journey is what the hero undertakes, which is both the source of the scheme's reach and the basis of the objection that it cannot be disconfirmed.

In practical use the pairing supplies screenwriters with a protagonist defined by function, not by qualities. The template survives translation into settings that have nothing else in common.

The terms overlap and are used inconsistently. Folk tale is the broader category, covering the whole body of traditional prose narrative, while fairy tale usually names the subset involving magic and enchantment, whether or not any fairy appears.

Complicating the pairing is that much of what circulates as fairy tale is literary rather than traditional, written by Perrault, Andersen or the Grimms' editorial hand, so the label often marks a style and a market as much as an origin.

The conventional folkloristic distinction turns on where the story is set and how it is held. Myth deals with gods and origins in a time outside history and is bound up with belief and ritual; legend is set in the historical world, attached to named places and people, and is told as something that may have happened.

The boundary shifts with the community doing the telling. The same narrative can be classed differently depending on who is asked.

Both are short narratives told to make a point, and they differ in cast and in how the point is delivered. The fable uses animals with fixed characteristics and usually states its moral outright; the parable uses human beings in ordinary situations and typically withholds the application.

The withholding is the parable's method, not an omission, since a story whose meaning must be worked out implicates the listener in a way an appended maxim does not.

Both are ancient theories of what a performance produces in the person watching it, and both are stated compactly enough to have generated centuries of commentary.

They are not equivalents. Catharsis is a single effect proper to tragedy, described in one unexplained clause; rasa is a system of distinct flavours, each with its own determinants and durable emotion, applying across the range of dramatic material. The Natyashastra sets out its scheme in far more detail than the Poetics offers for its own.

Both are East Asian structural patterns that organise a work without making conflict its engine, and both nest inside themselves at several scales.

They differ in what drives the movement: jo-ha-kyu is a principle of pace, running from slow introduction through development to rapid close, while kishotenketsu is a principle of information, in which a third section introduces something that reframes the first two.

World building is setting taken past the point where it can be assumed. When a story's location is a version of the reader's own world, most of its rules arrive free; when it is not, they have to be supplied, and the supplying becomes a substantial part of the work.

The craft question is how much of the constructed material should surface. Practitioners generally hold that the value lies in the constraint it imposes on the plot rather than in the exposition it makes available.

Both push the significant material out of direct statement, and they operate on different layers. Show, don't tell concerns the narrator's handling, replacing summary and assertion with rendered action; subtext concerns the characters, who say one thing while meaning another.

A scene can observe the first and lack the second, which is the usual failure mode: everything is dramatised and nothing is withheld, so there is nothing for the reader to do.

Both give access to a mind without quotation marks, and they differ in how much of the narrator survives. Free indirect style keeps the narrator's grammar and tense while borrowing the character's idiom and judgement, so two voices are audible at once.

Stream of consciousness attempts the thought itself, dropping the connective tissue that would explain it. The first supports irony, because the narrator is still present to be measured against; the second largely gives that up.

Both apply the techniques of fiction to material presented as true, and both sit on the same fault line: scene construction, dialogue and interiority require more than the record usually supports.

They differ in whose memory is at stake. The memoirist is the source and the subject and the reader knows it, while the reporter's claim rests on other people's accounts, which is why disputes about invented material have been more damaging to the second form than to the first.

Both make the work's own artifice part of what it is doing, one in prose and one on stage or screen. Addressing the audience directly and acknowledging that a novel is a novel are the same gesture in different media.

Neither is modern. The device is present in Aristophanes, in Cervantes and in Sterne. That makes its recurrent presentation as a contemporary innovation a reliable error.

Both supply a reason for the text to exist as an object inside its own world, a bundle of letters or a story told to someone, and both put at least one intermediary between the reader and the events.

The letter form adds a constraint the frame does not: everything must be written by a participant, at a moment when the outcome is unknown, to a specified addressee, which limits what can be reported and supplies a built-in reason for it to be shaded.

Beginning in the middle creates a debt that the flashback usually pays. Once a narrative opens with the situation already developed, the preceding material has to arrive somehow, and the two devices are therefore found together in everything from the Odyssey to the standard crime film.

The alternative is to leave the earlier material out entirely and let it be inferred, which is rarer and places considerably more weight on what the present action can carry.

Both tell stories through sequences of framed images, and both depend on what the audience supplies between one frame and the next. The difference is where control of time sits: film fixes the duration of every shot, while comics hand pacing to the reader, who can linger or skip.

The exchange between them has run in both directions for a century, in storyboarding practice, in shot composition, and more recently in the wholesale adaptation of one industry's properties by the other.

The Poetics is the origin of the standard objection to the device. Aristotle requires that the resolution of a plot arise from the plot itself, and says that the intervention of a god should be reserved for events outside the drama, either before it or after, not used to untie the knot on stage.

His named example is Euripides' Medea. The criticism has held for two and a half thousand years, and the phrase survives as a term of abuse, not a description of a technique.

The Ars Poetica repeats the prohibition in a single memorable line, advising that a god should not be brought on unless a knot occurs that is worthy of such a deliverer. Horace's version is a rule of thumb, not an argument, which is part of why it travelled.

Set beside his other precepts about decorum and consistency of character, it belongs to a practical code for poets rather than to an analysis of how plots work.

Brecht's epic theatre was defined by opposition to what he called the Aristotelian model. He argued that a theatre which sweeps the audience into identification and discharges their feeling at the end leaves them purged and passive, having experienced a resolution rather than examined a situation.

His alternative sought a spectator who watches critically and remains capable of judging, on the grounds that a social order shown as tragic and inevitable cannot be shown as changeable.

The Verfremdungseffekt was designed to prevent exactly the absorption that suspension of disbelief describes. Brecht used visible lighting rigs, placards, songs that interrupt the action and actors who report their characters rather than becoming them, so that the audience is never allowed to forget it is in a theatre.

The aim was not coldness but attention: a familiar situation made strange enough to be seen again and questioned, not accepted as natural.

Levi-Strauss's 1960 essay on structure and form praised Propp's descriptive achievement while rejecting its formalist basis, arguing that separating form from content leaves the analyst with an abstract sequence that cannot account for why the tales mean anything.

He proposed instead that the units be grouped by relation instead of read in order. Propp responded sharply, defending the limits of his own claim and objecting that his critic had ignored the empirical corpus the Morphology was built from.

Zipes has argued in detail that the Disney adaptations effectively repossessed the European fairy tale, replacing a plural, contested oral and literary tradition with a single standardised version that most audiences now take for the story itself.

Zipes's critique focuses on the flattening of the heroines, the suppression of the tales' harsher social content and the commercial enclosure of material that had been common property. The argument is contested by scholars who read the films as a legitimate branch of the tradition.

Propp did not live to read Booker, but his method supplies the standard objection to schemes of this kind. The Morphology insists that a classification must be derived from a defined corpus and tested against every tale in it, and that categories imported from outside the material will always appear to fit.

Booker's seven plots are drawn from a selection across world literature and grounded in a psychological theory rather than in an exhaustive corpus, the procedure Propp set out to replace.

The Poetics is a treatise on tragedy above all else, defining the form, ranking its six parts, specifying the kind of protagonist and the kind of error that produce the proper effect, and analysing plot into simple and complex kinds.

Its coverage of the other genres is comparatively brief, and the book on comedy that ancient sources refer to has not survived, which has given the Western critical tradition a detailed account of one genre and almost nothing on its counterpart.

The Natyashastra treats performance as a whole system, covering theatre architecture, gesture, costume, music, dance, character types and the emotional effects to be produced, in a level of practical detail no comparable ancient text attempts.

It frames drama as a fifth Veda, available to everyone regardless of the restrictions governing the others, which places entertainment and instruction on the same footing, not in tension.

Campbell's book reads myth psychologically and comparatively, setting narratives from unrelated traditions side by side and treating their common shape as evidence of a shared inner process rather than of contact between cultures.

Folklorists have objected that the evidence is selected to fit and that the specificity of each tradition is flattened in the process. The book's reach among general readers and screenwriters has nonetheless been far greater than that of its academic critics.

Goldman's Adventures in the Screen Trade is a working screenwriter's account of how films actually get made, and its most quoted line, that nobody knows anything, is an argument about the unpredictability of commercial outcomes, not a joke.

Written from inside the industry by someone with credits on hits and failures, it remains one of the few descriptions of development, rewriting and credit that treats the business arrangements as part of the craft.

Goldman held that screenplays are structure and said so repeatedly, treating the placement of scenes and the point of attack as the writer's decisive work rather than dialogue or character detail.

His emphasis on entering a scene as late as possible and leaving as early as possible became standard advice. He was nonetheless hostile to the seminar industry that grew up around structural teaching, on the grounds that a template cannot supply the material it organises.

Frye's account of comedy describes a standard movement from a society governed by an arbitrary or obstructive law toward a new one formed around the young couple, with the obstructing figures usually absorbed rather than destroyed.

He traced the pattern from Greek New Comedy through Shakespeare to the modern stage, arguing that the genre is defined by the shape of that transition, not by whether it provokes laughter.

Genette's treatment of narrative order gave the flashback a precise vocabulary, classing it as analepsis alongside its forward-looking counterpart prolepsis, and distinguishing how far back a passage reaches from how much ground it covers.

The apparatus makes it possible to describe what a particular arrangement achieves, not merely to note that the chronology has been disturbed, which is the difference between naming a device and analysing it.

Chatman's work treats narrative as a structure independent of the medium carrying it, and tests the claim by applying the same analytic terms to prose fiction and to film.

The comparison forces the differences into view, particularly around description, which prose must perform in time and film delivers instantly, and around interiority, which the novel accesses directly and film can only imply or narrate over.

Burke's dramatistic method treats every account of human action as a drama with an act, a scene, an agent, an agency and a purpose, and locates the interest in the ratios between those terms.

Applied to conflict, it shows that opposed parties frequently disagree about which term carries the explanation: one describes a situation as forced by circumstance, the other as chosen by an agent, and the dispute over the description is often the substance of the conflict itself.

Bruner argued that a life story is not a record of a life but a construction made by the same narrative means as fiction, selecting, ordering and supplying causes, and that people become the autobiographies they tell.

The position has consequences for how testimony and self-report are read, and it makes the memoir's characteristic difficulty, that memory is already shaped by narrative before the writing starts, a general condition rather than a personal failing.

Every narrative implies a position from which it is told, whether or not that position is occupied by a named figure, and the choice determines what can be known, withheld and doubted.

The range runs from an unlocated voice with unlimited access to a participant with an interest in the account. Booth's contribution was to insist that even the apparently absent narrator is a rhetorical construction, since deciding to report a scene without comment is itself a decision.

The phrase comes from Coleridge, describing the willing suspension of disbelief for the moment that constitutes poetic faith, and it names the contract an audience enters when it agrees to treat invented events as consequential.

Later writers, Tolkien among them, disliked the formulation, arguing that a well-made secondary world produces belief inside itself instead of requiring the reader to hold disbelief in abeyance by an act of will.

The rasa theory is set out in the sixth and seventh chapters of the Natyashastra, which enumerate the principal flavours, the durable emotions underlying them, and the determinants, consequents and transitory states from which each is produced.

The treatise presents the scheme as a practical matter for performers rather than as speculation, specifying the gestures, costume and music appropriate to each. Later commentators, Abhinavagupta most influentially, developed it into a full aesthetics.

In Campbell's scheme the figure appears as supernatural aid at the point of departure, and in Vogler's adaptation for screenwriters as the mentor, a named stage with a defined function: supplying the protagonist with what is needed to cross.

The role's characteristic exit is built into the pattern, since a hero accompanied through the ordeal has not undergone it. Removing the mentor before the crisis is a structural requirement, not a taste for tragedy.

The crossing of the first threshold is one of the pattern's named stages, and the guardian is whatever stands at it: a person, an institution, a physical barrier or a plausible argument for staying home.

The function is to test commitment rather than to prevent passage, which is why the figure is so often absorbed, outwitted or recruited instead of defeated, and why a story that kills its guardian outright usually has to supply another obstacle immediately.

The call to adventure opens the pattern, and the herald is whoever or whatever delivers it: a messenger, a summons, an arrival, a death, a symptom.

Vogler treats it as an assignable function, not a character. The role is so frequently filled by an event. The stage that follows in Campbell's sequence is the refusal of the call, so the herald's delivery is designed to be resisted before it is accepted.

The shapeshifter is one of the roles Vogler added when adapting Campbell for screenwriters, covering the ally whose loyalty is uncertain and the antagonist who may be an ally, and its function is to keep the protagonist unable to settle their assumptions.

Unlike the mentor or the guardian it corresponds to no single stage of the journey, since its usefulness lies in recurring at intervals and unsettling what has just been established.

The ordeal at the centre of the journey is characteristically a confrontation with the shadow, and the pattern treats the antagonist as a projection of the protagonist, not as an unrelated obstacle.

That is why the stage is so often described as a death and return rather than as a victory: what is defeated is a refusal of self-knowledge, and a version that merely kills an enemy leaves the structure's central movement unperformed.

The quest is the third of Booker's plots, covering narratives in which a protagonist and companions set out for a distant object, survive a sequence of ordeals on the road, and face a final obstacle at the destination.

Booker distinguishes it from voyage and return by the presence of a chosen goal, since the traveller in the second pattern is displaced rather than dispatched and wants only to get home.

Tragedy is one of the seven in Booker's classification, and he treats it as the pattern in which the protagonist's course runs the wrong way through the stages the other plots complete successfully, ending in destruction, not renewal.

The placement is where his scheme is most often challenged, since a category that has supported two and a half thousand years of independent theorising sits awkwardly as one slot in a list of seven.

Comedy appears in Booker's list as the pattern in which confusion, disguise and misunderstanding accumulate until a recognition dissolves them and the community reforms around a union.

His account owes a good deal to Frye's earlier treatment of the same movement, and like Frye he defines the genre by the shape of the resolution rather than by whether the material is funny.

The novel begins as a direct attack on the romances of chivalry, staging their conventions against a world that does not cooperate, and it retains that satirical machinery throughout.

What complicates the classification is the treatment of the target's believer. Cervantes makes his deluded gentleman steadily more sympathetic and the people who mock him steadily less so, until the satire's object has shifted from the books to the readers laughing at him.

Rakugo is a comic form in the strict sense: the repertoire is built toward a punchline, and the word itself refers to the fall or drop that ends each story.

Its comedy is generated almost entirely by character and timing, since the performer has no set, no costume change and only a fan and a hand towel, and must distinguish every speaker in a crowded story by voice and posture alone.

The novel is regularly named as the genre's starting point, most influentially by Brian Aldiss, on the grounds that its horror proceeds from a deliberate scientific act, not from a curse or a supernatural agency.

The claim is contested, since the science is gestural and the book's concerns are Romantic and Gothic. What is not in dispute is the pattern it established, of a created being that turns on its maker and argues its own case.

Four books of the poem are narrated by Odysseus himself at the Phaeacian court, so the Cyclops, Circe, the descent to the dead and the cattle of the sun all reach the reader as the hero's own account of himself to an audience he is trying to impress.

The arrangement is one of the earliest surviving embedded narrations, and it quietly places the poem's most fantastic material inside the testimony of a character the poem repeatedly describes as a skilled liar.

The poem opens in the tenth year of the war with a quarrel over the distribution of captives, and closes with a funeral, covering a few weeks of a conflict whose beginning and end both fall outside it.

The judgement of Paris, the assembly of the fleet, the wooden horse and the fall of the city are all known to the audience and none is narrated. The poem assumes the story and selects an episode from the middle of it.

The poem repeatedly tells the audience what is coming, announcing that a hall will burn, that a peace-weaving marriage will fail, and that the hero will die in his last fight, often many lines before the event.

The technique assumes an audience that already knows the legendary and dynastic material, so suspense is not available and is not sought. What the announcements produce instead is a steady undertow of doom beneath episodes of celebration.

The novel presents itself as a translation of a manuscript by the Arab historian Cide Hamete Benengeli, and the narrator repeatedly questions his source's reliability while depending on it entirely.

The device puts several layers between the reader and the events and supplies an excuse for gaps and contradictions, and it is also a joke at the expense of the chivalric romances, which routinely claimed a discovered ancient manuscript as their authority.

Each of the film's accounts comes from someone with a stake in how Kane is remembered, and the film supplies no neutral version against which to check them.

One sequence is narrated by a man recalling events he could not have witnessed in the detail shown, which the film neither flags nor corrects. The reporter's failure to reach an answer is by design, since the audience is left holding the same incompatible material he does.

The film's entire body is flashback, delivered as testimony at an inquest and framed by three men sheltering from rain at a ruined gate.

What makes the structure unusual is that the flashbacks contradict one another while being shown with equal photographic authority, so the convention that a visualised memory is a reliable record of events is used and then withdrawn.

The stolen technical readouts that open the film are a textbook instance: they set the pursuit in motion, everyone wants them, and their contents matter to the plot only as the location of a weak point.

The film spends almost no time explaining what they are, the treatment Hitchcock recommended, and the audience's interest transfers immediately to the people carrying them.

The book cuts between the family's last ordinary day and the two men driving toward them, so that domestic detail is read against an outcome the reader already knows and the participants do not.

The technique is borrowed wholesale from fiction, and it is one of the elements that made the book's status as reportage contentious, since the arrangement produces dread by construction rather than by disclosure.

Macondo is built up over a century of narrative time, from a village of twenty mud houses to a banana-company town and back to ruin, with its own founders, plagues, wars and weather.

The construction is what allows the marvellous events to register as local facts, not as intrusions: the town has a history within which insomnia plagues and four years of rain are simply things that happened there.

Horror depends on anticipation more than on disclosure, and its characteristic technique is to let the audience recognise the shape of what is coming while the characters do not.

The genre's most-repeated structural joke, that the audience shouts warnings at the screen, is a description of the device working. Withholding everything until the reveal produces surprise, which lasts a moment; signalling produces dread, which lasts as long as the film chooses.

A genre built on changing one condition of existence has to establish what the change entails, which means supplying the social, technological and physical rules of the setting as part of the narrative work.

The craft question is how to deliver them, since a reader who is told everything is being lectured and one who is told nothing is lost. The standard solutions, a newcomer to the world or a narrator who assumes it, are both devices for controlling that flow.

Tolkien's account of sub-creation makes world building the genre's central act rather than one of its techniques: the writer makes a secondary world with its own consistent laws, and the reader's belief holds only as long as that consistency does.

His own apparatus of invented languages, calendars and appended histories set an expectation of depth that the genre has been meeting, and sometimes drowning in, ever since.

Comics narrate through the arrangement of framed images and the gaps between them, and the reader supplies the movement, duration and causation the gutter leaves out.

The medium's theorists treat that inference as its basic operation, which puts comics and film in the same territory by different means: film cuts between images in time, comics place them in space and let the eye do the cutting at its own pace.

The memoirist narrates from inside the events, with an interest in how they are understood and access only to what was noticed and retained, which is the standard description of an unreliable narrator.

The better examples treat the condition as their subject instead of concealing it, acknowledging revision, gaps and the pressure of hindsight, since a memoir that presents recall as complete makes a claim its readers know to be false.

The parable characteristically withholds its application, narrating an ordinary situation and leaving the listener to determine what it is about and whether they are implicated.

The withholding is the form's method rather than an omission. A story whose meaning must be arrived at commits the listener to the conclusion in a way an appended moral does not. The form has been used so persistently for teaching under conditions where direct statement is unwise.

Shakespeare's plots run on gaps between what the audience knows and what the characters do: a disguise the audience has watched being assumed, a letter the audience saw planted, a death the audience knows to be feigned.

The technique carries both the comedies, where the gap produces delight and closes in recognition, and the tragedies, where it produces dread and closes too late, which is a strong demonstration that the device itself is neutral.

The novel applies interior monologue to several different minds and gives each its own vocabulary and rhythm, so that Bloom's practical, digressive attention is immediately distinguishable from Stephen's abstraction.

The final episode removes punctuation almost entirely for the whole of Molly Bloom's night thought, which is the passage most often reproduced as the technique's limit case and the one Joyce himself expected to be remembered.

The novel is built in three nested layers: Walton's letters to his sister enclose Victor's account, which encloses the creature's own narration of its education and rejection.

The structure controls sympathy precisely. The creature's case is the innermost and most articulate, but it reaches the reader through the man who abandoned it and then through a stranger inclined to believe him, so every judgement the reader forms has passed through two interested parties.

The difference is not only length but what length permits. A story can be built on a single situation and end while the meaning is still assembling; a novel has to sustain interest across a structure and generally has to account for consequences.

The economics diverge as sharply as the form. The short story has depended on magazines and now largely on institutions, while the novel has been a commercial unit for three centuries, which shapes what gets written as much as any aesthetic argument.

Radio must place everything in sound, using voice, effects, music and silence to establish where a scene is and who is present, and it can move between locations at no cost.

Film shows the place immediately and pays for every location. The constraint runs the other way for interiority, since a radio narrator can occupy a character's mind directly while film has to externalise it. The two media adapted very differently from the novel.

The realist novel defined itself against romance explicitly, rejecting the marvellous, the aristocratic cast, the errant structure and the idealised object of desire in favour of the verifiable, the ordinary and the causally connected.

The opposition is a founding gesture, not a neutral description, and the romance did not disappear when it was rejected: it persisted in popular fiction and returned, with the marvellous intact, in the fantasy that now outsells its supplanter.
