Both work by exposing incongruity and both depend on an audience that shares enough context to see it, and the two are frequently the same text read for different purposes.

The difference is in the intent behind the laugh. Comedy can be entirely without a target, ending in reconciliation and the restoration of a community, while satire requires one and generally declines to reconcile with it.

The modern term and the ancient one describe the same event from different critical positions. Peripeteia is defined by its relation to the plot's logic, arising by probability or necessity from what precedes it; the plot twist is defined by its effect on the audience.

The distinction matters in practice, since a twist that satisfies only the second requirement is the failure mode both terms are used to diagnose.

Diegesis is the telling and the told world, and the narrator is the position from which the telling issues, which is why narratology has generated so many terms for locating one relative to the other.

Genette's vocabulary of narrative levels does exactly this work, distinguishing a narrator outside the story from one inside it and tracking what happens when a character in an embedded tale begins to narrate in turn.

Bakhtin's term is a stronger claim than setting makes. Setting names where and when a story happens; the chronotope asserts that time and space are fused into a single category which determines what kinds of event are possible there at all.

The road produces chance encounters between strangers, the threshold produces crisis and decision, the provincial town produces cyclical time in which nothing arrives. Change the chronotope and the available plots change with it.

Both concern whose perspective a narrative carries, and they answer differently on whether one of them wins. Point of view describes the position from which material is presented, however many positions a work uses in turn.

Polyphony is Bakhtin's claim that a novel can hold several consciousnesses that are never subordinated to an authorial verdict, so the question is not which perspective is in force but whether any of them is finally authoritative.

Both name parts of the same transaction. Imitation describes what the work does in presenting an invented action as though it were an action; the suspension describes what the audience does in accepting it.

Aristotle's account makes the pleasure natural rather than negotiated, which sits somewhat against Coleridge's more contractual formulation, and the difference is still visible in disputes about whether an audience is persuaded, complicit or simply absorbed.

Breaking the frame is one method of making the familiar strange: an audience addressed directly stops watching a window and starts watching a performance.

The alliance is historical as well as conceptual, since Brecht's estrangement effect and the formalists' ostranenie describe the same operation, and Brecht's most visible instruments for producing it, direct address, songs, placards and visible lighting, all work by dismantling the wall.

Games borrowed film's visual grammar wholesale, including shot composition, editing, scores and performance capture, and for a period borrowed its structure as well by suspending play for cinematic sequences.

The medium's own resources pull the other way. A story delivered through what a player chooses to do and where they choose to look cannot be storyboarded in the same sense. Environmental narrative has largely displaced the cut scene as the form's distinctive method.

Both hold the audience's attention without meeting the conditions the protagonist's position usually implies, and both win by wit, nerve or opportunism, not by virtue.

The trickster is the older and stranger figure, frequently sacred and frequently a fool, capable of bringing fire or language to humanity and of being humiliated in the same cycle. The anti-hero is a narrower modern position with none of the mythic function.

The two describe the same figure from outside and inside. The monster violates a boundary the community depends on; the shadow is what an individual refuses to recognise as their own and therefore encounters in another form.

Stories that read the monster as a projection rather than as an intruder are drawing on both at once, and the sympathetic monster, whose grievance is legitimate and whose maker is the real offender, is the standard result.

Songlines carry narratives of ancestral beings whose journeys formed the country, which places them alongside origin narratives elsewhere in what they account for.

The comparison has limits. The songs are inseparable from specific country and from custodial responsibility, particular songs belong to particular groups, and performance is governed by conditions, so treating them as a body of detachable stories misdescribes both what they are and how they are held.

Greimas took the Morphology as his starting point and generalised its findings, and his actantial model is a direct restatement of Propp's seven spheres of action in a form that no longer depends on a Russian corpus.

The book reached him and the rest of French structuralism late: published in 1928, it was not translated into English until 1958 and into French shortly after. Its influence outside Russia belongs entirely to the 1960s.

Snyder's beat sheet is laid over the paradigm Field codified rather than offered against it, keeping the three acts and the two turning points and subdividing the space between them.

The lineage is visible in the method as much as in the shape: both writers give page numbers, not principles, on the assumption that a screenplay is a document of standard length whose structural events can be located by position. Field established that assumption; Snyder took it to its conclusion.

The beat sheet's adoption in development has been argued to have a measurable effect on studio output, with critics pointing to a period of releases that hit the same marks at the same minute.

The charge is contested by writers who point out that a tool used at the pitch and note-giving stage shapes what gets bought rather than what can be written, which locates the effect in the commissioning process, not in the manual itself.

Vogler wrote the seven-page memo in 1985 while working as a story analyst at Disney, and it spread by photocopy and fax to writers, producers and executives at other studios before it was expanded into a book.

What travelled was the checklist rather than the comparative argument, and its subsequent ubiquity in development notes is the main reason the hero's journey is now discussed as a screenwriting format, not as a theory of myth.

Booker grounds the seven plots in Jungian psychology, treating each pattern as a stage in a process of individuation and the recurring figures as archetypes in Jung's sense, not as literary conventions.

The commitment shapes the book's evaluative second half, in which modern works that decline to complete the pattern are read as symptoms of a culture that has lost its bearings, and it is the part of the argument critics have most consistently rejected.

Polti's thirty-six situations of 1895 is the nineteenth-century ancestor of Booker's project: an attempt to enumerate exhaustively the finite set of dramatic configurations available to a writer.

The two differ in what they count. Polti catalogues situations, defined by the roles and interests in conflict at a given moment, while Booker classifies whole plots by their shape from beginning to end, so a single Booker plot may pass through several Polti situations.

Yorke takes the three-act model seriously enough to ask why it works instead of treating it as a convention to be followed or rejected, and his answer is that its turning points mark changes in what the protagonist knows and wants.

His argument that a five-act shape sits underneath the three is a claim about the same material rather than a rival scheme, and it explains the midpoint that three-act teaching treats as an unexplained landmark.

Egri argued against the received ranking, holding that character generates plot rather than the reverse, and that a writer who knows a person completely will find that the events follow from what that person would do.

His method for arriving at that knowledge is the bone structure, a systematic account of a character's physiology, sociology and psychology built before the writing starts, and it is the earliest widely used version of the character questionnaire.

Harmon developed the story circle as a working tool in a television writers' room, and its spread owes as much to that context as to its content: it was published on a blog in instalments and picked up by writers, not by critics.

The scale it operates at is what suited it to serial television, since the same eight steps can be applied to an episode, a subplot and a season without modification.

The poem was completed around 8 CE, the year of Ovid's banishment, and he claimed in exile to have burned his own copy before leaving Rome, though others were already in circulation.

It is the work that made his reputation durable. His elegiac poetry was more scandalous and the Ars Amatoria more directly implicated in his fall, but the Metamorphoses is the book that later Europe read, quoted and painted from.

Virgil worked on the poem for the last eleven years of his life and left it unrevised, with several lines still metrically incomplete, which later editors preserved, not repaired.

Ancient sources report that he asked for it to be destroyed and that Augustus countermanded the instruction. The account is transmitted by later biographers rather than documented at the time, and its shape is suspiciously convenient for the emperor's reputation.

Dante composed the poem during the exile that occupied the last two decades of his life, completing the final section shortly before his death in 1321.

He titled it simply a comedy, in the technical sense of a work that begins badly and ends well and is written in a middle style rather than a high one. The epithet that made it the Divine Comedy was added by later editors.

Sterne published the first two volumes at his own expense in York at the end of 1759 and found himself famous in London within weeks, after which he issued the remaining volumes in instalments over eight years.

He wrote them while consumptive and increasingly ill, and the running joke that the narrator cannot outrun his own digressions acquired a second edge as it became clear the author might not finish either.

Tolkien worked on the book for some sixteen years, having been asked by his publisher for a sequel to The Hobbit and having produced instead something drawing on the mythology he had been developing privately since the First World War.

The division into three volumes was a publishing decision made on grounds of paper cost and risk, not a structural one, and he disliked the resulting titles. He always described it as a single novel in six books.

The third book of the Republic separates two ways of telling a story: the poet may speak in his own person, or he may speak as his characters, disappearing behind them.

Plato treats the second as the more hazardous, because the performer has to become what he represents, and habitual imitation of the disorderly will form a disorderly character. The distinction is the origin of the mimesis and diegesis pair, and it is a moral argument before it is a technical one.

Diegesis in the Republic is plain narration, the poet reporting in his own voice instead of assuming another's, and Plato prefers it because it keeps the distance that dramatic imitation collapses.

He demonstrates the difference by rewriting the opening of the Iliad into pure narration to show what is lost and what is gained, which is an unusually early instance of a critic altering a text in order to expose its technique.

Aristotle studied at Plato's Academy for around twenty years, and the Poetics is legible throughout as an answer to his teacher's charges against poetry.

Where Plato treats imitation as a third remove from truth and a corruption of the soul, Aristotle treats it as natural, cognitively valuable and pleasurable; where Plato worries that tragedy waters the emotions, Aristotle argues it accomplishes a catharsis of them. The Poetics never names the objection it is answering.

The Poetics reads as a systematic reply to positions the Republic had established, and much of its apparatus exists to make the case that poetry can be analysed as a craft with rules rather than defended as inspiration or dismissed as a copy of a copy.

The two texts together set the terms of European criticism for two thousand years, and later theorists have tended to be recognisably on one side or the other of the argument between them.

The phrase appears in the fourteenth chapter of Biographia Literaria in 1817, where Coleridge is describing the plan behind Lyrical Ballads nearly twenty years earlier.

His own contributions were to take supernatural or romantic subjects and transfer enough human interest and semblance of truth to them to procure what he called that willing suspension of disbelief for the moment which constitutes poetic faith. It was a working note on a division of labour, not a general theory, and it has been carrying far more weight ever since.

Tolkien engaged with the formula in order to reject it. He argued that a reader who has to suspend disbelief by an effort of will is already outside the story, and that what a successful secondary world produces is not suspension but literary belief, holding as long as the internal consistency holds.

Tolkien's alternative account, that the maker is a sub-creator and the reader enters rather than tolerates the world, is a direct correction of Coleridge's phrase, not an independent proposal.

The commentary by Abhinavagupta, the Kashmiri philosopher writing around the year 1000, is the point at which rasa becomes a philosophical account of aesthetic experience, not a working scheme for performers.

His solution to the problem of why an audience seeks out grief or terror in the theatre is generalisation: the response is detached from the spectator's own circumstances and from any particular person's suffering, so what is savoured is the emotion in a universalised form, obstructed neither by self-interest nor by indifference.

The Abhinavabharati is the most influential surviving commentary on the treatise, and for several passages it is the main route by which the text has been understood, since the Natyashastra's compressed technical language is frequently obscure without it.

Writing roughly a millennium after the treatise took shape, Abhinavagupta also records and adjudicates between earlier commentators whose own works are lost, which makes his book a source for the history of the debate as well as a contribution to it.

Understanding Comics argues that comics are a medium rather than a genre, defined by deliberate sequence of images in space, and it makes the argument in comics, with the author drawn as a narrator on the page.

Its most used idea is closure: the reader supplies the motion and duration that the gap between panels omits, which locates the medium's essential operation in the audience. He classifies panel transitions by what that bridging requires and notes that the distribution differs sharply between American and Japanese traditions.

McCloud's account of panel-to-panel transitions is a direct counterpart to film theory's account of the cut, and he draws the comparison himself while insisting on the difference.

Film fixes the duration of every shot and delivers the sequence at its own pace; comics place the images in space and hand the pacing to the reader, who can hold a panel or skip a page. The same juxtaposition therefore produces meaning by different means in the two media.

Aeschylus is credited by ancient sources with introducing the second actor, which shifted tragedy from a form built on a single figure answering a chorus to one capable of dramatic exchange between characters.

His surviving work also shows the form at a scale later abandoned: the Oresteia is the only complete trilogy to come down from antiquity, and it carries a single argument across three plays, ending with the replacement of blood vengeance by a court.

The eleven surviving plays are the only complete examples of Old Comedy, and they preserve a form of theatre that later comedy abandoned entirely: topical, obscene, fantastical, and directed by name at living politicians and intellectuals.

His method is to take an absurd premise with complete seriousness and follow it through, which is the strand of comic invention that runs to satire and to the modern sketch, not to the domestic plot Menander established.

Aristophanes attacked Euripides repeatedly across his career, most extensively in The Frogs, where the tragedian competes with Aeschylus in the underworld for the right to return and save Athens, and loses.

The charges are that he lowered the register of tragedy, gave rhetorical skill to unsuitable characters and made the audience clever rather than better. Since Euripides is also the tragedian whose work most obviously survives in quantity, the parody is one of the fullest contemporary responses to a Greek dramatist that exists.

Menander replaced Aristophanes' political fantasy with domestic plots built on concealed parentage, mistaken identity, obstructive fathers and lovers who are reconciled at the close.

That apparatus, carried into Latin by Plautus and Terence and from there into Renaissance and modern drama, is the direct ancestor of the romantic comedy plot. It is also why the modern form so rarely resembles the Athenian comedy that shares its name.

Plautus adapted Greek New Comedy for Roman audiences and named Menander among his sources, and for most of history the adaptations were the principal evidence for what the originals contained.

The twentieth-century papyrus recoveries allowed the comparison to be made directly for the first time, and they show Plautus expanding the musical passages, coarsening the humour and enlarging the clever slave into a role his Greek model does not support.

The Roman comedies were in print and on school curricula throughout the Renaissance, and their stock figures pass more or less intact into the Italian companies' repertoire: the miserly old man, the boastful soldier, the parasite, the scheming servant.

The transmission is documented, not inferred, since the learned comedy of sixteenth-century Italy was explicitly modelled on Plautus and Terence, and the improvised professional theatre developed alongside it.

The Comedy of Errors is built from the Menaechmi, with a second set of twins added to double the confusion, and Plautine material surfaces elsewhere in the comedies.

Shakespeare's grammar school education would have included the Roman comedians as set texts. That makes this one of the few literary debts in his work that can be asserted from the record rather than inferred from resemblance.

The prologue to Amphitruo has the god Mercury explain that a play containing kings and gods alongside slaves cannot properly be called a comedy, and coins a compound naming it a tragicomedy instead.

The remark is a joke about decorum, not a theory of genre. Renaissance theorists, Guarini most consequentially, took it up in earnest as authority for a mixed form that could hold tragic danger without a tragic ending.

Moliere's company shared the Petit-Bourbon and later the Palais-Royal with an Italian troupe, and he is reported to have watched them closely.

What he took is visible in the physical business, the timing and the use of stock configurations, which he then attached to precisely observed French social types, producing a comedy that works as farce and as social criticism in the same scene, which neither source form does on its own.

Moliere's plays take a single social vice and build an entire household around a person consumed by it, which gives satire a dramatic engine rather than a rhetorical one.

The method proved dangerous in practice. Tartuffe, whose target is religious hypocrisy, was suppressed after its first performances under pressure from church authorities and took five years to reach the public stage, which is a measure of how precisely the play was understood to be aimed.

Moliere established the comedy of character, in which the laughter comes from watching a person act consistently on an obsession the rest of the world does not share, and in which the obsessive is usually the one with the power in the household.

His titles name the type, not the plot, and the type outlived him: the miser, the misanthrope and the hypochondriac are still shorthand, which is not true of the plots they appear in.

Chretien's five verse romances established the working shape of Arthurian narrative: a knight of the court leaves it, is tested by a sequence of adventures whose meaning is not immediately clear, and returns having repaired a fault he did not know he had.

He also introduced Lancelot and the affair with the queen, and in the unfinished Perceval he brought in the grail, which the continuations and prose cycles then made into the centre of the whole tradition.

The romance quest as later literature uses it is largely Chretien's design: a journey undertaken by choice, not compulsion, with the object frequently unclear at the outset and the real test located in conduct along the way rather than at the destination.

The grail is the extreme case. In Perceval the failure is not a battle lost but a question the hero neglects to ask, which sets the pattern for quests whose object is understanding.

Dante makes the debt explicit by putting Virgil in the poem as his guide through hell and purgatory, and has his own character address him as the master from whom he took the style that has brought him honour.

The arrangement is also an argument about limits. Virgil can conduct him as far as the earthly paradise and no further, because reason unaided by revelation cannot enter heaven, so the poem's greatest literary authority is also placed among the excluded.

The Aeneid is organised as a deliberate response to both Homeric poems, taking wandering for its first half and warfare for its second, and reworking specific scenes so that the correspondence is unmissable: games for a dead father, a descent to consult him, a shield described at length.

The difference is in the manner of composition. Virgil wrote against the Homeric text over eleven years. That makes the Aeneid the great example of an epic that is a work of reading as much as of invention, a mode Apollonius had already attempted two centuries earlier.

The sixth book takes Aeneas through the underworld to meet his father, who shows him the souls of the Romans not yet born and thereby supplies the poem's justification for everything the hero has endured.

The episode is the most imitated descent in European literature, and it is the direct model for Dante, who has Virgil conduct him through a far more elaborated version of the territory his own poem had mapped.

The Inferno is a descent narrative that keeps going: the poem passes down through hell to the centre of the earth and then climbs out the other side, so the journey to the dead is a passage rather than a visit.

Dante also literalises the convention that the traveller returns with knowledge. What his protagonist brings back is the poem itself, presented as a report of a journey actually made.

The poem takes transformation as its organising principle, which allows it to admit almost any myth and to run continuously from the creation of the world to the poet's own century.

Its effect on the motif is disproportionate: because so much Greek myth survives in Europe through this poem, not through its Greek sources, the transformations that later art and literature draw on are frequently Ovid's versions of them, with his emphases and his tone.

Ovid was a set text in Elizabethan grammar schools, and Shakespeare's early narrative poems draw on him directly, with Venus and Adonis and the Lucrece story both taken from his material.

The debt persists in the plays, most visibly in the mechanicals' Pyramus and Thisbe in A Midsummer Night's Dream, which is a comic performance of an Ovidian tale, and in Titus Andronicus, where a copy of the Metamorphoses is brought on stage as a plot device.

Chaucer drew repeatedly on Ovid for narrative material and for the model of a collection organised around a theme, and he names him among his authorities.

The Legend of Good Women is the clearest case, taking its structure from Ovid's letters of abandoned heroines, and Ovidian tales appear throughout the Canterbury Tales in the mouths of tellers who often misapply them.

Bakhtin built the concept on Dostoevsky's practice, arguing that these novels contain a plurality of consciousnesses that the narration never subordinates to a single verdict.

The evidence he points to is that the strongest arguments in the books are given to characters their author opposed, and are not answered on their own terms. The Grand Inquisitor chapter of The Brothers Karamazov is the standing example, and Dostoevsky's own letters record his anxiety that he had made the case too well.

Bakhtin's book on Dostoevsky, first published in 1929 and substantially revised in 1963, is the work in which the polyphonic novel is defined, and it reads the fiction as a formal innovation rather than as a set of ideas.

Bakhtin argues that what looks like ideological confusion is a deliberate structure in which no voice is finalised, and he distinguishes this from the monologic novel where every position is ultimately placed by the author.

Tristram Shandy addresses the reader constantly, argues with them, blames them for inattention, and interrupts its own chapters to discuss the difficulty of writing chapters.

It is the standing counter-example to the claim that self-conscious fiction is a twentieth-century development, and later self-referential novelists have tended to cite it, not to discover the devices independently.

Shklovsky used the novel as his demonstration piece, arguing that it lays bare the device by making the gap between the story material and its arrangement the entire subject of the book.

His conclusion, deliberately provocative, was that Tristram Shandy is the most typical novel in world literature, on the grounds that every novel deforms its material and this one does nothing else.

Tolkien supplied the genre with its most influential work and with the vocabulary it uses to defend itself, including sub-creation, secondary world and eucatastrophe.

He also supplied its default furniture so thoroughly that the genre spent decades reproducing it, which is a fair complaint against his imitators rather than against him. His own practice began from invented language and philological problems, which almost none of them shared.

The book withholds most of its constructed material from the narrative and puts it in appendices, alphabets, calendars, family trees and a chronology running thousands of years before chapter one.

The technique is the reason the world reads as prior to the story, not assembled for it: characters refer to things the reader will never have explained, and the sense of depth comes from what is not delivered as much as from what is.

Tolkien read Old Norse professionally and ran a club for reading the sagas and Eddas in the original, and the material surfaces throughout his fiction: the dwarf names in The Hobbit are lifted from a list in the Poetic Edda, and the pattern of doom known in advance and resisted anyway is a saga inheritance, not a romance one.

His scholarly argument about Beowulf, that its monsters are the poem's subject rather than a distraction from its history, is the same position stated in criticism.

Tolkien's 1936 lecture on Beowulf changed the poem's critical standing by arguing that the monsters are central rather than embarrassing, and that scholars had been mining a poem for historical data while ignoring what it was built to do.

The reading is inseparable from his fiction, where the elegiac register and the dragon at the end of a long life both descend directly from the poem he was defending.

The Aeneid is the model for the literary epic as distinct from the oral one: composed in writing, in conscious relation to earlier texts, with a structure planned across twelve books rather than accumulated in performance.

Every later European epic written with a Homeric ambition takes its bearings from this poem, not from Homer directly, since Virgil demonstrated what the form could be once it was made on the page.

The Commedia keeps the epic's scale, its journey and its underworld while replacing the collective hero with the poet himself and the founding of a nation with the salvation of a soul.

It also breaks with the tradition on language, choosing Italian over Latin at a moment when serious literature was expected to be Latin, which made the poem an argument about the vernacular as well as a work in it.

The poem is in hexameter and runs to fifteen books, which makes it formally an epic, and it opens with a proper invocation and a claim about the scope of what follows.

What it lacks is a single hero or action, which is the requirement Aristotle had made central. Ovid substitutes a continuous chain of stories linked by transformation, and the mismatch between the epic form and the anthology it contains is part of the poem's wit.

Tristram Shandy appeared while the English novel was still establishing what it was, and it is a counter-example built at the same moment as the model.

It has the apparatus of the form, a first-person life, named characters, a household, a chronology, and refuses to deliver any of it in order. It is read now as evidence that the novel's conventions were understood as conventions almost as soon as they existed.

The book is the genre's reference work, and much of what now reads as a fantasy convention is a feature of this novel repeated by others: the quest party of mixed peoples, the dark lord, the invented languages, the map at the front and the appendices at the back.

Its influence on the market was as decisive as its influence on the form, since the paperback success of the 1960s established that there was a mass readership for long secondary-world fiction.

Old Comedy included a set piece in which the chorus turned to address the audience directly on the playwright's behalf, breaking the action to argue about politics, rivals and the merits of the play being performed.

The convention was structural, not transgressive. That makes it a useful corrective to the assumption that direct address is a modern device: the earliest surviving comedies have it built into their architecture.

New Comedy runs on recognition. A foundling's parentage is established by tokens, a supposed slave turns out to be freeborn, and the marriage that the plot requires becomes possible at the moment the discovery is made.

Aristotle had ranked recognition by tokens lowest among the kinds, and comedy uses it constantly and without embarrassment, since the point there is not the tragic weight of knowledge but the mechanical unlocking of a situation.

Several of Moliere's plays rework material and business he had absorbed from the Italian companies, and his early touring repertoire in the provinces included farces built directly on their scenarios.

What distinguishes the adaptation from imitation is that the masked type becomes a named Frenchman with a specific social position, so the routine survives while its target changes from a generic old man to a particular kind of Parisian.

The Inferno's geography, its pattern of encounters with named shades who recount their own histories, and several individual episodes are worked directly from the sixth book of the Aeneid.

Dante's adaptation is also a correction. He keeps Virgil's underworld and rebuilds it on Christian principles, which places his guide inside a scheme that has no place for him, and the poem makes that predicament explicit rather than passing over it.

Flaubert worked on the novel for roughly five years, notoriously slowly, testing sentences aloud for rhythm and recording in his letters the labour of getting a paragraph to hold.

The method is inseparable from the result: the impersonality he aimed at, an author present everywhere and visible nowhere, required that every judgement be carried by arrangement and detail, not stated, which is expensive to write and is why the book took as long as it did.

Austen is reported to have said before writing it that she was taking a heroine whom no one but herself would much like, which is a description of the technical problem she set herself, not of the character.

The remark comes from her nephew's memoir published half a century later, so it is family recollection rather than a documented statement, but the book bears it out: the reader is kept close enough to Emma's judgement to share it and given exactly enough to distrust it.

Woolf described the method she developed for the book as digging caves behind her characters, so that a past could be excavated and delivered in fragments while the present day continued uninterrupted.

The two strands, the hostess and the shell-shocked veteran, were conceived as a single figure and separated during composition, which is why the pair never meet and why the death of one arrives at the other's party as a piece of dinner conversation.

Dickens wrote it for weekly rather than monthly instalments to rescue the circulation of his own magazine, which forced a tighter structure than his usual serial method produced.

The compression shows: the book is among his shortest and least digressive, with a plot that turns entirely on a single concealed connection. He also replaced his original ending on Bulwer-Lytton's advice, and both versions are now printed together.

Morrison had encountered the Margaret Garner case while editing a documentary history of Black life in America, and returned to it years later as the starting point for the novel.

She was explicit that she did not want to write a historical account and did not research beyond the fragment she began from, on the grounds that the interior life of the woman was the thing the record could not supply and the novel existed to reach.

Le Guin was commissioned to write a book for older children and used the occasion to build a world in which magic is a discipline with costs, not a convenience.

She later described the decision to make her protagonist and most of his people dark-skinned as a deliberate move against the genre's unexamined default, and spent decades objecting to cover illustrations and adaptations that whitened him.

Calvino built the novel on a scheme worked out in advance: ten opening chapters in ten different manners, each cut off, held together by a frame in which a reader pursues the missing continuations.

The procedure belongs to his involvement with the Oulipo group, whose position was that a formal constraint chosen beforehand generates material rather than restricting it, and this is the fullest demonstration of the claim in his work.

Borges turned to short fiction in his late thirties after a head injury and a long convalescence, having previously written essays and poetry, and produced the pieces gathered here over the following decade.

He kept his day job in a municipal library while writing them, and the stories' preoccupation with catalogues, indexes and infinite collections of books is not unrelated to it.

Chekhov finished the play while seriously ill and died within months of its premiere, and his correspondence with the Moscow Art Theatre during rehearsals is a running argument about what kind of play it was.

He insisted it was a comedy, in places a farce, and objected to a production that treated it as a lament for a vanishing class. Stanislavski staged it his own way and it succeeded, which has left the disagreement permanently open.

Andersen began the tales in 1835 as a sideline to the novels and travel writing he expected to be remembered for, and was reportedly irritated to find them overshadowing everything else.

Unlike the Grimms he was composing instead of collecting. The collection contains stories with no traditional analogue at all: a tin soldier, a fir tree, a darning needle, an emperor's new clothes.

The collection appeared in 1697 under the name of Perrault's son, which has left a long-running scholarly question about how much of the work was the father's.

The subtitle referring to Mother Goose framed the tales as nursery material, but the prose is a courtier's, the verse morals address adults, and Perrault was at the time a leading combatant in the literary quarrel over whether modern writers could surpass the ancients.

Hitchcock financed the film himself after the studio declined it, shot it in black and white with his television crew to keep the cost down, and took a share of the profits instead of a fee.

The decision to kill the apparent protagonist a third of the way through was the element everyone involved regarded as the risk, and it is the reason the film's exhibition was managed so tightly, with latecomers refused admission.

Miyazaki began the film without a completed script, which was his usual practice, developing the story as the storyboards advanced and discovering the ending during production.

He has said the film was made for a specific audience of ten-year-old daughters of friends, and that he wanted a protagonist who was neither brave nor gifted, only stubborn enough to keep working.

Disney is said to have mortgaged his house to finish the film, an account repeated in most histories of the studio, and the production was known in the trade as his folly on the assumption that no audience would sit through a feature-length cartoon.

The studio developed the multiplane camera and a formal story department for it, and both became standard. Credit for the result is genuinely distributed, since the supervising animators and story artists shaped it substantially, but the decision to attempt it was his.

The production ran far over schedule and budget, and Kurosawa is reported to have been confident it would not be stopped once the studio had committed, an account that comes largely from the people who worked on it.

His technical practice on the film, multiple cameras running simultaneously with long lenses, was adopted for action filming generally and is now unremarkable.

The play is usually dated to around 1606, shortly after the Gunpowder Plot and early in the reign of a king who had written on witchcraft and claimed descent from Banquo, both of which are visible in the material.

The surviving text is short and shows signs of later adaptation, including songs attributed to Thomas Middleton, so what we have is probably a revised playhouse version rather than the play as first performed.

The opening chapter of Mimesis, by the German philologist Erich Auerbach, reads the binding of Isaac against the recognition of Odysseus by his scar, and argues that the two passages represent incompatible ways of rendering reality.

The biblical narrative gives almost nothing: no landscape, no gestures, no interior states, no explanation of the command or of the father's thoughts on the three-day journey. What is unsaid is not absent but withheld. The text demands interpretation, not merely permitting it.

Auerbach takes the scene in which the old nurse recognises Odysseus by a scar and observes that Homer stops the action for seventy lines to narrate how the scar was acquired.

His point is that the digression is not suspense but the opposite: Homer admits no background and no perspective, placing everything in a uniformly lit foreground where nothing is left obscure. The style is not a limitation but a whole account of what representation is for.

The two texts are the standing comparison for two opposite narrative manners, set against each other most influentially by Auerbach.

Homer externalises: every object described, every motive stated, every digression fully narrated, with no depth left behind the surface. The Hebrew prose withholds almost everything, giving a bare sequence of acts and leaving motive, appearance and setting unspoken. One leaves nothing to be interpreted; the other cannot be read without interpretation.

Auerbach's book takes imitation as its subject in a historical rather than a philosophical register, asking not what representation is but how the range of what could be seriously represented widened over three thousand years.

His governing interest is the separation of styles, the classical rule that ordinary people and daily life belong to comedy and only the elevated to tragedy, and the successive breaches of it, which he traces from the gospels through Dante to the nineteenth-century novel.

Auerbach's account makes nineteenth-century realism the culmination of a long process, not a movement with a manifesto: the point at which an ordinary person's daily circumstances could be treated with full seriousness and situated in a specific historical moment.

His reading of Stendhal, Balzac and Flaubert emphasises exactly that historical embedding, and distinguishes it from earlier depictions of low life, which were available for comedy but not for tragic treatment.

Wolfgang Iser, a German theorist of reading, worked mainly on English fiction from Bunyan onwards, and his argument is that these novels are constructed around what they do not supply.

A text presents schematised views with gaps between them, and the reader's filling of those gaps is not interpretation added afterwards but the process by which the work is realised. On this account no two readings produce the same object, and the text is a set of instructions rather than a finished thing.

The implied reader and the implied author are the two halves of the same move, locating the work in a transaction, not in the text alone.

Booth reconstructs from the text the sensibility that shaped it, which is what allows a narrator to be judged unreliable; Iser reconstructs the position the text prepares for whoever reads it. Neither figure is a person, and both are inferred from the same evidence.

Bordwell treats film narration as a process that cues and limits the inferences a viewer makes, not as a story delivered to a passive spectator, and he built the account from formalist and cognitive rather than psychoanalytic sources.

His work on the classical Hollywood style describes it as a historically located set of norms with datable origins, which was a corrective to writing that treated those conventions as simply how films are made.

Bordwell carried the formalist distinction directly into film theory, treating the story as something the viewer constructs from the cues the film supplies rather than as something the film contains.

The move gives a precise account of how withheld information works on screen: the syuzhet controls what is available and when, and the fabula exists only in the viewer's head. Two people can leave a film having assembled different events from the same footage.

Hayden White, an American theorist of historical writing, argued that a historian faced with a chronicle must emplot it, choosing a story shape that the records themselves do not contain, and that the choice between romance, tragedy, comedy and satire determines the meaning of the account before any argument is made.

The claim borrows Frye's categories and applies them to writing that had understood itself as reporting rather than composing, which is why it was received as an attack, not a description.

White took the four narrative categories of the Anatomy of Criticism and used them as the modes of emplotment available to a historian, treating a body of literary criticism as an analytic tool for non-fiction prose.

The borrowing is explicit and was one of the routes by which Frye's scheme outlived its standing within literary studies, since it continued to do work in historiography after archetypal criticism had gone out of fashion.

The novel is the technique's demonstration piece. Emma's expectations reach the reader in her own vocabulary, borrowed from the romances she has read, while the sentences carrying them remain in the narrator's third person and past tense.

The effect is that the reader occupies her illusions and observes them at once, with no narrator intervening to supply a verdict. That is the impersonality Flaubert was after.

Austen keeps the narration inside Emma's judgement for most of the book without ever endorsing it, so the reader is given her confident misreadings as though they were assessments of fact.

The irony is generated structurally, not by comment: what corrects her is the plot, and on a second reading the sentences that misled the first time turn out to have contained the evidence all along.

The novel moves between minds within continuous passages, handing the narration from one character to another as they pass in the street or hear the same clock, without chapter breaks or announcements.

What distinguishes it from Joyce's practice is that Woolf keeps a narrating syntax rather than dissolving into raw association, so the prose stays hers while the perceptions belong to whoever is currently carrying them.

The novel withholds its central act and returns to it repeatedly, each approach delivering a little more, so the reader learns what happened at the pace the characters become able to face it.

The structure is an argument rather than a device: an event that has not been assimilated cannot be narrated in order, and the book's shape enacts the difficulty of telling it instead of describing that difficulty from outside.

The novel addresses its reader in the second person from the first sentence and keeps doing so, describing them finding a comfortable position, being interrupted, and losing patience with the book they are holding.

The device carries the book instead of decorating it. The reader is a character with a plot, and the ten unfinished novels inside the book exist to give that character something to pursue.

Several of the pieces are not stories but commentaries on works that do not exist, complete with bibliographies, variant editions and corrections of other scholars.

Borges offered the procedure as a labour-saving argument, on the grounds that writing a vast book is exhausting when one can pretend it exists and write the review. The collection is the founding reference point for later fiction that examines its own construction.

The estate is sold in the third act and almost nothing is said about it before or after by the people it ruins, who discuss a bookcase, a passing summer, a sound like a breaking string somewhere out on the land.

The play is the clearest demonstration of the principle that dialogue can carry its weight entirely underneath itself, and it required an acting method capable of playing what is not spoken.

The film has two reversals working against each other. The first is structural, killing the character the audience has been following and leaving them without a protagonist; the second is the conventional revelation at the end.

The first is the more radical, since it withdraws the guarantee that the person a film is following will survive it, and later thrillers have used the possibility ever since whether or not they act on it.

The witches tell Macbeth he will be king and do not tell him how, and the murders he commits to secure the prediction are the means by which it comes true.

The second set of prophecies works the same way in reverse: the assurances that no man born of woman can harm him and that he is safe until a wood moves make him reckless enough to bring about the confrontation in which both are satisfied on terms he had not considered. Nothing in the play requires the witches to have any power beyond being believed.

The audience is given the witches' terms and watches the protagonist take each of them in the wrong sense: a wood that cannot move, a man not born of woman, a security that is a trap disguised as a guarantee.

The irony runs the length of the play rather than sitting at a single revelation, and it converts the prophecies from prediction into cause, since it is his confidence in them that produces the actions bringing them about.

The gospels' parables are the form's defining instances and the reason the term exists in European languages: short narratives drawn from ordinary agricultural and domestic life, told to an audience and left without an application.

The withholding is explicit in the texts themselves, which show hearers failing to understand and record the telling as a deliberate filter, not an accident of style.

Most of the jatakas take the shape of an animal fable, with a monkey, a hare or a quail acting out a lesson in a single reversal, closed by a moral.

What distinguishes them from the Aesopic corpus is the frame: each is told on a specific occasion and closed by identifying which of the animals the Buddha had been, which turns a collection of independent fables into episodes of one continuous life.

Every tale in the collection is set inside an occasion of telling, with a present-day incident prompting the Buddha to recount a former life, and closed by a passage matching the characters in the story to people present at the telling.

The structure does substantial work: it converts a stock of popular tales, many of which circulate elsewhere without any Buddhist content, into a single biography spanning lifetimes.

The two are the major early South Asian frame collections of animal tales, and they are aimed at opposite ends.

The Panchatantra teaches statecraft and the management of allies, enemies and risk, with cleverness rewarded and scruple frequently penalised. The jatakas teach renunciation and merit, with generosity rewarded at enormous personal cost. Several individual stories appear in both. That makes the difference in framing easy to see.

The bathhouse is delivered as a working institution with staff, a hierarchy, a payroll, regular customers and a plumbing crisis, and the film explains none of it.

That refusal is the technique. The protagonist arrives ignorant and is given a job, so the audience learns the rules by watching her get them wrong, and the sense that the place existed before the film started comes from everything the film declines to introduce.

The assembling of a team of specialists, each given an introduction that establishes what they contribute, is among the structures Lucas has cited in describing what he took from Kurosawa, alongside the more frequently mentioned debt to The Hidden Fortress.

The pattern has since become a genre convention in its own right, used in heist films, war films and superhero ensembles, generally without any awareness of where it came from.

The film keeps the poisoned apple, the mirror and the glass coffin and changes almost everything else. The dwarfs are named and given personalities the tale does not supply, the queen's three attempts are reduced to one, and the ending replaces the Grimms' punishment, in which she is made to dance in heated iron shoes, with a fall from a cliff.

It is the standard case for the argument that the studio's versions have displaced the texts they were drawn from.

The collection occupies an unusual position in the form, since these are literary compositions by a named author that have entered general circulation as though they were traditional.

Most readers cannot say which of the famous tales are collected and which invented, and the mermaid, the ugly duckling and the emperor's clothes now function as folk material despite having a documented author and a first publication date.

Perrault's eight tales are the point at which several of the best-known stories acquired the shape they have kept, and it is among the earliest of the great European fairy-tale books, preceded in Italian by Straparola in the 1550s and Basile in the 1630s.

Its framing as nursery material has always sat oddly with its execution, since the prose is worldly, the verse morals are addressed to adults, and the wolf in the final moral is explicitly a figure for a particular kind of man.

Perrault's version supplies the details most readers take for the tale itself: the fairy godmother, the pumpkin, the midnight deadline and the glass slipper, none of which appear in the Grimms' Aschenputtel or in most recorded oral variants.

His ending also differs sharply in temper. The stepsisters are forgiven and married off rather than mutilated and blinded, which is characteristic of his handling throughout.

Perrault's telling ends with the girl eaten and no rescue, followed by a verse moral warning young women about the tame wolves who are the most dangerous kind.

It is the earliest surviving printed version, and setting it beside the Grimms' huntsman and the oral variants in which the girl escapes by her own wit is the standard way of showing how far a tale type's politics can shift between tellings.

The film moved horror out of the castle and the laboratory and into a motel off a highway, replacing the supernatural with a psychiatric explanation and a domestic interior.

Its influence on what followed is structural as much as atmospheric: the killer with a private history, the isolated location that looks ordinary, and the willingness to dispose of a sympathetic character established the terms the next four decades of the genre worked in.

The novel has the form's apparatus, a young protagonist raised out of his origins and educated into a new class, and uses it to arrive at the opposite conclusion.

What the education produces is snobbery, debt and shame toward the people who loved him, and the plot's revelation strips the whole ascent of its justification. It is the English novel's most thorough interrogation of the pattern it belongs to.

Beloved is regularly named in critics' polls as the outstanding American novel of the late twentieth century, and its standing rests on formal ambition as much as subject.

It admits the supernatural without hedging, distributes the narration across several voices including the dead, refuses chronology, and closes on a passage that instructs the reader in how the story has been handled. None of that is decoration; each is doing work the material required.

The book offered the genre a model built on restraint at the moment its dominant example was built on scale: a small archipelago, magic with a price, and an antagonist that turns out to be the protagonist's own released shadow.

It also established the wizard school and the apprenticeship arc as available structures, decades before either became a commercial default.

The novel's central action is a pursuit that resolves when the protagonist names the shadow with his own name and the two become one, which is a Jungian resolution stated almost without disguise.

Le Guin had read Jung and acknowledged the correspondence, while noting that she wrote the pursuit before reading him and recognised the pattern afterwards. That sequence is her own account, not an independently documented one.

The film is among the most widely imitated in cinema, and its influence is easiest to see in structure: a long first movement devoted to recruitment, a middle given to preparation and training, and a final battle staged with the geography made legible in advance.

Its technical practice, multiple cameras with long lenses catching action from several distances at once, became standard for shooting sequences that could not be repeated.

The book is one of the clearest demonstrations of what modernist technique took from and gave up on the nineteenth-century novel: it abandons plot, incident and the accumulation of circumstance, and keeps social observation and moral weight.

Its single-day structure, shared with Ulysses of three years earlier, treats the compression as an opportunity rather than a constraint, since everything excluded from the day has to arrive through memory instead.

The oracle is given to Laius before the child is born, and every action taken to escape it is a link in the chain that fulfils it: the infant is exposed and therefore survives among strangers, and Oedipus leaves the people he believes to be his parents and therefore meets his father on the road.

The play is the pattern's most rigorous instance, since no character acts irrationally and the catastrophe is produced entirely by reasonable attempts at avoidance.

The two devices are usually found together because the pattern depends on the audience holding information the character does not: the terms of the prediction, or the identity of a parent, or the sense in which a promise will be kept.

Without that gap the prophecy is merely a plot announcement. With it, every confident line the character speaks is heard twice, and the working out of the prediction becomes a slow revelation to everyone except the person it concerns.

The forbidden chamber tale carries its own type number and sits beside a cluster of closely related types in which a woman is taken by a supernatural or murderous husband and escapes by her own contrivance, not by rescue.

Separating them by number is what makes the comparison possible. Perrault's version, in which the brothers arrive in time, and the Grimm variant in which the youngest sister revives her siblings and smuggles them out in a basket, are different types telling the same story about the same marriage.

Perrault's telling supplies the elements that fixed the tale: the key that will not come clean, the sister posted at the tower to watch the road, and the brothers arriving at the last possible moment.

His verse morals are unusually shifty here. The first warns wives against curiosity, and the second observes that husbands of this kind no longer exist, which reads as a joke about the first and leaves the tale's actual subject unaddressed.

Perrault's version removes the assault that Basile's earlier Neapolitan telling contains, and keeps the long second half in which the prince's ogress mother attempts to eat his wife and children while he is away at war.

That second half is almost never included in modern retellings, which stop at the waking. The Grimms end there too, so the familiar shape of the tale is the result of two successive editors cutting in the same place for different reasons.

The Grimms' Briar Rose ends at the waking and the wedding, dropping the ogress mother-in-law entirely, which is the version that reached general circulation.

The brothers were aware the tale had come to them through Perrault's French text rather than from independent German tradition, and it is one of the entries that complicates the collection's framing as a record of national popular material.

The swan maiden is the shapeshifter in its oldest and least metaphorical form: a being whose nature is genuinely double and whose transformation depends on a physical object that can be taken from her.

What the tales dramatise is not treachery but captivity. The uncertainty runs the other way from the modern shapeshifter, since the audience knows exactly what she is and only the husband is pretending not to.

The type turns on a transformation that is undone, not imposed, which distinguishes it from the punitive metamorphoses that dominate the classical material.

The beast is enchanted before the story begins, and the plot is the working out of the conditions under which the shape can be released. Ovid's transformations are endpoints; here the change is the situation the narrative sets out to reverse.

The two types put a woman in the same position, married into a house with a husband whose nature she does not know, and resolve it in opposite directions.

In one the prohibition conceals murder and breaking it saves her life; in the other the prohibition or the appearance conceals an enchantment and her acceptance releases him. Told side by side they read as two answers to the same question about what a bride can expect to find.

Both patterns run on terms that are honoured exactly and ruin the person who accepted them, and they differ in where the trap sits.

A prophecy misleads by ambiguity and the victim supplies the actions that fulfil it; a bargain is stated plainly, with the duration and the price agreed, and the ruin comes from the bargainer having wanted the wrong thing. One is a failure of interpretation and the other a failure of desire.

Both figures depend on a substitution that is undetectable by looking, and both produce their unease from a resemblance that ought to be reassuring.

The changeling's version is domestic and specific: the person in the cot is the right size and shape and is not the child. Where the double threatens the singularity of a self, the changeling threatens the reliability of recognition within a family. The tales are so preoccupied with tests.

The sleeping hero is legend rather than myth in the folklorist's sense: it attaches to named historical figures, is located at a specific hill or cave that can be visited, and is told as something that may be true.

That attachment to real places and real kings is what has made it politically usable, since a movement claiming a returning ruler is drawing on a story its audience already half-credits.

The Sphinx's riddle is the event that makes Oedipus king of Thebes, and it happens before the play begins.

Sophocles uses it as a standing irony, not as a scene: the man who solved the riddle about the stages of a human life cannot answer the simpler question of whose son he is, and the play's investigation is a second riddle contest in which the solver is also the answer.

The riddle contest is a machine for generating the gap the device depends on, since the audience is given the answer, or given enough to reach it, before the person whose life depends on it.

The pleasure is in watching someone reason toward something already known, which is the same structure as a prophecy misread or a disguise unrecognised, compressed into a single exchange.

Propp's sequence has the hero tested by a donor and, on the strength of his response, given a magical agent, and the whole subsequent action depends on that transfer.

Identifying it as a function rather than an object is what makes the analysis work: it does not matter whether the agent is a horse, a ring, a bird or an ally, because the position in the sequence is the same and the tale proceeds identically.

Both are objects the plot is organised around, and they work in opposite ways.

The magic object has to have specified properties, because the hero will use it to do something the story requires doing, and a vague one is useless. The MacGuffin must not have them, because the moment the audience becomes interested in what it actually is, attention leaves the people chasing it. One is an instrument and the other is a pretext.

The type is the folk instance of the plot Booker classified, and it is more specific than his category in a useful way.

Booker's pattern requires a threat and a confrontation; the tale type also requires the impostor who claims the kill and the token that exposes him, which means half the story happens after the monster is dead. The classification loses that, and the loss is characteristic of what taxonomies at his level of abstraction cannot hold.

The final third of the poem is a dragon fight in the classic shape: a hoard disturbed, a countryside burned, an old king who goes to face it with a company that abandons him.

What the poem does not use is the second half of the tale type. There is no impostor and no token, because Beowulf does not survive to be displaced, and the aftermath is given over to the funeral and to the wars his death has left his people exposed to.

The Norse material carries the fullest early literary version of the type in the story of Sigurd and Fafnir, preserved in the Poetic Edda and in the Volsunga saga.

It has the elements the folk versions keep: the hoard, the killing from concealment, the tasting of the blood that confers understanding of birds, and the treachery of the companion who wants the credit and the gold.

The Gothic supplied modern horror with almost all of its early apparatus and with its basic proposition, that the past is not finished and will present its account.

What changed in the transfer is location and explanation. The threat moved out of the inherited castle and into the motel, the suburb and the body, and the source of dread moved from a curse to a psychology, but the structure of a protagonist who is slowly proved right to be afraid did not.

The novel carries the Gothic apparatus intact: transgression against a limit, an isolated maker, a pursuit across a wasteland, and a secret that destroys a family.

What it replaces is the source of the horror, which is a deliberate act performed with instruments, not a curse or an inheritance. That substitution is why the same book is claimed as a founding text by two genres that otherwise have little in common.

The name was a claim about lineage before it was a genre. Walpole subtitled his book a Gothic story to assert descent from medieval romance, and presented the first edition as a translation of an Italian manuscript of the crusading period.

What the Gothic took from romance is the castle, the inheritance, the prophecy and the marvellous, and what it discarded is the code of conduct that made romance a moral form. The remainder is the machinery without the ethics.

Northanger Abbey is built on the Gothic as a shared readership: its heroine's expectations are formed by Radcliffe, and the comedy comes from her applying them to an ordinary English household.

Austen's treatment is affectionate rather than dismissive, and the book withholds the easy conclusion. The general is not a murderer, but he is a bully who turns a young woman out of his house, and the Gothic reading turns out to have been wrong about the facts and right about the man.

Melodrama began as a specific theatrical form with music cued under the action, and dominated the nineteenth-century popular stage in France, Britain and the United States before the term became a general description of a mode.

Its stage machinery was substantial and part of the appeal, with fires, floods, rescues from moving trains and other spectacular effects developed alongside the plots that required them.

Both stage suffering and reach opposite conclusions about who deserves it.

Tragedy requires that the protagonist be implicated in what befalls them, which is what hamartia is for; melodrama requires that the victim be innocent and the persecutor culpable, so the moral accounting is clear and the appropriate response is indignation, not pity and fear. Critics long treated the difference as a hierarchy, which obscured what melodrama is actually built to do.

Silent cinema inherited the form directly, including the continuous musical accompaniment that the stage version had established, and the reliance on legible gesture suited a medium without dialogue.

The inheritance did not end with sound. The scored underlining of emotional beats, the last-minute rescue assembled by cross-cutting, and the clear moral positioning of a threatened protagonist remain the grammar of popular film whatever genre it is sold as.

Detective fiction is retrospective and thrillers are prospective, and almost every structural difference follows from that.

The detective story opens with a completed crime and moves backwards through evidence to an explanation, with the reader invited to reason; the thriller opens with a threat and moves forward under a deadline, with the reader invited to worry. One withholds a solution, the other withholds an outcome.

The genre's structural unit is the chapter that ends a moment before a resolution, which is why thrillers are written in short chapters and why they read quickly.

The device is doing the same work as in serial publication, but compressed: rather than securing a return next month, it secures the turned page, and the pacing of the whole book is built out of a repeated small refusal to let a scene finish.

Hitchcock worked in the genre for half a century and supplied it with several of its standing configurations: the innocent man wrongly pursued, the ordinary setting turned hostile, and the audience made complicit by being shown more than the characters know.

His conversations with Truffaut also gave the form a vocabulary for what it was doing, which is part of why thriller construction is discussed in technical terms more readily than most popular genres.

The film is built on the genre's forward motion and then breaks it, since the audience spends its first act worrying about a theft and a police pursuit that turn out not to be the story.

The misdirection is total: the money, which every convention identifies as the thing that matters, is a MacGuffin, and it ends in a swamp with the car it was hidden in.

The genre is a nineteenth-century development within the novel rather than an older form, and it required a prior change in how the past was understood.

Before history was thought of as a sequence of distinct social conditions, not a stock of examples, a story set two hundred years earlier had no reason to differ from one set in the present. The historical novel becomes possible when the difference between periods becomes the point.

Both take the reader into a past populated by knights, kings and battles, and they treat it in incompatible ways.

Romance uses the past as a permanent elsewhere with fixed conventions, where a twelfth-century audience and a fifteenth-century one find the same Arthur. Historical fiction insists the period is specific, researched and different from the present, and that its characters cannot hold modern assumptions without falsifying it.

Dystopia sits inside science fiction by the genre's own definition, since it proposes a change to the conditions of a society and follows the consequences.

What distinguishes it is that the change is political rather than technological, and that the extrapolation is aimed at the reader's present, not at a possible future. The technology in the canonical examples is deliberately modest, because the argument is about arrangements of power.

Both work by taking something the reader recognises and pushing it past the point where it can be defended, and both depend on the audience making the identification unaided.

The difference is duration. Satire can make its point in a paragraph and get out; the dystopia has to sustain the exaggerated world for a whole book. Its plots so often reduce to a protagonist being shown around and then punished.

Kurosawa acknowledged the American Western, and John Ford in particular, as a direct model, and the film's landscape framing and its treatment of the professional fighter without a place in the settlement he protects both come from it.

The traffic then reversed, since the film was remade as a Western in 1960, which makes this one of the clearest cases of a genre convention crossing between national cinemas and returning altered.

The Western is the American cinema's foundational genre and for decades its most productive, supplying the studios with a setting whose conventions the audience knew well enough that a film could depart from them and be understood.

Its later history is one of self-examination, as films from the 1960s onward reopened the questions of whose land the settlement was on and what the man with the gun had actually secured.

The guslar is the living tradition on which the modern understanding of oral composition was built, and its evidential importance is out of proportion to its size.

The singers work with a stock of themes and a metrical formula system that allows a line to be assembled in performance, which is why no two renditions of the same song match and why the notion of an original text does not apply.

Parry went to Yugoslavia in the 1930s because the tradition offered something the Homeric question could not supply, a living oral epic practice that could be observed and recorded, not inferred.

The recordings, made on aluminium discs and now held at Harvard, allowed the same singer's performances of the same song to be compared across occasions, which is the evidence the whole oral-formulaic argument rests on.

The repertoire covers the Kosovo cycle, the Ottoman wars and the outlaw hero Marko Kraljevic, performed at lengths that can run over several nights.

One singer recorded by Parry and Lord, Avdo Mededovic, produced a song of some twelve thousand lines, comparable in scale with the Odyssey, which was the demonstration that a poem of Homeric length could be composed without writing.

The sagas quote skaldic verse as evidence, introducing a stanza attributed to a named poet as corroboration for an event the prose has just narrated.

The practice works because the metre is so tightly constructed that a line cannot be casually altered without breaking it, which meant verse could travel through generations of oral transmission with far more stability than prose. Whether the attributions are reliable is a separate and much-argued question.

Skaldic composition is a professional oral art with an unusually demanding technical standard: internal rhyme, fixed syllable counts, alliteration on prescribed positions, and a syntax so displaced that a stanza can take considerable work to unpick.

The difficulty was the point. A patron paying for praise was paying for something that could not be produced by anyone, and the kenning system is the most visible sign of the craft.

The naqqal performs alone, without staging or accompaniment, carrying the whole cast and the narration in one voice and using the space of a coffeehouse floor as the entire theatre.

The repertoire is largely fixed and drawn from written epic, but the delivery is not, since the performer adjusts pace, emphasis and commentary to the room. A related practice performs the same material along a large painted cloth, moving through its scenes as the story advances.

The tradition's core repertoire is the Shahnameh, Ferdowsi's eleventh-century epic of the Persian kings, which the naqqal delivers episode by episode over successive sessions.

The arrangement inverts the usual relationship: here a written literary epic is sustained in popular circulation by oral performance, rather than an oral tradition being fixed by writing.

The changeling belief and its tales were among the most persistent material in the Irish repertoire, recorded extensively by twentieth-century collectors alongside stories of fairy abduction of adults, nursing mothers and the newly married.

The collectors were often recording from people who had grown up when the belief carried practical weight. The archive contains accounts of remedies and tests as well as narratives.

In the earliest surviving tragedies the chorus is not a commentator on the action but a participant in it, and in The Suppliants the fifty daughters of Danaus are effectively the protagonist.

Aeschylus is credited with introducing the second actor, which began the long transfer of dramatic weight away from the chorus and toward individual characters, so his own work stands at both ends of the change.

The chorus was a structural requirement of Athenian tragedy, not an option, funded by a wealthy citizen as a public duty and trained for the festival competition.

Its odes divided the episodes, which is where the division of a play into acts originally comes from: the acts are the gaps between choral songs, and they survived long after the songs that created them had gone.

Brecht's use of songs and direct address to interrupt the action and comment on it draws on the chorus's function of holding the audience at a distance from the events.

The borrowing is selective. He wanted the interruption and the commentary without the chorus's other role of representing a community's settled moral position, since the point of his theatre was that the audience's position should be unsettled rather than confirmed.

Both occupy a position between the events and the audience, and both can know more than the characters and address the audience directly.

The chorus differs in being present in the world it comments on, visible to the characters and unable to intervene effectively, which is a constraint no narrator has. That combination of full knowledge and complete powerlessness is the source of most of its dramatic effect.

Shakespeare used the convention to carry the material that later fiction would put into narration, giving the audience access to deliberation, self-deception and fear that no other character hears.

Hamlet's speeches are the standard examples, but Macbeth's are the more mechanically important, since the play's action turns on decisions he reaches alone on stage and the audience watches him argue himself into and out of them.

Both deliver a mind directly and neither claims to be a record of how thought actually proceeds.

The soliloquy is composed, argued and addressed, closer to a speech than to a reverie, while interior monologue drops the connective tissue and the addressee. The difference is largely a matter of what the surrounding form can support: a stage requires audibility and shape, a page does not.

The convention sits on the boundary the wall describes. A character alone on stage is not addressing the audience, and yet the speech exists only because an audience is there to hear it.

Productions decide the question in staging, not in text: the same lines can be played as private thought overheard or delivered straight out to the house, and the two choices produce different plays.

The play staged before the court is a play about the murder the play itself concerns, watched by the man who committed it while the man who arranged the performance watches him.

The device is doing plot work rather than decoration, since the reaction is the evidence Hamlet has been waiting for, and it also states the play's argument about theatre, that a fiction can compel a response reality has failed to.

Both nest one narrative inside another, and they differ in whether the inner one reflects the outer.

A frame is a container: the pilgrims tell tales that need have nothing to do with the pilgrimage. Mise en abyme requires resemblance, so that the inner version comments on the work holding it, which is why the play within the play is usually about the situation of the people watching it.

The novel contains ten openings of novels, and its frame concerns a reader trying to finish a book that keeps failing, the reader's own situation while holding it.

Calvino also gives the inner books titles that, read in sequence, form a sentence, so the fragments compose a text of their own at the level above the one they belong to.

Beginning in the middle creates the debt that exposition has to service, since everything before the opening must arrive somehow once the story is already running.

The two techniques are therefore usually discussed together in craft teaching, and the standard advice is to withhold as long as the audience can tolerate, on the grounds that information supplied before it is wanted registers as delay and the same information supplied when it is wanted registers as revelation.
