Greek drama solved the problem of prior information by having someone tell the audience directly, in a prologue or through the chorus's recollection of the mythic background, without pretending the address was to another character.

The candour of the arrangement is what modern naturalism gave up, and the devices that replaced it, the newcomer, the briefing, the letter, all exist to disguise a transaction the Athenians conducted openly.

The two share a name and almost nothing else. Verbal irony is produced by a speaker who means the opposite of what they say, and it fails if the audience does not detect the intention.

Dramatic irony requires no intention at all: it arises from a gap between what the audience knows and what the character does, and the character's sincerity is precisely what makes it work. One is a rhetorical act, the other a structural condition.

Both put the significant meaning somewhere other than in what is said, and irony is the sharper instrument of the two.

Subtext leaves the real matter unspoken and lets the audience infer it from evasion; verbal irony states something and relies on the audience to reverse it. A character who is ironic is displaying a judgement while declining to own it. The device is so useful for people who cannot afford to say what they think.

Austen's narrators state propositions the books proceed to demolish, beginning with the famous assertion about single men and fortunes, which is offered as universally acknowledged and is the opinion of the neighbourhood, not of the narrator.

The technique extends into the free indirect passages, where a character's confident formulation is reported without endorsement, so that irony and point of view become the same operation.

Both ask to be read as being about something other than their surface, and they differ in how completely the correspondence maps.

An allegory can be decoded element by element, with each figure standing for a specified thing; a parable presents an ordinary situation whose application is left open, and frequently supports several. The parable withholds the key. Interpretations of the same one have differed for two thousand years.

Dante's poem is built on the medieval practice of reading a text at several levels at once, and a letter attributed to him sets out that scheme explicitly for the Commedia.

The journey is at once a literal itinerary, a moral account of sin and its correction, and a figure for the soul's progress, and the poem's architecture is designed so that all three readings can be sustained simultaneously rather than in alternation.

Tolkien stated in a foreword to The Lord of the Rings that he disliked allegory in all its manifestations and had never been drawn to writing it, objecting particularly to readings of the book as a treatment of the Second World War.

His alternative was applicability, which he located in the freedom of the reader, not in the purposed domination of the author. The distinction has been argued about ever since, since a great many readers find the applicability suspiciously specific.

A motif that has been attached to a person or an outcome can be introduced before either arrives. That makes it a means of preparation that operates below the audience's notice.

Film scoring uses this constantly: a few notes belonging to a character are heard while the screen shows something else, and the audience registers the connection before it can articulate it. The literary equivalent is a repeated image whose weight is only settled retrospectively.

The reprise is the musical's version of the device: a song returns late in the show, sung by a different character or in altered circumstances, and the change carries the meaning.

The technique depends on the audience remembering the first statement well enough to hear what has happened to it. The form's most effective reprises come from its simplest tunes.

Omission is one of the primary operations by which an arrangement differs from the events it arranges, and the formalist distinction is what makes it describable as a choice, not a gap.

Genette systematised this under the heading of duration, treating the ellipsis as the limiting case in which a stretch of story receives no narration at all, which is a measurable relation between two things rather than an absence.

Both compress time and they do it by opposite means. A montage covers an interval by showing fragments of it, so the passage is narrated at speed; an ellipsis covers it by showing nothing and letting the audience register the jump.

The choice is not neutral. A training montage insists the work was done, while a cut to a competent protagonist three months later insists that the work was not the interesting part.

Ballads were sung, remembered and altered rather than composed and fixed, and the same story survives in dozens of versions with different names, different endings and different regions attached.

Their technique is shaped by the conditions of performance: entering the story late, leaping between scenes, carrying the action in dialogue, and repeating a stanza with a single element changed so that a listener can follow a sequence without being told it is a sequence.

Both are sung narrative verse and they operate at opposite scales and registers.

The epic is long, encyclopaedic and concerned with the fate of a people, delivered by a specialist over hours or nights; the ballad is short, elliptical and concerned with a single incident, generally a death, and can be carried by anyone who has heard it. What the ballad discards is precisely the connective and explanatory material the epic exists to supply.

Both narrate violent events with a restraint that modern readers find striking, reporting acts and speech and declining to report feeling.

The ballad's version is more extreme because the form is shorter: a mother's response to a son's death may be a single repeated line, and the effect depends entirely on what the stanza refuses to say. The two traditions are geographically adjacent and the shared reticence is not a coincidence.

The integrated musical is a dramatic form in which the songs carry plot and character instead of decorating them, and the convention it asks an audience to accept is precise: characters sing at the point where speech has run out.

Its development is usually traced through Show Boat in 1927 and Oklahoma! in 1943, which established that the numbers should advance the story, replacing an earlier practice of assembling songs around a loose comic frame.

The musical inherits directly from the nineteenth-century popular stage, where music ran under the action to underline emotional turns and where the moral positions were drawn clearly enough to be sung.

The continuity is institutional as well as formal, since the same theatres, audiences and production companies carried one form into the other as the older melodrama's spectacular effects moved to the cinema.

Both apply the techniques of storytelling to material presented as true, and both live with the same unresolved tension between shaping and reporting.

Grierson's description of documentary as the creative treatment of actuality is the film equivalent of the nonfiction novel's claim, and the objections raised against each are identical: that scene construction, selection and sequencing produce meaning the record does not contain.

Documentary is as old as the medium, since the earliest films were records of actual events, and the distinction between fiction and non-fiction filmmaking was drawn afterwards rather than found.

Flaherty's Nanook of the North in 1922 is the conventional founding work and also the standing problem, since sequences were staged, an igloo was built open-sided for the light, and the resulting film is both an ethnographic record and a construction.

The two forms make opposite bargains with continuity. The serial requires that events accumulate, so viewers must watch in order and characters change; the situation comedy requires that they do not, so any episode can be watched by anyone and the cast arrives at the next one unaltered.

The reset is what allows a comic character to keep failing in the same way for a decade, and its erosion in later television is why so many comedies now end after four seasons.

The arc requires that a character change; the situation comedy requires that they cannot, since a person who has learned from their mistakes is no longer available to make them.

The form's later history is largely the negotiation of that constraint, with shows granting slow change to some characters while protecting the comic engine of others, and the ones that let everybody grow tend to become something other than sitcoms in the process.

The situation comedy inherits New Comedy's machinery almost intact: a household or workplace of fixed types, a disturbance caused by desire or misunderstanding, and a resolution that restores the group.

What it adds is repetition. Menander's community reforms once and the play ends; the sitcom's reforms weekly, which converts a plot shape into a renewable format.

Kristeva introduced Bakhtin to French readers in the 1960s and coined the term while doing so, drawing on his account of the word as always already carrying the uses others have made of it.

The transfer changed the emphasis. Bakhtin was describing voices in dialogue within a social world; the term as it circulated became a claim about relations between texts, with the speakers largely dropped out of it.

Genette took the general proposition and built a taxonomy on it, distinguishing quotation and allusion from parody, pastiche, commentary and continuation, and treating a text that rewrites an earlier one as a palimpsest with the older writing still legible underneath.

The classification is the most systematic attempt to make the idea usable, since intertextuality in its broad form claims something true of all texts and therefore distinguishes nothing.

Ulysses is the standing example of a work built from other texts, since it takes its structure from the Odyssey, parodies the whole history of English prose style in one episode, and quotes advertisements, newspapers, songs and liturgy throughout.

It is also where the concept meets its limit, because a book this deliberately constructed is a matter of demonstrable influence, not of the general textual condition the term describes.

Recognition is the most common instrument of closure, because a narrative usually cannot continue once the withheld knowledge has arrived and been acted on.

Aristotle's preference for a recognition arising from the events rather than from tokens is a claim about closure as much as about plausibility: an ending produced by the plot's own logic feels finished, while one produced by an outside revelation feels stopped.

The modern short story is where the question of what an ending owes a reader has been argued most sharply, since Chekhov's practice of stopping while the meaning is still assembling became the literary default.

The form makes the choice unavoidable. A novel can dissipate an ending across fifty pages of settlement; a story ends on a sentence, and whether that sentence resolves or withholds is the largest decision in it.

The cliffhanger is closure deliberately denied, and it works only because the audience expects the other thing.

An instalment that ends on an unresolved threat is exploiting the discomfort that an unfinished story produces, which is the same impulse that closure satisfies. The two are therefore not opposites so much as the same mechanism operated in opposite directions.

The journey's stages are usually taught as an arc rather than an itinerary, with the ordeal at the centre understood as the point at which the protagonist's governing weakness is confronted, not as a physical crisis.

Vogler's adaptation makes the reading explicit, and it is what allows the pattern to be applied to stories with no journey in them at all, which Campbell's comparative version does not straightforwardly support.

The picaro does not change, and the form depends on it. He acquires tactics, survives more masters and arrives at the end of the book as he began, which is what allows the episodes to be extended indefinitely and reordered without damage.

That makes the picaresque the clearest counter-example to the assumption that a protagonist must develop, and it is the reason the form is so often described as shapeless by people applying the wrong criterion.

The screenwriting teacher John Truby organises his scheme around a weakness the protagonist begins with and a self-revelation they arrive at, with the plot's function being to attack the first until the second becomes unavoidable.

His distinctive move is to require that the opponent be the character best equipped to exploit that specific weakness. That makes antagonist and arc a single design problem, not two.

Truby's objection is that dividing a script into three blocks describes its proportions and says nothing about what has to occur inside them, so a writer can satisfy the model completely and still have no story.

His alternative is a sequence of steps defined by function, not by position, which he presents as organic rather than mechanical. Critics of his own scheme note that twenty-two required steps is a considerably more prescriptive object than three acts.

The script consultant Linda Seger treats the screenplay as something to be diagnosed and repaired, not admired, and it made rewriting a subject in its own right at a point when the manuals were almost entirely about how to begin.

Her questions are practical and unforgiving: what is this scene accomplishing, what does this character want in it, and what would be lost if it were cut, which is the working method of development rather than of criticism.

Seger's structural vocabulary assumes the paradigm Field had established, and her contribution sits on top of it: given a script built to those proportions, she asks why it is nonetheless not working.

The relationship is characteristic of the field's development, in which a widely adopted model generates a second literature devoted to the problems it does not address.

The five-stage scheme comes out of Todorov's structuralist work on narrative and is the most widely taught piece of it, largely because it can be stated in a sentence and applied to anything.

It belongs to the same project as his grammar of the Decameron, in which narratives are analysed as sequences of transformations of a state, and it is the general form of what that study derives from a specific corpus.

Both reduce narrative to a sequence of positions, at opposite levels of resolution. Propp's thirty-one functions describe a particular corpus in enough detail to reconstruct its tales; Todorov's five stages describe any narrative and reconstruct nothing.

The trade is the one every taxonomy of narrative makes, and the two schemes sit at the ends of the range. They are so often taught together.

The Homeric poems are the standard demonstration of the pattern, with speeches, digressions and whole episodes arranged so that the elements introduced on the way in are answered in reverse order on the way out.

The scar digression is a compact example: the narrative leaves the nurse's hands on the scar, travels back through the boar hunt and the naming of the child, and returns to the same hands, with the centre holding the material that explains the mark.

The structure suits performance conditions in which nobody can turn back a page, since the symmetry provides a listener with landmarks and lets an echo stand in for the rereading a page would allow.

It also assists the performer, because a nested arrangement gives each element a paired partner and therefore a cue for what comes next, which is the same principle that makes formulaic diction stable.

Chiastic arrangement is pervasive in the Hebrew Bible at every scale, from a single verse whose clauses mirror each other to whole books organised symmetrically around a central passage.

The pattern is a working assumption in biblical scholarship rather than a curiosity, since identifying the centre of a structure identifies where its argument sits, and that is frequently not where a modern reader expecting a climax would look for it.

Both are structural schemes in which the decisive material sits away from the end, and both are regularly presented as evidence that the climax-at-the-close model is a convention, not a necessity.

They differ in the mechanism. Ring composition places the turn at the centre of a symmetry that closes afterwards; kishotenketsu places it in the third of four parts and uses the fourth to reconcile what it introduced.

The form is named after him in most European languages, and the attribution is the point rather than the biography: almost nothing about the man is recoverable, and tales were assigned to him for centuries after any plausible lifetime.

What the name marks is a manner. A short prose narrative with animal actors, one reversal and a stated moral became the Aesopic type, and any story fitting it could be admitted to the corpus regardless of where it came from.

The two great early fable collections share animals, brevity and stated morals, and differ in what they are for.

The Aesopic tales stand alone and teach prudence to anyone: the strong will take what they want, boasting is punished, expect nothing from a benefactor. The Panchatantra is framed as instruction for princes and nested several layers deep, and its lessons concern the management of allies, ministers and enemies. One is folk wisdom, the other is a manual of statecraft.

In the central Akan tale Anansi buys all the world's stories from the sky god Nyame, whose price is a set of creatures nobody could be expected to catch, and takes each of them by a trick suited to its nature.

Stories in the tradition are called spider stories after him, which makes the trickster the proprietor of narrative itself. The arrangement is unusual: most traditions locate the origin of storytelling in a god or an ancestor, not in a successful con.

The Anansi cycle travelled with enslaved Akan people across the Atlantic and persisted in Jamaica, other parts of the Caribbean and the American South, where a figure who survives overwhelming power by wit had an obvious application.

The stories adapted rather than merely surviving, acquiring new antagonists and new settings, and they are among the clearest documented cases of a narrative tradition carried intact through forced migration.

The bargain has its own type number in the international index, in the group of tales concerning the rewards and punishments of the supernatural, and its variants include the contract escaped on a technicality as often as the contract enforced.

The folk versions are frequently comic, with a peasant or a blacksmith outwitting the devil over a term of years, which sits oddly beside the literary treatments and is the more common form in the collected record.

Both name a fault that is committed knowingly and is not wickedness, and both produce a catastrophe the person could have avoided.

The bargainer's error is characteristically one of valuation rather than of knowledge: the terms are stated plainly and accepted anyway, because what is being bought seems worth it and the price is distant. That makes it a version of tragic error suited to a Christian scheme, where the fault is a choice, not a mistake.

The sleeping hero is the archetype held in reserve. The figure has completed the journey, been withdrawn, not buried, and remains available for a return that never quite arrives.

The pattern's persistence has less to do with the individual kings attached to it than with what it does for a community under pressure, which is to convert a defeat into a postponement.

Scandinavian tradition attaches the pattern to Holger the Dane, who sleeps beneath Kronborg with his beard grown into the stone and will wake when the country is in danger.

The figure entered the material from the Charlemagne cycle and was thoroughly naturalised, which is characteristic of how the motif travels: the story is stable and the sleeper is local.

McKee works within the act model while treating it as a consequence, not a rule, arguing that acts are defined by the major reversals that close them rather than by page counts.

His unit of analysis is smaller than the act: the scene, which he holds must turn a value from positive to negative or back, and the sequence of scenes that builds to each reversal. A script that satisfies the proportions and fails at that level fails entirely on his account.

McKee's position is that character is revealed by choice under pressure and that the deeper the pressure, the more truthful the revelation. That makes the arc a by-product of escalating dilemma rather than something designed separately.

He distinguishes characterisation, the observable surface of a person, from true character underneath it, and treats the gap between the two as most of what a story is for.

The frame makes the device a matter of survival, not of appetite: the story must be unfinished at daybreak, because a king who has heard the ending has no reason to postpone the execution.

It is the clearest statement in any literature of what the technique actually does, which is to convert a listener's curiosity into an obligation, and every serial that ends an instalment on a threat is operating the same mechanism with lower stakes.

The fictional teller and the historical profession are doing the same job under different pressures. Both work by night, both perform long cycles in instalments, and both depend on breaking at a point that compels the audience to return.

The coffeehouse storyteller needed the audience back for a living; the character needed the king back for her life. The frame is a dramatisation of a working practice rather than an invention.

The stolen skin sits in the index among the tales of a supernatural wife, and the numbering makes visible how widely the same story is distributed: versions are recorded across Europe, Central and East Asia, the Pacific and the Americas.

The consistency of the detail is what strikes comparativists. It is almost always a garment or skin, almost always hidden, not destroyed, and almost always found by a child.

The transformation here is a natural capacity rather than an event: the woman is both things already, and the skin is the mechanism by which she moves between them.

That makes it the opposite of the classical pattern, where a metamorphosis is inflicted once and is usually permanent. What the tale takes from her is not her shape but her access to it. The recovery of the skin ends the marriage immediately and without deliberation.

The tale exists almost entirely in oral tradition, not in a canonical literary version. That makes it a useful demonstration of what that difference means.

There is no authoritative text to depart from, the sympathies shift according to who is telling it, and the endings vary from the wife's permanent departure to a negotiated return. Nothing in the record privileges one version, which is the normal condition of a folktale and the abnormal condition of a fairy tale.

The late plays, Pericles, Cymbeline, The Winter's Tale and The Tempest, take material that would carry a tragedy, including jealousy, a death sentence and a lost child, and resolve it through recognition and restoration.

The Winter's Tale is the extreme case, running three acts of destructive jealousy, killing a queen and a son, then jumping sixteen years and returning the queen as a statue that moves. Nothing in either genre's rules accommodates the manoeuvre.

Chekhov called his plays comedies and objected when they were staged as laments, which is the disagreement his work has generated ever since.

The texts support both readings because they refuse the tonal signals that would settle it: an estate is lost, a life is wasted, a shot is heard offstage, and the scene around each event continues in the register of people talking about the weather. Modern tragicomedy proceeds largely from this.

Tradition credits Valmiki not only with the Ramayana but with the shloka metre itself, in a story that has him utter the first verse spontaneously on seeing a hunter kill one of a pair of birds, the metre arising from grief.

The account is legendary rather than documented, and it appears within the poem it explains. What it records is a tradition's own understanding of where narrative verse comes from, and is valuable on those terms.

Tradition credits Vyasa not only with the Mahabharata but with arranging the Vedas and composing the Puranas, which makes him less an author in the modern sense than the figure a whole textual inheritance is attributed to.

He is also a character inside his own epic, the grandfather of both sets of warring cousins, appearing at intervals to advise and withdraw. The arrangement makes the poem's frame recursive: it is recited by a bard who had it from a disciple of Vyasa, about events Vyasa took part in.

The Homeric poems arrange speeches, digressions and episodes symmetrically around a centre, so that elements introduced on the way into a passage are answered in reverse order on the way out.

The technique is well suited to a listening audience that cannot turn back, since the return of an element signals where in the structure the performance has reached, and it gives the performer a set of paired cues, not a linear sequence to remember.

The poem's digressions have long been treated as interruptions and read better as structure: episodes about earlier feuds are placed so that they answer one another across the poem, with the material they comment on between them.

Tolkien's argument that the poem is balanced, not badly organised, opposing youth and age in two great movements rather than telling a life in sequence, is an argument about this kind of arrangement.

Sophocles enlarged the chorus from twelve to fifteen and used it as the voice of the community whose welfare the protagonist's actions are wrecking.

In Oedipus Rex the elders move from confidence in their king through unease to horror, and the audience's own position is tracked by theirs. The chorus knows less than the audience and more than it wants to, which is a considerably more useful dramatic position than omniscience would be.

Old Comedy attacked named living individuals from the public stage at a civic festival, with the target frequently in the audience, and nothing in the later history of the mode has matched that licence.

The method is exaggeration to the point of fantasy rather than distortion of fact: the demagogue is a slave running a household, the philosopher hangs in a basket studying the sky. Later satire's standard defence, that the reader is expected to supply the correction, is already fully operational there.

New Comedy's household of fixed types, disturbed each time by desire or misunderstanding and restored by the close, is the situation comedy's structure with the repetition removed.

The inheritance runs through Plautus, the Renaissance stage, the well-made play and radio serials, and each transfer kept the machinery while changing the medium. What television added was the requirement that the restoration be exact, so the same disturbance can occur again next week.

The play is the most compressed of the tragedies and the one in which the protagonist's deterioration is narrated by the protagonist, since he tells the audience at each stage what he is becoming and proceeds anyway.

Its unusual feature within the genre is how little external opposition it contains until very late. For most of its length the antagonist is the man's own imagination, which supplies the daggers, the ghost and the sleeplessness.

The play contains seven soliloquies, and they carry the material that makes it what it is: the deliberation, the self-accusation for failing to act, and the examination of whether to continue living at all.

They also create the problem the play is famous for, since a character who thinks at this length in public becomes more interesting than the revenge plot he is delaying, and four centuries of criticism have argued about which is the subject.

The novel is assembled from other books at every level: a protagonist constructed by reading, a narrator working from a manuscript by a fictional historian, a library inspected and burned volume by volume, and a second part populated by people who have read the first.

It also absorbs a rival, since Cervantes wrote a spurious continuation published under another name into his own text and had his characters meet its readers.

Borges's stories are built almost entirely out of relations to other texts, real, invented and deliberately confused, with genuine sources cited alongside fabricated ones in the same footnote.

One piece imagines a writer who reproduces Don Quixote word for word and argues that the identical text is richer for having been written three centuries later by a different man, which is the concept stated as a fable before the theorists arrived at it.

Dickens took the popular theatre's apparatus directly into the novel: the persecuted innocent, the unambiguous villain, the deathbed, the concealed parentage and the rescue that arrives in the final pages.

He was a theatregoer and an amateur performer, and he read his own work aloud on tour with the emphases of a stage performance. The critical difficulty with him has always been that the melodramatic machinery and the social observation are the same machinery.

Miss Havisham's house is a Gothic property transplanted into a novel of social realism: a stopped clock, a rotting wedding cake, a woman in a decayed dress who has not seen daylight for decades, and a young girl raised inside it as an instrument of revenge.

Dickens uses the machinery without the supernatural, which is the direction the mode took in the nineteenth century generally: the haunting is a person, and the curse is money.

The form's meaning is made in the cutting room more visibly than in most fiction, since the material was not staged and the sequence it is given is the filmmaker's argument.

The Soviet claim that meaning arises from the collision between shots applies with particular force here, because a documentary that juxtaposes an official statement with footage contradicting it has made an assertion that neither shot contains.

Both forms run on a fixed set of types whose traits the audience knows in advance, so that the comedy comes from the collision, not from the introduction.

The transmission is not direct, but the structural resemblance is exact: a small company playing the same characters indefinitely, a stock of reusable comic routines, and plots that exist to give the routines an occasion.

The situation comedy is the scheme's cleanest instance and also its exception. An episode opens in equilibrium, disrupts it, recognises the disruption and repairs it, all within twenty-two minutes.

What it declines is the model's last requirement, that the new equilibrium differ from the first. The comedy's whole economy depends on the restoration being exact, which is why the form is better described by four of Todorov's five stages than by all of them.

Both are sung verse from the same centuries and they belong to opposite social worlds.

The troubadour lyric is courtly, composed by named poets for aristocratic patrons, preoccupied with the service of an unattainable lady, and written down in songbooks. The ballad is popular, anonymous, narrative rather than lyric, concerned with murder and betrayal, and survives in variants because nobody was preserving an original.

Both are popular theatres in which music, dance, spectacle and star performance carry as much of the evening as the plot does, and in which an audience attends partly to see familiar material done well.

Both also developed conventions their audiences read fluently and outsiders find opaque: a set-piece pose held for applause, a number that stops the action to state what a character wants, and a company of specialists trained in a specific range of roles.

Both use a surface narrative to deliver something else, and the fable is the smaller and more transparent instrument.

A fable's animals stand for human dispositions in a single situation and the moral is usually appended; an allegory sustains a systematic correspondence across a whole work and expects the reader to hold the second scheme in mind throughout. The fable is an allegory that has agreed to be brief and to explain itself.

The dragon slayer is among the tales in Propp's corpus, and it demonstrates the method's central claim particularly well.

The villainy, the departure, the struggle, the branding of the hero, the unfounded claims of the false hero and the final recognition are all functions in his sequence, and the tale contains them in order. What varies between versions is entirely at the level of who and what, the distinction the Morphology was built to establish.

The type occupies one of the lowest numbers in the index, in the section devoted to tales of magic, and it is among the most widely recorded of all, with versions collected across Europe, the Near East, India and beyond.

Its entry is also a good demonstration of what a type is: the number covers a plot with a fixed sequence of events, not a subject, so a story about a dragon that lacks the impostor and the tokens belongs somewhere else.

The pattern occupies a cluster of adjacent numbers in the index covering the search for a lost husband, of which the beast bridegroom is one branch and the invisible or bird husband others.

Grouping them by number is what allows the ancient literary version in Apuleius to be read as a variant of the same tale as the versions collected from oral tradition in the nineteenth century, not as its source.

The type is one of the small number of entries in the index with a continuous literary as well as oral history, running from Basile through Perrault and the Grimms into film.

The documented sequence makes it unusually useful for showing how a tale is edited over time, since each of the three printed versions is available in full and each removes something the previous one had kept.

The magic object is a motif rather than a tale type, and separating the two is what Thompson's second index was built to handle.

A type covers a whole plot; a motif is a component that can appear in any number of them, and the object that grants invisibility or inexhaustible food turns up across unrelated tales in unrelated regions. Cataloguing at that level is what allows a comparativist to trace an element independently of the stories carrying it.

Auerbach devoted a book to Dante as well as a central chapter of Mimesis, and his argument is that the Commedia is the decisive breach of the classical separation of styles.

By placing real and recent people in an eternal scheme, and rendering them with full individuality at the moment their fate is settled, Dante made ordinary human character the subject of the highest available seriousness, which is the development Auerbach traces to the modern novel.

The novel closes on a short passage repeating that this is not a story to pass on, a formulation that works in two directions at once and has been read both as an injunction to forget and as an acknowledgement that it cannot be.

The ambiguity is the ending. A book about material that has not been assimilated cannot resolve into settlement, and the closing pages supply the formal signals of an ending while withholding the assurance they usually carry.

White's argument narrows the gap between the historical novel and the history it borrows from, since on his account both impose a plot shape on a record that does not contain one.

He was careful about what the claim did not mean, insisting that the events are real and only the emplotment is made, but the distinction has never fully protected the position from the charge that it makes the two forms equivalent.

The Hungarian critic Georg Lukacs argued that the historical novel became possible only after the French Revolution and the Napoleonic wars had made mass populations experience history as something happening to them, not as a succession of rulers.

His reading of Scott identifies the technical solution: a protagonist of middling rank and moderate convictions, placed between the contending forces so that both can be represented sympathetically and neither reduced to a villain. The mediocre hero is a structural device, not weak characterisation.

Ong's account of oral composition explains features of the ballad that look like defects on the page: the formulaic epithets, the repeated stanzas with a single word changed, the reliance on dialogue and the absence of connective explanation.

All are mnemonic and performative, not stylistic, and they mark a form composed to be held in memory and delivered aloud rather than one composed to be read.

Medieval interpretation developed a systematic method of reading scripture on several levels at once, literal, moral, allegorical and anagogical, and that apparatus is the origin of allegory as a European literary technique rather than merely a rhetorical figure.

Writers then composed for the method, building works designed to be read at all four levels. The great medieval allegories assume an audience trained in the practice.

The jatakas circulated as public preaching material and as popular entertainment long before and after they were fixed in the canon, and they were carried across Asia by monks, merchants and performers.

Their visual transmission is equally important: the stories were carved on stupa railings and painted on cave walls, which made them legible to audiences who could not read the texts and gave the tales an existence independent of any manuscript.

The singer works with themes that have their own internal shape, and the arrangement of an episode around a centre gives the performance a set of paired landmarks rather than a list to be recalled in order.

That is one of the mechanisms by which a poem of Homeric length can be produced without writing: the structure is generative, not memorised, and a singer who knows where he is in a pattern knows what has to come next.

The Iranian and Arab traditions occupy the same social space and work by the same means: a solo performer in a coffeehouse, a long epic or romance delivered in nightly instalments, no staging, and a livelihood dependent on the audience returning.

Both declined with broadcasting for the same reasons, and both have been revived as heritage performance in settings quite unlike the ones that sustained them.

The kenning is the skald's principal instrument, and its usefulness is metrical as much as decorative: a poet working under strict syllable counts and fixed alliteration needs many available names for the same thing.

Skaldic practice nests them, so that a phrase may require unpacking through several layers of substitution before it resolves into a sword or a ship, and the audience's pleasure lies in the unpacking. The difficulty is the craft, not an obstacle to it.

Irony is satire's default instrument, since a satirist who states the objection plainly has written an argument rather than a satire.

The technique's characteristic risk follows from the same dependence: a sufficiently deadpan proposal will be read straight by some part of the audience, and the history of satire is full of pieces taken as sincere by readers who lacked the context to reverse them.

Both concern how a reader learns the rules of a world, and they pull in opposite directions.

Exposition delivers the information; world building generates far more of it than can be delivered and relies on the excess to produce depth. The craft position that has hardened around both is that the constructed material should be visible in its consequences and largely absent from the dialogue, which is a way of saying that world building works best where exposition fails.

The nested copy is the oldest and most concrete of the devices metafiction uses, and it does not require the work to comment on itself in its own voice.

A play within a play makes the audience aware of watching without anyone announcing it. The device is available to writers with no interest in self-reference as a programme, including Shakespeare, who uses it repeatedly without ever stepping outside the fiction to do so.

Both concern an element introduced early and answered later, and they impose opposite obligations.

Chekhov's principle requires that anything planted be used, on pain of the audience registering a broken promise. A leitmotif is used continuously and never discharged: its whole function is to recur and accumulate, and a motif that resolved into a single payoff would stop being one.

Booker's scheme has a slot for comedy and a slot for tragedy and no accommodation for a work that declines to be either.

That is a fair illustration of what taxonomies of this kind cost. A play that runs three acts of tragedy and resolves in restoration has to be assigned to one category or treated as a failure of the pattern, and Booker's evaluative framework generally takes the second option.

Todorov's final stage is a formal account of what closure requires: not a return to the opening state but a settled one that has been altered by what happened.

Stated that way it explains why an ending that simply restores the beginning feels evasive and why one that leaves the disruption unresolved feels stopped, not finished. Closure is the recognition that a new stable state has been reached.

Adaptation is the most visible and most legally regulated form of the relation the broader concept describes, and it is the case where a text's dependence on another is declared on the cover.

That declaration is what makes it useful as a limiting case. Intertextuality claims that all texts are made from others, much of it unintended and reader-constructed; adaptation is the subset where the relation is deliberate, specific and acknowledged, and where a reader can hold both objects and compare them.

The Theory of the Novel, written during the First World War, describes the form as the epic of an age in which the totality of life is no longer directly given, so that a novel's hero seeks a meaning the world does not supply and the seeking is the book.

The formulation has outlasted the Hegelian scheme it was built in, and it remains one of the few accounts of the novel that explains why the form's characteristic subject is disappointment.

Lukacs defended nineteenth-century realism on the grounds that it could represent a society as a connected whole, showing how a private life is determined by forces operating well beyond it.

He distinguished this sharply from naturalism, which he regarded as a degeneration into unselected description, and from modernism, which he read as the surrender of that totality in favour of isolated subjectivity. The position was polemical and is still argued with, most sharply by critics who value exactly what he dismissed.

Old English verse uses the device continuously, and the poem's vocabulary for the sea, for a king, for a sword and for battle is largely built from it.

The compounds are less nested than the skaldic ones and correspondingly more legible, which has made them a standard difficulty and pleasure for translators: the choice between rendering the compound literally and preserving its strangeness, or replacing it with the plain noun and losing the texture entirely.

The kenning does exactly what Shklovsky described: it refuses the habitual word and makes the audience reconstruct the thing from an unfamiliar description, so the sea has to be arrived at, not recognised.

The formalists did not use Norse examples, but the device is one of the clearest historical instances of a poetics built on the principle that perception should be slowed rather than eased.

A large proportion of film has always been adapted from novels, plays, comics and earlier films, and the industry's dependence on existing properties is economic before it is aesthetic, since a known title carries an audience.

The recurring formal problem is interiority. The novel's direct access to a mind has no exact cinematic equivalent, and voiceover, performance, point-of-view shooting and score are the partial substitutes around which most adaptation criticism has circled.

The fairy tale is the limiting case for any argument about fidelity, since the material has no original: every version is a version, and the printed texts that look like sources are themselves adaptations of oral tellings that were never fixed.

That has not stopped audiences from treating a particular version as authoritative. The Disney adaptations are so often measured against the Grimms as though the Grimms were the source rather than editors working two centuries into the tale's life.

Noh's practice is adaptation of a particular kind: a long narrative is reduced to a single charged encounter, usually with a returning spirit, on the assumption that the audience knows the story and has come for the treatment.

The method inverts the usual anxiety about what an adaptation loses. Nothing is being replaced, because the source remains in circulation, and the play is a commentary on material the audience is expected to hold in mind throughout.

The play is among the most adapted works in existence, and its history runs in both directions: Shakespeare adapted legendary and dramatic material, and the result has since been transposed into opera, ballet, film in many languages, and novels told from the position of minor characters.

Kurosawa's and others' transpositions to entirely different societies are the standard evidence that what travels is a structure of obligation and delay, not a set of Danish circumstances.

Joyce's book is an adaptation in the strict sense and almost nothing that word usually implies, since it keeps the Odyssey's structure and discards its plot, setting, period, characters and register.

The correspondences were circulated privately in schemas rather than stated in the text, which means a reader can miss them entirely and still follow the novel. That is an unusual arrangement: the source is indispensable to the author and optional for the audience.

The film is the standing case in arguments about what adaptation does to a shared tradition, since it took material that belonged to everyone and produced a version that is both authoritative in the public mind and privately owned.

Its specific changes are also instructive: naming and individuating the dwarfs, reducing the queen's three attempts to one, and supplying a romantic resolution the tale does not contain, each of which serves a feature-length structure the source had no need of.

Capote's book and the observational documentaries of the same period are two branches of one impulse, to apply the resources of storytelling to actual events without an intervening commentator.

Both also ran into the same difficulty within a decade, as scrutiny of what had been staged, prompted or reconstructed made the claim of unmediated access untenable. The subsequent history of both forms is largely about acknowledging the shaping instead of concealing it.

The memoir has a structural problem the novel does not: its protagonist's development is constrained by what actually happened, and lives rarely deliver an arc on demand.

The form's characteristic solution is retrospective shaping, in which the narrating self imposes a trajectory the living self did not experience, the same operation Hayden White describes for history and which raises the same question about whether the shape was found or supplied.

Bruner's account of narrative identity holds that people construct a self by telling it, selecting and ordering episodes into a trajectory that makes the present intelligible.

That is the arc described as a psychological process rather than a craft requirement, and it explains why the convention feels natural to audiences: it is the same operation they perform on their own lives, applied to someone else's.

Retelling is the normal condition of narrative rather than a secondary activity, and the graph's own contents make the point: Greek tragedy worked from epic, Shakespeare from chronicles and novellas, the tale types exist only as variants, and the oral traditions produce a new version at every performance.

The idea that a story has an original from which later versions depart is comparatively recent, and it arrives with print, authorship and copyright, not with storytelling itself.

Myth is where most traditions locate the origin of narrative and the origin of everything else, and it supplies the material that the other forms then work on: epic versifies it, tragedy dramatises it, folklore domesticates it, and modern genres borrow its figures.

It also differs from the rest in what it is for. A myth is told within a community that has some stake in its truth, which is a relationship no other narrative form quite reproduces.

Every form in the graph descends from performance before an audience, and the features that look like the natural properties of narrative are frequently the residue of that condition: repetition, formula, episodic structure, the direct address, the pause before the outcome.

Writing did not end the practice, and the sequence is not a ladder. Oral traditions have continued alongside print and broadcasting, and several in this graph were recorded in the twentieth century from performers whose repertoires owed nothing to books.

Games took their visual grammar from cinema more or less wholesale, along with scores, performance capture and, for a long period, the practice of suspending play to deliver story in filmed sequences.

What the medium then had to develop on its own is everything that follows from the audience controlling the pace and the route, since a story that can be approached in any order or ignored entirely cannot be staged like a scene.

Long-form serial television is regularly compared to the nineteenth-century novel, and the comparison holds better than most such claims because the production conditions match: instalment publication, a large ensemble, plots developed over a year, and an audience whose response is known while the work is still being written.

Both also produce the same characteristic defect, which is a middle that sags because it was commissioned before anyone knew how it would end.

The comparison between Dickens's part-issue novels and serial television is made so often that it has become a cliche, and the mechanism behind it is specific, not atmospheric.

Both write to a schedule with the audience already watching, both end instalments on a hook to secure the next appointment, and both adjust course in response to reception: Dickens revived a character and expanded a minor one on the strength of sales, which is what a writers' room does with an unexpectedly popular performer.

The novel's relation to epic is the founding question of its theory, and the standard answers agree that the later form inherits the ambition of representing a whole society and loses the shared world that made the earlier one possible.

Bakhtin located the difference in the epic's absolute past, closed and unarguable, against the novel's contact with an unfinished present. Lukacs located it in a lost totality. Both are describing the same shift from a form that assumes a common world to one that has to construct one.

Both put more than one voice into a work and they do opposite things with them.

The chorus speaks as a collective and expresses a settled communal position against which the individual protagonists are measured, so the plurality resolves into one perspective. Polyphony requires that the voices remain independent and unresolved, with no authorial verdict placing them. Supplying that verdict is what a chorus exists for.

Drama has no narrator to restrict what an audience perceives. The analytic apparatus built for prose transfers badly to the stage.

The chorus is the nearest equivalent and works differently: it does not limit what the audience sees, since everything happens in front of them, but it supplies an interpretive position from which to see it. The restriction is of judgement rather than of information.

Both create a gap between what a text says and what it invites the reader to conclude, and they place the gap in different positions.

Free indirect style borrows a character's idiom inside the narrator's grammar, so the unreliability belongs to the reported consciousness while the narration stays trustworthy. An unreliable narrator moves the problem up a level, and the reader has to reconstruct the events from a source that is the only one available.

Barthes's argument that a text is a tissue of quotations drawn from innumerable centres of culture, and that a writer's only power is to mix existing writings, is the position the term names.

He drew the consequence in the essay on the death of the author, where the origin of a text is located in language and in the reader, not in a person with intentions. The concept arrived in criticism attached to a polemic.

Barthes's account of the hermeneutic code describes a narrative as a sequence of enigmas posed, delayed, partially disclosed and finally resolved, with the delay rather than the answer supplying most of the interest.

On that reading closure is what the whole apparatus exists to postpone, and a classic narrative is a machine for making the reader want an ending it spends its length withholding.

The Sense of an Ending, by the English critic Frank Kermode, is the standard treatment of the subject and locates the need for endings outside literature. His example is the clock: the sound it makes is undifferentiated, and a listener hears tick-tock, supplying an opening and a close to an interval that contains neither.

From that he argues that a plot is a way of humanising time, and that the ending is where a narrative's whole shape is settled, since it determines retrospectively what everything before it was leading to.

Both claim to describe all narrative and differ in how much they claim to describe about it.

Booker specifies seven distinct plot shapes with named stages and treats deviation as failure; Todorov specifies a single movement that any story performs and says nothing about content. The first is a taxonomy that can be wrong about a particular work, the second a definition that can only be trivially true, and the pair marks the range within which every general scheme of narrative sits.

Campbell's pattern and Todorov's differ most in what they require of the ending.

The monomyth insists on return: the hero comes back to the community with something it needed, and a journey without the return is incomplete. The equilibrium model requires only that a new stable state be reached, which may be somewhere else entirely, and it accommodates the many narratives in which nobody goes home.

Greimas describes characters as positions in a structure, defined entirely by their relation to the object and to each other, and an actant may be a person, an institution or an abstraction.

The arc describes them as psychological individuals who change. The two accounts are not compatible, and the gap between them is roughly the gap between structuralist analysis and screenwriting instruction, which use the word character to mean quite different things.

Both hold that a setting determines what kind of story can occur in it, not merely hosting one, and they arrive from opposite directions.

Bakhtin's term is analytic, derived from reading existing genres and identifying the time-space each depends on. World building is constructive, and its practitioners discover the same principle in practice: settle the rules of a place and the available plots narrow immediately, which is what makes the constraint useful.

Booth wrote a book on irony as well as the one on fiction, and it asks the practical question of how a reader knows to reverse a statement when nothing in the text says to.

His answer is that stable irony leaves detectable evidence, in contradictions of known fact, clashes of style or conflicts with the work's established norms, and that the reader reconstructs a position from which the statement makes sense. Where no such position can be built, the irony is unstable and the reconstruction never terminates.

Zipes's objection to the studio versions of the tales is an argument about adaptation rather than about films: that when material held in common is adapted into a proprietary version and marketed at sufficient scale, the adaptation displaces the tradition it drew on.

The complaint is not that changes were made, since every telling changes something, but that the changes became authoritative and the earlier variants stopped circulating.

Lord's account of how a singer learns comes from watching guslari do it: absorbing the themes and the formulaic system by listening, then producing a first performance that is already composition rather than recall.

His demonstration that a singer will insist he sang the song exactly as he heard it, while the recordings show substantial variation between his own performances, is the central evidence that an oral tradition preserves a technique, not a text.

The Sundiata material is the clearest available demonstration that an epic can exist entirely as performance, since it was still being performed when it was first written down and continues to be.

That makes it evidence of a different kind from the Homeric poems, which survive only as texts and whose oral history has to be reconstructed. Here the tradition and the transcription are both available, and the differences between recorded performances can be examined directly.

Both are professional poets attached to a ruling house, paid to praise a patron and to hold a lineage's record, and in both traditions the poet's account carries weight beyond the performance.

The difference is transmission. The skald's verse survives because its metrical strictness resisted alteration and it was later written down; the griot's survives because the office is hereditary and the repertoire is passed within families, which is a social, not a formal solution to the same problem.

Both tell a story through sung and spoken performance over an evening, and they differ in nearly everything else.

Pansori gives the entire narrative and every character to one singer with a single drummer, using an intentionally rough vocal technique developed over years; the musical distributes the material across a company with an orchestra and privileges vocal beauty. One is an endurance performance, the other a production.

The clown-servants of the Javanese shadow theatre occupy a position much like the chorus: attached to the heroes, outside the epic action they comment on, and licensed to speak to the audience about matters the dignified characters cannot.

They also do something the Greek chorus does not, which is to address contemporary affairs directly, so an episode of ancient epic can carry commentary on the present without disturbing its own material.

The Italian companies worked from a scenario posted backstage giving entrances, exits and the order of events, and improvised the dialogue and business inside that frame.

What made it possible was a stock of rehearsed comic routines that could be dropped into any scene, and character types so fixed that a performer might play the same mask for a career. The result looks like invention and is closer to skilled recombination, which is the same arrangement the oral epic singer works under.

The multi-camera comedy inherits the popular stage more directly than any other television form: a proscenium arrangement, a live audience whose response is part of the transmission, broad playing pitched to the back of a room, and entrances and exits treated as events.

What it drops is the moral polarity, replacing the persecuted innocent and the villain with a group of people who irritate each other and cannot leave.

The dystopia's plot is characteristically a thriller's: a protagonist who notices something, an authority that must not find out, a concealment, a pursuit and a capture.

The combination is efficient because a society organised around control supplies the surveillance and the deadline the genre needs, and because the thriller's structure gives an argumentative form somewhere to put its argument other than in a lecture.

The genre's ending is a recognition scene conducted as an explanation, in which the accumulated evidence is reordered so that a single account fits it and everyone present learns who they have been dealing with.

Aristotle would have approved of the construction and possibly not of the tokens, since fair-play detective fiction depends on physical clues, the cigarette ash and the timetable, which is the class of recognition he ranked lowest.

The mode is where the double becomes a standard figure, in portraits that age, twins separated at birth, respectable men with second identities and houses containing a hidden relative.

The device suits the Gothic's central concern, which is that a family's or a person's history is not finished and will present itself, since the double is that history walking around in a recognisable form.

The changeling is a monster defined entirely by category violation and not at all by appearance or threat: it looks like the child and is not the child.

That makes it a useful limiting case for accounts of the monstrous that locate the horror in the failure of classification rather than in danger, since the creature in the cot is helpless and is terrifying anyway.

The contest is the trickster's characteristic arena, since it is the one form of combat in which the weaker party is favoured and the rules cannot be enforced by strength.

Across unrelated traditions the pattern is the same: a small or powerless figure accepts a challenge from something enormous, wins by attention to the exact wording, and takes a prize that force could never have secured.

Rebirth is the seventh of Booker's plots and the one that completes his scheme, covering narratives in which a protagonist is held in a dark state, remains in it while it deepens, and is released rather than escaping.

It is the only one of the seven in which the central figure spends most of the book as an obstacle to their own story, which is why it depends so heavily on an outside agency to end it. Booker treats that dependence as the pattern's meaning, not a structural weakness.

Both patterns take a protagonist through a dark passage and return them altered, and they distribute the effort in opposite ways.

The hero's journey requires the ordeal to be undergone actively and the boon to be brought back; rebirth requires the protagonist to be incapable of releasing themselves, so the turn is delivered by someone else. One is a story about what a person can do and the other about what has to be done for them.

Scrooge is Booker's own example and the pattern's cleanest instance: a man sealed in a state he does not experience as a problem, shown his past, his present and his end by agencies he did not summon, and released by morning.

The structure explains a feature readers often note, that the transformation feels unearned. Nothing Scrooge does brings it about, and on this pattern nothing could, since a protagonist able to save himself would not be in the story.

Dickens wrote it in a few weeks in the autumn of 1843, at a point when his sales were falling and he needed a success, and published it at his own expense in an expensive illustrated edition that sold out immediately and made him very little money.

He had been reading reports on child labour and had considered writing a pamphlet, then concluded that a story would strike, in his own phrase, twenty thousand times the force.

The beast bridegroom tales are rebirth narratives told from the other side, since the enchanted figure cannot lift the spell and the release comes from a person who chooses to stay.

Booker classifies them under rebirth for that reason, and the placement highlights what the pattern requires: the transformation is a gift rather than an achievement, and the protagonist of the plot is arguably the one doing the releasing, not the one released.

The play was produced at the Dionysia of 431 BCE and placed third, which is the lowest position available and a reasonable indication of how the audience received it.

Euripides made a decision the tradition did not require: earlier versions have the children killed by the people of Corinth, not by their mother, and the change that makes the play unbearable appears to be his.

Medea escapes at the close in a chariot sent by her grandfather Helios, lifted above the stage by the theatre's crane, carrying the bodies of her children and beyond any reach of Jason or of law.

Aristotle named this ending when objecting that a god should not be used to untie a knot. Modern readings frequently defend it on the grounds that the arrival of a divine rescue for a child-killer is deliberately intolerable, and that the discomfort is intended.

The play tests the genre's requirements rather than satisfying them. Its protagonist is not a person of moderate virtue brought down by an error, and her catastrophe falls on other people while she survives.

What it does supply is the tragic recognition in an unusual place: Medea knows exactly what she is doing, states the case against it in her own voice, and does it anyway, which relocates the conflict from ignorance to will.

The first production in 1896 failed badly, and by the accounts of Chekhov and his friends he left during the performance and declared he would never write for the theatre again.

Stanislavski and Nemirovich-Danchenko revived it at the Moscow Art Theatre two years later, with a rehearsal process and an acting technique built to play what the text leaves unspoken, and it succeeded completely. The company adopted the bird as its emblem and still carries it.

The play is the example most often attached to the principle, since a gun is present in the early acts and the shot that matters is fired offstage at the end.

What is usually left out of the citation is the handling. The death is not staged, and it reaches the audience as a doctor's quiet aside to another character, delivered so that the people on stage do not hear it. The gun goes off, and the play declines to make a scene of it.

The characters discuss the theatre, a lake, a manuscript and the weather while every important thing goes unsaid: who loves whom, what a mother thinks of her son's work, and what a failure has cost.

The premiere's failure is generally attributed to a company playing the lines, not what sits under them. That makes the play's early history a demonstration of what the technique requires from performers as well as writers.

The trilogy won first prize at the Dionysia of 458 BCE, two years before Aeschylus's death, and is the only complete tragic trilogy to survive.

The satyr play that completed the group, Proteus, is lost, which means even this exception is partial: what survives is three quarters of a single day's programme, and no other author's connected sequence has come down at all.

Each play gives the chorus a different identity, and the sequence uses the shift as an argument. The elders of Argos are frightened and complicit, the enslaved women of the household want the vengeance, and the Furies are the vengeance, present on stage as characters with a case to make.

By the final play the chorus is on trial rather than commenting on a trial, which is a use of the convention that no later drama attempts.

The trilogy is the earliest surviving demonstration of what the form could do at scale, carrying a single argument across three plays and resolving it in an institution rather than in a death.

Its ending is unusual for the genre and was available only because of the scale: a cycle of retribution is stopped by the founding of a court, so the third play ends in a procession, not a catastrophe. Nothing comparable survives from any other tragedian.

Collins wrote much of the novel while in severe pain from gout and heavily dosed with laudanum, and later said he did not recognise parts of what he had dictated.

The circumstance matters because opium is also the novel's mechanism, and the solution depends on a man doing something under its influence that he has no memory of afterwards. The book was serialised in Dickens's magazine in 1868.

The novel's misdirection is built into its structure, not planted in its dialogue: each narrator reports honestly and partially, so the reader's wrong conclusions are assembled from accurate testimony.

A suspicious servant, a debt, a stain on a nightgown and a locked cabinet are all supplied with innocent explanations that arrive too late to be believed, which is the technique working exactly as intended.

The book assembles most of the genre's furniture in one place: a theft in a country house, a bungling local force, a celebrated detective from London with a private obsession, a false confession, a reconstruction of the crime and a solution nobody has suspected.

T. S. Eliot's judgement that it is the first and greatest English detective novel is a critic's opinion rather than a settled fact, and the claim is contested by readers who point to Poe two decades earlier.

The narrative is assembled from written accounts commissioned after the events by one of the characters, each contributor instructed to write only what they witnessed themselves.

Collins had legal training and the arrangement is a deliberate imitation of evidence: the reader occupies the position of a jury, holding several partial testimonies with no authoritative version among them, which is a considerably more demanding structure than a single narrator.

Collins wrote for weekly serialisation and worked to a maxim traditionally attributed to him, that the business is to make an audience laugh, cry and above all wait. The attribution is not secure and the same line has been credited to Charles Reade.

He engineered his instalment endings accordingly, and his sensation novels of the 1860s are among the clearest cases of a book's structure being determined by its publication schedule, not merely accommodating it.

Collins was Dickens's friend, collaborator, travelling companion and serial contributor, and they wrote several pieces together.

The influence ran in both directions and is easiest to see in the later Dickens: the tighter plotting of the final novels, the concealed identities and the unfinished mystery he was working on when he died all owe something to what Collins had been doing with sensation and suspense.

Christie credited the idea for the device to two separate suggestions, one from her brother-in-law and one from Lord Louis Mountbatten, who wrote to her proposing a story told by the murderer.

Her own account of the writing emphasises the difficulty of the constraint: the narration had to remain literally truthful throughout while concealing the one thing it knew, which required working out precisely what could be omitted rather than what could be said.

The doctor who narrates the investigation is the murderer, and the book is his written account, composed with the intention of being read.

The unreliability is entirely a matter of omission and framing. A key paragraph records his movements accurately and passes over a few minutes in a phrase, and every subsequent statement is true, and the book has become the genre's most examined test case for what a narrator owes a reader.

The reversal overturns not just the reader's suspicion but the position from which they have been reading. The book provoked an argument, not admiration in some quarters.

It also satisfies the harder half of the genre's requirement: on rereading the clues are all present, and the narrator's evasions are visible in the sentences that concealed them, which is what separates a twist from a cheat.

The novel arrived while the Golden Age was codifying its rules, and it forced the question of what fair play actually required, since the text withholds nothing that was stated and everything that was assumed.

Some contemporaries called it a breach of contract; Dorothy L. Sayers defended it on the grounds that the reader had been given every fact and had simply declined to suspect the one person convention placed above suspicion.

The film was commissioned for the twentieth anniversary of the 1905 revolution as one episode of a much larger planned project, and Eisenstein abandoned the rest to concentrate on the mutiny.

It was shot in a few months, largely on location in Odessa with non-professional performers, and the compression is part of the method: with no stars and no dialogue, the meaning had to be built in the cutting.

The Odessa steps sequence is the most analysed piece of editing in cinema, assembling a massacre from fragments of boots, faces, a pram and a broken pair of spectacles, with the geography of the steps established only to be violated for effect.

The massacre as staged did not happen. Killings occurred in the city in 1905 but not on those steps, and the sequence is a construction, which is the clearest possible statement of the argument that the meaning is made in the cutting.

Eisenstein's theoretical writing turned editing from a technique into a claim about how film means, arguing that two shots in collision produce a concept that neither contains, on an analogy he drew with the composition of Japanese characters.

He classified the available collisions by rhythm, by graphic direction, by tone and by idea, and the position was polemical: he was arguing against filmmakers, including Soviet colleagues, who treated the cut as a way of joining scenes smoothly.

Eisenstein's films and essays gave cinema its first fully worked theory produced by a practitioner, and the vocabulary he supplied is still in use by people who have never read him.

His practical influence is visible wherever a sequence builds an argument out of juxtaposition rather than following an action, which includes advertising, news editing and the standard training montage as much as the political cinema he intended it for.

The story was written in 1927 and collected in Men Without Women, and Hemingway reportedly regarded it as among his best.

It is also the purest application of his stated method, since the omitted material is not unstated but is the entire subject, and the story's effect depends on the reader arriving at what the two people are discussing without being told.

The narration reports the heat, the drinks, the beaded curtain, the bags with hotel labels and the line of hills across the valley, and enters neither character's mind at any point.

Everything the reader concludes about what these two people are to each other and what has already been decided comes from the arrangement of their sentences and from what one of them keeps not saying, which is the principle demonstrated at its limit.

Hemingway's stated principle is that a writer who knows what they are leaving out may omit it, and the omission will strengthen the story, with the dignity of an iceberg lying in the seven eighths below water.

The formulation is his own and the practice is not original to him, but the combination of a stated method and a body of stories demonstrating it made him the reference point, and the technique reached later writers largely through his version of it.

The story is a single scene at a railway station lasting as long as a train is delayed, with two characters, no history supplied and no outcome given.

It is the form's argument for itself: material that a novel would have to explain, and would probably weaken by explaining, can be presented complete in a few pages because the length forbids the explanation.

The pamphlet was published anonymously in Dublin in 1729, in the format and register of the improvement literature it imitates, and Swift had been writing seriously about Irish poverty and English policy for years before it.

That context is what makes it work. The proposal is monstrous and its economic reasoning is continuous with arguments that were actually being made, and the reader is meant to arrive at that unassisted.

The pamphlet is sustained irony without a single signal: the persona is earnest, the tone is reasonable, the figures are supplied, and nothing in the text steps outside the mask to tell the reader how to take it.

It is therefore also the standard demonstration of the technique's risk, since the piece has been read straight often enough that its title now functions as shorthand for a proposal not meant seriously.

The essay is among the most concentrated satires in English and a very clear case of the mode's method, which is to take a position the target already half occupies and follow it to a conclusion they cannot accept.

It belongs to the Juvenalian register, not the Horatian: there is no genial self-inclusion and no invitation to laugh, and the composure of the voice is what makes the anger legible.

Wagner wrote the librettos before the music and in reverse narrative order, beginning with the death of the hero and working backwards to establish what needed to precede it.

Composition ran from 1848 to 1874 with a gap of more than a decade in the middle, and the complete cycle was first staged in 1876 at a theatre he had built for it. He was his own librettist, composer, theorist and impresario throughout.

The cycle's musical fabric is built from short recurring figures attached to characters, objects, ideas and relationships, developed and transformed as their situations change and combined so that several can sound at once.

The effect available to no other narrative form is contradiction: the orchestra can state a connection the character on stage is denying, or recall a promise while the singer is breaking it. The term itself was applied by commentators rather than by Wagner.

The cycle is the form's largest single undertaking, four evenings running to some fifteen hours, and it was written for a theatre built to specification with a covered orchestra pit and no boxes.

Its scale is an argument about what opera was for: not a sequence of numbers with recitative between them, but a continuous dramatic fabric in which the orchestra carries as much of the narration as the singers do.

Wagner worked from the Poetic Edda, the Prose Edda, the Volsunga saga and the Nibelungenlied, and recombined them freely instead of following any one.

The changes are substantial: he takes the ring and its curse from the Norse material, the hero's name from the German, and supplies a governing scheme about power and renunciation that none of the sources contains. What most audiences now take for Norse mythology is frequently his version of it.

Opera has taken almost all of its stories from somewhere else, and the transposition is unusually revealing because the medium's demands are so specific.

A libretto must lose most of a novel or play's language to leave room for music, so what survives is situation and relation rather than dialogue, and the moments the composer expands are the ones where a character stops to feel something. The form selects for material with strong situations and unremarkable prose.
