The device belongs to opera before it belongs to film, and the theatre is where its full possibilities are available, since an orchestra can carry several motifs at once while singers are occupied with the text.

What film scoring took was the association and the transformation; what it largely left behind was the contrapuntal use, in which two figures sounding together assert a connection the drama has not yet made.

The two forms are related by descent rather than by kind, and the line runs through operetta and light opera into the twentieth-century book musical.

The conventional distinction, that opera is sung throughout and the musical alternates song with speech, holds for most cases and fails for enough of them that practitioners generally treat the boundary as a matter of institution, training and audience, not of form.

Bunyan was imprisoned for twelve years for preaching without a licence and wrote a substantial part of the book during confinement, publishing the first part in 1678 and a second, following his protagonist's wife and children, six years later.

He was a tinker by trade with little formal education, and the plainness of the prose was a choice defended in his own preface against readers who expected divinity to sound learned.

The book is the reference case for the mode because the correspondence is complete and declared: every place is a spiritual condition and every person is their function, from Mr Worldly Wiseman to Giant Despair.

What keeps it readable is that the vehicle is concrete where the tenor is abstract. The burden is a physical weight, the Slough is mud that clings, and the river at the end has to be waded. The story survives for readers who reject the theology entirely.

Iser's account of the implied reader is built substantially on English prose fiction from Bunyan onwards, and the allegory is a useful starting point because it appears to leave nothing for a reader to supply.

His argument is that even here the gaps decide the reading: the correspondences have to be recognised and applied by someone, and a reader who does not perform that operation is holding a travel narrative about a man with a heavy bag.

Stoker worked on the book for several years while managing the Lyceum Theatre, and his surviving notes show the vampire acquiring his name and Transylvanian setting late, having begun as an Austrian count.

He drew the geography from travel writing and reference books and never visited the region. The novel appeared in 1897 to respectable reviews and modest sales, and its dominance of the vampire in popular culture came later and largely through film.

The novel is constructed entirely from documents, and the range of them is the point: shorthand journals, letters, telegrams, a ship's log, newspaper cuttings and a doctor's recordings on phonograph cylinders, later transcribed and assembled by one of the characters.

The apparatus of modern record-keeping is set directly against a very old superstition, and the form supplies the corroboration that a single narrator could not.

The novel arrives a century into the mode and gathers most of it: the castle, the isolated traveller, the hereditary evil, the persecuted women and the invasion of a settled domestic world by something the past has sent.

What it adds is direction. Earlier Gothic sends the protagonist into the ancestral place; Stoker brings the ancestral place to London, which turns the mode's anxiety about inheritance into an anxiety about arrival.

The vampire is the category violation stated plainly: neither living nor dead, human in shape and appetite and not human in kind, and able to pass unremarked in a drawing room.

The novel is also careful to keep him mostly offstage. He speaks in a handful of scenes and is otherwise a set of effects reported by other people, which is why the figure has proved so adaptable and why almost every subsequent version has had to invent an interior life the book withholds.

Woolf drew the family closely from her own, and wrote afterwards that the book had the effect of laying her parents to rest, describing herself as having ceased to be obsessed by her mother once it was finished.

The account is her own and belongs to her diaries, not to any external record, but the correspondence of the household to her childhood summers is not in dispute.

The middle section covers ten years in a few pages, with the empty house, the weather and the dust doing the narrating, and the deaths of three members of the family reported inside square brackets in single sentences.

The technique inverts the usual proportions completely. A dinner party occupies a hundred pages and a war, a childbirth and a family's dismantling occupy a parenthesis, which is an argument about scale delivered entirely through what is skipped.

The book is among the clearest demonstrations of what the modernist novel put in place of plot: a structure organised by symmetry and by the return of images rather than by consequence.

Its three parts balance a long afternoon against a short decade against a short morning, and the expedition that gives the book its title is postponed in the first part and completed in the third by different people for different reasons.

The film opens with a paragraph of text scrolling into space, stating the political situation, the stakes and the position of the stolen plans before a single character appears.

The device was borrowed from the serials Lucas was drawing on and is unusually candid: instead of disguising the delivery as conversation, it hands the audience the necessary information in writing and then starts. Its imitation across four decades has made it one of the most recognisable openings in cinema.

The novel was written for weekly, not monthly instalments, which meant a break every few thousand words and far less room to build toward one.

The pressure shows in the construction: the parts end repeatedly on an arrival, a recognition or a threat, and the largest of them, the revelation of who has been funding the protagonist's gentility, falls at the close of a number rather than in the middle of a chapter.

The novel covers one day and reaches thirty years into the past without a single conventional flashback scene, delivering the earlier material as memory surfacing inside a present moment.

What is skipped is everything between: the decisions, the marriage, the war and the years of ordinary life arrive as fragments attached to a sound or a smell, and the reader assembles a history the book never narrates.

The film's breakfast sequence covers the disintegration of a marriage in a couple of minutes, cutting between successive breakfasts across years with the intervening time simply absent.

It is the technique's most quoted demonstration because nothing is explained: the audience reads the growing distance from the seating, the clothes and the newspapers, and the decade that produced it is never shown.

Christie's practice defined the interwar puzzle novel and set the terms its rules were written against, since her books repeatedly located the culprit in whichever position the convention had placed beyond suspicion.

Her commercial dominance also shaped the genre's economics. The Poirot and Marple sequences established the serial detective as a durable property, and her plotting rather than her prose is what later writers took. She is so much easier to imitate badly than well.

Christie's misdirection works by supplying the reader with a suspicious person to be busy with, and by attaching guilty behaviour to characters who are concealing something other than murder: an affair, a debt, a false identity, a theft.

Every false lead is therefore resolved, not dropped, which is what distinguishes the technique in her hands from simple withholding, and it is why the solutions account for everybody's behaviour and not only the killer's.

Stoker arrived a century into the mode and produced the version that displaced most of what preceded it, with the result that a great many readers now encounter the Gothic through him and through the films his book generated.

His structural contribution was to reverse the direction of travel. Earlier Gothic sends its protagonists to the ancestral place; Dracula brings the ancestral place to a modern city with railways, typewriters and blood transfusion.

The novel supplied the genre with a set of rules that later writers treat as inherited folklore rather than invention: the ground from home, the threshold that must not be crossed uninvited, the reflection, the stake.

Some are drawn from recorded belief and several are Stoker's own or his sources' recent embellishments, and the difficulty of telling them apart is itself evidence of how completely the book was absorbed.

Kermode treats plot as a way of humanising time: a sequence with a beginning and an end imposes on duration a shape that lived experience does not provide, since nobody occupies their own beginning or end.

On that account the interest of a plot is concordance, the fitting together of an expected ending with a middle that has to be endured, and the recurring literary problem is that endings which satisfy formally tend to falsify what they claim to describe.

Kermode's later work took up the gospel of Mark, and its subject is interpretation, not belief: why a narrative should contain so much that resists explanation, and what a tradition does with a text whose obscurities are structural.

He argues that some narratives are built to keep outsiders outside, and that the parables are described in the text itself as performing exactly that function. That makes secrecy a property of the writing and not an inadequacy in the reader.

The singer composes the poem while performing it, selecting from a stock of themes and a formulaic system that supplies phrases fitted to each metrical position.

This is the clearest available demonstration that improvisation is recombination, not invention. Singers insist they reproduce a song exactly as they learned it, and the recordings show substantial variation between one performance and the next, because what has been learned is a technique rather than a text.

Composition in performance is the normal condition of oral narrative rather than a special case within it, and the constraints follow from the situation: nothing can be revised, the audience is present, and the material has to be held without notes.

What looks like freedom is therefore heavily prepared. The epic singer, the commedia troupe and the rakugo performer all work from stocks of learned elements, and the art lies in selection, ordering and response to the room.

Bunyan produced the English allegory that everyone subsequently had to write against, and its reach was extraordinary: for two centuries it was a household book in places that owned few others.

His method is also why the mode fell out of favour. He demonstrated so completely what a fully mapped correspondence can do that later writers, when they wanted meaning without decoding, defined their practice by contrast with him.

The Pilgrim's Progress is regularly discussed among the works that prepared the English novel, though it belongs to a different intention entirely.

What it contributed is a sustained prose narrative following one ordinary man through a sequence of encounters in a specified landscape, written in the speech of people who were not gentlemen, at a moment when serious prose was expected to sound learned. The nineteenth-century novelists who grew up on it, Dickens among them, took the manner, not the scheme.

Swift is the standing example of the Juvenalian register in English: no geniality, no self-inclusion among the fools, and a composure that makes the anger legible rather than concealing it.

His method of adopting a persona completely and never breaking it set the hardest version of the form's problem, since a satire that supplies no signal depends entirely on a reader who brings the context, and his own work has been misread often enough to prove the risk is real.

Swift's irony is sustained rather than local: not a sentence that means its opposite but an entire argument conducted in a voice the author does not hold, with the reasoning kept sound so that the reader arrives at the objection unassisted.

The technique requires that nothing wink. A single lapse into the author's own voice would relieve the reader of the work, and it is that refusal to relieve them which makes the pamphlets uncomfortable, not merely clever.

Wagner wrote his own librettos, argued for a form in which music, poetry and staging would act as one instrument, and built a theatre to his own specification with a covered orchestra pit and no boxes.

His practical changes to how opera is performed have outlasted the theory: the darkened auditorium, the concealed orchestra and the expectation that an audience will sit in silence, not socialise are largely his, and they are now assumed everywhere.

Wagner developed the practice of attaching short musical figures to characters, objects, ideas and relationships, and of transforming them as the drama transforms what they refer to, until the orchestra can carry a commentary the singers are not delivering.

He did not name it. The term was applied by commentators, and his own writing preferred to describe the figures as melodic moments of feeling, which is a looser account than the labelling catalogues later attached to his scores.

Film scoring took its basic method from Wagner: an associated figure introduced with a character or an idea, varied as their situation changes, and used to tell the audience what to feel before the scene has told them anything.

The transfer happened early and through practitioners trained in the European tradition, and it has proved so durable that most audiences read the device fluently without ever having encountered it in the theatre it was built for.

The classical detective novel supplies the most complete closure available in fiction, since the final chapter accounts for every anomaly the book has raised and reassigns each one to a settled explanation.

Christie's endings are the form at its most thorough: the assembled suspects, the sequential elimination, the confession or arrest, and the restoration of a community that had been made unreadable by a single concealed act. Nothing is left for the reader to carry away unresolved, which is much of the pleasure and the standard objection.

Storr came to the subject from long-form journalism and from teaching, and the book grew out of a workshop he had been running, not the other way round, which accounts for its ending in a step-by-step appendix rather than a conclusion.

Its examples are deliberately mixed in register, taking King Lear, Jane Austen, Breaking Bad, The Godfather and children's stories as equally usable evidence, on the argument that if the mechanism is cognitive it should not respect the boundary between literature and entertainment.

Storr's account starts a level below craft. He argues that the brain constructs a controlled model of the world rather than perceiving it directly, that this model is silently edited to protect the version of ourselves we can live with, and that a story works by staging exactly that process in someone else.

On this reading storytelling is not primarily entertainment or instruction but a simulation of another consciousness under pressure, which is why the form is universal and why the questions it asks are the ones people ask about themselves.

Storr treats plot as a sequence of causally connected changes whose function is to test a character's model of the world, and he is insistent that change alone is not enough: unexpected change captures attention, and only cause and effect converts a sequence of events into a story.

He distinguishes plot as recipe, a shape imposed from outside and filled in, from plot as a symphony of change generated by who the protagonist is, and argues that the second produces the first, not the reverse.

Storr's use of neuroscience gives the oldest term in the tradition a modern restatement: if perception is itself a model the brain builds and continually corrects, then a story is not an imitation of the world but an imitation of the modelling.

The consequence he draws is practical. Precise detail works because it activates the same neural apparatus that would fire on encountering the thing itself, so specificity is not decoration but the mechanism by which a reader is made to build the scene rather than be told about it.

Storr supplies a physiological argument for the oldest piece of craft advice in the manual literature. Concrete, specific detail recruits the reader's own perceptual and motor systems to construct the scene, while abstraction and summary do not, so the difference between showing and telling is a difference in what the reader's brain is made to do.

He extends the same reasoning to metaphor, arguing that a good one is effective because it borrows an existing model instead of describing a new one.

Storr works with a five-act shape, not the three-act paradigm, on the grounds that five movements give the sacred flaw the room it needs to be tested, exposed and either surrendered or defended to the end.

His interest is not in where the acts fall but in what each has to accomplish to the character: establishing the theory of control, destabilising it, forcing a defence of it, breaking it, and settling whether the person changes. The structure is a consequence of the psychology rather than a container for it.

Storr treats an ending as the answer to the question the story has been asking about who the protagonist is, and holds that only two answers are available: the character changes, or refuses and is destroyed by the refusal.

He describes the moment at which the answer arrives as the point where control is finally surrendered or reasserted, and argues that endings which resolve the plot without resolving that question register as incomplete however neatly the events are tied off.

Storr devotes a section to cultural difference in story, drawing on research suggesting that perception itself varies, with Western viewers attending to focal objects and East Asian viewers to fields and relationships.

He uses it to argue that the individual protagonist driving a plot against opposition is a culturally specific arrangement rather than a property of narrative, which is the same conclusion the four-part scheme supports from the other direction: a complete story is possible with a turn instead of a conflict.

Storr draws on Bruner directly, including his account of narrative operating in two realms at once, a landscape of action and a landscape of consciousness, which maps closely onto Storr's own division between the plot and the question it is asking about the protagonist.

The wider debt is to Bruner's position that narrative is a mode of thought, not a decoration on it, which is the premise Storr's psychological approach requires in order to get started.

The two books arrived within a few years of each other and are frequently recommended together, and they reach compatible conclusions from opposite starting points.

Yorke works from the practice of drama production and argues that a five-act shape underlies the structures writers are taught; Storr works from psychology and arrives at five movements because that is what testing a flawed model of the world requires. Neither is derived from the other, which is part of why the convergence is interesting.

Egri argued in the 1940s that character generates plot rather than the reverse, and that a writer should build a full account of a person before writing an event. Storr's method is a psychologically equipped version of the same order of operations.

Where Egri offers the bone structure of physiology, sociology and psychology, Storr offers the theory of control and the flaw at its centre, and both treat the plot as the instrument that applies pressure to what has already been established.

Both are teachers with a seminar behind the book, and they ground their authority in opposite places.

McKee's warrant is the accumulated practice of the form, argued from films and plays and delivered as craft judgement; Storr's is empirical, argued from studies of perception, personality and memory, with the craft tradition treated as a body of findings arrived at without knowing why they worked. They agree substantially about what a scene must do and disagree about what makes the answer authoritative.

The book's account of character is its centre of gravity. A person is described as running a theory of control, a working model of how the world operates and how to get what they want from it, assembled largely in the first two decades of life out of what Storr calls origin damage.

The flaw in that model is sacred because it is not experienced as a flaw: it is defended, rationalised and frequently taken as a virtue, which is why plot events, not argument are required to expose it.

Storr reframes the arc as the dismantling of a specific false belief rather than a general improvement in a person. The ignition point is the first event that puts pressure on the sacred flaw, and each subsequent event tightens it until the protagonist has to answer the dramatic question of who they are going to be.

His case study is Michael Corleone, whose model of himself as an honest man apart from his family's business is systematically taken away until the final scene settles the question against him.

Every narrative is delivered from somewhere, and the choice of position determines what can be known, what can be concealed and whose judgement the audience is lent.

It is one of the few components with no default. A story must have events and agents to be a story at all, but the position from which they are reported can be moved anywhere from unlimited access to a single confused participant, and the same events become a different work at each setting.

Imitation is the oldest available answer to what storytelling is doing: presenting an action so that an audience experiences something of what witnessing it would be.

The term carries the field's founding argument with it. Plato treated the imitation as a danger, at a remove from truth and corrupting to whoever performs it; Aristotle treated it as natural, pleasurable and a source of understanding, and every later defence of fiction is a version of the second position.

Telling is the other half of the pair, and in prose it is the more fundamental of the two, since a narrative made of language can only ever report.

The term also came to name the world of the story itself, everything that exists for the characters. Film criticism distinguishes sound the characters can hear from score they cannot. Both senses concern the same boundary: what is inside the told world and what belongs to the telling of it.

The Poetics is the first surviving attempt to treat storytelling as a craft with describable parts, not as inspiration, and almost every term the tradition still uses for the analysis of plot comes from it.

Its range is narrower than its influence suggests, since it concerns tragedy and epic in a particular city over a particular century. What made it general was later use: the six parts, the priority of plot, and the demand that events follow by necessity have been applied to novels, films and television by people the treatise could not have anticipated.

Ong's contribution is to insist that the medium is not neutral: how a culture stores and transmits words determines what kinds of story it can hold, and what a literate person takes for the natural properties of narrative are frequently the properties of writing.

Repetition, formula, episodic structure and the aggregative style are strengths where nothing can be looked up and faults where it can, which reframes a long list of supposed primitivisms as engineering.

Frye's ambition was to describe literature as a single ordered system, with works no longer judged one at a time, and the Anatomy of Criticism sets out categories intended to make criticism cumulative in the way a science is.

Whether the system holds is disputed. What survives is the underlying claim that the recurrences across unrelated works are structural, and that a critic's job includes describing the pattern rather than only the instance.

Burke treated narrative as the basic form of human reasoning about motive, not as a literary genre, and analysed any account of an action, including a legal argument or a political speech, with the same five terms.

The consequence is that storytelling stops being a special activity performed by artists and becomes the ordinary means by which people explain themselves, which is the position later work on narrative identity and on historiography proceeds from.

Kermode's question is why the shapes fiction supplies should be needed at all, and his answer is temporal: people are always in the middle, without access to their own beginning or end, and borrow from narrative a concordance that experience does not provide.

That makes the appetite for endings a property of the audience rather than of the form, and it explains why the arrangements that satisfy formally are so often the ones that falsify what they claim to represent.

White's argument extends the reach of narrative analysis into writing that had understood itself as reporting instead of composing, holding that a chronicle becomes a history only when a story shape is imposed on it.

The implication runs both ways. If history is emplotted, then the techniques catalogued in this graph are not confined to fiction, and the choice of which shape to impose is an interpretive act performed before any evidence is weighed.

The novel is the form that has taken on the most of what storytelling can do, absorbing letters, essays, documents, other genres and other voices, and it is the one with the fewest external constraints: no running time, no cast to pay, no audience present to lose.

What it gives up is everything performance supplies. There is no voice, no face and no room, and every effect a performer would produce has to be built out of sentences.

Drama is storytelling with the narrator removed. Nobody explains, nobody reports what a character is feeling, and the audience is given only what people do and say in front of them, which is why so much dramatic technique concerns getting necessary information onto a stage plausibly.

It is also the form in which the audience is physically present and collective, so the response is part of the event, and a performance changes according to the room it is played to.

Film controls what is seen and for exactly how long. That makes it the most directive of the major forms: attention can be placed on an object for a second and withdrawn before the audience has decided anything about it.

Its distinctive resource is the cut, which allows time, place and viewpoint to change instantly and lets meaning be produced by juxtaposition. What it cannot do directly is interiority, and the workarounds for that limitation account for a large part of its grammar.

Gottschall wrote the book as a general-audience synthesis of a research programme he had been pursuing academically, in which literary questions are approached with the methods of the sciences rather than of criticism.

The position was contentious within his own discipline, where the application of evolutionary explanation to art has been resisted both on methodological grounds and on the argument that it explains the appetite without explaining any particular work.

Gottschall's question is prior to every craft question: not how a story should be built but why an animal that needs to eat and avoid predators should devote so many of its waking and sleeping hours to events that never happened.

His answer is that the appetite is adaptive rather than incidental, and the evidence he assembles is convergent, not experimental: children's pretend play is universal and preoccupied with danger, dreams are largely narrative and largely unpleasant, and the fiction people choose is overwhelmingly about trouble.

The book supplies a functional explanation for the thing craft teaching simply asserts, that a story needs trouble.

If narrative is a simulation for rehearsing predicaments, then a story without a predicament is a simulation of nothing, and the appetite for difficulty is not a convention of the form but the reason the form exists. It is one of the few accounts that explains why audiences seek out experiences they would avoid in life.

Gottschall's simulation argument requires that people actually enter the imagined situation instead of observing it from outside, and that entry is what the transportation research measures.

The two lines of work support each other: the psychology establishes that absorption happens and has consequences for belief, and the evolutionary account proposes why a mind would be built to permit it.

The two books are the main popular statements of the empirical turn in writing about story, and they divide the territory between them.

Gottschall asks why the species tells stories at all and answers in evolutionary terms; Storr takes the appetite as given and asks what the machinery of perception and personality implies about how a particular story should be built. One is an account of the audience, the other a method for the writer.

Transportation is the measurable version of what Coleridge described from the inside. Where the older formulation asks what a reader agrees to do, the psychological account describes a state that can be scored on a scale and correlated with outcomes.

The research also embarrasses the older account slightly, since transported readers show altered beliefs whether or not they have been told the story is fiction, which suggests the suspension is less voluntary than the phrase implies.

The transportation findings give the tradition's oldest worry an evidence base. Plato held that imitation works on an audience below the level of judgement and shapes them whether or not they consent, which is close to what the research reports.

Where the two part company is on the verdict. The psychology describes reduced counterarguing as a property of absorbed reading; whether that is a danger or the mechanism by which fiction teaches anything is not a question the measurement settles.

Peter Brooks, an American critic, published the book in 1984, at a point when structuralist and deconstructive criticism had largely displaced plot as a subject on the grounds that it was the naive part of a text.

His argument for taking it seriously is that plot is where a narrative's force on a reader actually operates, and that a criticism which can describe everything about a novel except why anyone keeps turning the pages has mislaid its object.

Brooks redefines plot as a dynamic rather than an arrangement: the design that a reader constructs in the act of reading, driven by an appetite the text has aroused for an ending not yet available.

His formulation is that the anticipation of retrospection is the reader's chief instrument, since every element is held provisionally until a conclusion arrives to determine what it meant. On that account a plot is not in the book but in the transaction between the book and someone reading it forward in time.

Brooks's account of the middle explains why endings carry the weight they do. The narrative arouses a desire for the end and then insists on postponement, and the deviations, subplots and delays are not obstacles to the plot but the plot itself.

He takes the model from Freud's account of an organism that must reach its own end by its own path rather than by the shortest one, which supplies a reason why an ending arrived at too quickly or too easily reads as a failure, not an efficiency.

Brooks builds his model on Beyond the Pleasure Principle, taking from it the idea of a drive toward an end that must nonetheless be delayed and made to follow its own circuitous route.

The transfer is deliberate and openly methodological. He is not psychoanalysing characters or authors, which is the practice the approach became notorious for, but borrowing a shape of argument about desire and delay and applying it to what a text does to a reader.

Brooks accepts the formalist separation of the events from their arrangement and objects that it stops short, since it describes a relation between two static things and says nothing about the force that moves a reader through the second.

His addition is temporal and motivational: the reader is constructing the story from the discourse while still inside it, without access to the ending that will settle the construction, and that condition of provisional reading is what the formalist pair leaves out.

Janet Murray, an academic working on digital media, wrote the book from within a computing institution rather than a literature department, and it appeared in 1997, before the forms it describes had commercially arrived.

That timing accounts for both its influence and the objections to it, since the argument had to be conducted through thought experiments and early prototypes, not through a body of work, and later practitioners have disputed predictions the book could only make speculatively.

Murray's separation of immersion, agency and transformation gave the field its first usable vocabulary, and her definition of agency is the demanding part: the satisfying power to take meaningful action and see the results of decisions, which is not the same as being given things to press.

She also identified the computer's procedural character as the property that matters, meaning the author writes rules that generate events, not the events themselves, which is a different job from writing a sequence.

The book's title question is what becomes of a story when its audience can act inside it, and the answer it works toward is that authorship moves up a level, from arranging events to designing the system that produces them.

The difficulty it identifies has not been solved since: a narrative's power depends substantially on inevitability, and a participant's satisfaction depends on consequence, so every interactive form has to trade one against the other rather than combining them.

The title's thought experiment is deliberately provocative: place a Shakespeare tragedy in a system where the audience can intervene, and ask what is left.

Murray's point is that the play's effect depends on watching a man fail to act while being unable to help him, so an audience given the power to intervene would be given a different work entirely. The example marks the limit of interactivity rather than its promise, and she uses it to define what the new medium would have to invent instead of inheriting.

Murray's account of immersion treats a constructed world as something an audience enters and tests rather than observes, and holds that the pleasure comes from the world's rules holding under investigation.

That sets a harder standard than prose world building requires. A novel's setting is only tested where the narrative goes; a system's is tested wherever a participant chooses to push. Environmental consistency became a production problem, not a stylistic one.

The American media scholar Henry Jenkins had been working on audiences and participation since the early 1990s, when treating fan writing as a serious cultural practice was itself unusual, and the 2006 book extends that position into an account of the whole media environment.

Its argument is that convergence is happening in the audience, not in the hardware: people are moving across platforms and assembling what they find, whatever the industries producing it intended.

Jenkins gave the practice its name and, more usefully, its condition: each medium should contribute something distinctive to the whole, so that a comic tells what the film cannot and the game is not a retelling.

That requirement is what separates the concept from adaptation and from licensed merchandise, and it is also the reason relatively few commercial attempts satisfy it, since the economics favour repeating a story in every available format rather than distributing it across them.

Adaptation retells a story in another medium, so a reader who knows the novel and a viewer who knows only the film have each had the whole thing.

Transmedia distributes it, so the parts are not substitutable and the complete work exists only in an audience that has assembled several of them. The distinction is clean in principle and blurred in practice, since most commercial franchises do both at once and rarely say which is which.

The arrangement is older than the term. Mythological and religious material has always circulated simultaneously through recitation, ritual, drama, sculpture and painting, with each carrying episodes and emphases the others did not, and no single authoritative version holding all of it.

What is new is ownership and planning. A myth is distributed because nobody controls it; a transmedia franchise is distributed because somebody has decided where each piece should go.

Games are the component that most often carries the distinctive contribution the arrangement requires, because they can occupy the parts of a world that a film has no time for: the intervening years, the minor faction, the city the plot passes through.

The relationship also runs the other way, since a game built inside an established world inherits an audience that already knows the rules, which removes most of the exposition problem the medium otherwise struggles with.

Jenkins's work on fan practice reframes what adaptation is by widening who is permitted to do it: rewriting, continuation, recombination and correction of an existing story are treated as ordinary audience behaviour, not as infringement or eccentricity.

That position sits awkwardly with the legal apparatus around adaptation, and the tension between an audience that assumes participation and an owner that assumes control is the subject a good deal of his later work takes up.

The paper takes its premise directly from Vonnegut's proposal that a story's shape can be drawn as a line running from good fortune to ill across its length, and that a small number of shapes recur.

He had submitted the idea as a master's thesis in anthropology at the University of Chicago and it was rejected. He continued to deliver it as a lecture, drawing the curves on a blackboard, and the researchers cite the lecture rather than any published argument.

The two are rival answers to the same question and were reached by incompatible methods.

Booker derived seven plots from reading, over decades, and grounded them in a psychological theory that determines in advance what the categories mean. The paper measured emotional valence across successive passages of 1,327 texts and let three separate statistical methods converge on six shapes. What the second cannot do is describe content: an arc is a curve, and a rise-fall-rise says nothing about who anybody is.

The steady rise is one of the six shapes the study recovers, and it corresponds roughly to the pattern folklorists and Booker both identify.

The correspondence should not be overstated. The method tracks the emotional colouring of the language across a text and not the fortunes of a character, so a rise measures how a book sounds and says nothing about what happens in it, and the two coincide often enough to be interesting and not reliably enough to be a translation.

Rise-fall-rise is among the six shapes, and the authors label it after Cinderella, following Vonnegut, who used the tale in his lectures to demonstrate a staircase of small improvements, a catastrophe at midnight and a recovery.

The labels are illustrative rather than analytic. They name each curve with a story whose reputation matches its shape, which makes the finding legible and slightly overstates how much the measurement knows about the tale.

The paper is the largest empirical test yet made of the claim that stories fall into a small number of shapes, and its limits are as informative as its finding.

The corpus is English-language, out of copyright, drawn from one digitisation project and filtered by download count. That makes it a sample of what an anglophone public has chosen to read for free, not of human storytelling. A recurring shape in that corpus is evidence about a readership as much as about narrative.

Le Guin wrote the essay in 1986 and it runs to a few pages, borrowing its premise from Elizabeth Fisher's proposal that the container rather than the weapon was the decisive early technology.

Its argument is that a literature built on the hunt, the spear and the killing has taken a late and specialised activity for the whole of human life, and has produced a hero whose story requires someone to be defeated in it.

The essay is the sharpest available objection to the assumption that narrative requires opposition.

If a story is a bag rather than an arrow, then what it does is hold things in relation to one another, and the requirement that something be fought and beaten is a property of one kind of story, not of the form. Le Guin's target is not conflict in a plot but the doctrine that a plot without it has failed, which is what most craft teaching in this graph assumes.

Le Guin's essay is an argument against exactly the pattern Campbell describes, and against the cultural authority it has acquired.

Her objection is not that the hero story is untrue but that it is one story, that its universality is an artefact of who has been doing the collecting, and that a form built around a single figure who leaves, kills and returns cannot hold the material she was interested in writing. She had used the pattern herself and spent the rest of her career working around it.

Both undercut the same assumption from unrelated directions. The four-part scheme demonstrates that a complete and satisfying story can be built on a turn, not a fight; the essay argues that the fight was never the centre of human life and should not be the centre of its literature.

Neither is a proposal for a new structure. Both are evidence that the conflict-driven model taught as a general law describes a particular tradition.

The essay was written eighteen years after Le Guin's own hero narrative, in which a young man of great power pursues a shadow across the sea, and it reads in part as an argument with her earlier work.

The Earthsea book already qualifies the pattern, since the pursuit ends in naming rather than killing and the victory is a reconciliation. What the essay proposes is more radical: not a gentler version of the hunt story but a different container altogether.

Harari's argument moves narrative out of art and into political and economic organisation, holding that large-scale cooperation among strangers is possible only where enough people hold the same story about something that does not physically exist.

Money, nations, corporations, laws and gods are his examples of such imagined orders, and their power is real because the belief is shared. On this account the species' distinctive skill is not tool use or language as such but collective fiction.

Harari treats myth as a functional category rather than a historical one, covering any shared story that coordinates behaviour, which puts a corporation's legal personality and a limited liability agreement in the same class as a creation narrative.

The extension is deliberate and is where historians have pushed back, since a category broad enough to include both explains the resemblance by construction, not by evidence.

Taleb named the fallacy in The Black Swan and treats it as one of the principal reasons rare events are not anticipated: a record of what happened can always be assembled into a story, and the story feels like an explanation.

His illustration is the market report that attributes a day's movement to a news item chosen after the fact, and his broader claim is that the same operation is performed on careers, wars and lives, producing causes that were not available to anyone at the time.

The two arrive at a similar observation and take opposite attitudes to it.

White argues that a historian must impose a plot shape on a record that does not contain one, and treats this as a condition of the discipline to be understood; Taleb argues that fitting stories to sequences manufactures false causation, and treats it as a defect to be guarded against. Both agree the shape is supplied, not found.

Forster's distinction between a story and a plot turns on causation: events in sequence become a plot when joined by because rather than by and then.

The fallacy is that operation performed on material that does not support it. What is a virtue in fiction, where the causes are constructed and the writer is responsible for them, becomes an error applied to a historical record, where the connections are supplied by the reader and mistaken for evidence.

Almost everything else in this graph treats narrative as a way of understanding: Bruner's mode of thought, Gottschall's simulation, Storr's model of the world, Kermode's concordance. This is the standing objection to all of them.

The case is that the same machinery which makes experience intelligible also makes it feel more explicable than it was, supplying agents where there was chance and reasons where there was noise, and that its persuasiveness is precisely what makes it unreliable.

The two describe the same property from opposite ends. The psychology measures how readily an absorbed audience accepts what a narrative asserts and how little they argue back; the fallacy names what follows when that acceptance is applied to accounts of the real world.

Taken together they make the uncomfortable point that a story's persuasive power is not proportional to its accuracy, and that the better it is made the less it is examined.

Gottschall's later work turns on the material his earlier book celebrated, arguing that the same persuasive machinery which makes fiction useful also makes propaganda, conspiracy and grievance narratives effective.

The shift is a useful corrective to the optimism of most writing in this area: if story is a simulation that teaches, then it teaches whatever it simulates, and nothing in the mechanism distinguishes a true account from a compelling one.

Storr's method depends on the transportation literature, since his argument that a story hijacks the reader's model of the world requires the reader to be inside the model rather than watching it.

His practical advice follows from the same research: specificity, sensory detail and cause-and-effect sequence are recommended because they are what the measurements associate with absorption, not because good writers have always done them.

The two books are companions on the same question and were published within twenty years of each other.

Kermode asks why an audience needs endings and locates the answer in the human condition of being permanently in the middle; Brooks asks how a text exploits that need and locates the answer in the delay it constructs. One accounts for the appetite, the other for the machinery that feeds it.

The transportation research gives the oldest note in craft teaching an evidential basis, since imagery is one of the components the measures track and concrete sensory detail is what produces it.

A reader constructing a scene from specifics is engaged in the activity being measured; a reader receiving a summary is not. That does not make the rule universal, since summary has its own uses, but it explains why the advice keeps being given.

The book's Matrix case study treats the game as a necessary component, not a tie-in, since it carried plot material the films assumed and did not show, including a character's actions between instalments.

Jenkins uses it to argue that games are particularly suited to the role because they can occupy a world's interstitial spaces, the journeys and side conflicts a film has no time for, without requiring the main narrative to make room.

Jenkins argues that serialised television was where audiences learned the habits convergence depends on: following long arcs, holding detail across gaps, and pooling interpretations with strangers between episodes.

His examples include the forum communities that assembled around puzzle-driven series, which he treats as collective intelligence rather than obsession, and as the behaviour producers subsequently began designing for.

Vonnegut's proposal is the most compact structural claim anyone has made: that a story's shape can be drawn as a single line on two axes, fortune against time, and that the recurring shapes are few and simple enough to teach in minutes.

He delivered it as comedy, which is part of why it was dismissed, and the joke conceals a serious reduction. Nothing about character, meaning or language survives the abstraction, and what remains turns out to be measurable.

Vonnegut used science-fictional premises throughout his fiction while objecting to being shelved in the genre, and complained that critics treated the drawer as a urinal.

The ambivalence is itself part of the genre's history, since he is among the writers whose commercial success outside it helped make the material respectable, and his invented figure of a neglected science fiction author appears across several of his books as a running joke about that reputation.

Taleb's objection applies with particular force to any first-person account of a life, since the narrator knows the outcome and cannot unknow it while describing the years before.

What comes out is a record in which early events acquire a significance they did not have at the time and the alternatives that were live are quietly dropped. He treats biography and autobiography as the genres in which the fallacy operates most freely and is least noticed.

The two make the same observation about how the mind works and disagree entirely about what follows.

Bruner holds that narrative is one of two irreducible modes of thought, not a lesser version of the logical one, and that constructing a life as a story is how a self is made. Taleb holds that the same operation systematically manufactures causes that were not there, and should be resisted wherever the stakes are real.

Shelley began the novel at eighteen during the summer of 1816 at a villa on Lake Geneva, where the party set itself to write ghost stories.

Her account of the origin comes from the introduction she supplied to the 1831 edition, fifteen years later, and describes a waking vision of a pale student kneeling beside the thing he had put together. It is her own retrospective telling and the only account there is. The novel was published anonymously in 1818 with a preface by her husband, which led several reviewers to assume he had written it.

The claim that Shelley began the genre rests on what her horror proceeds from: a deliberate procedure carried out with instruments by a man who has studied, rather than a curse, a pact or an inheritance.

Brian Aldiss made the case most influentially, and it remains contested by critics who point out that the science is gestural and the book's concerns are Romantic. What is not contested is the pattern it fixed, of a made being that turns on its maker and argues its own case.

Frankenstein arrives half a century into the mode and rearranges it. The pursuit across a wasteland, the isolated transgressor and the family destroyed by a secret are all inherited; the source of the horror is not.

Shelley also gives the monster the most articulate voice in the book and places his account at the structural centre, which is a considerable departure from a genre whose threats had generally been left unexplained.

Walpole published it anonymously in 1764, framed as a translation by one William Marshal of a manuscript printed at Naples in 1529 and found in the library of an old Catholic family.

He acknowledged authorship in the second edition the following year and added the subtitle that named the genre. Some reviewers who had praised the supposed medieval original turned against it once it was known to be modern, which is an early demonstration of how much a frame can do.

The novel is the genre's origin point by common agreement and contains most of its apparatus in eighty pages: the usurped inheritance, the castle with subterranean passages, the tyrant pursuing a young woman through them, the prophecy, the animated portrait and the giant helmet that opens the book by crushing the heir.

What it does not have is the atmosphere later Gothic runs on. The events arrive at farcical speed, and the mode's slow dread was developed by Radcliffe a generation afterwards.

The first edition's preface is an elaborate fiction in its own right, supplying a translator, a printing date, a provenance and a scholarly opinion about the manuscript's likely composition during the crusades.

The device solved a practical problem: a marvellous story could be offered to an eighteenth-century readership as a curiosity of a credulous age rather than as something its author expected them to believe. Gothic novels went on using discovered manuscripts long after the excuse had stopped being needed.

Poe published the tale in Graham's Magazine in 1841 and wrote two further Dupin stories, which is the whole of his output in a form he invented.

He called them tales of ratiocination and was dismissive of the achievement, remarking that they owe their popularity to being something in a new key and that where the reader's ingenuity is not equal to the author's the appearance of profundity is easily produced. The assessment is his own and unusually accurate about the genre that followed.

The three Dupin stories established the amateur reasoner, the slower official police, the narrating companion, the locked room, the wrongly accused suspect and the armchair solution, and left later writers the task of elaboration.

Doyle acknowledged the debt without reservation, describing Poe as the father of the detective tale and observing that each of his stories is a root from which a whole literature has developed. The Moonstone and the Golden Age both proceed from this base.

The tale contains the genre in miniature and gets there before the genre exists to be joined.

It opens with several pages of essay on the analytical faculty, demonstrates that faculty by having Dupin read his companion's train of thought from his movements in the street, and only then supplies a crime. The solution turns on a physical impossibility resolved by an explanation no reader is expected to reach, which sets the standard the Golden Age would later try to make fair.

Poe's review of Hawthorne sets out the earliest clear theory of the short story: a work that can be read at one sitting, designed backwards from a single preconceived effect, with no word admitted that does not serve it.

The argument makes brevity a formal principle rather than a limitation, and it underlies the tradition of the constructed, unified story that runs through the nineteenth century until Chekhov begins dismantling the requirement for a designed ending.

Poe moved the genre's machinery inside a mind. The threat in his tales is generally a compulsion, a guilt or a decay that the narrator reports while insisting on his own soundness, and the reader is placed inside an account they can see is unreliable.

Lovecraft's survey of supernatural horror treats him as the point at which the form became art, and the tales of premature burial, telltale heartbeats and self-destroying narrators have been rewritten continuously since.

Scott published it anonymously in 1814 and maintained the anonymity for more than a decade, partly because a poet of his standing writing novels was thought to be lowering himself.

He had abandoned the manuscript years earlier and is said to have rediscovered it while looking for fishing tackle. The account comes from his own later preface, which is an interested source, and the book's success was immediate enough that everything after it was advertised as by the author of Waverley.

Scott made the past a subject rather than a costume, and the technical solution he arrived at defined the form: an ordinary protagonist of divided loyalties placed between contending forces, so that a society in the act of being destroyed can be shown from both sides.

His influence was European and immediate. Balzac, Manzoni, Pushkin, Tolstoy and Dumas all worked from the model, and Lukacs's account of the genre is substantially an account of Scott.

The novel is the genre's founding instance and demonstrates its central manoeuvre. Its protagonist is neither a Jacobite nor a convinced Hanoverian but a young man susceptible to atmosphere, and his susceptibility is the device that lets the book give the losing cause its full appeal.

Its subtitle places the action sixty years before the time of writing, which is close enough for witnesses to survive and far enough for the world to have gone, and that distance is the one the form has worked in ever since.

Lukacs took Scott as the historical novel's decisive figure and read Waverley as the demonstration of what the form could do that history could not.

His argument is that the mediocre hero is a structural necessity: a protagonist with strong convictions would settle the question the novel exists to hold open, while one who can be moved by both sides allows the conflict to be presented as a collision of social forces rather than a contest between a hero and a villain.

Giambattista Basile, a Neapolitan courtier and poet, wrote the tales in Neapolitan and they were published after his death by his sister, in two instalments in 1634 and 1636, under an anagram of his name.

He spent his working life as a courtier and soldier in the service of various Italian nobles, and the collection is aimed squarely at that audience: learned, allusive, extravagantly figurative and entirely uninterested in children, who were not the intended readers of fairy tales for another century and a half.

The collection is the earliest substantial body of European fairy tales in print and contains the first known literary versions of several of the best-known stories.

Reading it beside Perrault and the Grimms shows the direction of travel: the tales become shorter, cleaner, more moral and considerably less violent at each stage. Basile's are the versions before any of that editing, and they are startling to a reader who has only met their descendants.

The frame is a fairy tale rather than an occasion for one. A princess who cannot laugh is cursed to marry an enchanted prince, is displaced by a slave who steals her place by trickery, and regains it by having the false bride's own appetite for stories used against her.

Ten women tell fifty tales over five days to satisfy that appetite, and the last of them exposes the substitution, so the storytelling is what resolves the frame.

Basile's version, in which the sleeping woman is discovered by a passing king, raped while unconscious, and gives birth to twins who wake her when one sucks the splinter from her finger, is the earliest known form of the tale.

The story then continues for as long again with the king's jealous wife attempting to have the children cooked and served to him. Perrault removed the assault and kept a version of the second half; the Grimms removed both.

Basile's Cinderella is an active participant in her own ill-treatment: prompted by her governess, she kills her first stepmother by dropping the lid of a chest on her neck, and is then betrayed when the governess marries her father and installs six daughters of her own.

Nothing of that survives into the versions that followed, and setting it beside Perrault's patient and forgiving heroine is the clearest single demonstration of how much editing separates a printed tale from its predecessors.

The Russian folklorist Alexander Afanasyev assembled the collection between 1855 and 1863, working principally from manuscripts held by the Russian Geographical Society and from other collectors rather than from his own fieldwork.

His editorial practice was unusually restrained for the period. He printed variants side by side rather than merging them into a single authoritative telling, and preserved dialect and irregularity, which is why the collection functions as evidence where more heavily edited ones do not.

Propp drew the hundred wonder tales of his Morphology from this collection, working through a numbered sequence of its entries, and the scope of his conclusions is the scope of what Afanasyev happened to have gathered.

He was explicit about the limitation and later readers have generally ignored it. The thirty-one functions describe Russian wonder tales as collected by one man in the mid-nineteenth century, which is a firmer basis than most narrative taxonomies have and a narrower one than they claim.

The collection is the Slavic counterpart to the Grimms and differs from it in method as much as in material.

Its contents are the source of what most readers recognise as Russian folk narrative: Baba Yaga in a hut standing on chicken legs, Koschei who has hidden his death inside an egg inside a duck, the firebird, the grey wolf and Vasilisa the Beautiful. Because variants were kept rather than harmonised, the same tale can be read in several forms within the same volumes.

Capote went to Kansas in 1959 to report a murder for the New Yorker, stayed six years, and was present through the investigation, the trial and the executions.

He took no notes during interviews and reconstructed conversations from memory afterwards, a method he defended as more accurate than transcription and which is the origin of most of the doubts about the book. Harper Lee accompanied him and did a substantial share of the early interviewing, which his own account of the project underplays.

Lucas wrote and directed the 1977 film after several years of drafts that shifted almost everything except the general shape, and he took a reduced fee in exchange for sequel and merchandising rights that the studio did not value.

His stated sources are serials, Kurosawa, Westerns and Campbell, and the relative weight of each has been disputed ever since, partly because his own accounts of the process have changed over time.

The attribution is traditional and contested. The novel appeared anonymously in 1592, a decade after Wu's death, and his name was attached to it in the twentieth century largely on the strength of a local gazetteer listing a work of the same title among his writings.

Some scholars accept the identification and others hold that the book is a compilation with no single author, since the material had been developing in oral, dramatic and written form for four centuries before the novel fixed it.

Ferdowsi worked on the poem for around thirty years, completing it in about 1010, and drew on an earlier prose compilation of Persian royal traditions as well as on oral material.

He states within the poem that he has revived the Persian language by writing it, and later tradition has taken the claim as fact. The stories of a promised reward that arrived at the gate of the city as his funeral left it are legend, and they are told about other poets as well.

The Shahnameh is generally described as the longest epic composed by a single known author, running to some fifty thousand couplets, and it is organised as a continuous history rather than around one action.

Its three movements move from a mythical age through a heroic one dominated by the warrior Rostam to a historical section ending with the Arab conquest, so the poem narrates its own culture's defeat and was composed in the language that defeat had displaced.

The naqqal's core repertoire is the Shahnameh, performed episode by episode over successive evenings in coffeehouses, with the Rostam cycle as the material audiences returned for.

The relationship inverts the usual one between writing and performance. Here a written literary epic is kept in popular circulation by oral delivery, and the performer works from memory and from prompt books rather than reciting the text, so the poem exists simultaneously as a fixed work and as a living tradition.

The episode of Rostam and Sohrab is among the poem's most performed and is a tragedy of recognition arriving too late: the hero kills a young champion in single combat and learns afterwards that the man was his son, who had come looking for him.

The pattern of a father killing an unrecognised son occurs independently in Irish, Germanic and Russian material, and this is its fullest and best-known telling.

Spiegelman serialised the work over eleven years in Raw, the magazine he edited with Francoise Mouly, and built it from taped interviews with his father Vladek conducted across the same period.

He has been consistently uncomfortable with its reception. It received a Pulitzer special award in 1992 because the existing categories had no place for it, and he has described the anxiety of a work about mass murder becoming a career.

Maus is the work most often produced to settle the question of what the medium can carry, and it makes the case through form rather than despite it.

The animal masks let a reader look at material that photographs make unlookable; the panel grid controls the pace of testimony; and the drawn present-day frame, in which a son records a father he finds difficult, sits on the page beside the past it is trying to reach. None of that is available to prose in the same way.

The book is two memoirs at once, the father's account of survival and the son's account of extracting it, and the second is what distinguishes it.

Spiegelman includes his own bad behaviour, his father's, the tape recorder, the commercial success of the first volume and his inability to draw the thing he is drawing. The result is a memoir whose subject is partly the unreliability of the form it belongs to.

The wartime narrative reaches the reader inside the present-day one, delivered in a father's voice under his son's questioning, and the two are cut against each other continuously rather than being separated into sections.

A further layer appears in the second volume, where a strip Spiegelman drew years earlier about his mother's suicide is reproduced inside the book in a different style, so a third version of the past is set beside the other two.

The series is the standing example of what the form can do that an episodic structure cannot: hold a hundred characters across five years, allow consequences to arrive several seasons after their causes, and give each season to an institution rather than to a plot.

It also declines the form's usual compensations. Investigations fail, reforms are reversed, and the closing sequence of the final season shows the same positions filled by different people.

The comparison with the nineteenth-century novel is made about this series more than any other, and the resemblance is structural rather than flattering.

Both work at a scale that lets a whole society be shown through the interlocking of separate worlds, both were released in instalments to an audience whose response was known while later parts were being written, and both use recurring minor figures to carry the sense of a populated place. The series' creators have invoked Dickens directly, sometimes to reject the comparison.

David Simon has described the show as Greek tragedy with modern institutions in the place of the gods: postmodern forces that are indifferent to individuals and cannot be successfully opposed.

The framing is his and not a critical consensus, and it accounts for a real structural feature. Characters who behave well are destroyed as reliably as those who do not, and the destruction follows from position rather than from any flaw the tradition would recognise.

Flaherty had shot an earlier film of the same material and lost the negative to a cigarette fire in an editing room, and he raised money from a fur company to return and start again.

He spent over a year in the north for the second attempt, screened rushes to the people he was filming and took their suggestions, and directed scenes that he knew to be reconstructions. Allakariallak, the hunter credited as Nanook, died within two years of the film's release.

The film is treated as the form's first feature and as the first demonstration of its central problem.

Flaherty staged and directed extensively: a hunting method already replaced by rifles was revived for the camera, an igloo was built with one side open so the interior could be lit, and the family group was cast rather than found. He argued that one sometimes has to distort a thing to catch its true spirit, which is the defence every subsequent documentary has had either to make or to refuse.

The film and the nonfiction novel run into the same objection forty years apart: that arranging true material by the methods of storytelling produces meaning the record does not contain.

Both are also defended on the same ground, that a bare record conveys less of a situation than a shaped account of it. What separates them is that Flaherty's staging is visible on the screen while Capote's reconstruction of unrecorded conversations is not visible on the page.

The broadcast is the medium's most famous single transmission and a demonstration of what sound alone can do: it establishes a music programme, interrupts it with bulletins, sends a reporter to a field in New Jersey and then cuts him off mid-sentence into silence.

The silence is the effect no other medium can produce as cheaply. Radio drama's whole resource is what a listener supplies, and a dead microphone supplies a great deal.

The programme is a drama pretending to be the interruption of a programme, so the form the audience is actually listening to appears inside the fiction as the thing being broken into.

That nesting is what produced the effect, since a listener who had missed the announcement had no frame available except the one the broadcast was imitating. A trick of this kind is available to a medium roughly once, before its audience learns the format.

Welles directed and narrated the broadcast for the Mercury Theatre on the Air in October 1938, with a script by Howard Koch adapting the Wells novel to a contemporary American setting.

His own account of the panic grew more colourful over the years, and he enjoyed the reputation it gave him. Later research into the ratings and the complaints suggests the audience was modest and the alarm limited, and that the story of a nation in flight was substantially a newspaper construction.

The play is among the most frequently performed in the repertoire and is one of the clearest cases of what noh does with a long prose source.

It takes a single episode from the Tale of Genji and stages neither the affair that caused the jealousy nor the wife's death that follows, only the spirit's appearance and subduing. The sick woman is represented by a folded robe on the stage floor and never appears, which is the form's compression carried about as far as it will go.

The play works from the chapter in which Genji's neglected lover, the Rokujo lady, becomes a living spirit and attacks his pregnant wife at a carriage procession where she has been publicly humiliated.

The adaptation assumes the audience knows all of that and stages none of it. What the play supplies is the encounter itself and the spirit's own account of her shame, so the source is not retold but answered.

First staged in 1840 for Ichikawa Danjuro VII, the play belongs to a category performed against a painted pine backdrop in imitation of the noh stage, and it is among the form's most celebrated vehicles for a leading actor.

Its reputation rests on two sustained performances: the improvised reading of a blank scroll under interrogation, and the beating of a disguised master, played so that the audience watches the retainer's grief and the barrier keeper's decision to be deceived.

The play is taken from the noh Ataka and keeps its situation exactly: a barrier, a disguise, a suspicious keeper, a subscription list read from an empty scroll, and a servant striking his lord to complete the deception.

What kabuki adds is duration and display. The noh play is spare and fast where the kabuki version expands each confrontation into a set piece, and the transfer is the standard example of how the two forms handle the same material.

Chunhyangga is the most performed of the five surviving works and the one most often used to introduce the form.

A complete performance runs several hours with a single singer and one drummer, and the singer plays the heroine, her mother, the two magistrates and the narrator without leaving the mat. The best-known passages, the parting and the torture scene, are performed as excerpts in their own right.

The story existed as popular narrative before it existed as pansori and circulates simultaneously as prose fiction, film, television and stage drama.

Its material is folk in origin and its politics have been read as such: a courtesan's daughter who refuses a magistrate's demand and is tortured for it, vindicated when her husband returns as a secret royal inspector. That shape has made the heroine available as a national figure at several points in Korean history.

The film is the paradigm's standing teaching example, and Syd Field used it as such: the first act closes when the farm is destroyed and the protagonist has no home to return to, and the second when the rescue is complete and the assault on the station begins.

The fit is close enough to have been used for decades in seminars, and close enough that the film's own influence has helped make the model look like a description of how films naturally work.

The play is among the most cited examples of the five-act shape, with the ghost's charge, the growing suspicion, the play within the play at the centre, the consequences of the killing behind the arras, and the duel.

The division is partly editorial. The early quartos are inconsistent about act breaks and much of the marking in modern texts was supplied later, so the structure is at least in part something imposed on the play by people who expected to find it.

Freytag built his diagram from Greek tragedy and Shakespeare, and this is the play it fits most exactly: an opening that establishes a plague and an investigation, a rise through the interrogation of witnesses, a peak at the recognition, and a fall through the queen's death and the blinding.

The fit is partly circular, since the model was derived from a corpus this play dominates, and applying the same shape to a modern narrative that ends at its climax is where the diagram stops working.

Propp's corpus was Russian, but the functions describe the Grimm wonder tales just as closely, which is part of why the analysis travelled.

A lack is established, a hero departs, a donor tests him, a magical agent is transferred, the villain is defeated, the hero is branded, a false claimant appears and is exposed, and there is a wedding. The sequence holds across tales with entirely different casts, and where a Grimm tale departs from it the departure is usually traceable to Wilhelm's editing.

The film is regularly used to illustrate the four-part scheme, and the fit is in what it declines to supply: the antagonist is not defeated, the bathhouse owner is not punished, and the resolution comes through understanding a situation instead of overcoming an opponent.

The turn is the discovery of the river spirit's name, which recasts everything the protagonist has assumed about who she is dealing with, and the final section reconciles rather than triumphs.

Child, an American philologist at Harvard, worked on the collection for most of his career and died before the final part was issued, leaving a colleague to complete it from his notes.

He was a philologist by training and treated the ballads as texts to be established rather than as songs to be heard, printing no tunes at all. That omission is the collection's main limitation, and it left the musical side of the tradition to be recovered by later fieldworkers with recording equipment.

The collection is the form's reference corpus, and its arrangement demonstrates what a ballad is better than a definition could.

Each entry gathers every version Child could find, so the reader sees the same story with different names, regions, motives and endings, and no version claiming priority. A ballad on this evidence is not a text with variants but a set of variants with no text underneath them.

Child's method anticipates the type indexes by a generation: numbered entries, all variants preserved, and comparison across languages and borders treated as the basic analytic move.

He was working on sung narrative rather than prose tale, and the two fields developed separately, but the underlying problem is identical and so is the solution. Aarne's index does for the folk tale what Child's numbering had already done for the ballad.

Hammerstein wrote the book and lyrics and Richard Rodgers the music, in a partnership formed after Hammerstein had spent a decade with no substantial success.

The show was widely expected to fail: it had no chorus line at the opening, a murder in the second act and no star names. Its run of more than two thousand performances changed what producers believed a musical had to contain.

The show is the standard example of the integrated musical, in which numbers carry the story instead of pausing it.

Its opening is the demonstration: a woman churning butter and a man singing about a morning offstage, which establishes place, period, temperament and relationship before any dialogue. The dream ballet later stages the heroine's fear of a man she cannot refuse in words, and it is the only place in the show that material appears.

The show is drawn from a 1931 play about the same characters, which had a modest run and is now remembered almost entirely because of what was made from it.

The transfer shows what the musical adds and removes. The play's dialogue is compressed to leave room, the ambivalences are simplified, and in exchange the form gains the ability to put a character's interior state on stage in a way the source could only report.

Harmon created the series and developed the story circle during its production, teaching it publicly at the same time on a blog and in podcasts.

The show is therefore an unusually direct test of a structural scheme, since the episodes and the theory were being made by the same person in the same years, and the parody episodes are the strongest evidence for it: a western pastiche or a documentary spoof holds together as a story because the eight steps are underneath it.

Episodes are built on the eight steps, and the constraint is what makes the show's formal experiments work rather than collapsing into sketch.

An episode can become a paintball western or a stop-motion Christmas special and still run through comfort, want, unfamiliar situation, adaptation, getting the thing, paying for it and returning changed. The circle operates at the level of the group as well as the individual, which is how the same eight beats serve an ensemble.

The series works the form's central constraint as a subject. Its characters are held in a study group they have no practical reason to remain in, and the show repeatedly acknowledges that they should have graduated, moved away or grown up.
