It also tests how far the reset can be stretched, since some episodes leave permanent consequences and others end with the group back at the same table as though nothing had occurred.

The game demonstrates what the medium can do that adaptation from film cannot supply. Its protagonist's abilities are written as speaking characters who argue with him and with each other, so the mechanical layer that other games keep on a menu is the narration here.

It also removes combat entirely and makes failure productive, since a failed check often opens material that success would have closed, which turns the usual relationship between skill and story on its head.

The game takes the genre's structure and applies its pressure to the investigator instead of the crime. There is a body, a suspect list and a solution, and the more demanding question throughout is who the detective is, since he begins with no memory of himself.

The political convictions he can be given over the course of the case are treated as evidence about him in the same way as the physical clues are treated as evidence about the killing.

The game satisfies Murray's demanding definition of agency, in which choices must have consequences the participant can perceive, rather than the appearance of choice on a branching menu.

It also illustrates her point about procedural authorship. The writing is not a sequence but a system of checks, thresholds and internal voices, and no two players assemble the same protagonist out of it, which is authorship at the level of rules.

Orwell wrote the novel on the island of Jura while seriously ill with the tuberculosis that killed him two years later, typing the final draft himself in bed because he could not find a typist willing to come.

He had been working on the argument for years in essays about political language, propaganda and the falsification of the record during the Spanish Civil War, where he had seen newspapers report battles that had not happened.

The novel is the genre's most widely read instance and supplies its standard furniture: the telescreen, the ministry with an inverted name, the rewritten archive and the language engineered to make dissent unsayable.

It also sets the pattern its imitators follow structurally, with a protagonist who notices, a forbidden relationship, a document explaining the system, and a capture. What most imitators decline to copy is the ending, in which the protagonist is not martyred but corrected.

The book's argument is delivered inside a pursuit plot, which is how it avoids becoming the lecture most dystopias become.

A concealed diary, a room rented in secret, a paperweight, a hidden telescreen and a shopkeeper who is not a shopkeeper all belong to the machinery of suspense, and the reader's dread is generated by the machinery rather than by the exposition it carries.

The novella established the form: an autobiographical narrator of the lowest social standing, a chain of masters, an episodic structure that could be extended indefinitely, and a survey of society conducted from below.

Its protagonist does not improve morally and is not intended to. He learns each master's particular cruelty, adapts, and arrives at an accommodation he declines to look at closely, which is the shape every later picaro follows.

The book's targets are clerical, and it does not hedge: a pardoner who stages a fake miracle to sell indulgences, a priest who keeps his bread locked in a chest while his servant starves, a friar with unexplained business outside the monastery.

It was placed on the Spanish Index in 1559 and circulated afterwards in an expurgated version with the worst of the clergy removed, which is a fair measure of how the satire was received.

Eliot combined two separate projects while writing, a study of a provincial doctor and a story about a young woman with unusable ambitions, and the interlocking of the two is what gives the book its scale.

It was issued in eight parts across 1871 and 1872 in an unusual format devised for it, longer than a serial instalment and shorter than a volume, which allowed her to work at length without the monthly pressure Dickens accepted.

The novel is the English realist tradition at full stretch: a town rather than a household, several plots that affect one another through money and reputation rather than coincidence, and a narrator who analyses motive without excusing it.

Its particular contribution is refusing to let any character be furniture. Even the figures the plot requires the reader to judge are given the reasoning from inside, which is the technical form of its moral argument.

Eliot uses the technique to move between a character's self-justification and the narrator's assessment within a single paragraph, often without a marker to signal the shift.

Where Austen uses it for irony at a character's expense, Eliot uses it for sympathy at their expense: the reader is given the reasoning that makes a selfish decision feel reasonable from inside, and is left to supply the judgement.

Stowe wrote the novel in serial parts for an abolitionist weekly, prompted by the Fugitive Slave Act's requirement that northerners assist in returning people who had escaped.

She drew on published accounts by formerly enslaved people and on her own contacts, and published a documentary volume of her sources the following year in response to accusations that she had invented the conditions she described.

The novel runs on the mode's full apparatus: virtue in visible distress, an unambiguous villain, a flight across breaking ice, a child's deathbed and a moral scheme in which suffering redeems.

Its stage afterlife made the identification permanent. Hundreds of unauthorised adaptations reached audiences far larger than the book's, and they hardened its figures into the types that the title character's name now stands for.

The book is the standing historical example of fiction changing what a large public believed, and of the mechanism the transportation research describes operating at national scale.

It is also the standing example of the associated risk. Its sentimental method carried an argument against slavery to readers who would not have read a pamphlet, and fixed a set of racial types that outlived the argument by a century, which is what a persuasive story does whether or not its account is accurate.

Thomas Malory, an English knight of the fifteenth century, compiled the work in the 1460s, largely in prison, from French prose romances and English sources, and asks at the end for prayers for his deliverance.

His practice was to translate, cut and reorder rather than invent, and the achievement is one of arrangement: three centuries of accumulated material in several languages made into a single narrative with a beginning and an end. Caxton printed it in 1485 and divided it into books and chapters himself.

The book is the form's great late compilation and the point at which it becomes English.

It carries everything the genre had accumulated, the quests, the tournaments, the enchantments and the code of conduct, and it also carries the material's own critique: the grail quest finds most of the fellowship unworthy, and the order is destroyed by a love affair its own rules made inevitable and could not accommodate.

The grail quest occupies a substantial portion of the book and is the pattern's most searching treatment, because the object cannot be won by the qualities the rest of the narrative has been rewarding.

The best knights by every established measure fail, and the ones who succeed do so on grounds the fellowship has no way to recognise. The quest that was meant to crown the order is what breaks it.

Ford made the film in 1956 with John Wayne in a part that inverted the persona he had built with the same director, and cast his own regular company around him.

He shot in Monument Valley for the fifth time, on the Utah and Arizona border, several hundred miles from where the story is set. The landscape is not the Texas of the plot and has come to stand for the frontier generally largely because of these films.

The film is the genre's most examined work and the one that turns its central figure inside out.

Ethan Edwards has every competence the Western asks of a hero and a racial hatred the film neither shares nor explains away, and the search he conducts is for a girl he may intend to kill. The closing shot leaves him outside the house he has made safe, which is the genre's standard ending emptied of consolation.

The film's protagonist holds the position without supplying what the position implies: the audience follows a man whose stated intention through most of the film is to murder his own niece.

What keeps the attention on him is competence and force rather than sympathy, and the film's refusal to redeem him fully at the close is what separates it from the many later Westerns that borrowed the figure and softened him.

The play belongs to the group of late works written around 1610 and 1611, after the major tragedies, and adapts a prose romance by Robert Greene, a writer who had attacked Shakespeare in print two decades earlier.

Shakespeare keeps Greene's plot and changes the ending: in the source the queen is genuinely dead and stays dead, and the statue that comes to life is his own addition.

The play is the mode's most extreme English instance. Three acts of jealousy kill a child, apparently kill a queen and expose an infant on a foreign coast; the fourth jumps sixteen years into pastoral comedy; the fifth returns for a reconciliation.

Nothing in either genre's rules permits the manoeuvre, and the play makes no attempt to disguise it, having Time appear as a chorus to announce the gap and ask the audience's indulgence.

The sixteen-year gap is the boldest ellipsis in English drama and is handled with deliberate effrontery: a personified Time walks on, states that he will turn his glass, and asks the audience to accept the leap.

What is skipped is a childhood, a marriage that does not happen and a kingdom's decline, none of which the play needs. The device also draws attention to the convention rather than concealing it, which the late plays do repeatedly.

The play was produced in 405 BCE, months before Athens lost the war, and was awarded first prize and the rare honour of a second performance.

Sophocles and Euripides had both died within the previous year, which is the occasion for the premise that no capable tragedian remains alive. The advice the chorus gives the city about recalling its exiles was taken seriously enough to be cited later as a reason for the honour.

The play is Old Comedy operating at full range: a god as an incompetent protagonist, a slave who is smarter than he is, a chorus of frogs, direct political advice delivered to the audience, and a contest of literary criticism conducted with a set of scales.

It is also the form's clearest demonstration that topical, obscene and serious are not exclusive categories, since the joke about which poet should be resurrected is a real argument about what the city needs.

The contest gives Euripides his charges in his own idiom: that he lowered tragedy's register, taught the audience to argue, gave rhetorical skill to slaves and women, and wrote prologues so mechanical that a single phrase can be appended to any of them.

Aeschylus wins by weight, with his verses proving literally heavier on the scales. As criticism it is a parody, and it is also the fullest contemporary account of how a Greek dramatist's work was received.

The saga is among the longest and best regarded, and it departs from the form's usual restraint in one respect: its protagonist's interior life reaches the reader through the poems quoted in the prose.

Everything else is characteristic. The killings are reported without comment, the lawsuits are given in detail, the genealogies are exact, and a man who murders a boy at the age of seven is described in the same register as one who buys a farm.

Egill is the tradition's most celebrated practitioner and the saga is the fullest portrait of what a skald was: a court poet who composed praise verse to order, and who on one occasion saved his own life by delivering a poem to a king who intended to kill him.

The lament for his drowned son is the most affecting verse in Old Norse, and the saga gives it a function in the narrative, presenting it as the thing that stopped him starving himself.

The performance is the tradition's best-documented single achievement and the specific evidence on which the oral-formulaic argument rests.

Mededovic produced some twelve thousand lines over several days, composing in performance rather than reciting, and separately performed a song he had heard once from another singer days earlier, at several times its original length. Neither feat is possible for a memorised text.

Parry recorded the performance in 1935 as the centrepiece of fieldwork designed to test what could be inferred about Homer, and the scale was the point: a poem of comparable length to the Odyssey, produced by a singer who could not read.

The recordings and transcriptions are held at Harvard with the rest of his collection, and they remain the largest body of evidence about oral epic composition gathered anywhere.

Julia Kristeva, a Bulgarian theorist working in Paris, coined the term in the mid-1960s while introducing Bakhtin to French readers, describing any text as a mosaic of quotations, built by absorbing and transforming others.

The formulation deliberately removes the author's reading from the question. Where influence asks what a writer had encountered, intertextuality describes a property of language itself, and the relations it covers include ones no writer arranged and only a reader can construct.

Kristeva encountered Bakhtin's work as a graduate student newly arrived in Paris and presented it in a seminar and in essays that reached a readership his own country had largely denied him.

The transfer changed the emphasis. Bakhtin was describing voices in dialogue within a social world, with speakers and situations attached; the concept as it circulated in French theory became a claim about relations between texts, with the speakers dropped out.

Stanislavski's system supplies the practical technique for playing text whose meaning is not in its words: the actor works from what the character wants in each unit, from the circumstances surrounding the scene, and from the intention beneath the line.

The approach was developed largely on plays that require it, and it makes explicit what a naturalistic script assumes, that dialogue is behaviour rather than statement.

The Moscow Art Theatre's 1898 production rescued a play that had failed badly two years earlier, and the difference was a company trained to play what the text withholds.

Stanislavski's production notes are unusually detailed, filling in pauses, business and off-stage sound, and Chekhov objected to a good deal of it as too heavy. The disagreement between a writer working by omission and a director filling the omissions is the founding argument of naturalistic theatre.

The collaboration made both reputations and neither party was entirely satisfied with it.

Chekhov's plays needed an acting technique that did not yet exist, and Stanislavski's technique needed plays whose meaning sat under the dialogue. They disagreed permanently about register: Chekhov called the plays comedies and complained that the productions were staged as laments, and the theatre's success meant his objection lost.

Radcliffe supplied the mode with the atmospheric method it is now identified with: extended landscape description, sustained uncertainty, a heroine of sensibility in an unfamiliar building, and dread produced by delay.

Her explained supernatural, in which every apparition is eventually given a natural cause, split the genre. Writers who found the explanations a betrayal, Lewis among them, wrote the other kind, and the division between suggested and shown has organised horror ever since.

The essay published after Radcliffe's death distinguishes terror from horror on the grounds of their effect: terror expands the soul and awakens the faculties through uncertainty and obscurity, while horror contracts, freezes and nearly annihilates them by making the object plain.

The distinction remains the most quoted piece of theory the genre has, and the argument between filmmakers who show the creature and those who withhold it is still conducted in her terms.

Northanger Abbey is built on Radcliffe specifically. Its heroine has read The Mysteries of Udolpho, expects an English abbey to behave like a Radcliffe castle, and is corrected.

Austen's treatment is affectionate rather than dismissive, and she borrows the method she is parodying: the suspicions are aroused, sustained and then explained away, which is Radcliffe's own procedure applied to a laundry list and a locked cabinet.

Radcliffe took Walpole's apparatus and supplied what he had not: duration, atmosphere and a reason to be afraid for a specific person.

Otranto delivers its marvels at farcical speed and explains none of them; Udolpho withholds, delays and finally accounts for everything. The genre as it was actually read and imitated for the next century is closer to her practice than to his, though the name and the machinery are his.

Lucas has spoken publicly and repeatedly about Campbell's importance to him, and the two appeared together in a widely broadcast series of conversations that fixed the association for a general audience.

What is disputed is the chronology. Scholars working from the surviving drafts have argued that the pattern was applied to material already in progress rather than used to generate it, and Lucas's own accounts have varied over the decades.

The two are the central figures in the argument for comics as a serious medium and worked at it from opposite ends: Spiegelman by producing the work that could not be dismissed, McCloud by supplying the theory.

Both also made the case in the form itself, Spiegelman by including his own difficulty in drawing his subject and McCloud by writing a work of theory as a comic, which is an argument that the medium can carry abstraction.

Capote claimed to have invented a form, the nonfiction novel, and the claim is overstated in a useful way: reportage using the techniques of fiction predates him, and no earlier example had the commercial reach or the confidence.

What followed was the New Journalism of the 1960s and 1970s, whose practitioners took the scene construction and the interior access while disagreeing sharply about how much reconstruction the claim to truth allows.

Perrault's collection appeared six decades after Basile's and treats several of the same tales, and the transmission is generally accepted even though Perrault never names him.

The Italian collection circulated in French court circles where the fairy tale had become a fashionable form among women writers, and the versions Perrault produced are recognisably the Neapolitan ones with the violence removed, the sexual content excised and a verse moral attached.

The Shahnameh is the model for the Persian epic and for the literary epics of the wider Islamic world, and it demonstrates a use of the form the European tradition has few examples of: an epic composed to preserve a culture's past at the moment that past has been politically defeated.

Its scale is also exceptional. At some fifty thousand couplets by a single named author, it is longer than the Iliad, the Odyssey and the Aeneid together.

Simon created the series and wrote or co-wrote a substantial share of it, working with the former police detective Ed Burns and recruiting crime novelists including George Pelecanos and Richard Price to the writing staff.

The practice of hiring novelists rather than television writers is part of why the show reads as it does, and Simon has said the aim was a visual novel, with each season a chapter and no obligation to resolve anything within an episode.

Simon's first book came from a year spent inside a homicide unit with the notebook open, and the immersion method is the reportorial tradition applied at length.

What he then did with it is unusual: rather than continuing in nonfiction he transferred the material and the method into drama, where invented characters could carry patterns that no single real case demonstrated. The relationship between the two forms in his work is the argument about what fiction can report that journalism cannot.

Simon's work is the standing case for what the form can do at length, and its influence has been on ambition more than on technique.

After it, a season devoted to an institution rather than a plot, a cast that turns over across years, and a refusal to resolve became available options for prestige television. The commercial argument that audiences would not follow it was harder to make afterwards.

Mededovic produced the poem over several days of recorded performance in 1935, composing as he sang rather than reciting a fixed text, and it runs to some twelve thousand lines.

Authorship is the wrong word for what he did and there is no better one. He did not write it, could not have read it back, and would not have produced the same poem twice, which is precisely the condition the Homeric poems are now thought to have been made in.

Mededovic is the guslar tradition's best documented practitioner and its most capable, and the recordings of him are the largest single body of evidence about oral epic composition anywhere.

He worked as a farmer and butcher, could neither read nor write, and had learned his craft by listening in coffeehouses. Everything he demonstrated about scale, elaboration and composition in performance had to be inferred from texts before he was recorded doing it.

Parry sought out singers of exactly this capacity because the Homeric question needed a living example rather than an inference, and Mededovic supplied the strongest one available.

The experiment that mattered most was deliberately designed: Parry had him listen to another singer's song and then, days later, perform it himself, which produced a version several times longer and demonstrated that what had been transmitted was a technique and not a text.

The play is generally attributed to Zeami, most often as a revision of an older piece rather than an original composition, which is the usual situation with the noh repertoire.

Attribution in the form is unreliable for a specific reason: plays were held and reworked within performing families as professional property, and the treatises Zeami wrote for his own successors were unknown outside them until the twentieth century.

The play runs the three-part movement at the scale of a single work: a slow opening in which a medium is summoned and the sick woman's condition established, a development in which the spirit appears and states her grievance, and a rapid close in which she is subdued by an exorcist.

Because the pattern nests, the same shape governs the individual dance within the final section, and a performer working inside the slow opening is expected to observe it there too.

The parable appears in the gospel of Luke among a group of three concerning things lost and found, and it is the longest and least schematic of them.

The first two, a sheep and a coin, are recovered and celebrated with no complication. The third supplies a second son who did not leave, resents the celebration and is still outside when the text stops, which is the departure that makes it literature rather than illustration.

The story is the form's clearest instance because of what it withholds. Nothing is allegorised, no figure is labelled, and the application is never stated.

It also declines to close. A story that ended with the feast would supply a moral about forgiveness; this one adds a brother with a legitimate grievance and leaves the argument in the yard unfinished, which obliges the listener to take a position rather than receive one.

The younger son's arc is the pattern in miniature: a fall into a state he cannot recover from by his own effort, a recognition of it while feeding pigs, and a restoration delivered entirely by someone else.

His prepared speech is interrupted before he can offer to work as a hired man, which is the pattern's characteristic move. What restores him is not the plan he has made but a decision taken about him.

Booker uses the film as an instance of the pattern, with a community under threat from a power that destroys planets and a protagonist who confronts it at its own centre.

The fit is neat and slightly too neat, since the same film is the standing example of the hero's journey, of the three-act paradigm and of the MacGuffin. A work that illustrates every scheme equally well is evidence about the schemes as much as about the work.

Propp's Morphology could not have been written without the collection, and the relationship between them is the clearest case in this graph of an analysis being shaped by the corpus available to it.

Afanasyev's practice of printing variants rather than merging them is what let Propp see that the characters change while the sequence of actions does not. A more heavily edited collection would have concealed the regularity he found.

Animal Farm maps the Russian revolution onto a farmyard with a completeness that allows most figures to be identified, and Orwell described it as the first book in which he tried to fuse political and artistic purpose.

The method sits awkwardly beside his stated dislike of writing that conceals its argument, and the book has been read against his intentions often enough that he complained about it, including by readers who took the pigs to indict revolution as such.

Orwell's satirical method is closer to Swift's than to Horace's: no geniality, no self-inclusion, and a straight face maintained throughout.

His essays argue the case directly, holding that stale and evasive language is not a stylistic failing but a political instrument, since a phrase that has stopped meaning anything can be used to describe an atrocity without anyone picturing it. The fiction acts on the argument the essays make.

The novel is the historical case most often produced when the question is whether fiction changes what a public believes, and the evidence is unusually strong: sales without precedent, hundreds of stage adaptations, and a measurable shift in northern opinion before the war.

It is also the case that shows the mechanism working independently of accuracy, since the same book fixed a set of racial types that outlasted the argument it was written to make.

Ford made the genre's grammar: the small figure against enormous landscape, the doorway framing the wilderness from inside a home, the cavalry column, and the community dance interrupted by news.

He also spent his career complicating what he had established, giving the frontier's cost more weight in each decade, and his late films reopen the treatment of the people the settlement displaced. The genre's self-criticism begins inside his own work.

Kurosawa named Ford as a direct model and the debt is visible in his composition, his use of weather and movement, and his treatment of a group of professionals defending a community they cannot belong to.

The exchange then reversed, since Seven Samurai was remade as a Western and A Fistful of Dollars was taken from Yojimbo without permission, which makes the two traditions a circuit rather than a line of influence.

Hammerstein established the working assumption the form has operated on since: that a musical is a play whose songs do the dramatic work, and that a number which stops the story to entertain is a fault.

He also insisted on subjects the commercial theatre avoided, including racial prejudice in Show Boat and South Pacific, and his position that a song can carry an argument as well as a feeling is the reason the form was available for that material at all.

Flaherty established the form's characteristic method of long immersion with a community, and its characteristic problem in the same films.

He returned repeatedly to the same procedure in Samoa and on the Aran Islands: live with people for a year or more, decide what is essential about their way of life, and stage it. Grierson's phrase about the creative treatment of actuality was coined in a review of Flaherty and describes his practice exactly.

Malory is the channel through which Arthurian material reached English-language fantasy, and the debt is largely unacknowledged because it arrives through so many intermediaries.

The sword in the stone, the round table, the enchanter, the quest for an object that tests the seeker's worth and the doomed fellowship are all in his compilation in the form later writers use, and Tennyson, Twain, White and Steinbeck all worked directly from him.

The book is itself an adaptation, assembled from French prose cycles and English poems, and it demonstrates how completely a good compilation can displace its sources.

Almost no English reader encounters the French romances Malory worked from, and the Arthurian material now circulates in a shape he gave it in the 1460s. Caxton compounded the effect by dividing the text into books and chapters and supplying the title.

Sun Wukong is among the most durable trickster figures in world narrative: a monkey who acquires immortality by fraud, defeats a celestial army, is imprisoned under a mountain for five centuries and is then attached to a pilgrimage as a penance.

He holds the position without its usual ambiguity of allegiance, since he is bound to the quest by a headband that tightens when he misbehaves, and the tension between his nature and that constraint is most of the novel's comedy.

Lazarillo had been in circulation for half a century when Cervantes was writing, and Don Quixote carries its inheritance visibly: the road, the episodic structure, the social panorama seen from below and the pairing of a master with a servant who eats better than he does.

What Cervantes declines to take is the first-person rogue. His protagonist is a gentleman with an idea rather than a survivor working upward, which changes the meaning of every encounter on the road.

The hymn names her within the text, which is the basis of the attribution and the reason she is described as the first named author.

The claim needs qualification. The surviving copies are scribal exercises made some five centuries after her lifetime, no contemporary manuscript exists, and some scholars hold that the ascription is traditional rather than evidence of composition. What is not disputed is that a named individual is being credited, which is itself the innovation.

The poem is the earliest surviving text in which a speaker claims a specific identity, a personal history and an occasion, rather than voicing a community or a rite.

That move is the precondition for most of what this graph contains. Once a text can say who made it and why, authorship, attribution, reputation and eventually the whole apparatus of literary history become possible, and the shift is visible here four thousand years before it is theorised.

Carter wrote the collection after translating Perrault, and she was direct about the relationship between the two projects.

She described her method as extracting the latent content of the traditional stories and objected to being read as writing versions for adults, which she considered a misunderstanding of what the tales had always contained. Several of the pieces were adapted for radio, and one became a film she co-wrote before her death at fifty-one.

The title story narrates the tale from the bride's position and changes the rescue.

In Perrault the brothers arrive; here the mother does, having sensed something wrong, and shoots the husband through the head at the edge of the sea. Carter also gives the girl a curiosity that is sexual as well as investigative, which removes the moral the verse epilogue had attached to the tale for three centuries.

Three of the collection's stories work the beast marriage, and none resolves it the same way.

In one the girl is won at cards and the beast is a tiger who does not become a man; instead she sheds her skin and becomes an animal herself. The pattern's usual settlement, in which acceptance restores a human shape, is refused in favour of a transformation running the other direction.

Carter's collection is the point after which rewriting the tales became a recognised literary project rather than a children's exercise, and a great deal of subsequent fiction works in the space she opened.

She also worked on the material as an editor, assembling two volumes of tales from around the world with a preference for the bawdy, the practical and the cruel, which is a corrective to collections shaped by the nursery.

Carter takes the mode's apparatus seriously and inverts its politics. The castle, the aristocratic predator, the isolated bride and the locked room are all present, and the position of the person moving through them is not.

Her prose is deliberately ornate where the Gothic is usually functional, which is part of the argument: the excess is the pleasure the form has always offered and has generally been embarrassed about.

Zipes reads the fairy tale as a social document whose editors carried their values into it, and Carter's collection is that argument conducted as fiction.

Both treat the printed versions as interventions rather than records, both are interested in what was removed, and both hold that the tales' subversive potential is what makes them worth returning to. Zipes has written on her work directly and has included her in his accounts of the tradition's modern life.

The historian Marina Warner recovers the tellers the printed collections obscured: the salon writers of seventeenth-century France, many of them women writing under constraint, and the nurses, servants and grandmothers whose repertoires the male editors gathered and attributed to the folk.

Her larger argument concerns the figure of the old woman as narrator, invoked on title pages as Mother Goose and simultaneously derided as a gossip, which she traces through the tales' own recurring hostility to ageing women.

Warner's study of the Nights follows the collection's European life rather than its Arabic origins: what Galland added, how the tales were read as evidence about the East, and how they supplied the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries with a vocabulary of enchantment.

Her interest is in the traffic itself, in a body of stories that has no stable original and has been remade at every point of transmission, which makes it the best available case study of how a tradition actually moves.

The two are the principal historians of the fairy tale in English and approach it from complementary directions.

Zipes works from the social and economic conditions of the tales' production and is concerned with who controlled them; Warner works from iconography, gender and the figure of the teller, and is more interested in what the stories did for the people telling them. Neither treats the collections as records of an oral past.

Hurston collected the material on two field trips in the late 1920s, funded by a white patron whose contract required her to submit what she gathered for approval, an arrangement she found constraining and has been criticised for accepting.

She returned to the Florida town she grew up in to do the work, which gave her access no outside collector would have had, and the book's frame makes that position visible rather than concealing it behind a scientific voice.

The collection is a substantial body of African American oral narrative recorded in performance conditions and presented with them intact.

What distinguishes it from the standard collections is the frame: tales arrive in the middle of arguments, competitions and courtships, told by named people for reasons the reader can see, so the book documents the practice of telling rather than only its products.

Hurston's position as a trained anthropologist collecting inside her own community produced an account of oral performance that outside fieldworkers were not placed to give.

She recorded the competition between tellers, the interruptions, the way an audience shapes a telling and the difference between what is performed for the group and what is offered to a visitor, and she was explicit that a collector who is not trusted receives a different repertoire.

The material Hurston collected is the material her fiction is built from, and she made no separation between the two activities.

Her best-known novel gives its narration to a woman telling her life to a friend on a porch, which is the situation her folklore book documents, and its prose carries the rhythms, proverbs and figures of the tellers she recorded. The anthropology and the fiction are the same project by different means.

Butler has said the book began from an argument with a fellow student who dismissed the older generation for not resisting harder, and that she wanted to put a modern person on a plantation to see how long the attitude survived contact.

She researched the period closely and reported finding the published slave narratives sanitised, since their authors were writing for a nineteenth-century readership and could not describe what had been done to them.

The novel solves the genre's central problem by refusing its usual solution. Historical fiction generally supplies a protagonist of the period whose assumptions the reader must accommodate; Butler supplies a protagonist from the reader's own time and removes the distance entirely.

What the device produces is a measurement rather than a fantasy, since the interest is in how quickly a modern woman's reflexes are replaced by the ones survival requires.

Butler declined the label for this book, calling it a grim fantasy on the grounds that it contains no science and offers no mechanism for the time travel it depends on.

The distinction matters to the genre's self-definition. If cognitive extrapolation is the criterion, a novel that simply asserts its premise and follows the consequences falls outside it, and yet the consequences are followed with exactly the rigour the genre asks for.

Butler wrote hierarchy, coercion and unequal bargains into a genre that had generally preferred competent protagonists solving problems, and her premises rarely allow a clean refusal.

Her influence is now substantial enough that the tradition she is credited with opening has a name and an institutional presence, and her working conditions, decades of manual jobs and predawn writing, are part of what the record of that influence has to include.

Mantel spent years on the research and was explicit about the method it produced: where the record says something, the novel follows it, and where the record is silent the fiction works.

She wrote about the discipline directly in lectures, arguing that a historical novelist's obligation is not to invent freely around the facts but to inhabit the gaps between them, and that the temptation to improve on the evidence is the form's characteristic failure.

The novel is the form's most influential recent example and its technical innovation is a tense.

Writing in the present, in a close third person that frequently declines to name its subject, removes the retrospective knowledge that historical fiction usually supplies and that every reader brings to the Tudor court. The result is a protagonist who does not know he is in history, which is the condition everyone is actually in.

The book's celebrated difficulty is a pronoun. Cromwell is so consistently the centre that he is often simply he, including in sentences where another man has just been named, and readers regularly lose the thread on a first encounter.

Mantel defended the choice as the point rather than an obstacle: the reader is placed inside a consciousness that does not announce itself, and the discomfort of that position is the effect the technique exists to produce.

Mantel's practice is the sharpest available test of Lukacs's account, because it succeeds by doing the opposite of what he prescribed.

Lukacs held that the historical novel requires a protagonist of middling rank and divided loyalties, so that the contending forces can be shown without the book taking a side. Mantel puts the reader inside one of the period's most consequential actors and never leaves, and the result is a novel about historical process seen entirely from within the machinery.

Kingston assembled the book from family history, Cantonese legend, invention and her own childhood, and declined to mark which was which.

The publisher classified it as nonfiction, a decision she did not make and has discussed since, and a substantial part of the argument about the book proceeds from that shelving. Read as memoir it is unreliable; read as what she calls talk-story it is doing exactly what the form does.

The book has the memoir's first person, childhood and family, and refuses the form's central undertaking, which is that the reader can tell what is being claimed as fact.

One of its five sections is a legend narrated in the first person as though it happened to the author. Another opens with an instruction never to repeat the story that follows, which the existence of the book has already broken. The result is a memoir about the impossibility of the genre's premise.

The central section retells the legend of the woman who takes her father's place in the army, and puts the narrator inside it in the first person.

Kingston's version departs substantially from the ballad it derives from, adding a period of training in the mountains and carving the family's grievances into the heroine's back. Critics working from the Chinese sources have objected to the alterations, and she has answered that the material arrived to her as talk-story and was never fixed.

The Dutch narratologist Mieke Bal separates focalisation from narration more sharply than Genette by giving it a layer of its own, so a text has a narrator who speaks, a focaliser who perceives, and events that occur, each analysable independently.

The refinement lets her track focalisation that shifts within a sentence and identify embedded focalisation, where one character's perception is presented through another's, which the two-part model handles awkwardly.

Bal's system is built on Genette's and departs from it on the point of layers.

Genette works with story and discourse and locates focalisation within the narration; Bal inserts a third level between them, which she argues is necessary because the arrangement and perception of events is a separable operation from the telling. The disagreement is technical and consequential, and most subsequent narratology follows one or the other.

Bal's later work takes the analytic apparatus out of literature entirely and applies it to painting, sculpture, exhibition design and video, on the argument that narrative is a mode of organisation rather than a property of texts.

The move tests the vocabulary. Asking who focalises a painting, or what the fabula of an installation is, either extends the terms usefully or exposes them as literary in origin, and the debate about which has continued since.

Liu Xie, the earliest systematic literary theorist writing in Chinese, completed the treatise around 501 while working in a Buddhist monastery, where he had gone after being orphaned and unable to marry, and where he catalogued the collection of scriptures.

The bibliographic training shows in the organisation. The book proceeds from first principles through a systematic survey of genres to questions of composition and finally to the critic's own faults, which is a structure no European work of the period attempts.

The two are the founding systematic works of their traditions and are unalike in almost every respect.

Aristotle analyses one genre in detail and reasons from the structure of a well-made plot; Liu Xie surveys thirty-odd genres, derives all of them from the classics, and is at least as interested in ornament, temperament and the relation of writing to the natural order. The Poetics asks how a work is built; the Chinese treatise asks what writing is for.

Liu Xie's account places writing within a cosmological order, treating pattern in language as continuous with pattern in nature, and derives the genres from the classics as branches from a trunk.

His practical chapters are recognisable to any modern editor: how to plan before writing, how to cut, why a piece loses force when its ornament exceeds its substance, and why writers of every generation believe their own age has declined.

Jin Shengtan, the seventeenth-century critic who treated vernacular fiction as seriously as the classics, produced the edition that displaced all others for two centuries, cutting the novel to seventy chapters and supplying an ending in which the outlaws' triumph is revealed as a dream.

His running commentary is the achievement. He annotates how a scene has been prepared several chapters earlier, how a character is established by a single refusal, and how the reader has been manoeuvred into an expectation, which is close narrative analysis three centuries before the term existed.

Jin Shengtan argued that vernacular fiction deserved the attention given to the classics, and demonstrated it by supplying that attention.

His commentaries treat structure, characterisation, pacing and the management of the reader as technical matters open to analysis, and they place a novel and a play alongside the canonical texts in a list of works he considered works of genius. The position was heterodox and his editions were nonetheless enormously popular.

The book is among the earliest full-length Chinese vernacular novels and shows the form emerging from performance material rather than from literary prose.

Its sequential construction, in which each outlaw's arrival is given a self-contained account of the injustice that produced him, is a storyteller's architecture: any section can be delivered alone, and the whole accumulates by addition rather than by developing a single action.

The novel was assembled from cycles that had circulated for centuries in marketplaces and theatres before any text fixed them, and the prose retains the marks of that origin.

Chapters end at moments of suspense with a formula inviting the audience to hear the outcome next time, and set-piece descriptions recur in fixed wording, both of which are performance habits carried into print rather than literary devices.

Cao Xueqin, born into a family ruined by imperial displeasure, worked on the novel through the last decade of his life in poverty outside Beijing, revising repeatedly, and it circulated in hand-copied manuscripts among a small circle before his death.

The printed edition of 1791 supplied a conclusion in forty further chapters, generally attributed to the editor Gao E working from notes or from his own invention. Whether that ending is what Cao intended is the central question of an entire field of Chinese scholarship.

The book is the summit of the Chinese vernacular novel and works almost entirely without event.

Several hundred characters occupy a single household, and the narrative advances through poetry contests, illnesses, quarrels over servants and the gradual disappearance of money, with the family's ruin arriving as an accumulation rather than a catastrophe. Its psychological attention to a large cast of young women has no European parallel at its date.

The novel is enclosed in a mythological frame: a stone left over when the goddess repaired the sky asks to be taken into the world, is inscribed with the story that follows, and is found later by a passing Daoist who copies it out.

The device gives the whole a retrospective and elegiac character before a word of the household narrative begins, since the reader is told at the outset that what follows has already ended and been recorded.

The middle commentary by Ibn Rushd, the twelfth-century Andalusian philosopher known in Latin Europe as Averroes, is the most instructive misreading in the history of criticism, and the misreading is structural rather than careless.

Working from an Arabic translation of a Syriac version, in a culture with no theatre, he had no way to picture what tragedy and comedy were. He rendered them as the poetry of praise and the poetry of blame, and produced a coherent and intelligent account of an art form he could not have seen.

The commentary is the standing demonstration of what a chain of translation can do to a text. Aristotle's Greek reached Ibn Rushd through Syriac and then Arabic, and the words for tragedy and comedy arrived without the practice that gave them meaning.

What resulted was not an error to be corrected but a coherent alternative poetics, and it circulated in Latin Europe alongside the Poetics itself. A concept can survive translation grammatically and still lose the thing it names.

Borges wrote a story about the commentary in which the philosopher works through an evening trying to establish what the words tragedy and comedy can mean, while children in the courtyard below play at being a muezzin and a congregation.

The reader sees the answer being acted out under the window and the philosopher does not. Borges closes by admitting that his own attempt to imagine Ibn Rushd is the same failure at one further remove.

Ibn al-Muqaffa', a Persian convert to Islam working as an administrator in eighth-century Iraq, made the Arabic version from a Middle Persian translation of the Sanskrit, and what he produced is a rewriting rather than a rendering.

He added a preface of his own about how the book should be read, and the prose he established became a model for Arabic literary style. He was executed in his thirties, and later accounts of his death are lurid enough that they are generally treated with caution.

The Arabic version stands at the centre of the most consequential chain of transmission in narrative history: Sanskrit into Middle Persian, into Arabic, and from Arabic into Hebrew, Latin, Castilian, Greek and most European vernaculars.

Every later European encounter with this material runs through this book, and the animal fables that reached medieval readers as ancient wisdom arrived by way of a Persian convert working in eighth-century Iraq.

The book is the clearest available demonstration that an adaptation can outlive and outrank its source in the traditions it reaches.

For a thousand years European readers knew this material only through descendants of the Arabic text, and the Sanskrit original was not available to them at all. What travelled was not a story but a chain of rewritings, each made for a different court, a different faith and a different purpose.

The Kashmiri poet Somadeva compiled the collection in the eleventh century, reportedly to divert a queen of the Kashmiri court during a violent period of dynastic conflict, which is a frame situation the collection itself would recognise.

He states that he has abridged an earlier and larger work, the Brihatkatha, now lost, and that he has preserved its substance rather than adding to it. His version is the fullest surviving descendant of that source.

The collection is the deepest nesting structure in world literature. Tales contain tellers who tell tales containing further tellers, and a reader can be several levels down before the sequence unwinds back through each frame in order.

The architecture is not decorative. Stories inside are offered as arguments, warnings or delays within the situations that contain them, so each level has a reason to be telling the one below it.

Several tales in the Nights have close analogues in the Sanskrit collections, and the transmission route from India through Persia into Arabic is the same one Kalila wa-Dimna travelled.

What the two share more fundamentally is the principle that a frame can be an engine: telling to postpone, to instruct or to survive. Whether specific stories moved or the structure was arrived at independently is disputed, and the collections are contemporaneous enough that both are possible.

The Heike was a performance repertoire before it was a book. Blind reciters delivered it in instalments over many evenings, chanting to their own accompaniment on the lute, and organised into a guild that controlled training and performance rights.

The surviving text is a written record of that practice rather than a work the performers were reading from, which is why its episodes are shaped to end where an evening should end.

The tradition is among the best documented cases of a professional oral narrative practice with a formal institutional structure: licensed training, ranked grades and a monopoly on the repertoire.

It is also a case where blindness and the profession were bound together, since the guild provided one of the few recognised livelihoods available to blind men in medieval Japan, which shaped who carried the material and how it was passed on.

The Heike is Japan's principal martial epic and differs from the European examples in its governing attitude.

It opens by stating that the proud do not endure and that the mighty fall like dust before the wind, and then narrates a specific dynastic collapse as the demonstration. Sympathy runs to the defeated clan throughout, and the individual deaths that receive the most attention are the ones that accomplish nothing.

The noh repertoire returns to the Heike more than to any other source, and the form's characteristic structure is suited to it exactly.

A warrior killed in the war appears as a ghost at the place of his death, recounts the battle to a travelling priest and asks for prayers, so the epic's dead are given a second telling in which they narrate their own defeat. Atsumori and Tadanori are among the most performed plays in the form.

Coyote occupies the trickster position across a great many Indigenous North American traditions, and the figure is not one character but many, differing substantially between nations that are unrelated in language and culture.

Where he appears the doubleness is unusually pronounced. The same figure who arranges the seasons, brings fire or establishes the fact of death is defeated in the next story by his own appetite and left ridiculous, and neither role is treated as the real one.

Coyote narratives frequently account for how the present order was established, and the accounts characteristically arrive by accident or by botched improvisation rather than by design.

A world is arranged carelessly, a decision about death is made in irritation and cannot be revoked, a container is opened when it should not have been. The pattern gives a cosmology in which the arrangement of things is neither perfect nor malicious but the residue of somebody's bad afternoon.

The two are the most widely distributed trickster figures in their respective continents and share the position's defining instability: creator and fool, benefactor and thief, admired and never trusted.

They differ in what the trickery is for. Anansi's cycle is preoccupied with acquiring stories, food and status by outwitting the powerful; the Coyote narratives are more often concerned with how the world came to have the shape it has, including its unsatisfactory features.

Both carry a work into conditions it was not made for, and both generate the same argument about fidelity.

The difference is what is held constant. An adaptation keeps the story and changes the medium; a translation keeps the medium and changes the language. Neither can hold everything, and the interesting cases in both are the ones where the loss is acknowledged in the work rather than concealed by it.

Most people meet most stories in a language other than the one they were made in, which makes translation a component of the practice rather than a service attached to it.

The graph's own contents demonstrate the dependence: the Indian fables reached Europe through Persian and Arabic, Aristotle reached the Latin west through Syriac and Arabic, and the Homeric poems, the sagas, the Nights and the Chinese novels are all read by most of their readers as somebody's decisions about English.

The book is the most consequential chain of translation in narrative history and shows what accumulates along one.

Sanskrit to Middle Persian to Arabic to Hebrew, Latin, Castilian and onward, with each stage rewriting rather than rendering: material added, framing changed, the religious and political purposes of a new court served. What arrived in medieval Europe as ancient Indian wisdom had been remade at least four times before it got there.

The Grimms were translators as well as collectors, and the fact is generally left out of the collection's framing.

Several of their tales came from informants of Huguenot descent whose repertoire derived from Perrault's printed French, so material presented as German popular tradition had crossed a language boundary twice before it reached the page. The brothers noticed the problem and moved some texts further from their French versions in later editions.

Cao's book stands at the head of a field of Chinese scholarship devoted to a single work, and its influence inside the tradition is closer to that of Shakespeare in English than to that of any one novelist.

What it demonstrated was that a vernacular novel could sustain psychological attention across hundreds of characters without incident, which is a claim about the form that Chinese fiction had not previously made and that European fiction arrived at separately a century later.

The hymns predate the earliest biblical material by well over a thousand years and share the Mesopotamian world it emerged from.

The relationship is contextual rather than one of descent. What the Sumerian and Akkadian material establishes is a body of temple literature with named priestly composers, direct address to a deity and a first-person voice in distress, all of which the later psalms operate within.

Ibn al-Muqaffa' is the founding figure of Arabic literary prose, and he arrived at it through translation rather than composition.

Working from Middle Persian into a language whose prose tradition was still forming, he had to invent much of the register he needed, and the style he settled on became the model others worked in. The case is a useful corrective to the assumption that translation is a secondary activity.

Kingston's term talk-story comes from the Cantonese practice her mother worked in, and she uses it for a mode with no boundary between family history, warning, legend and invention.

Her books reproduce its conditions rather than describing them: a story is told for a reason, adjusted to the listener, contradicted later by another version, and never fixed. What arrives on the page is a written record of a practice that resists being written down.

Somadeva's collection and the Nights share tales, share the principle of a frame that generates its contents, and sit on the same transmission route from India through Persia into Arabic.

Whether specific stories travelled or the architecture was reached independently is disputed. The collections are close enough in date that either is possible, and the Sanskrit material is demonstrably older in several individual cases.

Marie names herself in the general prologue of the Lais, states that she has turned Breton lays into rhyme so they will not be lost, and dedicates the collection to a king generally taken to be Henry II.

The self-naming is the reason she exists to us at all. Almost every other vernacular narrative poet of the period is anonymous, and her explicit claim that she wrote them so she would be remembered is unusual enough to be worth reading as a statement about authorship rather than a formula.

The lais are contemporary with Chrétien's romances and work the same courtly material at a fraction of the length, which changes what the form can do.

There is no room for the sequence of adventures that constitutes a romance quest, so what survives the compression is the situation: a wife shut in a tower, a knight who is a werewolf, lovers who cannot survive their own success. The supernatural is admitted without apology and the endings are frequently unresolved.

Marie's collection of a hundred-odd fables is the earliest in French and among the largest medieval descendants of the Aesopic tradition.

She names her source as an English version made by King Alfred, which cannot be verified and may be a claim to authority rather than a record. Her morals are unusually pointed about power, repeatedly observing that the strong will justify whatever they were going to do to the weak in any case.

The two are the major named vernacular narrative poets of the later twelfth century and worked the same Breton and Arthurian material for overlapping courtly audiences.

They divide the territory by scale and by interest. Chrétien builds long romances organised around a knight's public reputation and its repair; Marie writes short poems organised around a private situation, and is markedly less confident that the social order can accommodate what her characters want.

Madame d'Aulnoy, a French salon writer, published the collection in 1697, the same year as Perrault, and the title she chose gave the genre its name in French and eventually in English.

She wrote considerably more tales than he did, at greater length, and was the more celebrated of the two at the time. The reversal of their reputations happened later and tracks the genre's reclassification as children's material, which suited his short moralised versions and not her long courtly ones.

The genre is named after her book, and the salon culture she belonged to is where the literary fairy tale was made.

That culture was substantially female: a group of women writing tales for adult audiences, using the marvellous to discuss marriages they could not choose and constraints they could not name directly. The collections that followed, and the histories written from them, largely replaced this with an image of anonymous peasant tradition.

Warner's history is substantially a recovery of the salon writers, and d'Aulnoy is its central case: a woman who named the genre, wrote most of its early canon and was displaced from its history within a century.

The displacement is Warner's real subject. She traces how a form invented by educated women for adult listeners came to be presented as the artless production of nurses and grandmothers, and how the figure of the old woman teller was simultaneously invoked and ridiculed.

The two published in the same year, drew on the same salon fashion and were read together, and their reputations have since diverged completely.

Perrault's versions are short, plain and closed with a verse moral, which made them portable into nurseries and schoolbooks. D'Aulnoy's are long, ornate and ironic about their own conventions, which did not. What survived was the format the nineteenth century could use rather than the one contemporaries preferred.

Behn published the work in 1688, the year before her death, and claims in it to have been present in Surinam and to have known the man whose death she narrates.

The claim cannot be independently verified and has been argued over for three centuries, with positions ranging from documented residence to complete invention. The narrative's authority rests entirely on it, which makes the book an early and unresolved case of a text whose value depends on a testimonial claim it cannot support.

Behn is among the small number of English prose fiction writers working before the form consolidated, and her practice anticipates several of its later features: a narrator with a stated position, a claim to reportage, and a plot turning on money, contract and betrayal.

Her commercial position matters as much as the writing. She earned a living by it, in the theatre as well as in print, at a point when that was not available to women, and later women novelists worked in a space she had established.

The book raises the form's founding problem four centuries before the form was named: a story about real events whose authority depends on the narrator's claim to have been there, and which cannot be checked.

Behn's narrator is also compromised in a way modern reportage rarely admits. She is sympathetic to the enslaved prince, socially embedded in the colony that kills him, and absent at the critical moment, and the text does not resolve what her position amounts to.

The novel was published in 1847 under the name Ellis Bell, and reviewers who assumed a male author found it brutal, while those who suspected a woman found it improper.

Her sister's preface to the posthumous edition apologises for the book's harshness and explains it as the product of a solitary temperament in a rough district, which has shaped the novel's reception ever since. Almost nothing about Emily's working life survives to set against it.

The story reaches the reader through two interested parties. A visiting tenant records what a housekeeper tells him, and she was a participant with her own stake in how events are understood, having withheld letters, concealed illnesses and taken sides throughout.

Nothing in the book stands outside them. Every judgement about the characters is somebody's judgement, and the reader is given no vantage point from which to correct it.

The novel takes the Gothic apparatus of inheritance, confinement, revenge and a returning past and relocates it from a castle to a working farmhouse in Yorkshire.

What it declines to supply is the mode's usual moral positioning. There is no innocent to be rescued and no villain who is not also a victim, and the ghost at the window may be a dream. The horror is a family destroying itself across two generations with complete plausibility.

Published in 1847 under the name Currer Bell, the novel succeeded immediately and its authorship was speculated about for two years before Charlotte acknowledged it.

She had told her sisters she would write a heroine as plain and small as herself, on the argument that a woman had to be beautiful to interest a reader and that the assumption was false. The stated intention is family recollection recorded later, and the book bears it out.

The novel follows its protagonist from a hostile childhood through a charity school and a governess's post to an independence achieved on her own terms, which is the form's standard shape.

What differs is the endpoint. The German model ends in accommodation with society; Jane refuses two offers of a settled place, one bigamous and one loveless, and returns only when the terms have changed. The formation produces a woman less willing to be absorbed than at the start.

The novel's power is in its address. A poor, plain, dependent woman narrates in the first person, argues with the reader, and asserts an equality her circumstances entirely deny, and the most quoted sentence in the book reports her marriage directly to the reader rather than describing it.

Contemporary reviewers found the tone presumptuous, which is a reasonable index of how unusual the position was.

The novel imports the mode's machinery into a realist frame: a great house with a locked upper storey, laughter in the corridor at night, a fire, and a secret that makes a marriage impossible.

The woman in the attic has generated more argument than any other element, since the book requires her to be an obstacle and gives her no account of herself. A later novel written from her position is among the best-known responses one work of fiction has made to another.

Du Maurier wrote the novel in Egypt while accompanying her husband on a posting, and described it later as a study in jealousy rather than the romance it was marketed as.

She was accused of plagiarising a Brazilian novel with a similar situation and successfully defended the case. The book has never been out of print, and its commercial success is part of why she was dismissed as a popular writer for most of her life.

The situation is Brontë's, restaged: a young woman without money or standing marries a wealthy older man with a house and a first wife who will not stay dead in the required sense.

Du Maurier reverses the moral arrangement. Here the first wife is not confined but admired, the second is not the moral centre, and the revelation that reverses the reader's sympathies makes the husband guilty of something Rochester was not. The unnamed narrator is her own addition.

The novel is a Bluebeard in which the forbidden room is a whole wing, kept by a housekeeper rather than a key, and the previous wife is a presence rather than a corpse.

The tale's usual moral is also inverted. The narrator's curiosity is not punished, and what she discovers does not endanger her; it implicates her, since the truth about the first marriage binds her to her husband rather than freeing her from him.

Hitchcock filmed the novel in 1940, his first American production, and was required by the censors to change the central fact: the first wife's death could not be a killing that goes unpunished, so it became an accident.

The alteration removes the book's mechanism, since the plot turns on the narrator's relief at learning her husband is a murderer. The film is nonetheless faithful in atmosphere and keeps the narrator unnamed throughout.

Jackson wrote the story in a morning and sold it to the New Yorker in 1948, and the magazine received several hundred letters in response, more than for any fiction it had printed.

Most were hostile or bewildered, and a substantial number asked where the ceremony was held and whether it could be watched. Her own account of the reaction, written later, is drier than the letters and treats the assumption of literal truth as the more interesting result.

The story produces its effect entirely by register. The prose is flat and pastoral, the villagers discuss tractors and taxes, the children gather stones early on and nothing marks the detail, and no interior access is offered to anyone.

Withholding comment is the whole technique. The horror is not a revelation about the supernatural but the recognition that everyone present regards what happens as normal, which the narration also does.

Jackson moved the mode into the American domestic interior and left its central question open on principle.

Her haunted house novel is the standing example: a woman with no place of her own arrives at a house that may be malevolent or may be finding the fault line in a personality already breaking, and the narration is placed close enough to her that no reader can adjudicate. The technique is now a genre standard.

O'Connor's craft position is that fiction is an incarnational art that operates through the senses, and that a writer's business is the concrete particular rather than the idea it might illustrate.

Her working advice follows: that a story cannot be summarised without loss, that a writer who knows what a story means before writing it will produce an illustration, and that the reader must be shown a world at the level of dust, weather and the exact make of a hat.

O'Connor's stories are built to a shape she defended explicitly: an ordinary and self-satisfied person meets a moment of violence or grace that the story has been preparing, and is left changed or dead.

She justified the violence on rhetorical grounds, arguing that a writer addressing a hostile or deaf audience must shout and draw large startling figures. The argument is unusual for treating the reader's resistance as the technical problem to be solved.

O'Connor held that a story's ending should be both entirely unexpected and entirely inevitable, and that the moment of grace must be something the reader could not have predicted and cannot afterwards deny was prepared.

The formulation is close to Aristotle's requirement that a reversal arise by probability or necessity, arrived at independently and from a theological rather than a structural premise.

Atwood began the novel in West Berlin in 1984 and applied a rule throughout: nothing would be included that had not already been done by some government somewhere.

She has kept the file of clippings and produced it when the book has been called far-fetched. The rule is a claim about the genre as much as about the book, since a dystopia assembled from precedent is making an argument about the present rather than a prediction about the future.

The novel supplies the genre's standard elements, a totalising state, a controlled language and a protagonist who remembers a previous life, and adds a device most of its imitators leave out.

The closing section is a transcript of a conference two centuries later at which a male academic discusses the narrative as a document, makes a joke at the narrator's expense and declines to condemn the regime. The warning is thereby aimed at the reader's own interpretive habits as well as at the state.

The historical notes reframe the entire novel retrospectively as a transcription of tapes found in a footlocker, assembled in an order the editors chose and given a title they invented as a joke.

That undermines the account the reader has just accepted as immediate, and it does so at the point where it can no longer be recovered from. The narrator's voice turns out to have been reconstructed by people who find her chiefly interesting as evidence.

The two corresponded and reviewed each other, and disagreed publicly about genre labels.

Atwood reserved science fiction for stories with technology that cannot yet exist and preferred speculative fiction for her own work; Le Guin objected that the distinction was a way of protecting literary standing and that her own field was being used as the disreputable term. Both positions are on the record and neither conceded.

Lady Gregory, the Irish folklorist and co-founder of the Abbey Theatre, collected over many years in cottages, workhouses and by roadsides in Galway and Clare, recording belief alongside narrative and returning to the same tellers repeatedly.

Her practice is closer to modern fieldwork than to the antiquarian collecting of her period: she recorded what people held to be true about the fairies as well as the stories, noted who said what, and treated her informants as authorities rather than as sources of raw material.

Gregory's prose versions of the Ulster and Fenian cycles put the Irish heroic material into English for a readership that could not read the originals, in a register built from Irish syntax that became known by the name of the district she gathered it in.

The versions are compilations from several manuscripts rather than translations of one, and they are the form in which most English-language readers have met Cuchulainn and Finn ever since.

Gregory co-founded the theatre that became the Abbey, managed it for decades, and wrote a substantial number of the plays it performed, mostly one-act comedies in the speech she had spent years collecting.

The folklore and the theatre are a single project. She was assembling a repertoire for a national drama out of material she had gathered from people who had never been to a theatre, and the register she developed for the page was written to be spoken.

Adichie delivered the talk in 2009 and it has become among the most watched recordings of its kind, used in school and university curricula worldwide.

She builds the argument from her own errors as well as others', including her assumptions about a poor family who worked for her household and her acceptance of a single narrative about Mexico, which prevents the piece from resolving into a complaint by the represented against the representers.

The talk's proposition is that the problem with a single story is not falsity but monopoly: an account may be accurate and still do damage by being the only one in circulation.

It connects that to power directly, arguing that who tells a story, how often it is told and who controls the means of telling it determine what a people are taken to be, including by themselves. It is the clearest short statement of the position that narrative is a political instrument rather than a neutral one.

Both concern the damage a story does by being persuasive, and they locate the fault in different places.

Taleb's objection is epistemic: a narrative manufactures causes that the record does not contain. Adichie's is political: a narrative that is not false can still function as a lie by crowding out every other account. The two together make the case that a story's power and its reliability are unrelated properties.

Sayers's 1928 introduction to an anthology of detection is among the first substantial histories and theories of the form, tracing concealment and detection through ancient and biblical material to the modern puzzle and setting out what fair play requires.

She also argued that the genre had a structural ceiling: a form built on a puzzle cannot admit full characterisation without breaking the puzzle, and would exhaust itself unless it found a way to. Her own later novels are attempts on that problem.

Sayers defended Christie's device against the charge that it broke the genre's contract, on the ground that the narration states no falsehood and that a reader who assumed a narrator must be innocent had made an assumption the text never underwrote.

The defence is the clearest articulation of what fair play actually requires: that the evidence be present, not that the reader's conventional expectations be honoured.

Jane Ellen Harrison, a classicist and the leading figure of the Cambridge ritualists, reverses the assumed order between story and ceremony. Where myth had been read as a primitive attempt to explain the world, she treated it as a later formation: a rite performed for reasons long forgotten acquires a narrative to account for it.

The ritual theory was pushed too far by her successors and has been substantially revised, and its influence on twentieth-century work on tragedy, comedy and the origins of drama was very large, including on Frye.

The Cambridge group Harrison led argued that Greek drama grew out of ritual practice rather than from literary invention, with the chorus as the surviving trace of a communal ceremony and the tragic pattern as a seasonal rite of death and renewal.

The specific reconstruction is no longer accepted, and the general position that the form has ritual origins remains the standard account of where the chorus and the festival context came from.

The anthropologist Mary Douglas supplies the argument this figure rests on and is rarely credited with. Her position is that pollution is a matter of classification: things are found abominable when they fall between the categories a culture uses to order the world, not because of anything they contain.

Applied to narrative, that explains why the creatures that disturb most are the ones that are neither living nor dead, neither animal nor human, and why the horror survives when the creature is harmless.

Douglas's late work argues that a great deal of ancient literature, including biblical books, is composed as a ring, with the elements arranged symmetrically around a centre that carries the meaning.
