Her claim about modern readers is the sharper part: trained to expect a climax at the end and an argument that proceeds in a line, they read the middle as a digression and the whole as badly organised, and consistently locate the point in the wrong place.

The study by the American theorist Barbara Herrnstein Smith of how poems end supplies the technical account that Kermode's philosophical one does not attempt.

Her argument is that the sense of an ending is produced by specifiable means: the completion of a formal pattern the work has established, a shift of register at the close, the exhaustion of a structural principle, or an explicit assertion of finality. Closure becomes a describable effect with causes rather than a feeling a reader reports.

The two books appeared within a year of each other and divide the subject cleanly.

Kermode asks why human beings require endings and answers from the condition of being permanently in the middle of things; Smith asks how a text produces the sense that one has arrived and answers from prosody and structure. Neither displaces the other, and closure is unusual among critical topics in having both accounts available.

Mulvey's 1975 essay argues that mainstream narrative cinema is built so that the camera, the male protagonist and the spectator occupy a single position of looking, and that women appear within it as the object of that look.

Her structural point is that the arrangement affects narrative and not only representation: the moments organised around display arrest the story while they last, which makes the pattern a matter of how films are constructed rather than of what they depict.

Mulvey's contribution to the analysis of narrative position is to insist that the question of who looks is not exhausted by describing where the camera is.

A point of view in film is assembled from the camera's placement, the character whose looking it reproduces and the spectator's identification with both, and her argument is that these are conventionally aligned in a particular direction. Later work, including her own revisions, addresses what happens when a viewer does not occupy the position built for them.

Mulvey's essay uses Hitchcock as its principal case, on the argument that his films make the mechanism unusually explicit rather than concealing it.

Rear Window and Vertigo are her examples: films in which a man watches a woman, the audience watches with him, and the plot consists of the consequences. Her point is not that he was unaware of this, since the films are about looking, but that the awareness does not dismantle the structure it displays.

Woolf's essay on women and fiction treats Behn as the decisive figure, on economic rather than literary grounds.

Woolf's argument is that Behn proved a woman could earn money by writing, which converted the activity from an aristocratic accomplishment into a possible living, and that every woman writing afterwards was working in a space she had opened. The passage asking that flowers be let fall on her grave is the most quoted thing anyone has written about her.

The sisters published in the same year under names chosen to conceal their sex, and their two novels are the period's clearest demonstration that a shared upbringing produces nothing predictable.

Charlotte's book gives its heroine the first person and an argument with the reader; Emily's withholds any reliable narrator at all. Charlotte's preface to the posthumous edition of her sister's novel is also the first act of interpretation performed on it, and a defensive one.

Brontë's contribution is a narrating position the English novel had not previously granted: a woman without money, beauty or standing who addresses the reader as an equal and expects to be taken seriously.

Contemporary reviewers registered it as presumption rather than technique, which is the surest sign of its novelty. The first-person heroine with a claim on the reader's attention rather than their pity is standard afterwards.

Du Maurier kept the mode's houses, secrets and menace and removed its supernatural guarantees, so the threat in her books is a marriage, a housekeeper or a first wife's reputation.

The result is a strand of twentieth-century writing in which a woman arrives somewhere she has no standing and slowly discovers what the place requires of her, and it runs directly into the domestic suspense fiction that remains commercially dominant.

The collection is one of the two founding books of the literary fairy tale, published in the same year as Perrault's and considerably longer.

Its tales are courtly rather than nursery material: elaborate, ironic about their own machinery, and preoccupied with women whose marriages are arranged for them and whose escapes are managed by wit. What the genre kept from it was the name; what it discarded was the length, the irony and the audience.

Adichie's fiction covers the Biafran war, the Nigerian middle class and the experience of migration, and it reached a large international readership without adopting the explanatory register that African novels published abroad have often been pushed toward.

Her stated position is that the pressure to explain a society to outsiders is itself the single story operating on a writer, and that the remedy is to write as though the reader already lives there.
